chapters.title: The Guest of Suvarnapur
paragraphs: The Guest of Suvarnapur A weary waste expanding to the skies: Where’er I roam, whatever realms to see ... Bless’d be that spot, where cheerful guests retire To pause from toil, and trim their ev’ning fire; Bless’d that abode, where want and pain repair; And every stranger finds a ready chair.⟨fn:1⟩ Suvarnapur is situated where the river Bhadra meets the Arabian Sea. It is spread out on the slope of a hill cradled by the sea with riverine hands like a child held at the waist. In th­e month of Magha, a vessel laid anchor in the harbour of this town. Small and large boats went up to the vessel to unload its cargo and passengers. Some merchants climbed onto one such boat. A young man got off with them and sat on the side of the boat, as if concealing himself. His eyes moved between the sea and Suvarnapur, almost in response to the boat swaying on the sea waves or like a child imitating the movements of the boat. The man appeared to be twenty-three or twenty-four years of age. His clothes were not bright; his face was withered. While he did not betray signs of dejection, his visage suggested that many a sigh filled his heart. His beauty was illuminating, his features delicate.

These set him apart from the rest of the merchants with their harsh country-folk features, immersed in joyous revelry. The boat came ashore, and passengers disembarked with their bedding and baggage in a hurry. He too walked ashore, melancholic and somewhat indifferent. For a while he stood there, gazing into the distance, his hand on his chin. People were walking in the direction of the town. He slowly began to walk the other way. He walked apart and alone on a road surrounded by an expanse of trees and bushes, like a lone engine on a wide bridge. He carried a small bundle and walked with a steady step, looking in turns at the sky, the earth, the road before him, and behind. The young sun of the early morning suited him, dressed as he was in light clothing, and yet at times a strong gust of wind would force him to cross his arms over his chest. The effort of walking and the sun caused a film of perspiration to appear on his large forehead. His lotus-like face and cheeks turned red. At last, he reached a Shiva temple. Looking around, he entered its gates. This was the temple of Rajeshwar Mahadev. It was built by the ancestors of Buddhidhan, the Counsellor of Suvarnapur. The temple was surrounded by a tiled square, and a roofed corridor bound it. A stone wall plastered with dung, built years ago, skirted this corridor. A small window-like opening led to a courtyard out back. In the courtyard there were fruit and flowering trees appropriate for the worship of Mahadev, as also a bel tree. This courtyard was encircled by a cactus fence with a few gaps in it. On either side of the corridor there were two large platforms. Towards the right was a small lake with an embankment, called Rajsarovar. On the other side, facing the temple, was a well. When crowds gathered at the temple on festival days, worshippers could stand on the well’s high platform and have a darshan of Mahadev. The entry to the temple was slightly elevated but was purposefully placed lower than its threshold. The idea was that anyone entering the temple would—knowingly or unknowingly— have to bow before the deity on entering. The corridor was paved and wayfarers used it as a dharamshala. The paving had come loose at places but had been patched afresh. Travellers had inscribed their names with stone, brick, or coal on the walls of the corridor with a view to seek immortality, fame, or out of sheer playfulness. Some had even etched their names with nails. These ‘writings’ included crude poetry, correct and incorrect verses, idioms, foul abuses, blessings, advice, threats to the owner of the dharamshala, dates that signified arbitrary events; images of Gods and other beings drawn well and not so well could be seen at every step. The Shiva temple itself stood in the middle of the square. It was unremarkable: it had the requisite ten or twelve steps, a platform, and a Nandi. Upon entering the temple, the newcomer looked around and gazed into the sanctum sanctorum. He climbed its steps, rang the bell that hung from the outer dome and perfunctorily bowed to the God. He sat on the threshold of the sanctum sanctorum and placed his bundle in front of him. The priest performing rituals inside signalled to him, so he got up and sat outside. Murkhdutt, the priest, was a brahmin, about thirty to thirty-five years of age. He had an unkempt stubble and appeared careless and unconcerned. His association with the family of the Counsellor and the habit of imitating the servants of that family had given him some semblance of civilised conduct. His natural language was crass and of the mofussil, yet he could pepper it with smart turns of phrase on occasion. He was given to speaking for long, would try to please and plead, and would succeed in small deceits but get caught when he tried treachery in any important matter. He was given to scolding insignificant persons and strangers in the name of the powerful to satiate his ego. One moment he would quarrel with the Counsellor’s staff, and the next, join them in some petty conspiracy. He made a show of being a poor priest in front of the Counsellor’s family, sought pity and got his way. Despite this, the Counsellor considered him a naïve simpleton and provided for him. When he saw the young stranger, Murkhdutt made a show of elaborate worship. He poured enough water to cause a flood, placed a heap of bel leaves and flowers on the Shivalinga, and belted out his impure chanting. The temple was at a distance from the town and therefore rarely visited. However, since the festival of Shivaratri was approaching, Murkhdutt was inebriated with the thought that the Prince and his retinue, the family of the Counsellor, and the townsfolk would soon visit the temple. The youth’s arrival was an auspicious beginning, and it had an intoxicating bhang-like effect on Murkhdutt. The young man watched the scene without so much as blinking an eyelid. He smiled at this show of ever-increasing worship. Murkhdutt felt that his display was having its desired effect. Pleased with himself, he concluded the ritual and loudly clearing his throat, unfurled a string of questions with much pomp: ‘You appear to be a believer. What is your name? From where have you come? Are you thinking of doing some job or business here? How come here, at this time? You seem new to this town. I am the hereditary priest of this Mahadev. My name is Murkhdutt.’ And then he got up and brought the flowers and bel leaves placed on the Linga to the youth. The young man touched the consecrated offering to his eyes and said, ‘My name is Navinchandra. I am a brahmin. I disembarked at the harbour and came straight to the temple. I wish to stay in this dharamshala for a few days, for which I need your assistance. I have no objection if you want to cook my meals with yours.’ Murkhdutt was surprised at the phrase ‘no objection’, at which point Navinchandra threw a rupee onto the floor. The clink of the coin on stone captivated the priest and silenced all further queries. He welcomed Lakshmi, the Goddess of Wealth, and rose as if in a trance or a joyous dream. He led the way, and as Navinchandra followed him, Murkhdutt let loose his tongue. ‘Bhai Navin Chandar, your name is difficult on the tongue! I will call you Chandar Bhai, and you, like all the others, should call me Dutt. Come along, Chandar Bhai! I have a room in the corridor where I cook. If you have any valuables keep them in my trunk; you may keep the key if you wish. There is a courtyard at the back and a pond adjoining it. You may bathe in the pond, or pour water over yourself in the courtyard. I will call you when the food is ready; you wouldn’t like to sit in the smoky kitchen and will prefer the courtyard to the corridor outside. Moreover, tomorrow is Shivaratri. The women of the Counsellor’s family are expected to visit to oversee arrangements for the rituals, and if you are in the courtyard they will be shielded from your gaze. Come along. This is my room.’
chapters.summary: A melancholic young Navinchandra arrives in Suvarnapur, seeking solace and shelter at the Rajeshwar Mahadev temple, where he encounters the talkative priest, Murkhdutt.

chapters.title: Buddhidhan's Family
paragraphs: Buddhidhan’s Family⟨fn:2⟩ Navinchandra went into the courtyard. Clouds of smoke billowed out of Murkhdutt’s room. Soon, the creaking and squeaking of carriages and trotting hooves could be heard. Murkhdutt, his hands covered with dough, rushed to the front of his room, craned his neck to look out, tried to arrange his shikha with his wrists, and rubbing his eyes looked in the direction of the gate. Just then, four or five beautiful young women walked in, their anklets tinkling as they climbed up the temple steps with evident effort. Two women led the group. At the front of the train was Buddhidhan’s daughter Alak Kishori, about twenty to twenty-two years old. There was about her an air of unrestrained sensuality. Walking a step behind was a girl of fourteen or fifteen. Her charm was tender, her beauty like the breaking dawn—calm, despite the exhilarating passions suited to her age. Her gait was swan-like. She was Kumud Sundari, the new bride of Buddhidhan’s son, Pramaddhan. Lightning dazzles and brightens a dark night, but when the rain-laden clouds disperse, it is gentle moonlight that illuminates the sky. Likewise, Alak Kishori’s splendour was followed by the soothing beauty of Kumud Sundari. She was shy, restrained, with the hint of a smile on her lips; she illuminated the temple with her radiant beauty.

The differences in appearance, disposition, demeanour and thought between the two sisters-in-law were apparent. This was in large measure due to their respective families, their histories, and education. The seeds of this difference were sown from birth, but their lived contexts had contributed to the growth of these innate dispositions. Alak Kishori was what women would describe as gorgeous. Her golden complexion glowed like the mid-day sun. She attracted and impressed all those who set eyes on her. Her body was proportionate and full: the eyes of the beholder were ‘filled’ by her figure. Her demeanour was restless, forceful and authoritative. Those who faced her experienced the anxiety of facing a large assembly. She spoke as one used to exercising authority; most people felt naturally inferior in her presence. Just as Buddhidhan ruled by the power of his office, Alak Kishori ruled with her captivating gaze. Most people with average intelligence believed that she owed her power to her physical beauty. They were not wrong. Bedazzled in her presence, their judgement was paralysed. However, those capable of more real and detailed analysis, or who thought about her in her absence, found themselves able to think of Alak Kishori’s many shortcomings. But even such persons found themselves helpless before her captivating beauty. And if someone still felt an impulse to rebel, just the presence of this doe- eyed beauty melted their pride and they felt stupefied in the face of her vibrant sensuality. Her unrestrained, passionate youth attracted a large group of admirers, and she wielded over them a power akin to that of a goddess. Alak Kishori’s mother Saubhagya Devi was a woman of average beauty and qualities. Buddhidhan was fond of her because of her maturity. Alak Kishori was spoiled by her father’s affection from an early age. Buddhidhan’s preoccupation with public affairs left him little time to pay attention to household matters. Saubhagya Devi did not necessarily approve of everything her daughter did, but her own unwillingness and inability to bear the burden, her retiring disposition, and Alak Kishori’s own forceful character led this unabashed young
chapters.summary: Alak Kishori and Kumud Sundari arrive, their contrasting beauty and demeanors illuminating Buddhidhan's courtyard, hinting at the complex family dynamics unfolding.

chapters.title: Buddhidhan
paragraphs: woman to wield authority over Buddhidhan’s household, his family, clan, relations, and when possible, even in affairs of state. Nothing happened in the household without Alak Kishori’s approval. No one could point out her shortcomings. No one could impede her. Outsiders saw her as the very life-force of the Counsellor’s family. They sought to influence the Counsellor through her and showered her with praise and flattery. Some even believed that the family would be plunged into darkness the day Alak Kishori left for the house of her in-laws. The Counsellor was aware of this and always on his guard, lest someone take advantage of the situation. He always had his way, but kept up the pretence of his daughter’s authority. He did not have the power to change what the world believed, and he did not want to use his power in a way that would hurt his daughter’s pride. He was also curious about the blind ways in which the world formed its opinions. Sometimes however, without his knowledge, Alak Kishori actually wielded power, thus reinforcing the common belief. The household of the Counsellor of Suvarnapur functioned in this manner. Alak Kishori was still childish. She had never as much as seen poverty. She always got her way, did exactly what pleased her, issued orders, and ensured that they were obeyed. She knew only praise. The ascendancy of the Counsellor coincided with her birth. She had seen people superior to her in age, wisdom, experience and beauty remain subservient to her. No one told her what was right; no one dared tell her what was wrong. It was in no one’s interest to point out to her desirable from undesirable, or cause tedium and boredom by recounting to her stories of the family’s past. It was believed that to point out to her the future that awaited her would cause a strain upon her imagination and pain her. Hence, her gaze was fixed on events unfolding in the present and her vision limited by the immediacy of the obvious. Consequently, arrogance like a dangerous snake lurked in her delicate mind. It swayed upon her brows, danced in her eyes, hissed through her tongue and endowed her body with a poisonous vibrancy. She did not possess the nectar of knowledge that could have countered the poison since she had never experienced the goodness and bounty of association with the righteous. Her hauteur was contained only by the natural goodness of the Counsellor’s family. Her glory was like the sun at high noon. Her in-laws obeyed her wishes. Her haughtiness pricked her husband, but causing injury to her heart appeared to him ungrateful. People had hoped that her brother Pramaddhan would marry at the right age and become a householder, thereby deflating Alak Kishori’s arrogance as the Counsellor’s family would then be ruled by someone else. But those who had harboured such hopes were soon forced to reconsider. Counsellor Buddhidhan’s son Pramaddhan had received many marriage proposals. But the parents and the daughter differed in their estimation of the girls’ beauty, virtues, and lineage, which is why his marriage could not be fixed. Finally it so happened that Kumud Sundari, daughter of the Minister of Ratnanagari, Vidya Chatura, became available for marriage. Kumud Sundari was previously betrothed to Sarasvatichandra, the learned son of Laxminandan, a wealthy and reputed merchant of Bombay. As the day of marriage drew nearer, God knows why, Sarasvatichandra suddenly disappeared without a trace. Ultimately, Vidya Chatura received a letter from Sarasvatichandra, posted from Bombay. Therein he had written: ‘There is a reason why I have left my home and identity behind. I do not desire marriage. Like a wave in the ocean of life, I shall roam the world alone and unrecognised. I will not be traceable. Do not worry about me. It would have been my good fortune to marry the virtuous Kumud Sundari, but I cannot convince myself that I could have given her any joy. Please get her married. May she experience everlasting conjugal happiness’. Upon receiving the letter, and ascertaining its veracity, Vidya Chatura had become dejected and anxious about Kumud Sundari’s fate. She had crossed the marriageable age and he could not think of a match comparable to Sarasvatichandra for her. He had a younger daughter, Kusum Sundari. He had no son, but his two jewel-like daughters gave him immense joy. The thought of Sarasvatichandra and Kumud Sundari as a couple had filled his heart with supreme bliss. Hence, this misfortune grieved him even more than a son’s death would have. Vidya Chatura could not fathom what had possessed his intelligent and wise son-in-law- to-be. Resigned, and with the thought that such was God’s will, he let bygones be bygones and looked towards the future. The news spread far and wide, was published in newspapers, discussed in the community and outside of it. Learning was blamed. Sarasvatichandra’s juvenile conduct was on every tongue. Pramaddhan read and heard about it, and talked of it at meal time. Kumud Sundari’s misfortune was discussed; everyone took pity on her. Somehow, talk veered towards her virtues and beauty. Suddenly, Alak Kishori said, ‘Isn’t that girl a suitable match for my brother?’ Saubhagya Devi said she was suitable. Buddhidhan said Vidya Chatura was an old friend, that he was high born, and that his wife was intelligent, virtuous and literate. Saubhagya Devi said, ‘I have seen the girl. We met during Rajchandra’s marriage and sang songs together. She is beautiful and intelligent’. Alak said someone should be sent the next morning to seek Kumud’s hand in marriage. Everyone agreed. The family priest, also present at the meal, declared, ‘The following morning is auspicious; the proposal will be accepted’. Pramaddhan followed the goings-on, spent the day in a spirit of festivity, and the night as in one long, sweet dream. The next morning, a messenger left for Ratnanagari with the proposal. The Minister of Ratnanagari was still gripped by worries. It was his wife who ran the household. She found the groom and his family suitable. She had little idea about the groom, but she reasoned that since the family was good, the groom would be, too. She spoke to her husband. Agitated as he was, he agreed to the proposal without much thought. Buddhidhan’s messenger ran back to Suvarnapur with the good news. When Vidya Chatura regained his composure, he reconsidered the decision; but having agreed to it, he could not now decline the proposal. If it is God’s will, it must be for the good, he reasoned and stopped worrying. The marriage was solemnised, and Kumud Sundari had barely spent ten, fifteen days with her in-laws when the incident narrated at the beginning of our story took place.

The credit for finding such a fine match for Pramaddhan was accorded to Alak Kishori. The mother gave birth to him, and the sister found him a wife. Alak Kishori’s prestige in the household rose even higher; the brother loved her even more. Kumud Sundari’s placid disposition was amenable to this domestic arrangement. Gunasundari, Kumud Sundari’s mother, and Vidya Chatura were married as young children. She had not been to school. Her husband, who was learned, and who had the opportunity, conviction and enthusiasm, imparted to her a little learning before she gave birth to their first child. Gunasundari was clever, quick-thinking, and emotional. But she was practically illiterate when she got married and could not fathom his deepest concerns. She would often ask, ‘Beloved, what causes you such grief?’ Vidya Chatura would let out a deep sigh, put his hand on her shoulder, and think to himself, Oh, sweet bird! Your voice is sweet, but only if a mynah could understand human grief could you understand my pain. What good is it to tell you? Weep at my tears like a child, my sweet bird, and make me weep even more. He would then immerse himself in his books or worldly affairs. His face shone with joy when he read good books, thought new thoughts, heard news about the country’s welfare, or when God’s lila filled his mind. At such times, his wife would gaze upon his moon-like face, and an innocent but uncomprehending joy would envelop her. But there were times when her heart ached because she could not partake of his joys and sorrows, and when sorrow pierced his heart, she felt helpless. Sometimes words that came naturally to her or actions that were insignificant caused her husband disproportionate pain, who made as if he had lost his all to a shipwreck. Other times, even the most gigantic efforts on her part seemed inconsequential to him. Her deepest joys seemed to him childish. This caused her great confusion and turmoil. There was no way out of this. Gunasundari would shed silent tears lying on her bed, or with her head on the dressing table, while looking out onto the river, the fields and the sky from her window, or when she lay her head on her husband’s lap.

One day, the couple was up on the terrace. It was midnight and a huge moon was overhead. It was as if spring had embellished her friend the sky with jewel-like stars and white clouds. The unrestrained moonlight played with this beautiful woman. Vidya Chatura was reclining on a bolster, gazing at the moon, lost in thought. Gunasundari lay with her head in his lap, holding his hand in hers and ignoring the magnificent moon, she gazed at the resplendent visage of her husband. For a time, they lay together in silence. Then, of a sudden, from his poet’s heart sprang a song: Touching foreheads we remained Conversing in soft whispers As if for the first time We spoke in endearments Our hands held in close embrace And in this chosen dream, was the night spent.⟨fn:3⟩ Smiling childlike and innocent, morning breaks And stands before our bed Suddenly shy, sensuality Hides in the blush of your cheek The joy of togetherness sleeps in our eyes. As his song rose and reverberated through the skies, the lovely Gunasundari was entranced, captivated by the sonorous sounds. Satiated and joyous, the words receded and merged into each other, finding repose in the last stanza. Gunasundari asked, ‘Beloved! What was it you sang? What do these beautiful words mean? Explain it to me.’ The poet hesitated, ‘Will you understand...? But of course, you will.’ And Vidya Chatura explained the narrative and the song to her at length. As she listened, enrapt, her liquid eyes shone. She responded, ‘Oh, it is beautiful indeed! I tremble with joy, my very hair stands on end. How can I understand your song for myself? You fulfil all my desires. I am dependent on you for life and shall forever remain so. But I cannot understand your thoughts or fathom your mind. I do not want to stare blankly at you at such moments and in times of joy and sorrow. Tell me, what am I to do?’ Vidya Chatura smiled, ‘Come, even that will happen. You will learn what I shall teach, will you?’ The very next day Gunasundari commenced her studies, and she persisted with them through the course of her first pregnancy. Thereafter, she became embroiled in household matters and motherhood, and had to give up her lessons. But she was no longer discontented. True, her learning was of no use in her husband’s affairs. But she felt worthy of entering the sanctum of his heart, sharing his bed, his pleasures and his delights. While lessons with the husband had to cease, as she matured, Gunasundari learnt to disentangle herself from her household tasks and further her learning. Eventually, her efforts and enthusiasm bore fruit. In their moments of leisure and pleasure, the potent seed of Vidya Chatura’s learning and his aesthetic sensibility impregnated Gunasundari’s eager mind. This light grew daily, and young Kumud Sundari benefited from it. A renowned scholar has likened men to tailors. Each wants others to be dressed in his own likeness, and if possible, in clothes of his own making. It is a general principle: the literate desire that all should be literate. While Kumud Sundari was still an infant, Gunasundari, in her love for the child and passion of first motherhood, decided to educate her. In our country, many obstacles are placed in the way of women’s education. If they do go to school, what girls typically study is worthless. And after they marry and become householders, study becomes even more difficult. Although knowledge is worshipped, household duties, association with illiterate female friends and relatives, the need to satisfy the base animal instincts of the husband and oneself, caring for one’s children, the many ailments that women have to bear, and the lack of belief, ability and opportunity in women’s education do not allow Hindu women to acquire learning. Gunasundari, intelligent and persevering, overcame these obstacles and acquired some learning. She was determined that her daughter should study before such obstacles were placed in her path and before she became a householder. Vidya Chatura was increasingly embroiled in public affairs, which cast a shadow over all his other activities. Even so, he supported, facilitated, improved, guided and furthered Gunasundari’s commendable enthusiasm, insistence and effort in their daughter’s education. In conversation, humour and by example, he helped bridge the gap and overcome the shortcomings of this effort. In just a few years, Kumud Sundari learnt much. She learned to think for herself, and her parents could rejoice that their efforts had borne fruit. She began to learn English and Sanskrit before marriage. The duties of a householder, aesthetic sensibility and refinement, worldly wisdom, and moral conduct which act as custodians of a householder’s life, came to her effortlessly and stood guard as this princess entered the temple that was Buddhidhan’s household. Her parents desired the learned Sarasvatichandra to be the consort for their princess. Though his refusal and disappearance pained and disappointed them greatly, Kumud Sundari bestowed heavenly bliss on her parents. Kumud Sundari was quite different from Alak Kishori in appearance. Her complexion was fair, her structure delicate. She embodied the description: ‘a delicate woman with a pearl nose-ring’. She did not attract by virtue of dazzling beauty. Her bearing was not haughty. Some thought she was a meek cow; some said she was worthless. Anyone could look upon her face. She wore the markers of a married woman but little else by way of ornamentation. Her clothes had simple, muted patterns and covered her entire body, except her childlike and delicate hands and equally dainty hennaed feet. Her movements were imperceptible, and she rarely emoted through bodily gestures. Like the outline of the moon shrouded by clouds in spring, a faint smile would play on her face. She spoke little, but when she did, her sweet voice had a silvery, bell-like ring to it. The virtuous could rest their gaze upon her and feel a natural, innocent and quiet attraction. Male aesthetes could discern about her visage a pure beauty. Intelligent women found her eyes alive and expressive. Middle-aged women found her mature. Charming young women were entertained by her conversation. Refined women liked to keep her company, observed her demeanour, her manner of speech, imitated her, and asked other women to do the same. Her delicate bearing, beauty, intelligence, modesty, charm and tenderness were observed, analysed and discussed in her absence. Children would stop playing and gather around her. Anyone who pointed out aspects of her beauty was praised; others joined in with their own views. Blessings were showered upon her as if unbidden. All those who looked at Kumud Sundari, heard her or conversed with her felt the same sensation of having bathed in gentle moonlight—they were immersed in nectar and showered with joy. For Kumud Sundari, Buddhidhan’s household was a world apart. She had settled in well with her in-laws. Alak Kishori ruled by habit; Kumud Sundari had learnt obedience. Women of the Counsellor’s family did not have to do household work, which is why there was no conflict between them. Of money there was plenty; desires could be fulfilled without discrimination. Moreover, Alak Kishori was given credit for suggesting this match; therefore dressing up the bride, bringing her to the fore, adding to her glory, introducing her to the community, and acquainting and instructing her about the family customs were also her responsibility, and Alak Kishori performed them with enthusiasm. In all such matters, Saubhagya Devi’s consent was perfunctorily obtained, Buddhidhan merely informed, and Pramaddhan’s preferences sought. The family servants spoke about the new bride to her husband to seek his favour. Alak Kishori indulged in banter with her brother. The family’s time was thus spent in this newfound and innocent joy. When she first moved to her in-laws’, Kumud Sundari still remembered Sarasvatichandra and shed silent tears. When alone, she sighed deeply, and when with others, she participated in their play and festivities with an empty heart. Her lacklustre smile hid a wounded and broken heart. However, this was seen as bashfulness and her tears seen as tears of joy. She wished and attempted to forge a bond with Pramaddhan, but her heart trailed behind. Even so, the force of time, the experiences of a new life, the surging joy of others around her, her young mind’s capacity for adjustment to the new, the intelligence to obey the imperatives of God’s will, the wisdom to cede to forces beyond her control, and the knowledge that so much as thinking of another man violated her virtue enabled the young but determined woman to rein in her mind and perform the duties expected of her. Gradually, the past began to recede; joy returned to her face. However, her happiness was like the waning moon at dawn, and no one but Gunasundari could have discerned this. If she were with her daughter, her loving heart would have shattered. Pramaddhan’s joy was a superficial one. To him, as to other onlookers, it was apparent that Kumud Sundari had attained the zenith of bliss. What they did not see they were not capable of seeing. There was no one in Buddhidhan’s household to nurture Kumud Sundari and her refined ways. Pramaddhan had been an errant student. Student life had seemed constricting; he felt belittled at school. Studies were to him a source of boredom and drudgery, and learning, merely a poor man’s means of earning a livelihood; and if it had any other use, he believed he could avail of it by retaining educated men as servants. The school teacher was a case in point: a respected man of learning, but his advice was never sought in the administration of the state. Pramaddhan believed that English education was glorified because it was a foreign language—the language of the rulers. Sanskrit was for him the language of the shastris, who, despite their learning, were poor and dependent. He considered mathematics, philosophy, Vedanta, and other such subjects fit only for the purposeless, the old, mendicants, people without means, and others who, though respectable, were in a real sense good for nothing. His father was the source of such notions, but Pramaddhan had nourished them owing to his own lazy disposition. He reasoned that as a dutiful son, it was not given to him to challenge his father’s ideas. His associates flattered him and there was no one to tell him bitter truths. He had no disagreeable experiences. For these and other reasons, like many others, he too harboured a high opinion of his own intelligence. Pramaddhan led a wanton and dissolute life. He took the family’s wealth and prosperity for permanent and, eyes closed, floated along on the tide of time, believing, however, that he swam on the back of his own strength. Having done with his political intriguing, he read novels or whiled away his time in the company of friends who praised him, belittled others, and narrated their encounters with women. He behaved fancifully, imagined exciting situations, and wandered about freely anywhere any time. His speech was indiscreet. The Counsellor’s son considered such a course of things to be his lot and a good use of his wealth. Apart from this, his character was good, his temperament joyous and content. He aspired to satisfy all of Kumud Sundari’s desires and strived conscientiously to make her happy. He took pride in her beauty, praised her learning, and considered their union as precious as that of a jewel with gold. The conduct of Pramaddhan, Alak Kishori and the entire household of the Counsellor of Suvarnapur were wholly foreign to what Kumud Sundari had been used to at Vidya Chatura’s. Her natal home and her in-laws’ household differed from each other in demeanour, in what constituted pleasure, thought and action. Believing that her new home would have books as well, she had brought none with her. In this new world, she had only one thing that linked her to her past and reminded her of it. Alongwith his letter to Vidya Chatura, Sarasvatichandra had also sent a letter for Kumud Sundari. The letter contained just one verse, written in golden ink. The handwriting was familiar to Kumud Sundari, as was the verse, which is how she knew who the author was. Enchanting Night! Do not allow separation from the waning moon to blind you By day, holding the hands of the one you desire, Become a joyous bride.

She had neither shown nor shared this verse with anyone. She guarded it in her blouse, close to her heart. In opportune moments of solitude she would take it out to read, although she knew it by heart. She would hum it to herself and weep. If she saw anyone approach her, she would quickly hide the letter, compose herself and be on guard. She often looked at the letter angrily, her eyebrows raised. At such times, her face reflected pity, pain and anger simultaneously. She would look up at the sky, sigh deeply, and wipe away her tears. In her new household, she could mask her feelings and no one could gauge her troubled emotions. In the eyes of the world, there was nothing amiss. To all outward appearances, the Suvarnapur Counsellor’s family seemed festive and joyous. The nubile beauties of this family gracefully climbed up the stairs of the Rajeshwar Mahadev, their breathing heavy with effort. None but the priest Murkhdutt witnessed this scene. If a Yaksha were to behold them, he would be pardoned for believing that these were celestial beings rarely seen by mortal eyes, come down to earth to imbue it with life-giving nectar and worship the God of the Gods, Mahadev. The priest hurriedly washed his hands, wiped them on a piece of cloth, adjusted his dhoti, and rushed out to receive the ladies. ‘Welcome! Welcome!’ he exclaimed and entered the sanctum of the temple. He took some bel leaves and other consecrated offerings and gave them to the women saying, ‘Behn! Everything has been arranged just as you desired. All items required for the Shiv puja have been procured. I will follow your orders.’ In the company of these beautiful women, Murkhdutt reminded one of Mahadev’s ghostly attendants standing beside Parvati. Just as he was receiving instructions for the following day’s festivities from them, a soldier rushed in, ‘Behn, Behn! The Counsellor is on his way here, possibly accompanied by the King!’ ‘Is it possible for us to return unseen?’ ‘No, the flag-bearers and riders can be seen where the road forks.’ ‘What then?’ asked Alak Kishori, flustered. Those who have had to deal with certain situations know best how to respond to them. Murkhdutt rushed down the steps and said, ‘Come, follow me to the courtyard. The King has only come for darshan and will not spend much time here. I will lock you in and open the door only after their party has left.’ Murkhdutt had forgotten that Navinchandra was in the yard. The women followed him. Alak Kishori turned to Kumud Sundari and said, ‘We will be confined here for at least an hour or two. The King has not come merely for darshan. He will spend some time here. It was a mistake to come at this hour; it completely slipped out of my mind!’ Kumud Sundari looked up at her sister-in-law to indicate that she understood it was no one’s fault that this had happened, delicately withdrew her gaze and kept on walking with her eyes lowered on the ground. The women entered the yard. Murkhdutt quickly banged the door shut and locked it behind him.

Rajeshwar Mahadev was at a distance of four to five miles from Suvarnapur. Not many came that way. It was therefore a place for the secret rendezvous of rich wastrels and those bent on political intrigue. This contributed substantially to Murkhdutt’s income—he had learnt the craft of pleasing all patrons by accommodating their needs and demands. Most times, patrons informed him of their meetings beforehand, thus avoiding the awkwardness of encountering others. However, the two persons meeting here at this point in our story were no ordinary men. One was the ruler of the city, and the other the patron of the temple. It was the duty of the priest to ensure that they were left undisturbed. ‘Your kindness be upon us all, Your Grace!’ announced the usher, as the ruler of Suvarnapur entered the temple accompanied by Buddhidhan. The princely retinue spread out a carpet woven with gold thread near the Nandi. Both men sat on it, and the servants left them to their conversation. Murkhdutt kowtowed thrice to them in greeting and then returned to his room to resume his cooking. Like the moon and a solitary star visible through a break in the clouds on an overcast monsoon night, the King and his Counsellor were left alone in the temple.⟨fn:4⟩

Rana Bhupsinh was about thirty-seven or thirty-eight years old. The previous ruler had left no legitimate male heirs. His administrators and queens had failed to install an heir after his death. Their machinations to foist a ruler of their choice failed because of divisions in the ranks. Bhupsinh was a close cousin of the deceased king. Through the influence and cunning of his family, and support of the British Resident, he had ascended the throne. He had, by now, ruled over Suvarnapur for three, four years. Rana Bhupsinh had had a normal upbringing, under ordinary circumstances. As a child, he had been shielded from the poisonous air of the palace. This was why he was still in possession of common sense. He had known poverty. Therefore, while not generous, his own memories of deprivation ensured that he was benevolent to the poor. He had dealt with administrators, officials and soldiers while trying to protect his father’s garas, the family inheritance. He had had to plead and please, submit to insults, face wily officials, offer bribes, and suffer being pushed around. Therefore, he had an inkling of the difference between outward expressions and genuine feelings of love, trust and respect, even among those in the ruler’s inner circle. He had heard of and experienced the wilful conduct of palace officials. He had resolved to put these learnings and experiences to good use after assuming the throne. He was personally acquainted with many in the state administration. He felt duty-bound to avenge the insults heaped upon him in the past and took pride in rewarding those who had stood by him. Bhupsinh had not the faintest idea of the real duties of a ruler: he firmly believed that by punishing insults and rewarding supporters, he would be performing his duty and securing glory. This belief stemmed from his past and was nurtured by his present. The rumblings beneath the surface were ever ready to erupt. When Bhupsinh assumed the throne, the chief administrator, the Karbhari of Suvarnapur palace had offered no resistance; he had changed his colours and displayed generosity. The wily administrator’s scheming seemed to have borne fruit—Bhupsinh’s temperament had seemingly undergone a change. The leisure and pleasures of the palace had doused his fire. His anger and thirst for revenge had subsided under the coat of gratification. And the old palace guard had heaved a collective sigh of relief. In the torpor of power, in unthinking selfishness, in the inebriation of passion, in the grandeur of ostentation, in the web of everydayness, encircled, slumbering, comatose, bedazzled and enmeshed, as the change of ruler became a thing of the past, the old and new guards grew negligent. The only person who remained awake and vigilant was the Counsellor of Suvarnapur, Buddhidhan. He observed, listened, thought ahead and devised new manoeuvres. While the world around him slept, Buddhidhan kept awake like a doctor keeping vigil by the side of an ailing patient, or like an ever-watchful lion with his sight fixed on his prey, lest it escape. His aspiration was that the administration of Suvarnapur be regarded as the finest. He desired that his authority should take root, and thus render the state his plaything. This would ensure that the ruler and the populace of Suvarnapur became the bountiful kamdhenu for him and his family. Such thoughts constantly haunted Buddhidhan and kept him awake and restless. Perchance if another thought entered his mind and blurred his vision momentarily, he would soon return to his obsessive ambition. This unceasing worry corroded his joy, his being. It was not given to ordinary eyes to either witness or comprehend this churning. Some four or five generations ago, Buddhidhan’s ancestors had been the chief administrators, the karbharis of Suvarnapur. They had since lost this position; but the family continued to accept even lowly work in the state administration just in order to keep a foot-hold in the Suvarnapur palace. Wheels of fortune move rapidly, not only changing from one generation to the next but also within a single generation itself. This family, which had once taken pride in its wealth, had to see its riches dwindle to rags. Buddhidhan had inherited nothing but a strong sense of family pride from his father. This pride brought with it certain other qualities as well. His mother was intelligent and wise. She maintained the household even in poverty, but was equally capable of generosity in times of prosperity. It was said of her that had she been a man, she would have reclaimed the post of chief administrator for the family. Her son had inherited these qualities from her. As they observed his abilities flourish and grow day by day, his parents anticipated and hoped for a better, brighter future. Shivaji Maharaj was raised and encouraged by his mother Jijabai. Similarly, Buddhidhan’s mother told her son rousing stories about his ancestors; how Ramrai had obtained the position of chief administrator; how young Laxmanchandra had gained the ruler’s confidence and affection; how Krishnadas had amassed amazing riches and lifted the family’s fortunes under the rule of Sundarsinh. The child Buddhidhan listened attentively to all these stories, hanging onto her every word. His illiterate mother’s descriptions were not refined, but her narration had a natural flair, an innate charm, an attraction, and the power of suggestion. It had the delicacy of a woman’s tongue and the cultured air attendant to it. The unadorned prose of this wise and beautiful woman unobtrusively etched itself into the mind of her young listener. The dreams and aspirations of the mother mingled and became part of the child’s unconscious, and there they flowered effortlessly. His father boastfully recounted past glories of the family and blamed fate for allowing the new rank of uncultured youth, born in poverty, to rule and rise arrogantly in power. He laughed disdainfully at such officials and considered them of no significance. Buddhidhan’s tender mind was filled with such ideas, and he resolved young that he would rectify Brahma the Creator’s error and attain a position of power befitting his significant abilities. The boy destined to be chief administrator went to school, but found education purposeless and spent many days in a quandary. Eventually, he realised that literacy was a craft, a means to a livelihood, and that those who possessed it could write dazzling prose and decipher obscure documents. The mother argued that education enhanced intelligence. The son never challenged this view, but was convinced that on this score his mother was in error. Believing this, he studied little at school, and instead spent time observing the school master at work, how he increased his number of pupils, how he flattered their parents, and how he dealt with dullards. He also observed how the students played pranks on the master behind his back. Buddhidhan found such observations both pleasurable and instructive. Initially, in his ranking of the most intelligent persons, the second slot, after his mother, had belonged to his school master. However, he was soon dropped from this exalted position. Gradually, the master became for him a specimen of stupidity and low intelligence. Buddhidhan satisfied the master with his learning and intelligence, and by also giving him money. As he entered the real world, Buddhidhan was armed with the conviction that all educated men must be like the school master. He changed his opinion only later in life, following a handful of instances, when faced with irrefutable proof to the contrary. Success in the real world was harder than success in school. Over time, Buddhidhan experienced much that was new which would cause him to change his mind. As a child, he had dreamt of an easy and rapid rise to power. Bitter lived experiences doused this dream. Buddhidhan decided that he had no choice but to be satisfied if after years of toiling, he was mid-way but on course to his desired destination. The ultimate position he desired, for which he would have to overcome many obstacles by dint of hard work, face agonising disappointments and allow for the vagaries of fate, would only come to him gradually. Having taken this decision, he set himself adrift in the sea of the world without a raft. Buddhidhan never thought highly of his father’s intelligence, but benefited from his experience. While he often disregarded his mother’s lessons and instructions, he was often forced to go back to her to seek counsel. Despite the fact that his mother’s instruction was agreeable to him, day by day, his estimation of her intelligence lowered. He began to be moulded by worldly experiences, and with age his intellect matured. He increasingly found his mother’s domestic wisdom wanting and fit only for women; his father he found weak in body and in mind. The young bird was learning to fly alone. The role of the parents became confined to expressions of endorsement or anxiety. As their ability to deal with his world decreased and their focus shifted to other concerns, their resolve weakened and their affection for their son deepened. This they expressed amply. The son recognised that it was his duty to ensure that their affection was not wasted like rain on barren land. He realised that it was his duty to respond to it in equal measure and give them joy. It did not come naturally to this worldly- wise man to make a display of his emotions, which usually remained unseen, unrecognised. But his reasoning enabled him to express a recognisable verisimilitude of filial love. Buddhidhan was now required to decide the stream he would follow, to get to the port where he would cast anchor. His aged parents tried to mould his thinking to their aspirations. The father wanted to see his dream realised within his lifetime. He wanted to use his family connections and be instrumental in Buddhidhan making his acquaintance with the ruler of Suvarnapur. Poor as he was, he wanted this to be his inheritance to his son. The chief administrator was a distant relative of Buddhidhan’s mother. Through the intercession of her cousin, she desired that her son be given a position higher than others of his age and stature. The old couple endlessly discussed the relative merits of their proposals. Buddhidhan understood the purpose of these discussions. But he wanted his own desires fulfilled, using the means suggested by his parents. They all agreed that wealth must be obtained, for it was a means to other ends. Their differences were over the source of this wealth. Political power or trade—which was it to be? Trade involved the risk of loss, needed initial capital, the goodwill of officials, and was a source of perpetual worry. For these reasons, Buddhidhan decided to seek wealth through the state. His concern was to find a way of achieving this. If he were to join the state service, his first job would be petty, bring in little money and no prestige. Political power would be a distant dream and he would be at the mercy of strange and stupid officials. Consign such a job to the flames. Throw dust over it! Business, however difficult, would not be so disagreeable. Buddhidhan was plagued by such doubts. He vacillated day and night, at home and in the world, solitary and deep in thought; he sought a solution to this dilemma. Often, even in the company of his parents, his heart empty, his gaze vacant, his ears would shut out all sound.

Sitting by himself, he would imagine thousands of situations, study how other people carried on their livelihoods, sincerely ask them how they had found this resource initially, and consider if these means were available to him. One path would appear unsuited to his temperament; another would not be free of risk; a third would not bring him riches; and a fourth was hazardous and full of obstacles. He measured each path and calculated on his fingertips, in the air, scribbled in the dust; but it would all come to naught. He would murmur to himself: What is to happen I do not know. I fear a failed future, I preempt, resolving it all in my mind. But even this seemed to him foolish and at times he would laugh out aloud at himself. Finally, Buddhidhan decided to look for a job. He decided to wait patiently and secure suitable employment. His parents were unaware of what was raging in his mind. Sometimes they would ask, ‘Bhai! What is it that you wish to do?’ No response was ever satisfactory. Through all of this, Buddhidhan appeared outwardly cheerful. He found ways to keep himself occupied, and his mother supported his endeavours. Though not deeply enamoured of learning, he went to the Kazi Sahib, an old acquaintance of the family, and learned Persian. This gave him gravitas and an air of wisdom. He heard instructive stories from the shastris and puranis. Moral sense tempered his conscience. He kept the company of ascetics and obtained peace and calm, while acquiring some understanding of the nature of divinity. This also helped him cultivate a philosophical attitude in his dealings with worldly matters. In his spare time he indulged in banter with old men who, in the strength and intoxication of youth, had done things great and base, had fallen and plotted, seen success and defeat, had been tempted and entangled, and had even managed to salvage themselves. Some were administrators, others traders. Some had wasted their youth in the company of prostitutes, while some in their stupidity had seen nothing of the world. Some had been lazy and allowed things to take their own course; others had been victims of intrigue. These wizened men narrated their stories variously, some without regret, some with a touch of pride, some with dejection. All these tales seeped into Buddhidhan’s heart. At times, irrespective of whether the occasion demanded it or not, Buddhidhan would recite Persian verses, narrate instructive tales, or illustrate a point with a story told by one of his elderly companions. On these occasions, his mother would join in enthusiastically with stories of her own. These stories came alive for Buddhidhan and were etched permanently on his mind. Like Brahma who witnessed happenings in this illusory world without the necessity for action, Buddhidhan’s father, the family patriarch, witnessed all this and experienced a quiet joy. While cleaning his teeth, bathing, at lunch and dinner, while lying in bed, sitting around a winter fire, chatting on a moonlit night, in the cool nights of summer, while listening to the rain fall from laden clouds on dark monsoon nights, the ‘chief administrator’s family’ of Suvarnapur, without a teacher or text, unconsciously learnt lessons from the world. The delicacy of a woman’s charm, imagination, metaphor, affection, aesthetic sensibility and sensitivity now entered the conscience of this man who had hitherto harboured little regard for womanly intelligence. It had the same beautiful, nourishing and positive effect that the morning breeze wafting in from over a river has on the human body. The Persian couplets, moral lessons, verses, and idle chatter of old men became easily digestible for Buddhidhan owing to the nurturing touch of this woman—his mother. Buddhidhan’s father, like his ancestors, was entitled to a privy purse of two hundred rupees annually. The amount came in handy in hard times and gave them prestige among the people. Once a year, the new administrators were reminded of the ‘chief administrator’s family’. Buddhidhan’s ancestors had amassed wealth and acquired land. From this holding, only enough survived to pay the land revenue. If Buddhidhan were to gain political power, he too would amass wealth anew. But for his family, such power was a thing of the past, not reclaimable even in their dreams. Money begets money, but his family had no wealth; which is why entry and success in palace politics through bribery was difficult to accomplish. They had to submit to the wealthy and influential, and could hope to secure justice only when the competition was level; even this hinged upon the industriousness, enthusiasm, and alertness of the concerned official. Nevertheless, affairs of the household rolled on. This was due to the able intelligence and parsimony of the woman who ran it. The family faced no apparent hardship. In any case, they were used to bearing difficulties. Leisure and pleasure were regarded as unpalatable. The joys, riches and pleasures of the family were confined to the chatter of the mother and son. Buddhidhan was betrothed to a girl of a family living in similar circumstances. Her mother was dead; she was raised largely by Buddhidhan’s mother, and under her upbringing she had acquired her true potential and capabilities. Her father-in-law had named her Saubhagya Devi. The young couple was the only wealth of this impoverished household—and their only hope. Days passed. The haughty inebriated world did not cast so much as a glance in their direction. Buddhidhan’s condition was like that of a potent seed growing underground, unknown even to the rays of the sun. He had passed through no fiery ordeal. His only real concern was to acquire power and to be considered important. This desire plagued and consumed him like a constant low fever. Not even his family knew what ailed him. Only he felt the torment in moments of solitude. But this did not last long. Troubles burst upon this growing sapling. The father suddenly died of cholera. Buddhidhan was in no way prepared for this. The blow was sudden and swift. His resolve seemed to crack. Given his character, he was unlikely to find a virtuous companion among the pleasure-seeking youth. His poverty precluded any friendship with the rich, except one based on flattery; the poor were not similarly cultured. Even if he found a friend, the difference in intellect always remained apparent. Buddhidhan was friendless. In his moment of crisis there was no one to give him solace—save for his mother who was now a widow and herself submerged in grief. It became Buddhidhan’s duty to give her succour. The avalanche of difficulties had not yet subsided.

When parents are alive, their words should be implicitly obeyed. After death, on their death anniversary, the Shradh should be performed with generous offerings of food. At least once in a lifetime, Shradh (Pind Danam) should be performed in Gaya. These three actions alone make a son worthy of being called a true son. This verse resonated within the brahmin youth. He found it pleasing. Reformers believed that a son following his own inclination also brings prestige to his father. Buddhidhan wanted to be a good son by fulfilling his father’s aspirations. He drowned the sorrow of his father’s death by dealing with the exigencies of daily life and thus proved himself a model son. He suffered agonies; he borrowed money; he worked hard. Hardships fell on him like axe blows on a sandalwood tree. His body withered, but his innate intelligence blossomed. Difficulties encircled him, but he pushed them aside and moved on ahead. He had no opportunity to turn back and ponder over the past. Alone and without support, Buddhidhan used all his strength to confront the hardships that threatened to crush and overwhelm him.
chapters.summary: Alak Kishori’s formidable influence guides the household, leading to an unexpected marriage proposal for Pramaddhan and Kumud Sundari after Sarasvatichandra vanishes.

chapters.title: Buddhidhan (Continued)
paragraphs: Buddhidhan (Continued) The motherless Saubhagya Devi had lived with her in-laws since she was a child. She was no longer a child. Her body and mind changed, visibly and invisibly. With the death of her father-in-law, her widowed mother-in-law observed confinement. Saubhagya Devi had to shoulder the entire burden of the household. Her mother-in- law instructed and guided her from her room, and it was Saubhagya Devi’s duty to obey her, even anticipate her wishes. She thus became a householder even before she was married. Hitherto, she had not spoken with Buddhidhan. But in these difficult times, gradually, unseen by others, and with trepidation, the two began to converse, initially standing well apart from each other. However, the young unmarried couple, in anticipation of pleasures to come, began to experience sensations hitherto unknown. Their hearts blossomed under force of youthful passion and even in the midst of very real difficulties, this tender attraction, unbeckoned by either, grew and dreamt innocent dreams. Neither was aware of this. In moments of playfulness, worldly responsibilities receded into the background; but their everyday lived reality compelled them to forget their tenderness. They had little scope to comprehend the two conditions. Sometimes their awakened desires sought to play themselves out and their growing familiarity allowed the playfulness of touch. Still children, they were in ‘love’. If this sorrowful world was a sari dark as a moonless night, their love was resplendent like the Milky Way; in the belief that the whole world slept, it twinkled brightly. Sorrows and joys do not come in monotones. Flung against the rocks of difficulty, Buddhidhan’s courageous mind grew tougher. At the same time, he was also tempered by delicate feelings. A love of pleasure and passion took root deep within his grave and sombre disposition. No one in the world was aware of this development. One day, the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law sat reminiscing about the past. The mother-in-law was overcome with emotion. Not wanting the child to see her tears, she sent her out of the room, saying, ‘Daughter-in-law, will you get me some water?’ The girl promptly got up to fetch water. She went to the other part of the house and filled a tumbler from the pot. Buddhidhan was sitting on a swing, deep in thought. He stopped swinging when he saw her, the one who brought a sparkle to his eyes, the light of the house. He stared unblinking at Saubhagya Devi as she filled water. He looked at her face and eyes, which were uncovered, but his imagination led him to visualise her tender and sensuous body which was covered. He oscillated between that which was seen and that which was imagined. Saubhagya Devi grew aware of his intense gaze. Both stared at each other, and they forgot all else. She forgot that her mother-in-law had asked for water. Meanwhile, the mother-in-law had shed her tears and regained her composure. She wondered where Saubhagya Devi was, and felt that her daughter-in-law had understood her pain and was probably crying all alone somewhere. She stepped out of the room, forgetting that she had to observe a widow’s customary confinement. She mumbled to herself, You are the good fortune of this house, our hope, the goddess who will perpetuate our lineage. Can you ever be happy while I’m drowning in sorrow? Dear God! she sighed and stepped out. She retreated the moment she saw the tender young couple. She could not believe her eyes. Overcome with curiosity, and to be certain, she looked on, hidden from their view. This beautiful and joyous sight melted away her pain and sorrow. Just a moment ago her pain had been unbearable, but now she thanked God. Her moist eyes forgot that an elder was not supposed to witness such tender scenes. She stood there, transfixed.

Buddhidhan and Saubhagya Devi gazed at each other unblinking, as if in a trance. The spell was about to break. Any moment, Buddhidhan expected Saubhagya Devi to sprinkle water on him, and he was prepared for it. But the expected did not happen. Instead, he saw her eyes well up with tears. He got up. He took the tumbler from her and put it aside, then took her hand and asked, ‘What is the matter?’ In response, she broke down and began to sob quietly, her eyes downcast. He drew her close, embraced her and gently caressed her back. Buddhidhan’s mother suddenly realised that she had broken the customary limit. She retreated back to her room, deep in thought. She knew she had seen what was not for her to see. Saubhagya Devi, too, realised what she had done. She freed herself from his embrace, and said, ‘Nothing, nothing at all,’ picked up the tumbler of water and hurried back to where her mother-in-law was waiting for her. Buddhidhan kept standing there, surprised, stupefied. This was the first time they had crossed the limit. Both experienced new desires surface in their mind and body. Deep in thought, Buddhidhan slowly walked back to the swing. The mother surmised that the wise step would be to solemnise their marriage immediately and not wait for her husband’s death anniversary to pass. She felt some remorse, but she forgave them as she recalled the days of her own youth. It is the natural instinct of Indian mothers to try and cover up the indiscretions of their children. The girl had reached puberty, but her father-in-law’s death had delayed the marriage. The mother in her wisdom realised that God’s will knew no such barriers, and hearts already united would not wait long for the marriage to be solemnised. But there was another reason as well that delayed the marriage. Buddhidhan was required to incur the customary expenses on death rituals. To then spend money on a wedding was to invite trouble. But he could not bring himself to say this to his mother. The marriage was organised, and the bride and groom were declared a couple in the eyes of the world. The festivities were over. They were householders now.

Buddhidhan now had to face his debts and creditors. The household expenses could be met from the privy purse, but that was not enough to pay back the creditors. The family felt in want of various things for the new household. The produce from the land was not sufficient. Buddhidhan could not share his concerns with either his mother or his wife, for it would cause them much anxiety. He had to be the man of the house and keep up pretenses. Alarming the women would be like cutting off his feet himself. Buddhidhan’s body withered, his face lost its lustre, his body appeared drained of blood, and although young, he soon started looking aged. Even so, a solitary lamp spread light and hope. At the end of a tiring day, he would sit down and talk to his widowed mother. Saubhagya Devi would join them with her childlike innocence. Finally, alone with her, he would be able to listen to her sweet voice, her melodious song and experience a nectar-like passion. Tired and fatigued, with her he would experience a momentary bliss. This was the only source of joy in a life otherwise full of sorrow and strife. The height of a householder’s joy is attained only while living in poverty. This dream, too, proved short-lived. The joys of domesticity were not a remedy to his problems. Buddhidhan began to have bouts of fever. He did not submit to them, but the fevers soon developed into a chronic condition. His body was aflame and ultimately he was bedridden. In his state of acute anxiety, no medicine, no remedy could alleviate what ailed him. There were many vaidyas in town, but most of them were quacks. Each one suggested a different concoction. Although poor, the ‘chief administrator’s family’ still commanded some prestige in Suvarnapur. Many visitors crowded around Buddhidhan’s sickbed, irritated him, found faults in the welcome accorded them owing to the absence of another man in the house, commented upon the family’s circumstances and criticised the family members. They felt or feigned compassion, cast lecherous glances at the young woman who sat beside the ailing man, made many conjectures, stole what they could, made a lot of noise, and rose and left for their homes with or without taking the family’s leave. Saubhagya Devi and her mother-in-law were grief-struck; these random comings and goings only alarmed and distressed them further. No remedy seemed to work and every visitor added to their confusion by suggesting new potions. Finally, the widow decided to come out of her confinement and sat by her ailing son when he had visitors. The young daughter- in-law, nervous and anxious, somehow managed the house. But the sole hope and support of the family, Buddhidhan showed no signs of recovery. Suffering followed suffering. A year passed since Buddhidhan’s father died. The administrator refused to continue the privy purse. Secretly, they were informed that the allowance could continue if the palms of the administrator and other petty officials were greased. This was impossible for the impoverished and hard-pressed family. The women felt helpless and distraught, but they did not inform Buddhidhan. His illness was a prolonged one. There was no money in the house, the income had stopped, and in the absence of a man to look after affairs, produce from the land declined further. There was no one who could go to the market. The vaidya lost interest in administering the medicines and his visits became infrequent. The visitors too became disinterested and stopped visiting. The house fell silent; there was nothing to draw attention away from the ailing man. The two women also began to look ill. Their suffering seemed endless. They had nowhere to turn but the sky above them and the water below. Buddhidhan’s distress increased as newer diseases assailed him. Bedridden, with sunken eyes and vacant gaze he stared at his old mother and childlike wife. His wife shed silent tears. Her eyes became swollen and bloodshot. The mother’s anguish knew no bounds. She looked at her son and daughter-in-law, and smote her forehead in vain when she was alone. She nursed her son courageously, stayed close to her daughter-in-law and ensured she was not left alone with her consuming worry. Finally, all visits ceased. Only the vaidya, moved by compassion, administered his preparations to the poor man. In addition, one elderly neighbour, whom Buddhidhan had spent hours listening to before his illness, continued to visit him, sit by his side and give him solace. It was this same man who now helped the widow by running errands to the market and the vaidya’s house; it was also on his counsel that Buddhidhan had not been informed about the cessation of the privy purse. One day, feeling unwell, the old man could not visit Buddhidhan. The vaidya too had not been around. The widowed mother who was in confinement, found herself in a quandary. Sending her daughter- in-law out of the house seemed to her inappropriate. Therefore, early next morning, the doting mother decided to abandon societal norm and custom. She told the daughter-in-law not to feel embarrassed and to sit by her husband’s side in her absence. Then like a thief stalking the shadows, she walked to the vaidya’s house. The daughter-in-law closed the door behind her and sat by her husband’s bedside. Buddhidhan was asleep. His weak and withered body looked lifeless as he slept. A dhoti covered his torso; one emaciated hand rested inert by his side. The mother-in-law’s absence allowed Saubhagya Devi to give vent to her grief. She looked at the shriveled body and withered face of her loving husband, and her heart cried out in anguish. Tears streaming down her eyes, she sang softly to herself. Sad is the wife whose husband is away For she is content only in his presence My only beloved Give up your foreign land and return For my heart breaks when you are away ... when you are away As she sang, her eyes on the deathly pallor of his face, her imagination ran wild. Inauspicious images flashed before her eyes as if in a macabre dance. The force of these visions was such that emotions buried deep within burst forth. She could no longer contain herself and let out a loud wail, ‘Hai!’ She smote her head against his feet and sobbed without restraint, not realising she might wake him. Her warm tears wet the bed. Buddhidhan woke up startled. For days now, he had not been able to as much as sit up in bed unsupported. Who knows from where he now found the strength. He pulled his wife close with his skeletal hands and weakly tried to press her to his emaciated chest. It was futile, since what little strength he had was already spent in this exertion. Buddhidhan was profoundly saddened at the sight of his agitated and frightened wife. He fathomed instantly the cause of her grief. He regained his calm; his eyes were moist with unshed tears. His voice trembled and broke as he said, ‘Devi! Why are you doing this? Be patient. God is with those who have no one else.’ Saubhagya Devi continued to gaze intently at Buddhidhan as if crazed. The torment in her eyes seemed to admonish God as it were, convinced that His will did not favour her. She put her hands on her husband’s shoulders and kept sobbing with downcast eyes as she haltingly spoke. ‘What can I do? I cannot bear it any longer! Mataji did all she could. She sold her ornaments and paid off our marriage debts. She bears the household expenses with what little remains. I beg and plead with her, but she refuses to sell my ornaments. Now, disregarding her confinement, she has gone to the vaidya’s house. Hai! O why did God create me? You had to incur debts to marry me. I am so utterly useless that I cannot even leave the house, and Mataji was forced to go despite her confinement. Who else could do what she has done! Her life is fulfilled. Alas, I am utterly useless, so are my ornaments. You could not make use of them. If the Privy Purse has been stopped, so be it—but what about my ornaments? If they are of no use to you, I do not need them either. What use are they to me!’ And saying so, one by one she removed all her ornaments and flung them against the wall in helpless rage. ‘I am born accursed because I have to see you in this state. I cannot bear it anymore!’ she wailed. Buddhidhan felt even more helpless and wretched. ‘Why are you doing this, Devi? Why was I not told that the Privy Purse has been stopped? So be it. You are not useless. Why would you think so! You are my support, my beloved. Be patient, my Devi. Those who have no one else have God. These auspicious ornaments are symbolic of our union. Do not throw them away.’

‘Who can be more auspicious for me than you? I have no fondness for ornaments. Where has the lustre of your face gone? God helps those He wants to, but what am I to do? Oh God! Do lie down, you will get weaker. Even at such times, I only add to your suffering!’ She composed herself and helped him to lie back in bed. There was a knock at the door just then, and Saubhagya Devi hurriedly went to open it. The mother entered the house. She looked dejected. Her face hid neither her rage, nor her red and moist eyes. She saw her distraught son and daughter-in-law, and the gold ornaments strewn about the room. For a moment, worry and suspicion assailed her. Her lips quivered and her heart pounded. In a voice weak with exhaustion, Buddhidhan said, ‘Ma, where have you been? Was it right not to inform me about the Privy Purse? Why do you appear so shaken?’ Realising then that he knew, the mother cast a reproachful look at her daughter-in-law. Saubhagya Devi got up, embraced her and wept, ‘Mataji, please forgive me! But at least put my ornaments to some use!’ she pleaded. Shutting the door behind them, both women sat near Buddhidhan’s bed. ‘Devi my daughter, you are still a child and immature. Why won’t we use your ornaments? We will have to when the need arises. Let me take care of you while I’m there. May God preserve these ornaments upon your body forever. Do not weep, my daughter, put them on.’ And wiping her tears, the mother let escape a deep sigh. ‘Son, what shall I say? What all shall I recount?’ The vaidya had gone out of town. His wife was a lowly character. The vaidya had not told her that he was treating Buddhidhan for free. There were many needy persons who could not pay, but the vaidya incurred his wife’s wrath if he gave them free medication. The wife had abused and driven away Buddhidhan’s mother without disclosing where her husband was. A compassionate neighbour had then informed her that the vaidya had to suddenly leave town on work. She had to return dejected. On her way back, she decided to pay a visit to the administrator, a distant relative, to discuss the matter of the privy purse. On reaching his house, she encountered his daughter at the threshold. The latter made a face and mocked her. But need can compel one to make a mother of a donkey; so disregarding the mockery, she entered the house. The administrator was in the courtyard, brushing his teeth, surrounded by servants. The moment he saw her, he knew why she had come. He also knew there was nothing to be gained from someone who lived a hand-to- mouth existence. Not wanting to waste his morning on something so futile, his face expressed displeasure. He sent a servant to say that ‘the Kamdar is busy. Go back. Send your application to the palace.’ She had hesitantly crossed the threshold; she now quickly turned back. She had only walked a few paces when she saw a woman come out of the administrator’s house and catch up with her. Though a widow, the woman had adorned and embellished herself. ‘You must have gone to the Kamdar’s house to speak about the Privy Purse.’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Your work will be done if you follow my advice.’ ‘I have no money to pay a bribe; I am poor.’ ‘You have something more valuable than money.’ Startled, Buddhidhan’s mother looked at the woman with suspicion and fear. ‘What?’ she asked. ‘Send your daughter-in-law to me. I will ensure that your work is done. The Kamdar’s son and I have good relations. I suggest this for your own good.’ A poor man’s wife is sister-in-law to all. The old widow clenched her teeth and pursed her lips. Anger shone through her eyes. But she knew it was dangerous to get into a verbal duel with this shameless and unchaste woman. So concealing her righteous anger, she simply said, ‘I do not want the Privy Purse,’ and walked away, not wanting even the shadow of this woman to fall on her. In native states, the son is the chief of police, the brother is the judge, and the father the administrator. Who is one to complain to, or seek justice from? Helpless, the poor woman quietly walked back home.

She had decided to keep all this from her son, not wanting to cause him greater distress in his already weakened state. But Buddhidhan had divined from her face that something untoward had occurred. To satisfy his curiosity, she merely said, ‘The fate of the poor is wretched. The vaidya is out of town.’ The rest she did not mention. They spoke of unrelated things which did not make many demands on the ailing man’s mind. Buddhidhan drifted back to sleep. Mother-in-law and daughter-in-law quietly got up and went to the adjoining room. The girl put her head on her mother-in-law’s lap and cried herself to sleep. The elderly widow sat deep in thought. She patted the daughter- in-law with one hand and tried in vain to wipe away the tears that flowed incessantly down her cheeks. Just then, the elderly neighbour Dayashankar opened the door. The widow signaled to him to enter quietly. He came in, closed the door, and sat down quietly. In low tones, he explained the previous day’s absence and asked after Buddhidhan. The old widow was overcome with emotion and wept anew. For when your own people appear Sorrow breaks through as if a gate has opened.⟨fn:5⟩ In company of a kindred soul, sorrow finds a voice. She narrated in detail to Dayashankar her experiences at the homes of the vaidya and the administrator. She also told him about what had transpired between her son and daughter-in-law. ‘Hai! What will become of this orphaned flower? Dayashankar, I am old. But if this child were to be widowed like me, how will I have the courage to face her? What hardships will she have to bear? I will die soon; then who will look after my Devi?’ The compassionate Dayashankar tried to console her. ‘Behn, have courage. Your fate will take a turn for the better. No doubt, Buddhidhan will certainly recover. He will come back with leonine strength. My conscience bears testimony to this, and you must believe it to be true. I have read your daughter-in-law’s birth chart, and it foretells that she is not destined to become a widow. This year is a bad one for Buddhidhan, but things will eventually turn for the better.’ It was not as if Dayashankar had deep faith in astrology, but his  words gave hope to the suffering widow. She felt better for having  unburdened herself. Her tears also ceased. Meanwhile, Saubhagya Devi awoke, and sat up with propriety. All of them went to Buddhidhan’s bedside. The rustle of Dayashankar’s feet had awakened Buddhidhan. Illness had made his hearing sharper. And he had overheard their entire conversation. As he listened to them, emotions of pity, helplessness, rage, hope, enthusiasm ... all swept through his mind. By the time the three of them came in, Buddhidhan had regained his composure. Dayashankar sat by his bed, put a hand on Buddhidhan’s forehead, and felt for his pulse. ‘Are you feeling better? You look better to me, but your face betrays anxiety.’ ‘Yes Kaka, I am better today. I felt angry when I heard what mother said to you. You see for yourself how cunning the Kamdar is. That entire clan is shameless and wicked; they work only for the benefit of a few.’ Buddhidhan appeared pensive as he said this, and seething in a quiet rage. ‘Bhai, that is just the way it is. Keep that in mind when you become chief administrator,’ Dayashankar said with a smile. ‘Behn, don’t think such a thing cannot happen. You know well that there was a time the present administrator had no food to eat. Who knows how the wheel will turn! You belong to the original chief administrator’s family. Fifty years later, you may well regain that position. Is anything impossible before God?’ Buddhidhan looked at the old woman. The widow sighed deeply and said, ‘We do not want to be administrators or any such thing, bhai. We are not going to get lakhs and become millionaires. My only consolation is these two.
