They are my heaven. Once my son recovers, finds an occupation, and they find happiness again, I will feel as fulfilled as if I had bathed in the Ganga. All this suffering and ignominy will then only be a memory. Then all I will seek and await is the call of God.’ The son keenly felt the mother’s pain. Dayashankar consoled, ‘Do not worry. All will be well. What do you say, bhai?’ ‘Kaka, I will feed you sweets when that happens. At this moment however, it seems like mockery. But I have taken note that this cunning administrator has heaped scorn upon my poor and virtuous mother, and that his son has insulted my family in hard times. Bear this in mind: Buddhidhan will have his revenge. In God’s plan, every misfortune has a silver lining. It is good that the Privy Purse has been stopped. Now I am no longer under the Kamdar’s thumb. I was unable to escape his power. That anxiety has now been taken from me—I am free. I am my own master. Thank God! The Kamdar has himself unwittingly removed these obstacles from my path. Now, I will get better. My desire to live has been rekindled. These two jewels are dearest to me—what would I not do for their sake! Yes, I am poor. I have neither money nor friends. Whether I become chief administrator or not is for fate to decide. But what is certain is that I will ruin this administrator. He shall be forced to acknowledge me, and to praise me. Yes, I have that power, and the world shall recognise it one day. Revenge: this fire will burn day and night in my heart, it will scorch the Kamdar and his family, and be quenched only thereafter. I too am a man born into a family of true administrators, not a family of savages like the present administrator. Ma, I was born of you! I do not wear bangles.’ Buddhidhan trembled uncontrollably as he spoke, twisting and turning in his bed, gritting his teeth and biting his lips, at times thumping his emaciated chest with frail bony hands. The effort of this long passionate speech completely exhausted the sick man. His hands fell limp and hung lifeless by his side, his eyes flickered unsteadily and started to close. Drained by the excitement, the patient soon fell into a deep sleep. Gradually, his extreme agitation and tremors subsided, but his eyebrows were still raised and his forehead remained creased in a frown, betraying that even in sleep, Buddhidhan was gripped by a powerful dream.

The three of them stared at him as if stupefied. As he drifted swiftly into sleep, they got up, anxious and pensive. ‘Let him sleep. Let him sleep,’ advised kindly Dayashankar and returned home. It was thought that Buddhidhan’s words were borne out of delirium and rage. But when the vaidya resumed his visits the following day, his medicines miraculously seemed to take effect. Within a few days, Buddhidhan was well enough to move around the house. Quite soon, he was completely rid of his disease. The only traces left behind were the fires of revenge and anger still burning inside him. Like the comet that blazes a trail in the midnight sky, his unceasing rage manifested itself on his perpetually creased brow. It was a sign that the administrator’s doom was certain.
chapters.summary: Buddhidhan battles severe illness and mounting debts, but a fiery resolve ignites within him, promising a dramatic shift in his future.

chapters.title: Buddhidhan (Conclusion)
paragraphs: Buddhidhan (Conclusion) The false utterances of the influential and important are often taken as true, while the honest words of the less important are dismissed as false. Kindly Dayashankar had laughed at the anger of the weak, ailing, impoverished Buddhidhan. In time, Buddhidhan’s family, too, forgot about it. God has made the minds and hearts of people inscrutable. While those of little or no means have occasion to fathom the thoughts of the rich and powerful, the latter—intoxicated and blinded by power—fail to read the minds of the poor and the wretched. Those whose vision is thus blinded consider the deeds of the poor innately meaningless, thoughtless, foolish, insubstantial, and transient. Even if there be in the company of the blind a one-eyed man who considers a poor man’s intelligence worthy of being tested, it is only to prove himself superior to the latter. Prior to his illness, Buddhidhan used to visit the administrator, Shathrai, on occasion. Despite the insult to his mother, after his recovery, Buddhidhan resumed these visits. During gatherings, when the administrator sat surrounded by sycophants, chatting, boasting, disparaging others, seeking pleasure and pride in another’s harm, indulging in depravities, plotting schemes, turning morality on its head, dreaming foolish and vile dreams fueled by a mistaken sense of superiority and abject flattery, Buddhidhan would sit at the back among the lowliest of workers and engage his eyes, ears and mind fully to observe this world. No one ever noticed him. Eyes fixed upon

Shathrai and his son Dushtarai, Buddhidhan would stoke the rage that burned within him. Sometimes Dushtarai would look at him from the corner of his eye, his gaze disdainful and arrogant, and gesture mockingly; this would remind Buddhidhan of his wretched and lowly status. The genuflection of his subordinates gave Dushtarai a supreme sense of power and authority. In comparison, Dushtarai’s father Shathrai was a better and more intelligent individual. Not that he was incapable of behaving like his son, but that he would do so only for a reason. In as much as was possible, nothing but pure self-interest moved him. Therefore, Buddhidhan had to rarely deal with Shathrai. However, on the occasions they did meet, Shathrai had realised that Buddhidhan was sharp and intelligent, albeit not as ‘sharp’ and ‘intelligent’ as himself. This assessment was in no way likely to either benefit or harm Buddhidhan, because Shathrai was unlikely to grant or deny him any favours because of his qualities. By the same token, Buddhidhan’s status was such that he was incapable of causing any harm to the administrator. For Shathrai, he was neither a friend, nor a foe. Whatever enmity there was burned secretly within Buddhidhan’s mind. This fire had been kindled, unbeknownst to them, by both the administrator and his son. Those without ordinary virtues are incapable of discernment; they see no reason for it either. But God punishes even those who falter unknowingly, and the consequences of indiscretion—realised or unrealised, seen or unseen—inevitably take root. When these consequences become manifest, ignorant men blame God. They forget their insolence, or are unable to see the link between their arrogance and the consequences thereof. Blessed are those whose conscience is shielded by virtue and right judgment, for they are enlightened by their power of discernment even in times of darkness and sorrow. Examining Shathrai and Dushtarai minutely, reflecting upon their crimes and their future implications in moments of controlled rage, Buddhidhan would ponder, and arrive at conclusions and decisions known to him alone. On one such occasion, seated right at the back of the gathering, Buddhidhan was deep in thought. Everyone had got up and left. But he continued to sit there and stare blankly ahead of him, as if seeing images flit past in a dream. Seated upon a window ledge, he was lost to the world. Just then, a sweeper entered the hall, swinging his broom. He thwacked the broom hard, releasing clouds of dust. Startled, Buddhidhan broke out of his reverie and realised he was alone. He got up, stretched his limbs and slowly walked to the door. Just outside Shathrai’s house, he met a Rajput Garasia. He wore a pagdi embroidered with gold and silver thread on his head, a tight- fitting intricately patterned angarkha, and tight pajamas buttoned at the ankles. He carried a silver hookah, a dagger, a sword, and a carved knife tied to his waist. The mojris on his feet had red embroidery. He was followed by another Garasia in simple attire, and a few others. They walked with slow deliberate steps. The Rajput Garasia leading them addressed Buddhidhan and said: ‘Buddhidhan Bhai, how are things? Where are you headed? Is the Kamdar at home?’ ‘Welcome, welcome Bhupsinhji! The Kamdar has just left.’ ‘I see,’ said Bhupsinh with a scowl. ‘Then why did he ask us to be here! So be it. It is his day today. Buddhidhan, why have I not seen you around? You should visit us sometime. The Kamdar’s house may be filled with gold, but none of it is going to be of any use to you. Instead of wearing your shoes out at his doorstep, if you were to come to us, we might be of some use to you. It is entirely up to you.’ ‘Why do you say this, Bhupsinhji? I have been intending to visit you for many days now’. From that day on, Buddhidhan strengthened his acquaintance with Bhupsinh. Bhupsinh was the closest cousin of Rana Jadsinh, the ruler of Suvarnapur. Because he was still a minor, Bhupsinh’s garas was under the Rana’s administration. The Receiver appointed to administer the land under the garas, together with Shathrai, had siphoned off as much revenue from it as they could. They had also tutored the Rana to treat Bhupsinh as just another cousin. To this end, Bhupsinh was only paid paltry sums from the revenues earned from his garas. Being a minor, he feared for his life and stayed with his maternal relations, away from Suvarnapur. However, having recently attained adulthood,

Bhupsinh now wanted his family inheritance returned to him. He had come back to Suvarnapur to claim it, putting his life in jeopardy. No one heeded his demands and he was pushed around. He therefore harboured considerable enmity for both Rana Jadsinh and Shathrai. But his anger was impotent; Bhupsinh was incapable of actually doing anything. He kept the company of lowly, scheming bureaucrats and through them sought ways of reclaiming his inheritance. The only way suggested to him was to bribe the administrator. Shathrai and his hangers-on demanded at least fifty thousand rupees. The Rana wanted the same amount as a gift. In times like these, the foe of a foe becomes a friend. Emboldened, Buddhidhan took up cudgels on behalf of Bhupsinh, who had the financial and moral support of his maternal family. Buddhidhan no longer had to worry about finding a source of income and livelihood. He decided to fight it to the finish with those who ruled the state. Owing to the people’s fear of Shathrai, Bhupsinh was friendless. Buddhidhan’s allegiance was therefore useful to him. Bhupsinh and his advisor would meet at night, contemplating their present and their future. They were not yet important enough to attract any attention. But in due course, their association became public knowledge and alongside the one, the other too came to be regarded as an enemy by Shathrai. And so eventually, Buddhidhan too felt the need to be prepared for a counterattack. He sold his house and land in Suvarnapur and decided to move out with his family to an area under British control. He later came to know that Dushtarai had hatched an evil plan to abduct Saubhagya Devi the very day they left Suvarnapur. This reinforced Buddhidhan’s conviction that his decision to move his family had been the right one. Buddhidhan and Bhupsinh both made Lilapur, a seat of British administration, their new home. Both rented separate houses in Lilapur. Some three miles from the village lived the Agent of the British Government, Colonel Buskin Sahib. Suvarnapur, Ratnanagari, a few other native states, and seven or eight taluks were under his jurisdiction. These native states were of different sizes and brought in revenues ranging from ten to fifty lakhs per annum. A military man, Buskin Sahib was a jolly fellow. He liked taking quick decisions and lost his temper if his orders were not carried out promptly, or if suggestions were made to the contrary. He always did things correctly and suspected others of wrongdoing. Even his strong sense of fairness did not prevent him from using all available means against such persons. He was capable of taking wise and insightful decisions, but preferred to work through his Shirastidar.⟨fn:6⟩ He would often seek the Shirastidar’s opinion about the goodness or otherwise of plaintiffs, and was pleased when his own views were confirmed. He had come to regard the Shirastidar as an efficient and a good man. This Shirastidar was a Dakshini⟨fn:7⟩ man called Sadashiv Pant whose command over the English language was good. He was clever and adept at conforming to the Sahib’s wishes whilst maintaining the façade of autonomy. He had once obtained the Dewanship of Shantigarh through the largesse of Buskin Sahib. Since he owed his position to the Sahib’s influence, he had come to regard that he had no duties towards the ruler of Shantigarh. When in need, he would flatter the courtiers, and discard them as soon as his ends were achieved. Therefore no faction regarded him as their own man. The newspapers praised Sadashiv Pant’s neutrality and fairness, causing him to rise in the Sahib’s esteem. This foreclosed any possibility of complaints against him, and the Shirastidar used this to satisfy his secret wants and desires, giving full play to his greed and brazenness. He appointed many outsiders in his administration on the grounds that the locals were incapable, unable to remain impartial, or unworthy of the responsibility entrusted. He could not but find anyone save fellow Dakshinis to fill these positions. Eventually, the ruler, the palace officials, Garasias, and the local people, everyone complained of his tyrannical ways. But the enemies of the state and the ruler went to

Buskin Sahib and attested to the Dewan’s fairness; so he disregarded these complaints. Once however, perceiving himself to be slighted, the ruler personally went to the Sahib with a complaint. Other palace machinations also surfaced. Buskin Sahib surmised that the Dewan was unable to manage competing factions due to his honesty. Sadashiv Pant was therefore recalled to his earlier position. The Sahib increased his personal allowances and promised him a higher position when the time was right. Buskin Sahib also exercised judicial authority over this area. Government pleaders were appointed for the same, and to liaise on account of native states. Buddhidhan approached the Sahib, and impressing him with his intellect, obtained a pleader’s license. With this, he acquired an individual income and the prestige of associating with Government officials. Befriending Sadashiv Pant, Buddhidhan then introduced Bhupsinh to him. He convinced Sadashiv Pant that Bhupsinh was likely to inherit the Suvarnapur throne, and was in a position to spend some money to obtain his garas. He also kept creating opportunities to see Buskin Sahib in a professional capacity, and he so impressed him with his honesty, cleverness and discernment that, although reliant on Sadashiv Pant for counsel in most matters, when it came to issues represented by Buddhidhan, the Sahib need heed no one else. Careful not to displease the Shirastidar, Buddhidhan would first meet him, humour him, and only then approach the Sahib. In this, he saw nothing amiss. However, as Sadashiv Pant cultivated relations with Bhupsinh, he began to see Buddhidhan as a thorn in his side. Buddhidhan had taught Bhupsinh to be generous, and his counsel was always sought in the exercising of this generosity. This practice ceased. Buddhidhan had calculated the worth of this relationship differently between the other two men. He felt that if Bhupsinh were to obtain his garas soon, he would squander it in pursuit of pleasure, which would douse his fiery aspirations. If this were to happen, Bhupsinh would not be in a position to cultivate relations with the British. Buddhidhan wanted to keep Bhupsinh in Lilapur primarily for this purpose, and to this end, though taking care to appear neutral, he would praise Bhupsinh in front of the Sahib. On the other hand, Buddhidhan fostered acquaintance with Sadashiv Pant in the hope that longstanding personal relations could be used to greater advantage in the future. Therefore, he also made no serious attempt towards claiming Bhupsinh’s garas immediately; he wanted to use this time to expand Bhupsinh’s understanding of the world. Sadashiv Pant foiled this plan. Bhupsinh and Buddhidhan drifted apart; but Buddhidhan pretended he was unaware of any such change in their relationship. He now plotted and schemed to counter the situation and right the wrong. The norm ‘good ends and good means’ was unknown to Buddhidhan. But because his conscience was clear, he instinctively searched for means that were pure. And yet, he was satisfied only when the ends were also beneficial. He believed therefore that good ends could be achieved by using any means. He had not been taught that this was wrong, and there was no one around him to do so now. In this instance, when pure means did not provide themselves, he felt it necessary to deploy impure ones. For the present, he gave up attempts to inculcate right thought and conduct in Bhupsinh, instead allowing their conversation to be mired in subjects of leisure and pleasure. Sadashiv Pant was addicted to liquor, a womaniser and a nocturnal creature. To profit from these weaknesses while himself remaining untouched, Buddhidhan masterfully created opportunities for Bhupsinh to indulge in them, but in ways that Bhupsinh never realised that he had done so. The young Rajput Garasia now began to idle away his days and nights at Sadashiv Pant’s residence. When the Shirastidar was busy with office work during the day, and when he headed out by night, Bhupsinh took up with his wife, Ramabai. Buddhidhan could no longer meet Bhupsinh at the latter’s residence. Even so, he would regularly visit his house and wait a while, keeping an eye on developments there. Bhupsinh’s wife Rajba had very high regard for Buddhidhan. Neither harboured unchaste thoughts about each other. However, in Bhupsinh’s absence, the two now had occasion to spend time alone with each other. Discontent and jealous of her husband’s debauchery, Rajba felt she was no longer bound by the chastity contingent to her wifely duties. And she gradually grew to be infatuated with Buddhidhan. One day as they sat talking, she abruptly fell silent and looked intently at him as if struck by a sudden thought. Buddhidhan met her gaze, and he saw her passion. His piety was shaken. They both stood up. Involuntarily, as if compelled by some unseen force, they drew closer together, and their fingers intertwined. Their pulses raced, their bodies trembled, felt fevered. They lost the capacity to think and could only look at each other, stunned. Rajba’s sari slipped off her shoulder. Just then there was a loud noise and the two were jolted back to their senses, their hands falling apart. Saying that he would return the next day, Buddhidhan walked out of the room, troubled and deep in thought. Rajba made as if to call him back, but the words failed her and she sat down petrified. Unable to think, in a state of extreme agitation, she sat there alone, crying. Then, like one reborn, with new resolve she sought to distract herself with household work. Buddhidhan’s conscience was aflame with repentance and remorse. He felt this incident was a bad omen. He resolved not to spend any more time alone with Rajba. But his imagination ran amuck and vivid images played and replayed in his mind’s eye. The vision of Rajba—her sari askew, standing before him, holding his hand in hers, intense and eager—refused to disappear; her image chased away his piety. Thus bewildered, distraught and pale-faced, he reached home. When Buddhidhan saw his mother’s face, she somehow seemed different to him, although nothing had changed. Feeling impure and incriminated, he stood at a distance and could not bring himself to look at her pious and radiant visage. Entering the bedroom, Saubhagya Devi greeted him with a loving embrace. But he stood petrified, unable to respond, as if his very touch would defile her. He made as if he were trying to shun this touch even in his mind. Burning with remorse, he felt as if he had been unfaithful to his wife, his Devi. He looked at her pure, innocent face. The thought that he had cheated on her troubled him. And that she had no inkling that the husband who now stood before her had been so wicked. He looked at her face again and found her even more beautiful—Rajba paled in comparison with his wife. He found repulsive the very idea that he had been attracted to her even momentarily and could not fathom why reason had failed him or how he had thought of forsaking his swan-like beauty for that ugly crow. He finally resolved that his virtuous wife alone was worthy of his affections, and he grew eager to reciprocate her love. He also decided he would not visit Bhupsinh’s home, but that if he had to do so, he would ensure that he spent no time alone with Rajba. Buddhidhan felt a deep gratitude that God had saved him from committing a great sin. Tension eased from his body as if he had received an oil massage followed by a bath, ministered by loving hands. He slept soundly, with his virtuous, beautiful and content wife by his side. Even in sleep, her image stayed with him. He dreamt that Saubhagya Devi was a deity in a temple: the temple of the heart, the Hriday Mandir. She was seated on a throne and emanated a light soft and soothing like the moon’s rays. Grateful and fortunate, he fanned his Goddess lovingly, held her insignias, and when some fifty-odd women resembling Rajba arrived at the temple gates, he chased them away. The Goddess chided him fondly saying, ‘Wait there, you crook!’ and raised her hand to give him an affectionate pat. Just then, Saubhagya Devi’s hand caressed his forehead: even in sleep, her lips quivered in a delicate smile. The following day, Buddhidhan became engrossed in his routine work. But when evening fell and it was time to visit Bhupsinh’s house,  he  remembered Rajba. Forgetting his resolve of the night before, he grew eager to see her. As he was dressing to leave the house, Saubhagya Devi came in to ask him something. Buddhidhan’s conscience reasserted itself—her mere presence ensured that he remained chaste and faithful. No! I am not going to visit Rajba, he firmly told himself, and went about other business someplace else. From that moment on, this thought lost its grip over his mind. But Rajba was a clever woman; she was obstinate and not one to give up easily. The Rajputani was also very courageous. Despite his promise, Buddhidhan had not come. He must be busy today; he will surely come tomorrow, she thought. Or the next day. Or the one after. Seven or eight days passed, but Buddhidhan did not come. Finally, one day as Bhupsinh was leaving the house to visit Ramabai as usual, consumed by jealousy, Rajba decided to follow him. She went back, and carefully disguised herself as a man, bearing a weapon at her waist. At around eight in the evening, she found herself in front of Buddhidhan’s house. She sent him the message that Bhupsinh’s friend Rajsinh was here to meet him and wanted a word with him in private. Surprised at the unfamiliar name, Buddhidhan came out and stood before her. ‘Rajsinh, please come in,’ he said, and took Rajba into the drawing room. He looked closely at the attire, the face, and was startled. Bewildered he said, ‘What’s this! You! Here, at this time?’ Imitating a man’s demeanour, Rajba sat up straight, her hand reaching to touch the dagger at her waist, but from habit, it petulantly came to rest on her hip instead. She thrust her chest out, but her shapely form only became more apparent. Moreover, she could not conceal her eyes and knew she was caught out. ‘Buddhidhan, you have done me wrong. Bhupsinh finds solace in Sadashiv Pant’s house. You promised to help me, but failed to keep your word. Does this befit our affection?’ ‘Rajsinh, I understand your pain. Bhupsinh is the reason for our relationship, and it would benefit neither of us to form an association independent of him. Bring Bhupsinh back in hand—my loyalties are with both of you. Bhupsinh should be the one to give you the succour you need,’ he said with brazen courage. ‘And what of your assurance, Buddhidhan? Your word? Your promise?’ ‘I am very sorry. A word wrongly given cannot be kept. I must break this promise, because I am bound by a greater one.’ ‘And what of me?’ ‘I have thought well of you, Rajba, and for you, too.’ ‘Are you certain of this? Be careful.’ ‘Yes. I am certain.’

‘Think again.’ ‘I have considered it well. Godspeed,’ Buddhidhan said, somewhat shaken, and got up. ‘I know what you think,’ Rajba said abruptly and she caught hold of his arm, forcing him to sit back down on a bolster. She stood close to him, her body touching his. Who knows from where she found the courage. A Rajputani, and so brazen! Freeing his hand and visibly squirming from her touch, Buddhidhan said, ‘Raj, this is enough. Send for me through Bhupsinh, and I will come.’ ‘Why, are you afraid of him?’ she laughed disdainfully. Then, bending over him, she put both her hands on his shoulders and stood very close, her chin touching his. ‘I am afraid of God. No one else.’ Realising she would not get her way, the Rajputani stood up straight, her eyes rolling in anger. ‘So be it. Be afraid of your God, Buddhidhan. Come when Bhupsinh calls you. But I will hold you to your word, or I am not a true Rajput. All right, I will be on my way now,’ and she pushed him aside in hauteur and left his house. Buddhidhan brooded over the incident for a moment, then returned to his business as if nothing had happened. He stopped visiting Bhupsinh’s house altogether. If the paths of the two friends ever crossed now, their salutations were perfunctory. Word of this trivial matter spread from ear to ear all the way to Suvarnapur. The world believed that something had caused a breach in Buddhidhan and Bhupsinh’s friendship. Queen Gossip provided thousands of explanations to people’s serpentine tongues. Buddhidhan’s chief concern now was to find ways of separating Bhupsinh and Sadashiv Pant, and to ensure that the Garasia was once more beholden to him. He clearly felt that he had erred in fostering familiarity between the two. But he had learnt his lesson: he resolved to no longer trust anyone, not consider anyone innately good, and never to allow his affairs to slip into the hands of others. He needed to wield influence over the Garasia to make him an instrument of his own success, but he decided not to count even Bhupsinh as his own.

Moreover, he now understood that he could not allow Bhupsinh to veer off the right path, because it was difficult to rein in a man who was in the wrong. It is possible to control him perhaps; but to do so one would have to stoop to his low, wicked ways. If Buddhidhan had given in to Rajba’s entreaties, for instance, Bhupsinh would have become a puppet in his hands. But this prospect did not appeal to his conscience, and it slipped away like mercury without leaving a trace. One day, on his way to the Sahib’s office, Buddhidhan found Bhupsinh walking ahead of him. Sadashiv Pant’s house fell on the same road. Ramabai was standing at a window on the first floor. She came down and opened the door. Bhupsinh entered the house, and the door closed behind him. Witnessing this scene, Buddhidhan sighed and walked away. As he sat in his office, his mind was not at ease. Just then Buskin Sahib called out to him, and Buddhidhan got up to go. The Sahib was seated on his chair, holding a quill between his teeth. Removing the quill, he said, ‘Buddhidhan, do you know in which year the Ruler of Suvarnapur had responded to the Garasia?’ Thinking a while, Buddhidhan turned to the Shirastidar and replied, ‘Pant, you took all these documents home to study three, four days ago. The answer is in there, and the letter also bears the date of the response.’ The Sahib said, ‘Send someone home and have the documents brought over.’ The Shirastidar submitted, ‘Sahib, I will look for them in the office today. If I can’t find them here, I will bring them over from home tomorrow.’ ‘Not at all. Either send someone, or go fetch them yourself right away,’ the Sahib commanded. ‘Buddhidhan, will you please send someone to my house?’ the Shirastidar asked. Buddhidhan found his opportunity. There was an office clerk called Narbheram, a wily, witty, jealous, garrulous and brazen mimic. He hated the Dakshinis and taunted Sadashiv Pant bitterly, ridiculing him behind his back for the freedoms he allowed Ramabai. But

Narbheram had proven himself useful to Sadashiv Pant in other ways, which is why the Shirastidar tolerated his mockery and believed Narbheram to be his man. Buddhidhan now chose Narbheram to locate and bring back the documents. On reaching Pant’s house, the clerk found the door firmly shut. Instead of knocking or calling out to anyone, he bent down and peeped through the keyhole. He saw Bhupsinh inside the house. Without drawing any attention to himself, he turned back. On his return, he whispered this juicy news into Buddhidhan’s ear. Buddhidhan told him to inform Sadashiv Pant. Narbheram went and stood before Pant. Concealing the glee in his heart, his face twisted in sorrow and anger, and he made as if he were at a loss for words. But of course, he told him all eventually. Sadashiv Pant’s face turned ashen. His head in a whirl, he sought Narbheram’s advice. Narbheram said, ‘It is best you ask Buddhidhan. He will know what to do. Personally, I think this wicked Bhupsinh should be exposed and beaten up.’ Narbheram thought, Now you’re caught, my boy! Bhupsinh is after all a man. It is you and your wife who will be exposed and derided. Before the frightened and distressed Shirastidar, Buddhidhan maintained a grave and concerned mien, and yet appeared disinterested. ‘Tell the Sahib that the document could not be found. Take his permission, and let us go to your house.’ All three thus headed to Sadashiv Pant’s house. Since a Rajput Garasia was involved, they also kept a few soldiers with them, anticipating a brawl. Looking in from the keyhole, they saw Bhupsinh going up the stairs. Narbheram signaled even the passers-by to stop. On his advice, the group climbed into the neighbour’s house and went up to the room adjoining the one in which Ramabai and Bhupsinh were. A wooden partition separated these two rooms. The three of them and the soldiers looked through the gaps in the partition. Sadashiv’s eyes were red with anger, his lips quivered and he looked like one possessed. ‘I will kill or be killed,’ he grimly announced. Standing behind him, Narbheram was beside himself with glee. He whispered to Buddhidhan, ‘Good! Much liberty is being taken. This madam is suitable for the Sahibs!’ A crowd gathered outside the window. Their noise attracted Ramabai’s attention and she alerted Bhupsinh. The Garasia was startled at first, then began to seethe with anger. He twirled his moustache, and anticipating that the crowd would come up the stairs, he took Ramabai under one arm and drew his sword half out of its scabbard with the other, declaring, ‘What can these effete men do! Even if Sadashiv himself comes here, I will pocket him and keep you in my house as a co-wife with Rajba. My sword is unyielding!’ Sadashiv was frightened. His anger drained away and he fell pathetically into Buddhidhan’s arms. Buddhidhan felt genuine pity for him then. ‘Sadashiv, you are no match for him. For the time being, forget what you have seen. You will either be killed by the Garasia’s sword, or be poisoned by your wife. Come, let us tell these people that nothing is amiss so they will disperse and this melee will cease. Take a few months leave from the Sahib and go back to your native place. We will tell him we could not find anything worthwhile in the document. Once at your native place, do what you will with Ramabai. Do not endanger your life here.’ The bystanders noisily dispersed and went their own way. Ramabai had opened the window partially to ascertain that they were actually leaving, and she recognised Sadashiv by his turban. Once the coast was clear, Bhupsinh quietly left for his home. There, he started ordering Rajba around as if he were her master. But Rajba was more than piqued. She had been told about the incident at Ramabai’s house, and she had decided she would create a scene and make sure that Buddhidhan was sent for. ‘Thakurani, fire the hookah.’ ‘That’s all I am good for now! For other things, you have someone else,’ Rajba retorted and burst into tears. ‘What’s all this?’ ‘As if you don’t know! Reclaiming the garas is hardly on your mind. You abandoned the friendship of a man like Buddhidhan and took up with a cunning fellow like Sadashiv and ...’ ‘And what?

‘Just that you no longer have any need of me. Of course—how can I compete with the beauty of a Dakshini!’ On the one hand, this dialogue commenced. On the other, Sadashiv Pant sought leave. But since there was no one who could replace him immediately, Buskin Sahib hesitated to let his Shirastidar go. Sadashiv Pant now considered Buddhidhan as his own man; so he requested him to take over his responsibilities. Buddhidhan, as if he were doing him a favour, agreed to step in. Even the Sahib approved of this arrangement. Buddhidhan ascended a step on the ladder towards his ultimate goal. Bhupsinh was left friendless. Ramabai had left. Rajba was playing hard to get. Bhupsinh had squandered away his money over Ramabai and Sadashiv Pant, and was now desperate for his inheritance. Thinking of his garas, he also thought of Buddhidhan and how he needed him again. But Bhupsinh would have chosen death over swallowing his pride. Rajba was equally obstinate; she had a message sent to Bhupsinh’s maternal family. Bhupsinh’s maternal uncle sent back word saying, ‘Befriend Buddhidhan—he has become a Shirastidar. Such cowardice and debauchery are not becoming of you.’ Since Bhupsinh now spent more time at home, Rajba would also keep nagging him saying, ‘With Buddhidhan, there is no question of pride. He is our well-wisher. It is because you went astray that he parted ways with you. He will be pleased to know that you are now reformed. He now has an office and will be of use to you’. Eventually, the Rajputani got her way. Tired of her insistence, the apathetic Bhupsinh started visiting Buddhidhan again. Then, Rajba died of a sudden illness. Buddhidhan therefore resumed visiting Bhupsinh’s house without a care. He even helped Bhupsinh financially, and the two became friends again. Buddhidhan was however careful to ensure that the resumption of their friendship did not become public knowledge. By then, Buddhidhan had been in Lilapur for five years. Saubhagya Devi had a daughter who was a year old. Their next door neighbour was a Bengali traveller whose wife had an unusual name, which they had all taken a fancy to. Buddhidhan’s mother had thus named the little girl Alak Kishori. Sometime after, a boy was born to them. His birth- chart determined that his name was to begin with the letter ‘p’. He was named Pramaddhan, to rhyme with Buddhidhan. The infant would lie in his grandmother’s lap quite idle and inert; so his father felt that his name was well chosen. Content that Buddhidhan had obtained the position of Shirastidar, his mother died at peace, surrounded by her beloved son, daughter-in-law and grandchildren. The house seemed painfully empty after her death, and the couple mourned her deeply. In time, as the son became engrossed with his new office and the wife got busy raising their two children, their grief became a thing of the past. Even so, Buddhidhan often felt that his children would not be raised very well, having been denied the care and upbringing of his loving, intelligent and wise mother. He had no time for them. And Saubhagya Devi, while virtuous and devoted, was not worldly-wise; she had never had to worry about things while her mother-in-law was alive. The old woman had trained her well when it came to household work, and she was now quite adept at it. But she had had no opportunity to learn about child-rearing. She didn’t even remember how she herself had been raised by the old woman, so how was she to act on her own? She was simple, good-natured, and of average intelligence. She believed the world was full of good people, like her husband and mother-in-law. Virtue and right conduct came naturally to her, and she believed that the wheels of the world turned on their own, without requiring a nudge and a push. Buddhidhan considered himself fortunate for having such a wife. He had never before seen such joyous days. He was now the Shirastidar of Lilapur, and his conjugal life was blissful. After the day’s work, he would sit with his wife and play with his children, then watch them sleep as he spent pleasurable hours with Devi. She would gently touch his face to wake him up every morning when the cool breeze wafted in through their widow. They would wake up quietly so as to not disturb the children. In his pensive moments, it would often seem to Buddhidhan that such beautiful, blissful days would never ever return. In his joy and gratitude, he would embrace Saubhagya Devi or his children. Sadashiv Pant found a good job in his native place. Buskin Sahib sent him a certificate of good conduct, and he made Buddhidhan’s position as the Shirastidar permanent, following which, his prestige climbed in the native states. In the belief that Buddhidhan and Bhupsinh had drifted apart, Buddhidhan’s appointment was appreciated in Suvarnapur as well, where he now cultivated relations with the ruling clique. The new Shirastidar visited Suvarnapur on work from time to time, and the administrator and his coterie began to accord him both respect and money. Dushtarai took the lead in praising and pleasing him, and Buddhidhan was now seated next to the Karbhari Shathrai in the Suvarnapur palace assembly. Every so often, Buddhidhan extracted bribes from these corrupt men, believing that he did no wrong. In fact, he used this opportunity to cultivate relations with the palace retainers so as to be able to closely follow the machinations of the royal household. In this undertaking, he freely used the money he had accumulated. Shathrai, however, still had some misgivings about Buddhidhan. Rana Jadsinh had no legitimate heir. He claimed one Parvatsinh to be his son. Shathrai kept Parvatsinh under his thumb by threatening to divulge the identity of his real parents. Parvatsinh was tired of such harassment. Garbaddas, the son of the previous administrator, was a state official. He had cultivated a relationship with Parvatsinh. Garbaddas engineered many a petition and complaint against Shathrai to the British Agent. He also fomented disaffection in the palace through various queens and palace servants. Even this faction had made a few overtures towards Buddhidhan. Parvatsinh was the main impediment in Bhupsinh’s way to the throne. Pretending to be a well-wisher, Buddhidhan informed Shathrai about the palace intrigues against him, after which he secured Shathrai’s trust. The Karbhari now began to solicit Buddhidhan’s advice even in personal matters and obtained bribes for him from the palace as well.

Ultimately, Shathrai succeeded in removing Parvatsinh from the line of succession, and in having Garbaddas dismissed, to boot. However, Garbaddas continued to trust Buddhidhan, not knowing that it was he who had betrayed him in the first place. From then on, Garbaddas not only confided in Buddhidhan, he also kept him apprised of Shathrai’s activities. Shathrai trusted Buddhidhan and believed that his relations with Garbaddas were purely instrumental. Buddhidhan, on his part, thought it no sin to cheat these two rogues, reasoning that since his goal was noble, using wickedness against the wicked was perfectly justified. With Parvatsinh’s removal it became imperative for the ruling clique to foist a new prince upon Jadsinh. Rana Jadsinh was a debauch and an addict who consumed various narcotics and intoxicants, including chemical preparations. As a result of these excesses, he had lost his virility. His queens did just as they pleased. But if a queen were to give birth to a son, she and her paramour would wield more power, which would reduce Shathrai’s influence over the palace. This was not acceptable to him; so Shathrai had set in motion schemes to find a false heir who would remain under his influence. Buddhidhan was aware of these plans, but the administrator had not yet confided them to him. While it was not possible for Buddhidhan to openly associate with Bhupsinh, he had learnt from experience that it was disastrous to allow Bhupsinh to come under anyone else’s influence. He also did not want to be seen as openly opposing Shathrai and his cohorts, but he knew he required an instrument with which to achieve this end. When Garbaddas visited Lilapur on work and met Buddhidhan, the two of them went to meet Bhupsinh. No false heir could be produced without the queen’s connivance. Garbaddas informed them that attempts were being made to include Jadsinh’s chief queen in this plot. Parvatsinh was no longer a contender for the throne; hence Garbaddas thought it beneficial to act as Bhupsinh’s secret informant. Buddhidhan’s plan succeeded: Garbaddas sought his counsel in all matters, and was therefore incapable of wielding independent influence over Bhupsinh. His allegiance, moreover, had been secured. Rana Jadsinh’s chief queen was of high birth, and she resented the machinations of the Karbhari. However, she gave in to temptation, and soon it became known that she was pregnant. Garbaddas and Bhupsinh sent many petitions to Buskin Sahib, claiming that the pregnancy was pure fabrication. Shathrai’s coterie congratulated themselves on the success of their scheme, but fear lurked within. Shathrai was required to visit Lilapur once. To test Buddhidhan, he raised the issue of Garbaddas’ petition. Buddhidhan replied, ‘Let him go to hell. Dogs often bark behind an elephant’s back. It is another matter that truth is on our side this time. But there might come a time when we would be required to do what is being alleged. We have to protect our interests.’ Shathrai did not show his cards on this occasion, and left Lilapur suspicious of Buddhidhan; but his suspicion did not last long. Bhupsinh’s garas was still in the keeping of the Rana’s Darbar. As Rana Jadsinh’s Karbhari, Shathrai contended that the Darbar had incurred large expenses for the marriages of Bhupsinh and his siblings, and on the death ceremonies of his parents, all of which had been paid for from the revenues earned from the garas. They also argued that due to drought, the yield from the lands was negligible. The administrator further contended that it was Bhupsinh who owed substantial sums of money to Jadsinh, and hence that his garas should remain in Jadsinh’s possession until such time as the debt was recovered. Bhupsinh, on Buddhidhan’s advice, sent a petition to Buskin Sahib asking for the reinstatement of his garas. Buddhidhan showed that petition to Shathrai, and received at least fifty thousand rupees from the Suvarnapur palace in exchange for a promise to help keep the garas from Bhupsinh. He leveraged the newfound confidence of the palace and used it to understand how the Karbhari forged state treasury accounts. He also convinced Buskin Sahib, forged the documents himself, and ensured that the garas would remain with the

Darbar for the next five years. Meanwhile, Bhupsinh knew that the fifty thousand rupees were in reality to help him secure the throne of Suvarnapur; so whilst appearing disgruntled in public, he was secretly satisfied with these developments. Shathrai was convinced that Buddhidhan was no friend of Bhupsinh’s, and that he was open to being bribed. This set his mind at ease. Henceforth, whenever the new Shirastidar of Lilapur visited Suvarnapur, the Karbhari of Suvarnapur would invite him home for meals, and they would talk freely. Other palace functionaries also developed familiarity with the new Shirastidar. In time, Buddhidhan came to know the Karbhari’s family intimately, and learned to fathom their minds. Also, Narbheram, who usually accompanied him, took great delight in finding the fissures in the family of Karbhari Shathrai. Shathrai had one daughter named Khalaknanda, and a daughter- in-law, Rupali. Every evening, a soldier named Jamal Khan was deputed to carry a lantern and accompany Khalaknanda to her in-laws’. Jamal Khan could sing, draw, and was quite a dandy. Sometimes, en route to her in-laws’ house, Khalaknanda would stop at Jamal Khan’s and spend a few quiet moments with him. Sometimes, she would disguise herself as a man and go gallivanting around town at night, arm in arm with the soldier. Rupali, Dushtarai’s wife, had found her own way. Dushtarai was the Faujdar, the police chief, and was required to travel to different villages. A Rajput soldier, Merulo, would stay in the house with Rupali. Merulo would also occupy Dushtarai’s bedroom whenever he was away. None of this had escaped the busybody Narbheram; he had witnessed some of these scenes himself and had heard of others. He apprised Buddhidhan of the same. The paramours of both these women had become the confidants of their husbands. Shathrai trusted Jamal Khan implicitly, as Dushtarai trusted Merulo. As the day neared for Jadsinh’s chief queen to announce that she had delivered a prince, the onus of finding and securing a suitable baby boy was assigned to these trusted men. Jamal Khan and Merulo saw each other as rivals. This responsibility only deepened their mutual animosity. Jamal

Khan located a Muslim boy, while Merulo found a Koli one. Shathrai trusted Jamal Khan, and chose the Muslim boy to be prince since he was good-looking; Merulo was disappointed. On Buddhidhan’s instructions, Garbaddas had cultivated relations with both these men. One day, an angry and disgruntled Merulo sat talking with Garbaddas and blabbered about what had happened. Cajoled and provoked by Garbaddas, he revealed more. Garbaddas rushed to Lilapur to consult Buddhidhan. It was decided they would waste no more time and not let this opportunity slip away. A petition was made to Buskin Sahib, and Bhupsinh sought an escort and the authorisation to intervene. Accompanied by Garbaddas and mounted soldiers, Bhupsinh rushed to Rana Jadsinh’s palace. Showing the Sahib’s authorisation, the contingent entered the palace and sought a private audience with the Rana. Bhupsinh reasoned with Jadsinh, ‘The Sahib knows everything. If you are implicated in this matter, you will lose your throne. Why worry about who will rule after your death? It will bring you no glory if the throne goes to a Muslim, and not your own cousin. It will bring you no merit in the other world either. And if you were to have a legitimate heir tomorrow, you would still have to give the throne to this boy who is not your own blood. The Sahib has sent us. You are answerable to him. You decide. This is your responsibility.’ Jadsinh was frightened at the mention of the Sahib; the letter was signed by him as well. It stated that the ruler should pay heed to Bhupsinh and provide him a satisfactory explanation. Jadsinh replied, ‘I know nothing about all this. I will ask the Karbhari and send my explanation. I do not love sons of Muslims and Kolis more than my own cousin Bhupsinh. I will do all that is in my power.’ Garbaddas asked, ‘Can all this be settled tonight?’ Jadsinh replied, ‘Bhai, who knows with these things? I will inform the Karbhari. What more can I do?’ Garbaddas: ‘Can’t you do anything about this yourself?’ Jadsinh: ‘Myself? Do you want me to do police work? Go and meet the Karbhari.’

The party rode back as fast as they had come. Suvarnapur was in a state of panic. Shathrai rushed to the palace. He was not satisfied with the Rana’s explanation. He knew that the matter would not end there. Lilapur was not far from Suvarnapur. Garbaddas reached Lilapur, met Buddhidhan and said, ‘You know that the Rana is incapable of doing anything himself. He blurted out something about Kolis and Muslims. There is substance to the charge. We came back because we knew that staying there was not to our advantage.’ Soon after, Shathrai’s messenger rode in, conveyed his salutations to Buddhidhan, and sought information. Buddhidhan said, ‘I cannot say much in this matter. The Rana said something about a Muslim or a Koli child, and also said that the Karbhari knew everything. The matter is for the Sahib to decide. It would be best if Shathrai were to abandon this plan.’ The messenger returned. Garbaddas took two thousand rupees from Buddhidhan and gave it to Merulo; with his help, they found the house of the Muslim woman and posted a few riders there to keep a watch over her. Garbaddas, Bhupsinh, and a few soldiers hid near the queen’s palace. Shathrai was frightened. He knew there would be an enquiry if matters were prolonged any further; his dirty ploy would come out as his own men had turned traitors. He feared the consequences of the Sahib’s enquiry and distrusted the Rana in this matter. But the queen’s pregnancy had already been announced, so he conferred with his clique. That night, they decided to announce after a couple of days that the queen had given birth to a still-born daughter, procure a dead infant, and bury her. They also decided to postpone procuring a male heir till matters had cooled down. Meanwhile, Rana Jadsinh received a letter from Buskin Sahib which said: ‘I am most distressed about this matter. I must state that I have reason to believe that you were also a party to this scheme, alongside the Karbhari, Shathrai. This time, I have decided not to inform the Government about what has happened. But you must be warned that if any such attempt is made in the future, it will not be in your interest. Moreover, you are instructed to inform the Government

Agent of any future pregnancy at the beginning itself. Any laxity on your part in carrying out this instruction will strengthen suspicion against you, and the Government will be duly apprised of the same. It  is hoped that your Karbhari will take cognizance of this, and comply. A copy of this communiqué will be kept in a special file in the Agent’s office.’ All those involved in the scheme were deflated by the letter. Correspondence ensued back and forth, but fear was etched in their minds. Buddhidhan received information about Shathrai’s activities from Garbaddas, and he used the money that Shathrai had given him to infiltrate his own house. Before the matter of foisting another heir could be resolved, Rana Jadsinh suddenly died, owing either to some illness or intrigue. This information was immediately relayed to Lilapur, and Suvarnapur was placed under the Agency’s control. Locks of flesh and blood in the form of guards were posted at the queen’s palace, the treasury, and the state offices. Wheels were set in motion to get Bhupsinh anointed the ruler of Suvarnapur. Officers and guards began to congregate around Bhupsinh’s house, which was a mere hovel. Shathrai took to visiting Buddhidhan often in a bid to have his crimes pardoned. Garbaddas’ influence increased. Buddhidhan could sense his star rising and smell prosperity in the offing, but he did not lose his composure. He remained industrious. He was not tempted; he did not commit haste, and he did not lose sight of his goal. Only Bhupsinh and Buddhidhan knew that the latter’s fortunes were tied to the former’s ascendancy. Everyone else saw him only as a Shirastidar for all times to come. Buddhidhan met Bhupsinh with a letter of felicitation from Buskin Sahib. Addressing him with just the words, ‘My Rana! The King of Suvarnapur,’ Buddhidhan’s voice choked and tears of joy rolled down his cheeks. Bhupsinh was overcome with gratitude. He embraced Buddhidhan warmly and said, ‘Buddhidhan, this day has come only because of you. I will never forget what you have done for me. Yes, I am now the King. And you are my Minister. Hardship will become a memory of the past as we both look to the future.’

Buddhidhan retained his poise in face of the new king’s emotional outburst, and his own memory of the intense desire for revenge. He did not want revenge to cast its shadow on auspicious beginnings. He did not want the Sahib to harbour any suspicion that the new ruler would use his authority to settle old scores. Nor did he want the worst fears of the old guard to come true and present them with an opportunity to commence new intrigues. These and other similar cogitations flashed through Buddhidhan’s mind, and he took immediate remedial measures. He advised Bhupsinh, ‘You should call upon the Sahib tomorrow and inform him of your intention to found an English school in Lilapur in memory of the years you have spent here. You should also tell him that you intend to commemorate your ascendance of the throne by establishing a ‘Buskin Garden’ in Suvarnapur. You should tell him that you intend to keep all the present palace officials in service, but also suggest that you need an honest, trustworthy and neutral person as an advisor. You should tell him: If you have come to trust Buddhidhan, depute him to me, or give me someone else.’ Bhupsinh did as he was counselled. Buskin Sahib had formed a favourable opinion of Bhupsinh over his dealings with the garas, and had sympathy for him. Hearing such noble thoughts from him on this occasion, Buskin Sahib was well pleased. The Sahib sent the Government a most favourable report on Bhupsinh and agreed to provide him with all support. He also agreed that Buddhidhan could join the new Rana’s service, if that was what Buddhidhan desired. On receiving Government clearance, Bhupsinh’s coronation was celebrated with much pomp and ceremony in Suvarnapur. On Buddhidhan’s advice, representatives of newspapers in Bombay were invited to witness the occasion, and well looked after. Buddhidhan met them as a neutral person and praised the new Rana. Newspapers, both English and vernacular, printed long and glorious reports about Rana Bhupsinh’s coronation. They praised Bhupsinh’s wisdom, and the world believed it to be true. As soon as a replacement for him was found in Lilapur, Buddhidhan took up the position of Hazoor Secretary, that is Principle Secretary to the Rana of Suvarnapur. Garbaddas was another trusted man of the new Rana. Buddhidhan secured a position for him in the accounts department. Positions of the other officials remained undisturbed. As time passed, Buddhidhan’s position was renamed ‘Counsellor’, and his pay was increased. Things inched back towards normalcy. If any intrigues smouldered, the Counsellor wisely doused them before they could catch fire. Small incidents did occur—there were internal rivalries and jealousies to deal with—but they were not apparent to an outsider. The Counsellor worked quietly, astutely, without intruding in anyone else’s business, guided everyone on the right path, reasoned with the Karbhari, and as a result, when the administrators met, there was no trace of discontentment to be seen. His prestige increased from day to day. He restored the temple of Rajeshwar Mahadev built by his ancestors. People looked upon him with hope. When he had occasion to go to Bombay, the Counsellor made it a point to call upon the British officials there. He accomplished his mission and received their praise. He kept in touch with priests and pretended he had faith in their rituals and observances. These were considered the Counsellor’s finest qualities, and as his influence over the Rana became apparent, they came in for even greater praise. So, these were the circumstances when the Rana and his Counsellor visited the Mahadev temple that day, some three or four years after Bhupsinh’s coronation. We had left the two of them in conversation at the Rajeshwar Mahadev, where Alak Kishori and Kumud Sundari had been confined in the same courtyard as Navin Chandra. We were distracted briefly by details about Buddhidhan’s past, and so lost focus of our main story. Dear reader, if you did not find this distraction necessary and useful, wipe it out now from your mind’s eye and pretend that it never happened. Forget the past and flow with the present, as it unfolds in the following chapter.
chapters.summary: Buddhidhan, burning with secret rage, meticulously observes Shathrai and Dushtarai, forming an alliance with Bhupsinh to subtly challenge the powerful administrators.

chapters.title: Intrigues in Rajeshwar
paragraphs: Intrigues in Rajeshwar One who is unattached achieves his ends while maintaining his silence. —Bhavabhuti Suvarnapur’s administration appeared to be slumbering, moving almost of its own volition. All except the Rana and his Counsellor were somnolent. Those who observed the state felt that this slumber was, in fact, the natural order of things, but those who remained wakeful desired this condition. Buddhidhan, the real manipulator of this apparent somnolence operated from behind the scenes. Each of the actors involved believed that their actions were autonomous, and that he, Buddhidhan, was one of them. The people believed that the Counsellor had the Rana’s ear; they did not however suspect that he was key to all the Rana’s decisions. But this perception and this sense of calm was also contrived by the Counsellor. The fire of revenge that had consumed him during his years of impoverishment still raged unabated within him; but even Bhupsinh himself was unaware of this. The Rana believed that Buddhidhan was subject to his wish and will, and thus showered him with unsullied affection. Buddhidhan had meanwhile turned Bhupsinh and his administration into mere instruments for his festering rage. However, it is also true that despite this, over time, Buddhidhan had come to grow a selfless devotion and friendship for

Bhupsinh. Buddhidhan’s ambition and desire for glory had taken root as well. Even so, this was not enough to calm his desire for retribution. In fact, this was daily stoked by the very sight of his enemies. For Buddhidhan, Bhupsinh’s hatred was a mere instrument to actualise his own animosity. He would do nothing, would remain unseen, act only through his instruments while others would act as directed by him. Buddhidhan would remain distant and indifferent like the sun and the moon, while the sea below him rose and fell in tides. He observed things unfold as desired by him. This was characteristic of the Counsellor; this was his strategy. For four long years, Bhupsinh, an instrument himself, could discern neither the means nor the fruit thereof. He became increasingly restless. This, too, was a part of the Counsellor’s strategy, and he was satisfied that it had taken root. Bhupsinh sat leaning against a bolster on a golden carpet. From where he sat, he could see the Shivalinga. No longer impoverished, the expected changes had occurred in his attire, his person, his face and disposition. In the past, a Garasia weary of the Karbhari’s machinations had required the help of a similarly poor advisor. Now, a Rana having exhausted his patience with his Karbhari sought help of his Counsellor. But the wants of the past were different from the needs of the present. Earlier, he had to plead and please an equal: his want was greater, and friendship was based on self-interest. Now, this was replaced by a certain impatience—he could now command, and their relations were guided by mutual affection and a sense of duty. This change was apparent; yet the affection of old often shone through. ‘Buddhidhan, you have done nothing all these years! How long do I have to bear this petty rascal Shathrai? How long do I have to address the man who gave me so much misery as my Karbhari? Should we not simply behead those who fed off my garas? I won’t rest as long as you don’t resolve this matter!’ Having raised himself up in excitement, Bhupsinh now sat back and glared at Buddhidhan. Buddhidhan sat next to the Rana, his feet turned away in respect from his ruler. He smiled and said, ‘Ranaji, be patient. You have become king—shouldn’t your enemies also get something under your rule? Do some good unto the wicked.’ He removed his turban and sat back quietly. Bhupsinh laughed out aloud, ‘Nice, very nice indeed! This is new. Do some good unto the wicked! Be kindly to the insolent and cause offence to a friend—this befits politicians like you. We are proud people. We could give life to the living and kill the dying. But you deal with friends and foes alike. Sweets and vegetables being sold at the same price can happen only in the city of the blind. Even a schoolboy knows this.’ ‘So be it. Give the order. It is in your power to dismiss the Karbhari tomorrow itself.’ ‘Oh stop fooling around and tell me what it is you intend to do.’ Both became grave. Then Buddhidhan began his discourse. ‘Ranaji, desires can be fulfilled both through haste and through patience. A weed that grows fast withers away soon. A tree has deep roots. For example, how deep are Shathrai’s roots? At the time of your coronation, all the officials owed their allegiance to him. He had his men in the palace. He is known both in the Agency and in the Bombay Government. The newspapers praise him. Russell Sahib, who replaced Buskin Sahib, trusts him. What ploy has he not tried to make me his confidant. If we had removed him outright, that boil would have become a festering wound. He would have tried a thousand machinations and caused all manner of trouble. He would have used all his power in the state and in the British Government to obstruct us. He would have destroyed your prestige before it could take root. What all would he not have done. And that would have been the outcome of haste.’ ‘Yes, that is certainly true,’ replied a subdued Bhupsinh. Buddhidhan, like a dexterous snake catcher, realised that the hissing snake was caught in his pincers. ‘Ranaji, we need time and patience before we can destroy him root  and branch and cast our own roots deep.’ The Rana looked dejected and slumped onto the bolster. Buddhidhan continued, ‘But we have overcome these obstructions. Our preparations are almost over. The outer shell of the building is ready and all the bricks are firmly in place. Now only the surface work remains to be done—only the plastering remains.’ Bhupsinh sat up and listened attentively. ‘All right, let us move ahead then.’ Buddhidhan abandoned the allegorical mode and laid out details of his plan before the Rana, who became immersed in this narration which appealed to his self-interest. ‘Our relations can no longer be concealed. People know about it since I joined your service. Naturally, Shathrai does not trust me, but he is a sweet-talker. We have not yet attacked him openly; hence his mistrust is not complete. And it is good that it is so. I do not openly meddle in his administration, therefore his machinations are subdued; but this will not last forever. We have made sure that his intrigues are rendered ineffective. Narbheram has been posted as his secretary. He indulges in mockery and participates in derogatory talks about me. The Karbhari trusts Narbheram completely. But you know well that he is our man. He has befriended Merulo; so we now know all that Dushtarai tells Rupali about his father’s and his own plans. ‘Shathrai and his brother Karvatrai, who is the chief judge, and son Dushtarai, who is the police chief, have tyrannised the poor people. Hitherto, we have chosen to look the other way, which has made them even more brazen and unrestrained. If they do not collapse under the weight of their own sins, a gentle nudge from us will do. It is for us to decide when to give that push. People are seething with anger at their unchecked oppression. People feel that the King is good, but that his Minister is wicked; their sentiments will catch fire when we fan them. And this would be a powerful justification, both for the people and for the Sahib, when we finally remove the Karbhari. No one will find fault with you, and everyone will be ready to kick the fallen. ‘The Karbhari liked our advice that an elephant remains untroubled by a barking dog, and so he refused to pay any money to the Bombay newspapers. When the Karbhari was away in Bombay, a few newspaper men had visited Suvarnapur. Merulo, spurred on by Narbheram, insulted them. Some of our people live in Bombay.

We give them respect and honour. But Shathrai’s pride is like that of Ravana. He behaves most arrogantly with such visitors, and they hate him after just one meeting. At times, Narbheram does not allow them to meet him. Other soldiers imitate Narbheram. If you want to know for yourself the outcome, here, read this newspaper. Once a thing is printed, no one can separate truth from fiction. In due course, I will demonstrate the impact that such writing has, both on the government and the people. ‘Russell Sahib is not a military man. Unlike Buskin Sahib, his mind is not easy to fathom. It is not in his nature to insult someone or even call a spade a spade. You and the others believe that the Sahib trusts Shathrai. But Russell Sahib is a deeper man. The incident of the Muslim woman’s son is recorded in a special file, and the Sahib knows about it, as is evident from this letter from Lilapur which you can read at leisure. The people’s complaints have reached the Sahib. He will bring this up with you when you meet him. I will dwell on this and tell you tomorrow how you can apprise him of facts without openly denigrating the Karbhari. At present, the Karbhari is responsible for all that happens, or does not happen, in the administration. ‘The chief judge, Karvatrai has done injustice to a bania. I have thought of a ploy to send the bania to the Sahib. It will not benefit the bania, but the matter will be placed before you by the Government, which will be good for us. ‘Gradually, we have removed all the old officials from the court and the palace, and sent them elsewhere on higher salaries. You know well that the new functionaries are trusted men. Shathrai has tried to make them his cronies, we know this. You are aware what use we want to make of Garbaddas. The time has come for it: we can use him whenever you desire. We will take this up after your meeting with Russell Sahib.’ The Rana stretched and relaxed his limbs once this ‘report’ was over. He stood up looking pleased. Buddhidhan also arose and said, ‘We have all the means for the action to begin. All we lack is a man with an English education.’

‘That is all right, look for one. But make sure that Shathrai does not stick around for another three-four years.’ ‘Ranaji, please be patient. The world knows when a child is born; it takes nine months, but no one knows what happens inside the mother’s womb. How long did you have to wait in Lilapur before you got the throne?’ ‘True, but that was God’s will.’ ‘That matter was also in your hands: you could have had Jadsinh killed, just as Shathrai got Parvatrai killed.’ The Rana had no further arguments. ‘So be it, bring on the delivery. But the fact of birth is known to all: pregnancy cannot be concealed.’ ‘But Ranaji, this child is going to be born without a pregnancy!’ The Rana was disarmed once again. ‘Very well then. Whatever you think and do is fine.’ The Counsellor followed his King as they walked out. ‘Ranaji, it is only a matter of a few days now.’ He moved closer and whispered something into the Rana’s ears. Bhupsinh was visibly delighted, turned around and patted the Counsellor on the back. He came out of the temple. ‘Your kindness is upon all, your Grace!’ shouted the ushers. The King sat in his carriage, the wheels moved, the horses trotted along, and the soldiers drew their swords. The procession left. Buddhidhan watched them go, and when they could no longer be seen, he turned back. He climbed up the steps of the temple and stood there with a hand on his heart, and his eyes over the horizon, murmured: God! I do nothing; it is only You who acts. God, I have never harmed anyone—not without reason—and will never do so in future either. Even You punish for a valid reason, don’t You? His heart was thus consoled and the thorn in his conscience removed. Cleansed, he suddenly became aware of his surroundings. He looked around and shouted for Murkhdutt. Murkhdutt came out running. He was cooking when the Rana arrived and thus had to stay put inside his room for the whole hour that the Rana was inside the temple. He had realised that Navinchandra was in the courtyard, and that he had sent the women from the Counsellor’s family there. Frightened, he had gone to the window that looked out over the pond and, holding on to its iron bars, had raised himself on his toes to look out. Fortunately, Navinchandra had not stayed long in the courtyard. He had bathed in the pond and when Murkhdutt saw him, he was wiping himself dry. The priest thought it unwise to shout to him, so he picked up some pieces of dry cracked flooring and threw them at Navinchandra. His hand did not pass through the iron bars and hence these pieces fell short of Navinchandra. At last, one such piece hit Navinchandra on his back, and he was startled. He turned around, looked up and saw Murkhdutt. He went up to the window. Murkhdutt softly told him about the visit of the Rana, the Counsellor, and the Counsellor’s family, and warned him to remain where he was and not go either to the courtyard or into the temple while they were present. ‘If you want to see the Rana, leave from the other side and stand near the gate.’ To pass the time, Navinchandra asked to take a book from his belongings. Murkhdutt was surprised that this man should, like a scholar, ask for a book! Navinchandra washed and hung his dhoti to dry, using it to shield his face from the sun. He liked the feel of the winter sun on his body. He sat down and opened his book to read, once in a while looking up to gaze around him. Murkhdutt went back to his cooking. He had just finished when the Counsellor called him. He rushed out with a, ‘Yes Sir!’, his voice resonating inside the temple dome. Buddhidhan asked, ‘Has no one come today?’ Murkhdutt replied, ‘Alak Behn and Bhabhisahib have come.’ ‘Where are they?’ ‘In the courtyard. Please come in, I locked them in there when the Ranaji arrived.’ The priest ran ahead, followed by Buddhidhan. ‘Aren’t there any travellers in the dharamshala?’ ‘Yes Sir, there is one. He must be somewhere near the pond.’ The lock and the door were opened.
chapters.summary: Buddhidhan cunningly reveals his elaborate plan to Bhupsinh amidst Rajeshwar's political intrigues, while Navinchandra discreetly hides, observing the drama.

chapters.title: Pleasure Garden
paragraphs: Pleasure Garden Flowerbeds of mogra, rose and champa had recently been planted in the courtyard behind the temple. In that garden was kept a bare and rickety string cot belonging to Murkhdutt. When alone, he was given to lying on it and singing rustic songs or reciting verses in his crude speech. Alak Kishori and Kumud Sundari now sat on one side of this cot. Their companions sat on either side of them in attendance. Alak Kishori plucked some flowers and offered them to the others. ‘Bhabhisahib, which flower would you like?’ she asked Kumud Sundari. ‘Whichever you choose to give me.’ ‘No, you select one.’ ‘Whichever you give me is the one I will like.’ ‘If you do this in all matters, it will be hard on you!’ laughed Alak Kishori. ‘I accepted the good brother you gave me. Why would I need to choose now?’ ‘Then take this sephalika—it has your delicacy and your complexion.’ Kumud Sundari smiled and took the flowers tenderly. Her extended arms resembled a river of clear sparkling water, and the flowers were like white lotuses floating in it. Alak Kishori: ‘Vanleela, have you ever seen hands as beautiful as those of my bhabhi?’ Radha: ‘Behn, she is your bhabhi; how could she lack in anything!’

Vanleela: ‘You have given her flowers, but you should string them and adorn her hair with it—these are the days of spring.’ Radha: ‘The spring is new, and so is she!’ Alak Kishori: ‘Yes, we will string these flowers together and tie them around her bed. We would make a veni of roses for her hair.’ Vanleela: ‘And tie some mogra and champa on her wrists.’ Alak Kishori: ‘And bhabhi, then you must dance for my brother.’ Krishna Kalika laughed: ‘Only courtesans dance to seduce.’ Alak Kishori: ‘Die, you wretch! Watch your words! Shame on you.’ Dark and pockmarked, Krishna Kalika was shapely. But her intelligence was limited and her conduct was lax, so this rebuke was wasted on her. She considered Alak Kishori a little too smart and over wise. She thought she had said nothing inappropriate. But Kumud Sundari’s face fell at that comment. She felt slighted. She realised it was only because of the lowly company she was in. She thought about her relationship with Pramaddhan; fulfillment of bodily passion was the basis of their relationship. Pramaddhan was the provider of comfort, and if that were true, Kumud Sundari asked herself, What is wrong with what was said? She remembered the books she loved. Sarasvatichandra would have satisfied all her wants, all her desires. She felt a profound discontent. Sarasvatichandra’s virtues came to mind, and suddenly overcome with emotions, her eyes became moist. The women assumed she was hurt by Krishna Kalika’s comment, so they chided Kalika, and pleaded with Kumud. Kumud Sundari wiped her tears and said she was not hurt by the comment. But she could not explain the real reason for her tears, so the women continued to believe that she was hurt by Kalika’s words. Sarasvatichandra and Kumud Sundari had met only once, many moons ago. She was intimate with Pramaddhan, knew his every desire. And yet, just as the moonstone melts at the touch of the moon’s rays, she too melted and shed melancholy tears every time she thought of her moon, her Chandra. It had never occurred to her if Sarasvatichandra was handsome or attractive, for it was through his letters and his words that she had grown infatuated with him. Pramaddhan was handsome, quite a dandy, and committed to opulence and sexual pleasure. And yet her attraction for Sarasvatichandra had remained undiminished. A woman should not be superior to her husband in age, beauty, learning, intelligence, wisdom, wit, and in her ability to experience aesthetic delight. Such a woman experiences the pain and inadequacy of an incompatible marriage. She remains discontented with her husband. She fails to respect him, feels no affection for him, and cannot unite her heart with his. If she is not endowed with virtue, she may even come to despise him. But God had endowed Kumud Sundari with virtue; she had been raised well by her parents and cultivated by education. The very air she had breathed at Vidya Chatura’s house had been different from the atmosphere at Buddhidhan’s. She felt affection for her husband and her in-laws. She wished them well and did not wish to harbour any sense of distinction or being apart from them. But there was a limit to her endurance. Like a fish out of water, Vidya Chatura’s daughter flailed in a house bereft of learning. With a great effort of will, she had calmed herself and regained her poise. But Krishna Kalika’s barb had brought Sarasvatichandra back into her consciousness. His last letter was still tucked inside her blouse. She could not take it out in plain sight, but her mind went to it and conveyed her desire to her heart which began to beat faster at the touch of the hidden letter. A shiver coursed through her body; her hair stood on end and she broke into a cold sweat. But Kumud Sundari alone was aware of this. She forced gaiety upon her face. The gaiety that had been disrupted returned as the women resumed their banter. The string cot felt rough against their soft skin, so they all got up. Vanleela and Kumud Sundari walked towards the pond, their fingers intertwined. Alak Kishori put an arm around Krishna Kalika and they strolled around the flowerbeds. Radha stood on one side, playing with the branch of a mogra shrub. Alak Kishori asked Krishna Kalika, ‘Now tell me the truth: yesterday, I made a face at Khalaknanda and Rupali when they were walking about accompanied by Jamal and Merulo. Did they comment on it later?’

‘No.’ ‘Kalika, you whore, speak the truth!’ Alak demanded, playfully pinching her dark cheek. ‘Fine! Let go of me. Why do you pinch me so! Is it only your family which rules over Suvarnapur!’ Krishna Kalika responded with a dismissive shake of her head. Alak Kishori caught hold of her with both hands and pressed hard. ‘Tell me, you imp!’ ‘She responded by the same token.’ ‘What did she say?’ ‘Khalaknanda said: This lass pretends to be so virtuous. I will break her pride.’ ‘The whore! Who is she to break my pride! What else?’ ‘Rupali said: This is like a sieve laughing at the husk!’ ‘I see. Who are they to talk about me? One can only draw water when there is water in the well. How can they talk about me when I am faultless?’ ‘Some speak the truth; others tell lies. Who can ascertain truth from lies?’ ‘I will pull out their tongues if they keep this up.’ ‘She is the Karbhari’s daughter.’ Alak Kishori pouted and said, ‘Good; we shall also see how long the Karbhari lasts.’ ‘But behn, we must not be so proud. Whatever we may think, Khalaknanda is after all from an influential family.’ ‘All right, then. I will never speak to them again.’ As this conversation was taking place, on the other side of the garden, Kumud Sundari and Vanleela walked leisurely. Vanleela was humming softly to herself ... Dejected, the passionate woman cries and pleads with her husband Feeling deeply dejected and spurned herself, Kumud Sundari was lost in her own thoughts. She drifted away from Vanleela. Walking by herself, she came to lean against the temple wall and looked out towards the pond. She repeated Vanleela’s song. And then of their own volition, two couplets sprang from her heart. O’ Moon, why have you abandoned the horizon? In darkness, your lotus withers Whatever came over you, O’ bee? How could you abandon your lotus? Her imagination was afire; its flames leapt around, changing hues, adding dashes of colour to her visions. Her mind and reason were bedazzled; her heart was in a frenzy; her senses, her eyes and ears abandoned her. Though awake, she was in a dreamlike state—and in her mind’s eye, she saw Sarasvatichandra. One moment he seemed to be standing below a tree in a large forest. The next moment, he was in a village, resting on a peasant’s cot, weary and fatigued. Then again, she saw him roaming through the streets of a city, solitary, unknown and unrecognised. Soon after, she had a vision of him lying ill and uncared for in a dharamshala. She felt that he was very near her, albeit in disguise, and his eyes almost seemed to rebuke her. Kumud Sundari often fell prey to this waking dream-state. But this went against her wifely virtues, and she wanted to remedy it. After having come to her marital home, Kumud had become emaciated, and she felt weak even in the mind. Some believed that newcomers took time to adjust to Suvarnapur’s water. Medicines, remedies and nutritious food were given to her, but to little effect. Buddhidhan believed that his daughter-in-law yearned for her parental home. He had given instructions that she should be engaged in fun and games and taken on pleasure trips. Buddhidhan also knew that Vidya Chatura’s house was that of a reformist, and that its women were used to a certain freedom of movement. Alak Kishori followed all his instructions wholeheartedly. But Kumud Sundari knew well what ailed her. She asked Pramaddhan for some books to be procured from Bombay.
