She believed that if she were to immerse herself in these books, she would be rid of the ghost of Sarasvatichandra. The books had not yet arrived; as she waited impatiently for them, she often found herself in these trance-like states. Today, however, these images had a different force, a different urgency to them. No one could have imagined the churning of her heart as she stood petrified against the temple wall, barely able to breathe. Vanleela walked towards her, singing a song. When did you become a foe, my friend? You awakened me from my sleep And tore me away from my beloved She stopped singing as she neared Kumud. ‘Bhabhisahib, look at this!’ she suddenly said aloud. In Kumud Sundari’s preoccupied state, the song registered before Vanleela herself did and its impact lasted longer than her call. ‘Bhabhisahib, oh do come and look!’ Vanleela entreated. Staring distantly at this ‘friend turned foe’ and returning to the present reluctantly as if from afar, Kumud asked, ‘What ... What did you say?’ ‘What a strange sight! There is someone sleeping here right on the edge of the pond, with an open book on his chest. What all people do! Taking a book to the pond of all things!’ ‘Let him be. What is it to us? Why concern ourselves with an unknown man?’ ‘But what if he were to turn on his side, bhabhisahib, or get up and fall straight into the pond?!’ ‘Wake him up then.’ ‘Bhai! O bhai!’ Navinchandra woke up, and looked up in the direction of the voice. ‘Move carefully. I woke you up just so you wouldn’t fall into the pond if you were to turn on your side.’ ‘That is most kind of you, behn,’ Navinchandra said, and sat up. For a fleeting moment, his eyes met Kumud Sundari’s. And, as if there was nothing uncommon about this sight, Navinchandra looked away. He was about to pick up his book when the ushers shouted out that the Rana was about to leave the Rajeshwar Mahadev. Navinchandra hurriedly got up to see the Rana depart, leaving his book and the two women behind. Poor Kumud Sundari! Her eyes trailed him as he walked away. Even as she and Vanleela turned to go back, her body pulled her in one direction, her eyes in another. This man so resembled the one whose image had possessed her mind for long now. Was this Sarasvatichandra? Did his wanderings bring him here? No, no ... That is unlikely, how could that be. Has he come here to see me in this pitiable condition? No, he would not ridicule my suffering. But, whether he accepts it or not, it is him. So be it. A deep sigh of dejection escaped Kumud. What is our relation now? I must purge my mind of these thoughts. Whether it is him or someone else, what is it to me? God has willed that I be with someone else: he is my truth; all else is deceit. And Kumud Sundari walked off with Vanleela almost against her own will. But, she thought again, it would still be nice if it were him. I have no interest in him now. Marriage has determined for me the object of my affection. But if he stays here, I might be able to hear him speak to someone else. If this man is indeed him, his learning will not remain concealed for long. At some point, his speech will spring forth, and in this land bereft of learning and culture, his sweet nectar-like words will reach my ears. No. Even that would be wrong. Why? What is wrong if relations are not physical, if bodies are not involved? But how can I be so sure that this man is him? He had the same face. And he had a book. But anyone can have a book. Who knows what all of this means! I only know it would be good if he stays on here. I would take delight in his wellbeing. And I would be cured—what more do I want? If this is the extent of our relationship, what could possibly be wrong? I will neither speak nor move with him. I won’t even look at him. I will only hear him speak to others. I would be free of worry if I just knew he was all right.

Kumud Sundari’s thoughts thus came round full circle as she and Vanleela walked back to the others. Seeing them, Alak Kishori came towards them. She looked at Kumud’s face closely, put her hands on her shoulders and asked, ‘Bhabhisahib, what is wrong today? You seem so pensive. Pain and suffering are not for you. Leave it to the karbharis to plot and plan and build and destroy in their heads. Tell me, are you longing for your parents, or craving for my brother?’ ‘God knows. I do not know why, but I feel most fatigued today.’ Just then the temple doors opened. Buddhidhan entered, followed by Murkhdutt. Murkhdutt had the lock and key in his hand. Alak Kishori, Kumud Sundari, Vanleela and Krishna Kalika entered together, and stood facing the Counsellor. Radha, who was still wandering about in the garden, saw the book lying near the pond. She picked it up. Whose is it? Who kept it here? she wondered, leafing through its pages. Then she hurried to join her group at the temple. She went and stood next to Kumud Sundari, leaning against her with one hand on her shoulder. Just then, asking, ‘Where is Radha?’ Alak Kishori turned around and saw her. Kumud had just taken the book from Radha’s hands. ‘What is that book?’ Buddhidhan asked. Kumud Sundari kept her eyes lowered on the pages of the book and shyly replied, ‘Radha had this book in her hands. It is called The Pandit: Kashividyasudhanidhi. It publishes articles in Sanskrit and English and also reprints sections from old books. My father also subscribes to it and receives a copy every month.’ The rest of the women stared at her, uncomprehending. Radha: ‘It was lying there on the embankment, so I brought it with me.’ Murkhdutt: ‘It belongs to the man who has come to live in our dharamshala, Navinchandra. He must be looking for it.’ Buddhidhan took the book from Kumud Sundari, and asked that Navinchandra be brought into the courtyard. The priest ran out. Navinchandra was looking for his book. Murkhdutt called out to him, ‘Come! The Counsellor has asked for you. It is a good opportunity to make your introduction. Your book is with him. Come.’ Both went into the temple courtyard together. Navinchandra greeted the Counsellor with a namaskar; Buddhidhan responded solemnly. The women stood at a distance. Kumud Sundari was trembling inside. The book had made her suspicions even stronger. She stood right at the back of the group so she could look at his face without being seen. She believed that if her suspicions were true, he would not be able to bear her gaze. Buddhidhan asked him, ‘Where are you from? There must be some purpose to your visit here.’ Navinchandra: ‘I come from Bombay. I wanted to see the native states for myself.’ ‘Are you a trader in Bombay?’ ‘Among us, there is a saying that Goddess Annapurna does not let anyone go hungry. I wished to experience that for myself. I was a student in Bombay; now I am a seeker of experiences.’ ‘Then you must find yourself a trade.’ ‘Trade gives you one kind of experience. I desire the whole gamut of experiences that life can afford.’ Buddhidhan found the man quaint and allowed himself a smile. ‘And how do you propose to accomplish this desire?’ ‘I can observe without speaking. I can keep to myself what I hear. I can experience all colours without being stained by any.’ Buddhidhan suppressed a laugh with some effort. ‘Is this your book, then?’ ‘Yes, sir.’ ‘What have you studied?’ ‘Some English and a little Sanskrit.’ ‘Where did you study?’ Kumud Sundari eagerly awaited his response. ‘In Bombay.’ The answer left her unsatisfied. ‘Here, take your book. What is your caste?’ ‘We belong to the same caste.’ ‘As long as you are here, please eat at my house.’ ‘As you please, sir.’

Kumud Sundari’s innermost desires were fulfilled; but her sense of duty towards her husband was not. Buddhidhan liked to collect interesting men around him. He was happy that one more was added to that collection. Alak Kishori was given the responsibility of looking after the new guest, a responsibility she accepted. The priest was asked to bring the guest over to the Counsellor’s house at dinner time. Throughout the conversation, Kumud Sundari looked intently at Navinchandra. Sometimes, he withdrew his gaze as if her look pierced him, but at other times he looked at her unblinking. And still other times, he looked away as if completely indifferent. In this examination, Kumud Sundari forgot her own confusion. She climbed into the cart with the other women, softly murmuring the couplets about the moon and the lotus to herself. Buddhidhan sat in his own coach and went away.
chapters.summary: Kumud Sundari finds solace in a pleasure garden, battling her longing for Sarasvatichandra, until a captivating stranger, Navinchandra, arrives at the temple.

chapters.title: At the Counsellor's House
paragraphs: At the Counsellor’s House Navinchandra started taking his morning and evening meals at the Counsellor’s house. Shathrai’s household was uncaring of its guests, their attitude being: ‘Dump the guest in the godown’. Those who ate in the Karbhari’s house felt as if they were fed scraps, like dogs. Shathrai would neither talk nor sit with his guests, and they invariably felt slighted. As a young man, Buddhidhan had also felt unwelcome in Shathrai’s house. However, if one did not accept the Karbhari’s invitation, and this came to his notice, one would also be considered swollen-headed. Sometimes, Shathrai would taunt his guests or ridicule them so, it would singe his visitors. Buddhidhan had always looked for reasons to steal away from that house. But this was in the past. Buddhidhan did, however, still remember it. And so he took care to ensure that no one felt slighted under his roof. He had therefore trained his children as well as his servants in the art of humility and civility. Navinchandra ate alongside Buddhidhan. There was not the slightest discrimination. Buddhidhan treated even a wandering wayfarer as an equal, in thought, word and deed. The honoured and loved Counsellor of the Ruler of Suvarnapur conversed interestedly with his guests, encouraged even the quiet and the reticent to speak up and engage in debates. In such discussions, he betrayed not a trace of pride and arrogance. Pramaddhan would also join in at mealtimes and ensure that the guests were comfortable. Saubhagya Devi, Alak Kishori and Kumud Sundari would quietly sit in a group and roll betel-nut leaves.

In Shathrai’s house, Buddhidhan had observed very different demeanour. Khalaknanda and Rupali would walk around noisily, talk loudly, laugh with the servants one moment and scold them the next. They were wealthy, wore ornaments in excess and behaved ostentatiously. But their sense of their own importance extended only to such display. Neither of them knew how to look after or manage the household. They never covered their heads. Sometimes their unkempt hair would come loose. At times their backs were uncovered, and they moved around the house without wearing a blouse sometimes. Petticoats seemed cumbersome to them, and the women did not care what happened to their garments when they sat down, got up, or moved about. Unknown men around the house did not feel the need to caution them, and if they did, felt ashamed in pointing such things out to women. The men of the house fooled around with other women and neglected their own household. As a result, visitors to the Karbhari’s residence could cultivate undesirable proximity with these women. Buddhidhan had observed this, and he felt a strong revulsion. He took care to ensure that such goings on would never transpire in his own house. In his caste, it was not customary for women to cover their faces. But the women took care not to appear before elderly men. Navinchandra was not considered an elder; he was a caste-fellow, and so the women could sit with him as he ate but they did not participate in conversation with him. Navinchandra was also quite shy. He did not interact with the women directly and placed no burden upon his hosts. His civility was endearing, his reticence charming, and within a few days, the Counsellor’s family came to consider him as one of their own. Buddhidhan had at their first meeting found the young man rather strange; but his opinion changed with time. Navinchandra would sit and converse with Pramaddhan before and after meals. Pramaddhan thought well of his ‘English knowledge’ and said as much to his father. Pramaddhan also learnt that Navinchandra often wrote for major English newspapers in Bombay. However, Buddhidhan did not immediately believe this about someone who seemed to be a complete vagabond.

One evening, Navinchandra arrived as usual at the Counsellor’s house for dinner. Buddhidhan was still busy at the palace and had not yet returned, although it was well past dinner time. Navinchandra sat with Pramaddhan in one of the drawing rooms. Some six or seven others who had come to meet Pramaddhan were also around. Pramaddhan lounged in an easy chair at the centre of the room. One of his hangers-on removed his pagri while another helped him with his angarkha, and a third helped him remove his jacket. A fourth person praised him, while a fifth chimed in, and the sixth abused Pramaddhan’s foes and competitors. Just then, the post arrived. All the letters were placed in Pramaddhan’s hands as he presided over the group. He opened the English newspaper first. He hurriedly scanned it, and said with evident joy and excitement, ‘Navinchandra, your article has been published!’ He had asked Navinchandra to write a piece so he could convince his father about Navinchandra’s abilities. ‘Is it published? Read it out aloud,’ one friend said. It was read out. Meanwhile, the master of the house finally arrived, and the party of hangers-on dispersed with alacrity, leaving only the family members at home. Pramaddhan and Navinchandra went into the dining room. There, Alak Kishori sat upon a wooden bench, leaning against a wall, with five or six other women surrounding her, gossiping. Saubhagya Devi sat on the floor near the brazier; old Dayashankar’s wife Jamna Kaki sat with her, warming her limbs. Kumud Sundari stood at a window by herself, resting her hand on the ledge. Alak Kishori now got up from the bench and went and stood with her sister-in-law, as Pramaddhan and Navinchandra sat down together side-by-side, their backs to the two women. Alak embraced Kumud fondly and whispered into her ears, ‘Now I am warm, bhabhisahib; your body is quite warm for a winter night!’ Kumud managed a faint smile. With every passing day, she felt a little less inhibited in Navinchandra’s presence. Buddhidhan came in, and the food was served. Over dinner, Pramaddhan spoke of Navinchandra’s article. Buddhidhan said, ‘Yes, I know of it. The Sahib’s Shirastidar was here; he read and praised the article. It is quite well written. Navinchandra, if you desire your gamut of experiences, stay here in Suvarnapur. We need someone who can write English. I will put it to the Rana at an opportune moment.’ It was late by the time everyone finished eating. It was decided that Navinchandra would stay the night at the Counsellor’s house. A bed was made for him in Pramaddhan’s drawing room. He lay down to sleep. Buddhidhan and Pramaddhan retired to the adjoining drawing room. Alak Kishori did not return to her husband’s house as it was already late. Her mother and sister-in-law advised her to send her in-laws a message that she would not be returning that night. At least let them know, they said. ‘What is the need?’ Alak replied, ‘They will come to know anyhow,’ and she did not send the message. Pramaddhan was not yet ready for bed, so the sisters-in-law sat around the brazier, talking. Buddhidhan had received much unusual news that day. The father and son sat conversing in the drawing room. ‘Pitaji, is there any news of Shathrai’s clique?’ ‘I think there has been a breach in our ranks. We need to ascertain who has done it, and how.’ Just then, a man dressed as a soldier sought permission to enter the room. It was Narbheram. He acted as a confidant to Shathrai, but in truth, he was one of Buddhidhan’s most trusted men. He sat facing father and son, and submitted, ‘Buddhidhanbhai, our task has become more difficult.’ ‘How so?’ ‘Until recently, Shathrai was in the dark about your relations with the Rana. Now the Karbhari knows that the two of you meet often, that you had gone on a hunt with him. He even knows that you met in the Rajeshwar Mahadev.’ ‘Is that all?’ ‘He removes anyone he suspects—that is his way.’ ‘Then what?’

‘He has fabricated letters between you and Rajba. He plans to show them to the Rana.’ Buddhidhan saw red. ‘Who is going to show him the letters?’ ‘The Rana’s old attendant, Mahva.’ ‘I see.’ ‘I myself wrote those letters,’ said Narbheram, and took out some fifteen-twenty letters and tossed them into the Counsellor’s lap. ‘When are they to be presented to the Rana?’ ‘After your return from the palace.’ ‘Let these remain with me for now. I will have them sent to you by noon tomorrow.’ Buddhidhan’s trust in Narbheram was reaffirmed. He had appointed trusted men both inside the palace and elsewhere; some were known to be his people while the identity of others had remained a secret. But he had not yet had the opportunity to put all of them to the test. Narbheram, however, had acquitted himself with a sterling performance. The Counsellor felt a newfound affection and gratitude towards him. But loss accompanies gain: as the saying goes, the uncle got married but the aunt became a widow. Buddhidhan trusted the Rana, but knew that he had to be very cautious. He had the Rana’s ear; but if something about Rajba were to take root in Bhupsinh’s mind, it would be difficult if not impossible to uproot, and all his ploys would come to naught. To this day, the Rana himself informed Buddhidhan about all palace intrigues. But now the Counsellor felt the need to appoint one of his own men to keep an eye on the Rana. Who should that person be? Garbaddas? No. Narbheram? Yes. Moreover, he reasoned, this appointment would also be a reward for Narbheram’s loyalty. All these thoughts flashed through the Counsellor’s mind much like lightning brightens up the entire sky in a fraction of a moment. This also clarified for him some other machinations that he had not quite been able to fathom. He had enough ammunition, but his conscience did not allow him to deploy it before his adversary made the first move. His resolve to fight back became stronger. The moment of doubt was over—now was the hour of decisive action.

‘Narbheram, a critical moment is upon us. Once the letters are placed before the Rana, he will pretend to trust Shathrai, and be angry with me. He will ask Shathrai to appoint a trusted man in his service. Can we ensure that Shathrai forwards your name?’ ‘Yes, that can be done. Today, Shathrai trusts no one more than he trusts me.’ ‘All right. Does Garbaddas visit him often these days?’ ‘Oh yes—I forgot to mention that. Rupalibai has ensnared him.’ ‘Correct. But keep a watch over his movements. These days, Garbaddas is playing a double game; he pretends to be a confidant of both parties.’ ‘And what would he gain by doing so?’ ‘Well, if the Karbhari and the Counsellor destroy each other, he could be the next Karbhari. Garbaddas thinks he has the Rana’s confidence and trust.’ ‘And what will you do about this?’ ‘We will deal with it. For the present, just keep watch on the plots he hatches.’ ‘Very well. I will take your leave.’ ‘All right; but you should come and see me more often.’ Narbheram left. Buddhidhan’s eyes followed him—his soldierly disguise was perfect. The Counsellor smiled at the sight. Then he turned to his son. ‘Pramad, be extremely careful about any food that might be sent from the Karbhari’s house. We should accept it, but bury it deep in the ground.’ ‘Why? Is he likely to poison us, you think?’ ‘It is said that Rana Jadsinh was murdered. And we know well that the Karbhari had Parvatsinh killed. Then how can we trust him? Now go to sleep.’ Pramaddhan was stunned, and went away without another word. Buddhidhan got up and paced up and down alone in the drawing room. He put a finger on his lips as he talked aloud to himself. May your face blacken, Karbhari. Finally, you have shown me your true colours. I did not attack you so far because you are a caste-fellow and also a relative. But, so be it. Let us fight this out. So far, our enmity has been disguised. Henceforth, it shall be an open one. Garbad, even you are trying to play smart. I did that once, too. But there is a difference; I did not get anyone killed. I fear God. What can I do if someone was killed without my having occasioned it? I cannot be blamed for Parvatsinh’s murder. No. But you, Garbad, you have gone one up on me. Plotting my death now, are you? If the Rana slips out of my hand, it will be difficult for me. It took me five-seven long years to extricate him from Ramabai’s clutches. Now he is besotted with Kalavati, and there appears to be no escape from this. Buddhidhan, if this happens, Bhupsinh will never be yours. Buddhidhan stood in his drawing room like a Brahmarakshas in a forest. His mind was aflame; his heart beat fast as his thoughts spun round and round. Murderer, would you murder even me! May you be destroyed root and branch, Shathrai! And where did you find Kalavati? Now that I know of your intrigue with Rajba, I understand your game with Kalavati. It is you who got the Rana besotted. It is a ploy to create a cleavage between the Rana and me. Rajba. That old incident came back to Buddhidhan. He saw Rajba, passion raging in her eyes, clasping his hand in hers. And suddenly he was frightened. He broke out in cold sweat and shivered. He sat down on the bolster. A woman dressed as Rajsinh stood before him. She leaned against him, and he felt her hands on his shoulders and chin. The Counsellor of Suvarnapur stared fixedly at the vision with bulging eyes and felt he was going to faint from fright. Just then, a door flung open and Saubhagya Devi entered the drawing room, smiling. The evil vision vanished the moment his eyes fell on his Devi. Besotted, the devotee gazed upon his goddess in blessed relief. ‘Dearest, you will soon become the Karbhari, and we will lose you. You will pass your nights just like this and will have no time for me. When we were young, we used to talk till midnight. But now all you care for is your Karbhar. I now have a co-wife, even without you having married again!’ Devi came and sat down next to him, her body touching his. She caressed his neck. Then, putting an arm around him, she led him to their bed chamber. Though parents of an adult son and daughter, Buddhidhan and Saubhagya Devi were still young of body and mind and not yet subject to the thoughts and aspirations of the old. Buddhidhan was murmuring in his sleep. ‘Shathrai, if you had resolved to kill only me, I would not have met with success. But you intend to kill even the Rana, which makes my task easier. The Rana will always be under my influence. You believe that once you remove Buddhidhan, you will control the Rana; and if he escaped your clutches, you would sacrifice him as well. Good. Excellent. But Dushtarai visits Kalavati ... which is also fine.’ Saubhagya Devi woke up hearing her husband’s blabbering. She pulled him closer to her and contentedly closed her eyes again. The comets of dreamland may at times become manifest through such delirious speech. The only witness to this was an inanimate lamp. In the grip of his dream the man attempted to turn sides, but his wife, even in her sleep, did not let him turn away and pulled him closer yet. And their creaking bed, like a sad bard, sang their song, but alas to a deaf bedroom. The long winter night thus became shorter.
chapters.summary: Navinchandra's article is published, while Buddhidhan learns of Shathrai's scheme to frame him with fake letters, leading to a night of tense revelations and dreams.

chapters.title: The Consequences of Intoxication
paragraphs: The Consequences of Intoxication Upon his return from Lilapur, the Rana’s generosity had allowed Buddhidhan to build himself a large and beautiful house. The gate opened onto an enclosed space, followed by a courtyard. On either side of this courtyard were spacious rooms. On one side, a room was divided to make a kitchen, a room for storing water, and a dining space. On the other side, the younger women held court. An enclosed passage, another room, and a store-room were to be found behind the main courtyard. Saubhagya Devi’s seat was in this enclosed passage. The front courtyard was partitioned from the inner living space with wooden planks. There was an English style ‘waiting room’ in the outer courtyard. During the day, the servants and soldiers of the family sat on the platform or otalo, and slept in this courtyard at night. A window of the women’s quarters opened on to a side-street. Pramaddhan’s bed chamber was above the women’s quarters. The floor above the courtyard was a large one. This space served as Buddhidhan’s drawing room. Pramaddhan had a drawing room adjacent to his bedroom, where he sat in the company of his friends. Buddhidhan’s bedroom was on this level. A window opened from his room onto his drawing room. The second floor was constructed above these rooms and it had an extended terrace, with partial enclosures encircling the rooms on it. These rooms had windows opening onto the terrace. Navinchandra’s bed was made in Pramaddhan’s drawing room. Pramaddhan saw to Navinchandra’s comfort and then proceeded to the Counsellor’s drawing room. Navinchandra was about to extinguish his lamp and go to sleep when he heard voices from either side of him. On one side, he could hear the Counsellor, Narbheram and Pramaddhan in Buddhidhan’s drawing room. On the other side was Pramaddhan’s bedroom, and since he was with his father, this is where the sisters- in-law sat chatting. The books that Kumud Sundari so wanted had finally arrived from Bombay a few days ago. Not satisfied with the solitary pleasure of reading them, Kumud read out parts of them aloud to Alak Kishori. She translated captivating passages from English and Sanskrit books for Alak, who listened to her meekly and attentively. ‘Alak behn, listen, this is most interesting. A woman forsaken by her husband laments her loss. Her words are haunting. Listen: “The peace which others seek, they find, as the heaviest storms do not last forever; for the heavens grant even to the guiltiest minds amnesty for what is past”. ’ ‘What does it mean?’ ‘It means, we feel guilt for our mistakes, but this burden does not last forever. There comes a time when we no longer feel the burden. Is this not amnesty granted by God?’ ‘Yes, of course.’ ‘The woman asks: “If the guiltiest of minds find amnesty, when will my God put an end to my sufferings? I am innocent: when will my sentence come to an end? I don’t ask for more, just that I wish to know the worst that will befall me. All that is left after that is for my heart to burst open, if God wills it”. ’ ‘What does that mean?’ ‘She says that she wants to know what awaits her, even if it means knowing that she will never meet her husband again. She cannot give up hope, but knows that her hope will not be realised; and hence her mind knows no rest. She feels, therefore, that all hope is in vain and peace can only come once her heart breaks completely.’⟨fn:8⟩ Kumud Sundari felt a deep ache in her heart as she spoke these words.

Alak Kishori said, ‘It feels wonderful to be able to understand such things. But what you sang yesterday was even better. I understood its meaning; you had explained it to me. But please sing it once more, bhabhi.’ Kumud sang again. Oh! Were he present, fondly would he seek, In secret whisper, that inviting cheek; Woo thee in close approach, his words to hear, And breathe these tender accents in thine ear. Goddess beloved! How vainly I explore The world, to trace the semblance I adore.⟨fn:9⟩ Explaining the meaning of the verses to Alak Kishori, Kumud said, ‘This is from Kalidasa’s Meghdoot. I had spoken to you about it yesterday. I have translated that passage for you.’ ‘Oh, you are so romantic!’ Alak Kishori exclaimed, enveloping Kumud Sundari in a tight embrace. She looked at her sister-in- law’s face, brought her lips close to her cheeks and teased, ‘Shall I be naughty, just like the song you sang? I would have definitely married you if you were a man, and not stayed away from you for even a day! Bhabhi, when one reads and understands words like this, how can one not be romantic? You do not speak about the things we do, but you understand them so much better. You are wise as a swan, dear bhabhisahib! You sing, and I will listen.’ Navinchandra had extinguished the lamp and lay in bed. In the adjoining room, Buddhidhan and Narbheram spoke frankly, while in the bedroom the sisters-in-law spoke softly. Although soft, their voices could be heard in the adjacent room. Neither group was conscious of Navinchandra’s presence, and hence did not lower their voices. Nothing could be seen through the door, but voices carried in the quiet of the night. Navinchandra was familiar with all these voices except Narbheram’s. His ears were drawn to both conversations. He rose from his bed and moved from one door to the other, placed his ears close to the door and listened intently. He did not intend to pass on these secret conversations or use them wrongly. He found the act of curious eavesdropping quite innocent. While the conversation between the sisters-in-law pleased and delighted him, he was astounded by the Counsellor’s conversation. Kumud’s poem, her song, her craving, melted Navinchandra’s heart. If the lamp could discern his expression, there certainly would have been cause for gossip. But that state lasted only briefly, and then his desire to learn the intrigues of statecraft drew him to the other side. He was surprised that Buddhidhan, who appeared happy and carefree, was actually neck-deep in worries. He remembered his own reading: ‘uneasy lies the head that wears the crown’.⟨fn:10⟩ Only the Karbhari knows his suffering; and even gold has impurities; such maxims took on new meaning for him. Navinchandra thought that the Counsellor was dissatisfied with his present position, and that he desired the post of the Karbhari. He felt that Buddhidhan’s desire was based on selfishness alone. He was astounded that one made so many enemies, played such intrigues, and associated with such persons to obtain the Karbhar. ‘The head of the avaricious reels in constant vertigo!’—he grasped the import of this adage anew overhearing Buddhidhan’s soliloquy. But he did not understand the part about Rajba, and was taken aback by Saubhagya Devi’s words. This set him thinking that the craving for sexual pleasure does not leave one even in advanced age; and that a man driven by worldly ambition becomes incapable of experiencing, of enjoying the everyday pleasures of the household. He also mused that a man married to money forsakes his wife. The Karbhar, all these murders, these intrigues—Why? How can one mind bear such terrible burdens? The ‘whitewash’ is only superficial; their insides are filthy. This is how God creates us: a beautiful body is nothing but a lump of meat. Dawn breaks out from an earth drowned in darkness. One should not ask about the history of the powerful, or else scandals would tumble out. The educated remain discontented despite hard work, riches elude them; while the likes of the Karbhari and others roll around in wealth. But such sentiments are misplaced. The worries, the intrigues, the wily ways, the dirty acts, and this whitewash all add up to some nominal prestige and some money—neither of which sustains and nourishes. Karbharis, keep your pleasures to yourselves! Perhaps, Karbharis who are learned are not faced with similar problems. Let it be. It is all the same; only the patterns differ. Reformed Karbharis will experience the pain of reformers. And all their wives would have the same complaints as Saubhagya Devi. The poor Karbharis and leading businessmen of Bombay—all of them lead lives of such miserable drudgery! Karbharis, you run the state, but look at your deeds! The foolish dance to your tunes, while you become one with the wicked and profit from them. It is not that you are not possessed of intellect or good conscience. Those who claim so are ignorant. But the very air you breathe is contaminated. How could that not pollute your mind and conscience? How contaminated are even the most learned minds? My experience in such matters is limited. What I witnessed today is the first lesson of my experiential learning. What all am I yet to witness, God alone knows. But, Kumud Sundari, whatever it may be, you ought not to be seen in this land. O Lotus, you belong to a lake. Vidya Chatura’s daughter—Who are you? And these people? Have these lowly beings become any better than you because of their Karbhar? Even beautifully arranged rows of crows on the mountain tops would not compare with swans. Royal swan, you are a child-woman. ‘Of the meritorious ones, the reason for their worship and reverence is not their seniority or age or some insignia of prestige that they bear, but their virtue.’⟨fn:11⟩ How do your days here pass, an immaculate beauty like you, in this dirty, sullied land?

Divine, sublime, royal swan Raised in Mansarovar, how do you live here? Pure lotus bloom, the wasps hovering around you Sup of your nectar, and drink your fragrance The wind carries your scent and pollen, Scattering it across the mountains You who were raised in Mansarovar find yourself In a frog-infested puddle, my fallen swan Raised in Mansarovar, how do you live here? Your wellbeing is drowned by someone else’s self-indulgence. You never knew this would happen, did you, Sarasvatichandra? You did wrong! Your learning is worthless! His mind was afire, as if the unrest of his heart had passed like electricity to his mind. Navinchandra, a vagabond wayfarer, slept in a large bed made for him in the drawing room of the Counsellor of Suvarnapur. He shivered in the cold, covered himself with a thick blanket, and exhausted by his emotions and excitement, finally surrendered himself to sleep. All members of the Counsellor’s family slept, and it felt as if Suvarnapur itself was asleep. Kumud Sundari’s body lay with her husband; her heart trailed the body, and finally she too succumbed to a tormented sleep. Alak Kishori slept in the room above the courtyard. The doors of the room were shut. She was in deep slumber. In her dream-state, her husband timidly asked her, ‘Why did you sleep there?’ She carelessly replied, ‘Whether I sleep here or there, what is it to you?’ Even before this dream was over, another joined itself with the previous one. Alak saw herself enacting the scenes from Meghdoot, that she had heard Kumud narrate, with Krishna Kalika. When Krishna Kalika responded to her amorous play, she scolded her. The Counsellor’s house was peaceful for about an hour. Some windows opened out onto a street outside the house. A handful of men had been observed loitering around there since eight or nine in the evening. Krishna Kalika had timidly apprised Alak Kishori of this; but the Counsellor’s daughter had paid scant regard to it.

She did  not  realise that small incidents can sometimes have large consequences. Some time ago, Alak Kishori had made a face at Khalaknanda and Rupali while they were sauntering about with their paramours. She had also told a few of her female companions her reasons for doing so, and had then forgotten about the incident. But Khalaknanda had not forgotten. She was also a proud daughter of a Karbhari, and not much younger than Saubhagya Devi. She saw Alak Kishori as an upstart. Some women had told her that Alak Kishori was encouraged by her mother. Hitherto, no one had the courage to say anything to Khalaknanda’s face; but they did tell her what Alak Kishori had to say about her. Imprudent as she was, Alak Kishori had also haughtily said that her father was going to be the new Karbhari. So the rivalry between the Karbhari and the Counsellor had now filtered down to the women and children of both families. Saubhagya Devi was a pious woman. Her daughter had inherited this quality. But there was a difference: Alak Kishori was self-righteous about her piety, and openly showed her disdain for the debauched women of the Karbhari household. She ruled over her husband, but did not care for any other man. Khalaknanda and Rupali were so incensed by this slight that they were determined to crush Alak Kishori’s pride. Rupali suggested a plan that Khalaknanda agreed to. They incited Jamal Khan, who gladly accepted the challenge; he believed that no one could check him. He thought he would kill two birds with one stone. He was dazzled by Alak Kishori’s beauty and wanted to possess her just as he had Khalaknanda. He was now being presented with this very opportunity. He hatched a foolish plan to abduct Alak Kishori on her way to her husband’s from her father’s house. To this end, Jamal Khan had been loitering around the Counsellor’s residence, along with three-four accomplices. Alak Kishori did not return to her husband’s house that evening. They waited till midnight, and by one in the morning, his accomplices had left the scene. Jamal Khan was also about to leave for home, when a plan came into his seething mind. Nothing could be worse than returning empty- handed, he thought. All this anticipation, this excitement would come to naught. All my brazen desires will go waste if I do not lay my hands on this fair damsel tonight. Every day, I chase thieves. Tonight, I shall be a thief myself. And he decided to scale the walls of the Counsellor’s house. Going around to the back of the house, he looked up at the roof, and saw a way in. He twirled his moustache as if in preparation, and began to climb. My friends proved effete, thought Jamal Khan. If they had stayed, they too would have shared in the fun. But leave them be to their fate. Good that they are gone! It was a dark night. Cautiously, climbing on all fours, he reached the roof. An owl hooted as it suddenly flew into his face on soft and silent wings. A bad omen, he thought, and threw a tile at it in anger. Come on, Jamal Khan, he reassured himself, What’s a bad omen to a Miyanbhai! He was now on the roof of the Counsellor’s house. Standing up, he looked around and saw no one. But far away, he espied a shadowy figure. Must be a thief, he thought. Let’s catch the bugger. But what do I get anyway? Forget it. I will get Alak Kishori. What a name! Alak Kishori. Alak Kishori! Alak Kishori! All right, this is all very well, but how do I enter the house? He slowly climbed down to the terrace. A window had been left open. He crouched and entered the room. Fortuitously for him, even the door to the staircase was left open! Jamal Khan came down the steps as if it were his own house, and soon, Shathrai’s lowly Musalman soldier stood before the bed of the Counsellor’s daughter. A castor-oil lamp burned in a niche. Like a tigress on a river bank, Alak Kishori lay resplendent upon her bed in the full bloom of her youth. The blanket she used to cover herself with had been flung aside, as if the cold dared not touch her. Her carefully arranged clothes had fallen out of place. The pleats of her sari unfurled between her legs like a rivulet flowing through the crevices of a hillock. The lamp threw her face and bosom into relief. The lamplight flickered, revealing glimpses of the beauty hidden in shadows, suggesting enchanting possibilities. The vision was captivating. Her long arms stretched out on either side of her, like wings. She looked fierce even in her sleep. It was as if the image of Ma Chandi about to slay the demon Mahishaasura was sculpted on the bed. Jamal Khan could not muster the courage to even touch Alak Kishori. Womankind, if you are determined, your splendour and radiance are immeasurable. Men lack the courage to take advantage of your vulnerability and violate your virtue. A single chaste, fiery glance from you is enough to keep the evil intentions of men at bay. This power is uniquely yours. Its use is a matter of your discretion and will. Alak Kishori’s eyes were shut. But like a serpent protecting precious jewels, her serpentine eyebrows protected her virtue. The Turk stood petrified—his arrogance and lust had no power over his movements now. An attack on virtue takes time. The Khan, though dandily dressed, was in attire which did not hamper his plans. He wore a beautiful Delhi-style cap of black velvet embroidered with zardozi over which he had draped a cloth that concealed his face. He had groomed his moustache and beard with perfumed oil. Being winter, he wore a woollen jacket with silver buttons, cut foppishly. He wore his dhoti tight and carried a small dagger tied at his waist. His shoes were English in style, but of local make. He had put kohl in his eyes, perfumed cotton in his ears, and sprinkled rosewater on his kerchief. He had washed and brightened his face. He was confident the damsel would find his youthful charms irresistible and become instantly infatuated with him. Khalaknanda had however warned him that this might not be, and had urged him to use force; he was prepared to, if she resisted. He believed that a mere woman was powerless before a man. He also carried a small thick black stick. Thus attired, arms crossed over his chest, legs grounded far apart, he stood close to the sleeping Alak Kishori’s bed, stupefied. He looked at the gorgeous form of this woman sleeping without a care before him, and his moist eyes shone with carnal passion. The awareness of place, time and power aroused him, and his mind and body were aflame with a terrible yearning. The lines between rapturous pleasure and unbearable agony grew blurred. Allah! What beauty! This divine face ... these rosy cheeks ... Allah! This is unbearable! Khalaknanda is nothing in comparison to this one. Come, my beautiful! He extended an ardent hand, and saw himself confidently climbing into her bed—but his courage failed him. He just kept standing there and staring at her, trying to think of his next move. His desire was aflame, but his joy was abject; his sensuousness stilled, his eyes glazed over, his legs trembled and he felt feeble from head to toe. There was no one there to prevent him from jumping onto the bed. But the sleeping Alak Kishori’s face was flushed with such radiance that the lecherous wretch could not bear her resplendence—he could not approach her fire. God knows what is happening, Jamal heard himself say, but I haven’t the audacity to step any closer. He had entered the palatial house of the Counsellor all by himself. If the Counsellor comes to know, what will become of me? Then Alak Kishori turned on her side. Her face was now turned away from him. All his qualms, his hesitation suddenly evaporated. His lust raised its fierce hood again, and Jamal Khan remembered Khalaknanda’s command. He silently removed his shoes and climbed into the bed. He lay against her side, unmoving and hesitant initially. But not for long. The Counsellor’s daughter woke up startled as if she had been singed by fire. Reacting even before she was fully awake, she flung away the offensive hands and feet which assailed her and leapt out of bed. This happened in the blink of an eye before she was even fully possessed of her senses. She tucked in her sari at her waist and glared at the beast in her bed with raging eyes. She screamed in wrath and fear, ‘Who is it? Wake up! Pramadbhai! Bapuji! Wake up! Thief! Thief!’ Jamal Khan composed himself, sat up and said, ‘My beloved, it is me, Jamal. Do not be afraid. I am so besotted with you that I had to visit you on this dark night.’ Kishori was somewhat less frightened, but her legs still trembled. ‘You!? Jamaliya, you rascal! Get up and get out, or I will teach you a good lesson. Do you take me for your Khalaknanda!’

‘Bai Sahib, do calm down, my sweet beloved.’ ‘You beast! I will cut off your tongue if you say more. I’m calling everyone,’ and regaining her courage, she walked to the window. Recognising danger, Jamal braced himself. Persuasion didn’t work. So he caught her by the arm to stop her from approaching the window, saying, ‘Wait ...’ ‘Leave my hand!’ Alak Kishori pulled herself free. But he caught her again and clasped her neck, ‘Why are you doing this, my love? Just wait ...’ Alak Kishori looked full at him, her eyes ablaze. She held his gaze briefly, then freeing her neck from his loathsome grasp, she drew herself up to her full height and clenching her teeth and her fist into a tight ball, she punched Jamal full on the mouth. She looked down, almost expecting Mother Earth to say, ‘Oh good! Well done!’ Jamal was momentarily dazed, his mouth stung by the unexpected blow. In anger, he grabbed her from the back. He was a powerful Musalman. She could not free herself from his grip, but did not lose courage and started screaming for help. Jamal pressed his hand over her mouth, but she screamed louder whenever his grip relaxed even slightly: ‘Bhai! Bapuji! Ma! Help me! O Help!’ There was an intense scuffle. Who knows from where Alak Kishori found the strength to not succumb. She tried to hit him hard on the chin, the face and the nose with her head every chance she got. Sometimes she succeeded; other times he fended off the blows. At some point Jamal Khan started chasing her around the room. Neither accepted defeat. Below them, there was a huge commotion in the house. Alak Kishori’s first scream had already roused the family. Each one tried to determine the source of the cry. Buddhidhan’s first thought was that Shathrai’s men had breached his house with murderous intent. Navinchandra heard the cry, ‘Thief!’ Startled awake, Kumud Sundari hurriedly woke up her husband. They thought the house was on fire. Saubhagya Devi recognised her daughter’s voice and she rushed out onto the terrace. The servants ran out into the courtyard, looking up in the direction of the floor above and questioned each other about the source of the commotion. Those asleep on the first floor assembled on the terrace. Pramaddhan opened the door to the staircase. Gathering at the entrance to Alak’s room, people shouted, asking her to open the door. Saubhagya Devi banged on Alak’s window to force it open. Next to his wife, Buddhidhan shouted, ‘Alak, don’t be afraid! We are here!’. Kumud Sundari stood behind everyone else, shaking with fear. Navinchandra tried to make his way to the front through the sea of servants. Buddhidhan, helped by a few servants, tried to force open Alak’s door. Pramaddhan, accompanied by a few others, climbed down to find another way into her room. In the meantime, Kumud shouted, ‘That window up there is open; he must have climbed in from it.’ Navinchandra heard this. He had learnt to climb and jump in the gymnasium. He looked at Kumud, tied his dhoti between his legs, and climbed up nimbly onto the roof. He saw the staircase, Alak Kishori’s lit room and heard all the noises coming from it. Inside the room, pit against the strength of a Musalman soldier, Alak Kishori was visibly tiring and running out of breath. But somehow, with tremendous effort, she kept dragging Jamal nearer to the lamp. The evil Turk realised that the others were closing in on him and that there was no way out. He was grimly resigned to face whatever consequences there may be. He also realised that those on the outside were unable to find a way in. This made him more brazen, and he became unrestrained and utterly vile. The use of physical force only heightened his sexual pleasure. Then suddenly, like a lamp dispelling darkness, an idea providentially came to Alak in a flash and she knew she was saved. As they neared the oil lamp, she swiftly pulled at Jamal’s dhoti and set it on fire. As it caught fire, he let go of her. Sensing victory, Alak ran towards the door, but she didn’t reach it— throwing off his burning dhoti along with his dagger, Jamal Khan leapt onto Alak before she could reach the door and pinned her down. Alak was completely helpless now. Her strength, her will to fight deserted her as she realised her subjugation. She lost the capacity to think and became numb. Her body was defiled at many places. Her sari had come undone during the scuffle and lay upon the floor, pleading with

Mother Earth for succour. Jamal climbed on top of her like a tiger on a cow. He caught her arms and said, ‘Beloved, do not be afraid.’ The moon was eclipsed by shadows. As she fell, disconsolate, Alak let out a heartrending wail: ‘Hai! O Ma! He has killed me!’ No one had heard such an anguished cry before. Their desperation mounted and the commotion around the window increased palpably, if in vain. The evil beast knew that no one was capable of breaking into the room; there was no one to stop him now. Alak’s tired hands were locked in a desperate struggle with his around the knot that held her petticoat in place. A moment’s delay and her virtue was certain to be violated, a permanent blot on God’s hands. Saubhagya Devi was hysterical and prayed fervently to the Goddess. God is the final refuge of the helpless. Buddhidhan had always staunchly believed this. Either the merits he had accrued or Saubhagya Devi’s prayers were responsible for what followed. Just at that critical moment, Navinchandra rushed down the staircase and landed a fierce kick on Jamal’s back, stunning the soldier. Then he grabbed the cloth around Jamal’s neck and pulled so hard that Jamal feared he would choke, and he let go of Alak Kishori. Navinchandra dragged him further away from her; but Jamal put his hand between the cloth and his neck so the noose would not tighten, then he turned around and broke free from Navinchandra’s clutches with a mighty heave. Navinchandra shouted out to those outside, ‘Don’t worry! I have saved  behn!’ Her  family members could breathe again. But in this interlude, Jamal Khan saw his chance—and he flew at Alak Kishori, who had barely regained some of her composure. At this renewed attack, she screamed in panic and dismay: ‘Navinchandrabhai, save me!’ and she ran and clung to him from behind. Navinchandra stood between them, shielding the doe-eyed one from the tiger’s paws. Jamal Khan was disappointed and could see no way out. Suddenly, he spotted his dagger and rushed to grab it. At the same moment, Alak Kishori let go of Navinchandra and made a dash for the door. Those on the outside were pressed against it and nearly tumbled into the room when she opened it. The Turk had leapt up the staircase, but

Navinchandra grabbed his leg and Jamal Khan fell hard, but as he fell he managed to plunge his dagger into Navinchandra’s shoulder. Saubhagya Devi was the first to enter the room. Her daughter rushed into her arms, crying, ‘Oh, Devi!’ Saubhagya Devi embraced and consoled her daughter who was sobbing uncontrollably. Buddhidhan and Pramaddhan stood close by, giving her strength. The servants caught hold of Jamal, who was sprawled on the ground. They kicked him in rage and held him so tight he could not move. Blows and kicks rained upon him mercilessly and he bore them in silence. Wounded by the dagger, Navinchandra lay inert upon the floor. He had lost much blood and had fainted. In all this melee, no one had noticed him. Only Jamal glared at him triumphantly even as he was being thrashed, saying to himself, Rascal, you deserved it! He looked longingly at Alak Kishori, and cursed the owl. He took solace in knowing he had touched her. In the struggle between the high and the low, the latter has nothing to lose; even in defeat, and even a slight gain to the low is like a two-fold loss to the high. When pure water meets filth, the filth is not cleansed; even if it is, it soils the water. This is as God wills it. Jamal Khan was dragged onto the terrace and brought down to the courtyard. When questioned, he brazenly said that it was Alak Kishori who had invited him up. This further enraged everyone. After more thrashing, the soldier came to his senses and told them who had sent him, and why. Saubhagya Devi sat on the threshold of the room above, as Alak lay sobbing into her lap with relief, still shaken by what had happened. Kumud Sundari and Pramaddhan were by her side, while Buddhidhan paced around the terrace, deep in thought. Even through her sobs, Alak Kishori heard Jamal Khan’s disclosure—and realised with shock that what had happened was the consequence of her own haughtiness. This heightened her distress no end. All this while, Navinchandra lay unconscious and unnoticed, his blood flowing unchecked. Kumud Sundari searched for him everywhere but could not locate him in the commotion. Finally, she saw his deathly pale body lying on the floor. Seeing him in that state, terrible inauspicious thoughts filled her mind, tormenting her tremendously, but she could not share her feelings with anyone. In the end, her heart won out over social stricture. ‘Oh God! Is this Navinchandra who is lying here?’ she said aloud for the others to hear. Hearing Kumud, Alak Kishori, too, forgot her woes, sorely repenting that she had allowed herself to forget even for a moment the timely kindness of the stranger. She got up and hurried towards Navinchandra. ‘Oh Devi! He has a dagger wound and it bleeds! Come soon, Devi, oh come fast!’, Alak urged her mother. The others gathered around. Kumud Sundari brought out the lamp and held it close to the body; she saw the wound and the spilled blood. Horrified and grief-struck, she quickly wiped her tears before anyone could see them. Keeping the lamp near the staircase so it would light the room better, she sat down next to Navinchandra’s body, facing her sister-in-law. Looking intently at his unconscious face, unnoticed by anyone else, Kumud lightly touched his forehead. Buddhidhan came in from the terrace. He at once instructed Pramaddhan, ‘Go, quickly bring me a clean piece of cloth and tincture iodine.’ He ordered a soldier, ‘Go fetch the vaidya.’ Tincture iodine, bought in Bombay, was kept in the house, but Pramaddhan was clueless as to its whereabouts. He rummaged about, asking, ‘Where is the tincture? What is it like?’ His sister got up. It was she who managed the household. She found the bottle, asked her brother to read the label, and brought it out; but they still could not find a clean rag. The houses of the rich have many fine cloths and garments, but no clean rags. While they took time searching for one, Buddhidhan grew angry. ‘How long does it take you to find a rag?!’ He looked at his own fine dhoti and thought of tearing it up. But before he could do so, like Draupadi had done for Krishna in Mahabharat, his young daughter-in-law tore a piece from her new sari, and hearing the cloth rip, Buddhidhan looked up at her. Buddhidhan and Pramaddhan applied the tincture to the wound and dressed it. The vaidya also arrived meanwhile. All this went on through the night. Regaining partial consciousness, Navinchandra moaned in pain. It was decided that he should be confined to bed in the Counsellor’s house for a few days until he had recovered his strength completely. He was lifted and taken to another room. Quite naturally, all his care became Alak Kishori’s responsibility. Attention now turned to Jamal Khan. They had to ascertain his real intent and determine how best to use him at an opportune moment. If his deed were made public, it would disgrace the Counsellor considerably. There was a Rajput soldier named Samar Sen whom Buddhidhan trusted completely. They had come in contact during Buddhidhan’s Agency days. The Rajput was immensely grateful to the man who had shielded him from the wrath of Buskin Sahib, and had hoped to return the favour some day. Buddhidhan had made him a caretaker and given him a room in a large building owned by the palace. The building had a cellar. Samar Sen was now ordered to take Jamal Khan there and keep him confined in secrecy. Kumud Sundari was still uncertain if Navinchandra was Sarasvatichandra. But her heartfelt desire wished this to be true. She carefully preserved the torn garment. ‘Bhabhi, go and take rest now. Devi and I will do what needs to be done,’ Alak requested Kumud. Kumud was duty-bound not to show even the slightest attachment for a man who was a stranger to her. With herculean effort, she tore herself away and went and stood, forlorn, at the door of her room. Pramaddhan got up saying, ‘Everyone is there. What more can we do now?’ and he gently led her inside. They spent the rest of the night in bed. She lay beside him, but her mind was in the adjoining room. The time her husband spent in sleep, she spent in silent and fervent prayer. Sleep finally came; and morning dawned, too. She arose singing the Gajendra Moksha, and was overjoyed to see that Navinchandra had fully regained consciousness.
chapters.summary: Navinchandra secretly listens as Kumud Sundari shares romantic verses, while simultaneously uncovering the hidden, troubling political machinations of Buddhidhan's household.

chapters.title: Instruments of Intrigue and the Warcraft of Karbharis
paragraphs: Instruments of Intrigue and the Warcraft of Karbharis Navinchandra’s care became Alak Kishori’s responsibility. Murkhdutt visited often and asked after him. The vaidya administered medication. The servants performed their tasks. Saubhagya Devi stayed downstairs but came up once a day to ascertain his well-being. Pramaddhan read him the newspaper and looked in on him every time he would pass by. He would also sit and chat by Navinchandra’s bed in the company of his friends. Buddhidhan visited him daily and spent some time talking with him. He had instructed the vaidya to report Navinchandra’s progress to him daily. Kumud Sundari never missed an opportunity to visit him whenever he had someone else for company. She would come in, keep her distance, and return feeling glad at the progress made by the patient. She would often sit in the adjacent room and listen to Navinchandra converse or make polite talk with visitors. If those visiting Navinchandra were not strangers, Alak Kishori would sit by his side, nurse him, chatter away innocently, and include Kumud or others in the conversation. At times, the sisters-in-law, their guest and Pramaddhan would play a game of dice. In a short time, the guest became one of the Counsellor’s family. His health improved. He no longer felt he was an outsider in a stranger’s house. These were pleasant times of peace and quiet for the Counsellor’s family. This was also around the time that the palace intrigues were at their height; and Navinchandra felt it was his misfortune that he was unable to witness this first hand. Rumours flew thick and fast; some even found their way to his chamber.

Since the incident with Jamal Khan, Buddhidhan had lost his equanimity. He imagined its roots to be much deeper than they actually were. Jamal Khan was held captive in the cellar. A clandestine search for him had been mounted. A worried Khalaknanda had incited her brother and compelled him to take certain actions. Buddhidhan had foreseen these events and was eager to turn the outcome to his favour. He could now clearly see on the horizon the advent of the day when he would need to confront Shathrai openly. The spark that Shathrai had lit by insulting the piety of his mother and Saubhagya Devi still smouldered within him; Shathrai’s intrigues had stoked the fire which burnt like live coal. The insufferable insult to Alak Kishori had added fuel to it, and fanned by Buddhidhan’s intellect, this fire of enmity now encircled Shathrai’s family and his Karbhar. Buddhidhan could also see his sun rise to its zenith. Kindly Dayashankar had taken the words spoken in anger by the young son of a poor widow to be the ranting of a sick, delirious boy. That affectionate man was still alive, though old and decrepit. Buddhidhan felt that what Dayashankar had laughed at was about to be realised, and it gave him pleasure. If only mother were still alive, what a support she would have been! At times, he felt that her absence would be the only blemish on his ascendant joy. But the thought that he would finally be able to complete his mother’s shraadha would make the son emotional. His mind was in a whirl and each day caused new ripples. This sea of emotions was made stormy by the insult to his beloved daughter. That night, as Jamal was being beaten up, when Alak Kishori lay numb and sobbing in her mother’s lap, Buddhidhan had been pacing up and down the terrace like a tiger, eyebrows raised, one hand twirling his moustache, muttering aloud, Beware Shathrai! I am no longer weaponless! In that commotion, no one had heard him or seen his expression in the dark. One morning, Buddhidhan woke up early. Usually Saubhagya Devi always rose before him, but that day she continued to sleep. He sat up in bed and looked at her face. He felt that his debt was still unpaid as her insult remained unavenged. Her delicate lotus eyes, her long black hair spread across the pillow, her glorious forehead, her full lips and fair delicate checks roused him. Her appearance had changed over the years, but her beauty remained undiminished. Buddhidhan was overcome with affection for her. But he felt that his affection, too, was a charade as long as the insult remained unavenged. He decided there and then to remove this blot for good and raised his hand in promise, speaking softly so as not to wake her, ‘Devi! Don’t take me to be a coward. Now when you hear a battle cry, you shall see my hand raised!’ He laughed and cupping her face gently in his hands, he bent over her and kissed her on the lips, and the nectar spread into her soul through them. She woke up smiling, and responded passionately to his kiss. Buddhidhan felt this was a beautiful and auspicious beginning to his campaign. He got up with renewed vigour and enthusiasm to set about his mission. This forceful stream merged with his ever-growing desire to obtain the Karbhar. On the other side, Shathrai had also decided to eliminate Buddhidhan. He had been a Karbhari for many years and his power had remained unchallenged. He was determined not to tolerate this thorn in his side anymore. He no longer feared Bhupsinh, but he had grown to fear Buddhidhan. This fear was deep-rooted. So long as he feared the Rana, the fear of the Counsellor had remained suppressed. Shathrai considered Bhupsinh insignificant, but Buddhidhan was potentially death itself. Shathrai was determined to annihilate him. He was also prepared to deal with Bhupsinh if he foiled his plan. Shathrai had already begun his preparations. It is known that one scabbard cannot contain two swords. So long as Buddhidhan and Shathrai remained deferential to each other, the situation remained under control. But ambition breeds opposition. Their hostility was hitherto concealed. But times had changed, and Buddhidhan felt that his foundations were now deep and secure—a structure could be built upon it. Shathrai had fathomed Buddhidhan’s anxiety; he felt that Buddhidhan’s cunning was precisely what would play Bhupsinh into his hands. Shathrai felt he could easily drive a wedge between the two. The Karbhari was a past master at intrigue and adept in the use of various machinations. His conscience never impeded his actions; he had much wealth and many supporters. Shathrai also believed that Bhupsinh’s benevolence, Buddhidhan’s own God-given intelligence and the fruits thereof, a few truly devoted men, and some money were all the means at Buddhidhan’s disposal. He  believed in fact that he could crush Buddhidhan as easy as a bed bug. Shathrai’s brother Karvatrai was the chief judge of the state; appeals against his judgment went to Rana Bhupsinh. The Counsellor sat in on the appeals alongside the Rana, and his opinion prevailed. Appeals were heard in the afternoon. This also gave the Rana and the Counsellor an opportunity to spend time together. Initially, Buddhidhan did not intervene in the process. But as the time for open conflict neared, more and more of Karvatrai’s judgements were reversed. As a result, the bribes that Karvatrai received also started drying up. Shathrai sought to remedy this situation. Dushtarai had brought a courtesan named Kalavati to Suvarnapur from Bombay. She was delicate, slender, fair and beautiful. She also sang melodiously. One day, she was invited to the palace for a performance. The Rana liked her singing. She soon became a regular feature of the court, and on the suggestion of some courtiers, began to stay back after the performance. The Rana did not object. In this small group, the appreciation moved from her singing to her shamelessly exhibited body. The foolish Rana would listen to this talk with interest, gazing enrapt upon her while she sang or danced, as if she had possessed him. He could not say much as he feared Buddhidhan’s censure. One day, in Buddhidhan’s absence, Kalavati’s beauty was much appreciated and a palace servant named Mahvo, who was one of Shathrai’s men, took upon himself the task of ensuring that the courtesan would soon present herself in the Rana’s service. The Rana did not object, and one afternoon Kalavati was brought to the palace. The palace was defiled, the body of the ruler of Suvarnapur became impure, and his mind corrupted. The people of Suvarnapur now had to contend with a lowly debauched woman as the consort of their Rana. Bhupsinh started having an aversion to the task of dispensing justice every afternoon and presiding over courtly matters. The hangers-on fathomed this. The Rana’s personal secretary Nichdas broached the subject with him: ‘Ranaji, God has not made you for such drudgery; let the Counsellor do that work.’ But who would tell the Counsellor this? Nichdas apprised Shathrai of this situation. In Buddhidhan’s presence, Jagabhai, the court bard, found occasion to sing this poem: O great and benevolent Rana Bhup: Your virtues and beauty are unmatched, To the care of your people night and day You devote your time, money and all, You have forgotten the simple joys of leisure and pleasure O great and benevolent Rana Bhup, you must now become a lion! You must hunt daily and in beautiful dense forests, roar! Be the King of the forest, O Rana, for what more need a ruler do? The bard stood with folded hands and said, ‘O benevolent Ranaji Bhup,  Saviour of the poor, the likes of me must deal with daily drudgery. But to see you toil thus—how can this be!’ Buddhidhan was astonished and looked at the bard with suspicion. The bard did not meet his gaze. Shathrai: ‘But Jagabhai, he has to rule, a king cannot be idle. Should he not dispense justice?’ Jagabhai: ‘My lord, if the Ranaji has to break his head over such things, what is a trusted and capable Counsellor for?’ With incidents like this, the grounds were laid, and Bhupsinh became less and less interested in matters of court and governance. In the afternoon he would send a message to Buddhidhan saying, ‘You begin—I will join in.’ He would eventually make an appearance, to put his signature on a few documents. Buddhidhan observed all this. Shathrai had not yet displaced him in the Rana’s affections, but the die was cast. Buddhidhan came to know that Kalavati visited the palace every afternoon, so he inquired into her past. She spent afternoons with the Rana, and Dushtarai spent nights with her. The Rana spent the money, so Dushtarai enjoyed himself for free. Merulo too was happy. He boasted to Narbheram, who informed the Counsellor. Gradually, the Rana became brazen, and an attendant named Raghi Khavasan remained in attendance while the Rana was alone with Kalavati. Raghi served Kalavati, and became their favourite. Raghi was having an affair with Mahva. He was cunning but felt helpless in face of his desire for Raghi; he would tell her everything. Mahva was debauched, while Raghi was greedy for money and ornaments. Raghi was foolish and playful, but she recognised Mahva’s vulnerability and managed to cheat him, scold him, rob him and have her way with him. The palace gave them ample opportunity to do as they pleased; such are the houses of the high and the mighty. In Shathrai’s house, Raghi Khavasan was feted. Taking the lead, Narbheram would quietly counsel her: ‘Bitch, you should be around to serve in every possible way when the Rana and Kalavati are alone together. This will earn you money; and someday you can also become a queen.’ Raghi took him seriously, and we know well what the outcome of that would be. Raghi felt beholden to Narbheram, and told him everything she heard. Even then, she did not divulge what Mahva had told her. One day Narbheram said: ‘Bitch, Mahvo can be said to be truly devoted to you only the day he brings you the nose-ring that the queen gave his wife. Otherwise, you are just a keep.’ Raghi said excitedly: ‘Of course he will!’ However, there was no way Mahva’s wife would give him the nose-ring. Mahva made excuses and reasoned with Raghi, but she did not budge. Narbheram would goad her in glee, ‘You deserve it. My Mahvo, my Mahvo, you would keep singing. But he proved otherwise. Time alone is the true test of things.’ Raghi could not break off relations with Mahva, but a wedge was driven between them. She now began to confide in Narbheram even things that Mahva would tell her. The Rana had a one-eyed usher named Ranjit. Before Merulo, he had been Rupali’s paramour. When the affair became known to him, Dushtarai decided to kill Ranjit. This was long ago, even before Buddhidhan had moved to Lilapur. In those days, Buddhidhan occasionally visited Shathrai’s house. It was here that he had come to know of Dushtarai’s intentions; Buddhidhan had then warned Ranjit and showed him a way out of this difficulty. Accordingly, Ranjit had met Shathrai and pleaded, ‘Sir, my enemies have spread lies about me to Dushtarai. Have mercy on me and transfer me out of here. If not, I will have to resign.’ Dushtarai could not divulge the real reason, and so he had let Ranjit go, saying, ‘Wretch, let him rot elsewhere’. This transfer eventually led to his becoming an usher. Ranjit was still grateful to Buddhidhan and remained a close supporter. Buddhidhan, through Samar Sen, taught him the next step: Ranjit flirted with Raghi, which resulted in their affair. Raghi Khavasan was also the favourite of the queens. Mahva’s secrets now began to tumble out one by one. And thus, through his intellect, the Rana’s court, the queen’s quarters, the palace intrigues, all became transparent before Buddhidhan. The Counsellor now believed he knew all that Kalavati did and said. So far, Shathrai had used her only to corrupt the Rana, for circumstances were not yet ripe for more. Then, she began to say things like, ‘We are condemned for our profession. But aren’t there women worse than us in the Rana’s harem? I have heard rumours— only God knows their veracity—who can talk about the queens? I have heard things about Rajba ...,’ and gradually Kalavati became increasingly brazen in her utterances. Finally, Buddhidhan went to the palace one morning with the letters that Narbheram had obtained for him. He threw them into the Rana’s lap and said tearfully, ‘I thought of Rajba like a mother. I tremble at these letters. Read them. Shathrai will send them to you through Mahva. If you have even a sliver of doubt, I will resign, and will remain content to see you rise.’ The Rana was moved. He got up and wiped his old friend’s tears. He said, ‘Buddhidhan, I have absolute faith in you. I owe my present to you. Let these forged letters be brought before me. I will hang the one who brings them. Why don’t you finish off Shathrai right now?’ Buddhidhan took back the letters and advised, ‘Take the letters that Mahva gives you. Pretend that you believe them all to be true. Show that you utterly detest me and are entirely willing to do Shathrai’s  bidding.’ And giving the Rana some other necessary instructions, Buddhidhan went home. That afternoon, when Mahva presented the letters to the Rana, Bhupsinh appeared duly outraged, he roared and vowed to destroy Buddhidhan. He called for Shathrai and confided in him. Shathrai was secretly overjoyed, and promised to ensure that the Rana would never have to see Buddhidhan’s face again. The Rana said, ‘Prepare someone who can take over the Counsellor’s responsibilities. Ensure that Buddhidhan remains in the dark until we have succeeded in our plans.’ The Karbhari thought for a while and said, ‘Appoint Narbheram as your Hazoor Secretary. That was Buddhidhan’s first post as well; he will not suspect this appointment, and Narbheram will soon learn on the job.’ This was done. The cycle of the new moon of Chaitra began a few days later. It was decided to bring everything out in the open on that day when the full court was assembled. Shameless Garbaddas had taken it upon himself to prove that Buddhidhan had accepted bribes in judicial work. Mahva’s brother Khodo had worked for a time in the postal department at Lilapur. It was decided that he would make Rajba and Buddhidhan’s letters public. He concocted a story about how he had come to be in possession of those letters. Narbheram was to provide testimony in this matter. It was decided that the enraged Rana would then order Buddhidhan’s arrest and the confiscation of his house. The Rana was told that he should depute Karvatrai to judge the charges against Buddhidhan. Dushtarai whispered to the Rana, ‘Once Buddhidhan is arrested, we will present all three women of his house to you. They are very beautiful.’ The Rana shuddered, but managed to hide his discomfiture. On their way back from the palace, Shathrai advised Karvatrai: ‘Why should you have to do all these things? The Political Agent might poke his nose into this matter. We will persuade Ranjit, Mahva and the others to finish him off. People will think he committed suicide. We will tell the Rana that even in death, Rajba was saved from public disgrace. This will work—short and swift.

Buddhidhan dead, the Rana in Kalavati’s clutches, and we will arrange a son for one of the queens; what more could we want?’ They plotted to keep a few pregnant women in the service of the queens so that a son could be easily foisted on the throne when the need arose, and the mishap with Jadsinh’s queen could be averted. Shathrai was certain that the Creator had destined that son Dushtarai would follow him as a Karbhari. A queen with an imposter son: both queen and son would remain under his thumb. The child’s birth was thus celebrated even before the wedding! The first day of Chaitra was also Rana Bhupsinh’s birthday. The full court assembled twice that day, once in the morning and again in the evening. It was decided that Buddhidhan would be stripped of his post and power during the morning assembly. He was to be arrested as soon as he emerged from the palace. Dushtarai was made responsible for this part of the plan. He was told, ‘Your soldiers should walk with him for a time and accord him full respect and honour; he should be allowed to move about freely. He should be taken out from behind the palace.’ The rear part of the palace had a large garden with a maze. The meandering lanes were covered with creepers which created dark spaces, where birds were kept. During Jadsinh’s reign, queens, palace servants, officials and courtiers all had their places of assignation in the maze. Behind the maze stood a Shiva temple. Women worshippers were lured, coerced, tricked, and even abducted and brought into the maze. Rana Jadsinh had himself taken part in the debaucheries of his courtiers and committed immoral acts here. During Bhupsinh’s reign, Buddhidhan had put an end to all these activities. This route was now used only by Kalavati. At the centre of the maze was a shallow pond. It was decided that Buddhidhan should be led towards this pond, where Ranjit and Mahva would attack him from behind, throw him into a ditch and strangle him to death. His body should then be thrown into the pond; thereafter Ranjit and Mahva should retrieve him and pretend to revive him. It should be declared that disgraced beyond redemption, Buddhidhan had committed suicide, and his body should be cremated immediately, they decided. It was also decided that Shathrai should make a show of excessive grief and mourning. Raghi divulged the entire plan to Ranjit, who naturally forewarned Buddhidhan. But Buddhidhan doubted Ranjit. The Rana was, after all, a Garasia—could he really be trusted to play his part? Moreover, he was also in Kalavati’s clutches. And could his ever faithful fiercely loyal Narbheram be trusted not to change sides in such dark times? Mired in mistrust, doubts, fear and anxiety, the Counsellor lost sleep. He worried night and day about the fate that awaited his precious Devi and the children. A broken hut, a wan wife, Wasted children: Will I ever see them again? Saubhagya Devi knew the Sudamacharita by heart. One day, Buddhidhan heard her and Vanleela sing stanzas from it. Overwrought as he was, his eyes welled up with sudden tears at the familiar words. He got up, washed his face and went back to work. Navinchandra observed all these happenings from his sick bed. He did not understand all of it, but was nevertheless surprised and he felt a growing empathy for Buddhidhan. Although emotionally distraught, Buddhidhan never once lost his patience. His genius did not wane, his intellect was not blunted. A lofty mind is not brittle; although delicate, it withstands worldly blows. It is aesthetically endowed and possessed of a refined sensibility which sharpens the intellect. Lofty minds are neither crass nor coarse; they are supple and subtle. A sword can suppress a cotton ball but cannot cut it down. If cut, it can be woven together again. An object that falls onto a hard rock either remains intact or shatters irrevocably. But when an object falls into water, the water parts momentarily and makes way for it, only to regain its original state. It is not that weapons do not wound the Gods, but their wounds heal on their own. Buddhidhan’s inner core was not immune to attack, but it had over time become ever more alert, agile and resilient.

Harder even than adamant and softer than a flower are the hearts of the super-eminent persons; who can correctly gauge them?⟨fn:12⟩ When he thought of his family, Buddhidhan’s heart was softer than a flower. When he thought of his worldly engagements, it became harder than stone; it hissed like a snake when gripped by revenge and turned into a raging ball of fire when confronted with the evil of Shathrai and his group. As he considered the future, his heart prepared for the ultimate sacrifice. Now that war was inevitable, he became hungry for battle. Taking stock of his enemy’s position, he grew eager in anticipation as he saw that his heart’s oldest desires were about to bear fruit. Buddhidhan was pleased that his rise was imminent, and his mind opened itself to receive the rays of the glorious rising sun. As the first day of Chaitra drew closer, the Bombay newspapers published a series of articles on Suvarnapur. The newspaper columns were full of stories about Shathrai’s administration, his tyranny, the urgent need for reform, his disastrous influence over Rana Bhupsinh, and rumours about Kalavati. The English newspapers did not accept articles from readers, but their letters to the editor were printed. The Karbhari camp read these articles and accused the Counsellor of inciting the newspapers. Narbheram pointed out, ‘This must be shown to the Rana. It is unbecoming of the Counsellor.’ Shathrai agreed, and Narbheram began to present and read out these newspaper clippings before the Rana daily.
