The Rana appeared angry; several times, Narbheram almost felt that the anger was genuine. The Rana was hurt by references to Kalavati. Buddhidhan had managed to get some articles inserted, and he had kept the Rana informed about this. But the Rana was surprised by Buddhidhan’s capacity to create this big a storm. Buddhidhan had also told him that he was not the one behind the Kalavati story, but he realised that on this matter, the Rana did not trust him. This was one reason for Buddhidhan’s own mistrust of the Garasia. The populace of Suvarnapur also sent petitions and pleas to the Rana. Narbheram did not allow them to be placed before Bhupsinh, and kept Shathrai informed of his actions. Shathrai’s trust in Narbheram was now sealed. It so happened that a bania had sent a petition to the English Sahib regarding an injustice done to him by the judge Karvatrai. The Government had sent that petition to the Agency, which in turn had sent it on to the Rana for remarks and clarifications. Narbheram, who was the Huzoor Secretary of the palace, sent this petition to the Karbhari. Acting at Shathrai’s behest, Narbheram put the bania in the dungeons, and got him to sign a letter stating that injustice had been done to him by the palace. The letter was sent to the Government, while the bania remained imprisoned. Buddhidhan had arranged for copies of the petition, the letter and newspaper clippings to be sent directly to the Sahib. He sent the bania’s wife to Lilapur, from where she filed another petition. Buskin Sahib had been transferred to a different province. Buddhidhan corresponded with him regularly and updated him on the challenges he faced. Buskin Sahib promised to mitigate his troubles. He also assured Buddhidhan that he would write to Russell Sahib and intercede on Buddhidhan’s behalf. Buskin Sahib’s wife was soon to return from England. She was to pass through Lilapur. Buddhidhan, along with Pramaddhan, met her. Madam Sahib arranged for his meeting with Russell Sahib, and Buddhidhan acquainted him with the goings-on in Suvarnapur. Satisfied with his explanations, Russell Sahib said, ‘When the need arises ask me; I will protect you.’ Buddhidhan also met Russell Sahib’s wife, whom he presented with sweets and dry fruits. As Bhupsinh had changed his mind about meeting the Sahib after Kalavati’s entry in his life, acting as the Rana’s emissary, Buddhidhan presented the Sahib with a letter from the Rana. In his response, the Sahib praised Buddhidhan.

Suvarnapur palace had appointed an advocate as its representative in Lilapur. This advocate sent false and exaggerated reports to the palace daily. He wrote with great flourish that he had spent two hours with the Sahib where the Karbhari and his administration were praised, and so on and so forth. He also reported the Counsellor’s meeting with the Sahib to Shathrai, in which he stated that the Counsellor had not been accorded any honour or respect by the Sahib. Shathrai was pleased. Buddhidhan had no interest in dispelling these rumours. Both the English Madams had gifted the Counsellor signed portraits. He showed these, along with Russell Sahib’s letter, to the Rana and expressed his satisfaction at the honours accorded him. The Rana was reassured that Buddhidhan’s prestige in the Agency was intact, and that he could have his way there. The Counsellor believed that by demonstrating his influence over the newspapers and the Sahib, he would continue to wield power over Bhupsinh. He was right. Buddhidhan had no intentions of attacking Shathrai directly: his ploy was to lead Shathrai into the grave that he had dug for Buddhidhan, and for this the wheels had already been set in motion. On the day of the assembly, he needed to shield himself from intrigue. Therefore, he had also ensured that Dushtarai’s police would come nowhere near him that day. He could not take anything for granted in these difficult times. It fell to Navinchandra to ensure that on the eve of the first day of Chaitra, the English newspapers would print favourable stories about the Counsellor. Navinchandra was now strong enough to sit up, and accepted the responsibility enthusiastically. He was eager to witness the court assemble on the first day of Chaitra, health permitting; Buddhidhan was also in favour of his attendance at the palace. Narbheram was charged with ensuring that Dushtarai would be required to rush home at the critical juncture. The idea was that in absence of their chief, his men would hesitate before attacking Buddhidhan. Should this not happen, Buddhidhan had also kept a team of soldiers in readiness to subdue Dushtarai’s men. Samar Sen’s older brother Vijay Sen was the commander of a troop. In times of peace under the British rule, the army rotted and was used only for ceremonial purposes. Whenever the court assembled and canons were fired in celebration, a troop of soldiers remained present at the palace, with their swords drawn. It was decided that Vijay Sen and his men would be present at the palace. Vijay Sen was unaware of the tumultuous events that were to take place that day. Buddhidhan had ordered Samar Sen to remain close to him during the assembly, and had briefed him on the instructions to be passed on to Vijay Sen, if the need arose. He also arranged for some trusted Rajput soldiers and Arab guards to be posted at his house while he was at court. They were instructed not to allow any stranger to enter the house until Buddhidhan returned from the assembly, and also to be wary of Dushtarai’s men. The womenfolk were asked to remain confined to the house while Buddhidhan was away. These were routine arrangements, but the instructions given appeared extraordinary to the family. They had no inkling of what was to come, and many conjectures were made as they prepared to carry out their part of the instructions. Everyone awaited the outcome of these strange events. This was the scenario on the dark last night of the month of Falgun. They waited for the new day to break to see what would unfold before it ended. Buddhidhan tossed and turned all night as if he slept in an airless room on a hot summer night. He stared at the ceiling continually. Even the comfort of Devi’s bed gave him no respite that night. Finally at two o’ clock, his overwrought mind and body succumbed to sleep. He slept rigidly, not so much as turning sides. Whether to ascertain if a heart gripped by the machinations of statecraft had any place for her in it, or to capture that heart for herself we do not know, but the sentient hand of the sleeping woman came to rest on the chest of her lifelong companion as he dreamed uneasily.
chapters.summary: Shathrai schemes to eliminate Buddhidhan, using Kalavati to distract Rana Bhupsinh, as Buddhidhan prepares his own forces for an inevitable, high-stakes showdown.

chapters.title: In Readiness for Court
paragraphs: In Readiness for Court The much awaited first day of Chaitra dawned at last. From early morning on, the homes of the courtiers were abuzz with activity. Shathrai bathed and dressed for the court. Narbheram was the first to arrive in attendance. Soldiers gathered noisily outside the Karbhari’s house. Shathrai relaxed on a mattress, leaning against a bolster. A servant brought him his jacket and helped him into it. Shathrai called for a mirror, admired his reflection and sat twirling his moustache. Narbheram was pacing about. He watched the Karbhari and muttered to himself: Look at him gaze at his face in the mirror; his heart is bereft of compassion and righteousness. ‘Oh God!’ he sighed aloud and walked away shaking his head. A group of policemen huddled outside Dushtarai’s quarters. The Faujdar sat on his bed, while his wife fetched his clothes and helped him dress. As he got ready, Dushtarai flirted with Rupali, bragged about his own intelligence, and mocked Buddhidhan’s fate. He spoke with much excitement and anticipation, ‘Tonight, Alak Kishori, Kumud Sundari and Saubhagya Devi will be subjected to some fine treatment, and I will prove just what kind of a man I am.’ His degenerate wife took delight in her husband’s licentiousness as if she had attained the height of good fortune. There was commotion all around. Everyone was busy chatting, roaming about aimlessly, showing their power, or obeying orders. Narbheram sought out Merulo. The soldier was busy folding

Khalaknanda’s clothes. Narbheram sat down on a large upturned copper pot, untied the knot of his tuft and said: ‘So, you are folding behn’s clothes today.’ ‘Of course, one has to do it.’ ‘True, she is ‘behn’ after all.’ ‘How can that be denied.’ ‘Yes, these are your lucky days, you are a Krishna among the gopis. If you don’t take advantage, you’d be a fool. Jamal has disappeared. So now you have two instead of one. Any news of Jamal?’ ‘Wretched Turk. Who knows where he rots. Good riddance!’ ‘But you changed the topic. You didn’t tell me about your behn.’ ‘Behn? She might well be a sister to others, Narbherambhai, but I am clear about these things. Those older than I are like mothers to me, and those younger are sisters.’ ‘And those of the same age?’ ‘Those I can take. If Jamal can take her, I can, too.’ ‘Isn’t Rupali jealous?’ ‘How can she be jealous! Am I jealous that now she has Garbaddas as well? She has two, so I have two!’ ‘Garbad, that rascal has it good.’ ‘Narbherambhai, what can I say. Garbad played mischief. Our Karbhari is busy with his administration, and the Faujdar is busy policing. Garbaddas would come to meet them when he knew that neither of them was home. He would wait for their return. The Karbhari was using Garbaddas to beguile and mislead Buddhidhan and had given him a free run of the house; so we had no authority to turn him away. He would sit alone in the drawing room, look out of the window, or waltz around the terrace.’ ‘What were you doing at the time?’ ‘I was busy with ... you know. Garbaddas took advantage of that. Sometimes Khalak—behn only to her brother—would be at her in- laws’, and Rupali would be alone at home. She would come out into the courtyard with her hair open, and he would be standing on the terrace, looking down.’

‘This was planned on purpose?’ ‘No, my dear sir. It all began unintentionally. Rupali is used to doing that, it is a habit with her. One day, Garbad could no longer contain himself and he coughed to draw her attention. What followed you know. The comings and goings began after that.’ ‘How do you know so much?’ ‘Some I witnessed. The rest she confessed, a bit by persuasion and a bit by coercion.’ ‘Then you will have fun today.’ ‘Of course! Important men will fight over the Karbhar in court, while men like me will take care of the ‘Karbhar’ of their homes. Rupali on one side, and on the other, the naughty one. But Narbherambhai, tell me how long will the assembly last?’ ‘They will be in the court till noon. You are the master of all you survey till then. Don’t you know how long they will be gone?’ ‘I know about the evening assembly, when Alak Kishori and the others will be arrested and brought to the palace. This means I am the master of the house till noon.’ ‘Today all the soldiers will also be at the palace. Don’t worry. I will be the first to come. I will warn you in advance.’ ‘I am grateful.’ ‘If fortune is not with you, you might be in for a surprise before noon.’ ‘My dear sir, with gopis on either side, this Krishna will carouse. At such moments, I am not one to be frightened even by Shathrai. One should keep doing what one is doing. I am a match for the best of them.’ ‘Lech! Two women, together!’ ‘Why not? These sisters-in-law may rule over the town; before me, they are meek as goats and cows.’ When elders are debauched, others in a family are also corrupted. Children and servants closely observe the conduct of their elders. If the elders are respected, so is their conduct, be it moral or immoral. That is considered best and is therefore emulated and perpetuated.

Their merits and sins affect not only their families but also those around them. How else could a lowly servant exercise such authority over the Karbhari’s own daughter and daughter-in-law? God grants heaven and hell in this world itself. This is exemplified by the homes of Buddhidhan and Shathrai. With these thoughts, Narbheram took leave of Merulo. Meanwhile, the entourage gathered. They hurriedly wore their footwear, and the procession left for the palace with due ceremony. Narbheram sought out Dushtarai and walked alongside him. Soon, the two were walking ahead of everyone else. Only a few soldiers stayed back as guards. Rupali watched them leave from a window. Dushtarai turned back once, looked up at her, and smiled. His chest, and his mind, swelled with pride. As the procession moved out of sight, Rupali came down. Merulo was working on the floor below. She came and hugged him from behind. In a while, Khalaknanda joined them. They both laughingly embraced Merulo from either side, rocking back and forth. Unmindful of the scene back home, Shathrai and party moved towards the palace, intent upon Buddhidhan’s destruction. The  certainty of this fact filled their minds, and their arrogance brimmed over. Narbheram: ‘So, Faujdar Sahib, you are in full force today!’ Dushtarai: ‘Of course!’ ‘Now your writ will run large, as it did in Jadsinh’s time?’ ‘Why not! Let us see.’ ‘But will you be able to turn the court into a house of pleasure as before?’ ‘That day, too, shall come.’ ‘Why not make an auspicious beginning today itself?’ ‘How so?’ ‘There will be a dance today at court.’ ‘So?’ ‘Won’t your Kalavatibai go in for a change of costume? You should follow her into the room. You have all the authority.’ ‘No, no, not today. There will be time for that.’

‘Courage, that is what you need. My dear Sir, be brave! He is gone. Finished. The Karbhar is yours. Make a beginning. But then, you know best.’ ‘It would be bad if the Rana gets to know.’ ‘Forget it, what does that Garasia understand! All he can do is smoke his hookah.’ ‘So, should I take the plunge? What is the problem in any case? It has been years since I took the liberty.’ ‘No problem. I will keep the Rana engaged.’ ‘Good. And what if father comes to know?’ ‘Oh, I have not seen anyone as cowardly as you! Didn’t your father do the same in his youth? Everyone is naked in infancy.’ ‘Fine. Then watch me.’ ‘So be it.’ ‘All right then, see what I do today. But don’t forget to play your part.’ ‘Of course, Faujdar Sahib!’ Narbheram said, muttering to himself, In case of any trouble, I will say what the fox said to the elephant: Please hold on to my tail! The crafty rascal. Reason fails before greed. As if it is your father’s rule! You will know for sure today. Go you wretches, you cunning asses! Narbheram bit his lower lip pensively. The Karbhari, judges, administrators and soldiers ambled along. Narbheram moved amongst them like a fly. Buddhidhan’s home was also bustling with activity. He had got up at four that morning, having slept only for two hours. He bathed, performed his ritual worship, and paced up and down his drawing room. Saubhagya Devi woke up early, bathed, marked her forehead with three lines of sacred ash and a red bindi at the centre, and commenced worship of Lord Shiva before sunrise. She had arranged silver utensils around her, lit two ghee lamps on either side of her and incense sticks which filled the room with their fragrance. She sat cross-legged on a low wooden stool with a woollen, multicoloured seat. She was the very embodiment of a chaste, pious woman. The sight of her reminded Navinchandra of Mahasweta from ‘Kadambari’, and he looked at her radiant face reverentially, as if she were a goddess to be worshipped. Kumud Sundari had studied English, but in matters of religion she was still a child. She was untouched by reformist ideas about faith or worship. She observed her mother-in-law offer puja, and was awed and attracted by the grandeur of the setting and the glory that Saubhagya Devi brought to it—it appealed to Kumud’s aesthetic sensibility. And so she had begun to learn the ritual of sun worship from Devi. Alak’s mind was not in such matters; Saubhagya Devi was happy that her daughter-in-law seemed keen on worship. Kumud Sundari had not yet learnt the full ritual, she therefore helped Saubhagya Devi by preparing the paraphernalia for the puja. Saubhagya Devi felt content and fulfilled that her daughter-in-law served her, just as she had served her own mother-in-law. The ritual was completed hurriedly as Buddhidhan had to leave soon. The puja over, Kumud Sundari got busy preparing breakfast for the men since the assembly was expected to be a long one. Navinchandra also woke up early. He brushed, bathed, and not having much else to do, sat on the terrace watching the auspicious beginnings of the day in the Counsellors’ house. Busy with arrangements, Kumud breezed in and out of the courtyard with a lamp in her hand, and occasionally looked up at the face, standing distant and above it all, which seemed at times to be looking down at her. Samar Sen arrived in the courtyard with some other men, adding to the noise and bustle. The servants busily cleaned and swept the house and obeyed a constant flow of instructions from Saubhagya Devi and Kumud Sundari. Pramaddhan sat by the side of a lamp and did the work assigned to him by his father. Having finished it, he came down and sent a man to fetch Dayashankar Kaka and some other relatives. Meanwhile, Alak Kishori arrived from her in-laws’ house, escorted by a guard. She, too, immediately busied herself with household work. Buddhidhan’s drawing room began to fill up with people. Dayashankar walked in, stick in hand, slowly climbed up the stairs and sat down on a couch. The headmaster of the school arrived wearing English ‘boots and stockings’, sat on a chair and began to read the previous day’s newspaper—it had an ‘article’ by Navinchandra, although written anonymously. Shastri Maharaj climbed the stairs reciting sacred verses, sat with Dayashankar and began to chat with him. The Qazi entered looking sombre, greeted all present with courtesy and sat down next to the headmaster. The City Judge who had recently passed the District Pleader’s examination joined in. He was an honest and frank man who often clashed with Karvatrai. Other officers used him when they had to send blunt messages to superiors, like the Rana, the Karbhari and the Counsellor. His intellect was pure and he did not like employing devious means; this made him quite unsuited to working in a princely state. The City Judge had acquired this position on Buskin Sahib’s recommendation, and he also had Buddhidhan’s protection. This was why, while all other state officials had gathered at Shathrai’s house, he had chosen to come to Buddhidhan’s instead. He was a genuinely carefree man. People knew they could get their work done by him as long as they praised his honesty and independence. His name was Tark Prasad. Corrupt and unctuous officers considered this straightforward man stupid and called him Dahyabhai. However, Dahyabhai had considered the situation quite thoroughly and come to his own conclusion: truth would eventually prevail and evil would be defeated. Shathrai would be destroyed and Buddhidhan would rise. This calculation also motivated his steadfast loyalty to Buddhidhan’s faction. On arriving, Tark Prasad greeted each present appropriately and slumped into an easy chair. Buddhidhan’s son-in-law, Vidurprasad also arrived. Sitting next to Tark Prasad on a chair without armrests, he engaged the Judge in conversation. He worked in the accounts department as an assistant to Garbaddas. He had also worked a short while in the police department, as also in the department that dealt with the cousins of the rulers—the Bhayats. Vidurprasad was a meek man; but sometimes, at his parents’ instigation, he harassed Buddhidhan and sought things that were beyond his station. He did not care if Buddhidhan faced any difficulty in meeting his demands. The moment one demand was met, he would come up with another.

If Buddhidhan ever did him a favour, he was given to saying, ‘So what? What is so unusual about it?’ He never allowed a sense of gratitude to enter his mind. But he was docile and submissive before Alak Kishori and therefore remained more or less quiet. Vidurprasad was a considerate man in some ways, but took interest in talks that degraded his father-in-law’s family, even though he was ultimately a well-wisher. He was a capable man, but made many mistakes in his work; Buddhidhan often spoke about them in the house. On such occasions, Vidurprasad accepted without protest Alak Kishori’s verbal lashings at night. Even his parents would go quiet when their proud daughter-in-law stepped into the house. They quibbled only behind her back. Dayashankar’s son Jaymalshankar joined the gathering. With monetary help from Buddhidhan, Jaymal had studied English and had passed the Matriculation examination from Bombay. He was a well-built, impressive-looking and practical man. He was related to Shathrai on the maternal side; he was given a post dealing with the petty expenditure of Bhupsinh’s palace. Shathrai had given him this position—on Narbheram’s suggestion—knowing that Buddhidhan would not object to the appointment. Jaymalshankar had been sent by the Rana to fetch Buddhidhan. He now sought the Counsellor out and whispered into his ear, ‘Bhai Sahib, Kalavati spent all night in the palace and went home only at four in the morning. Ranjit asked me to tell you that she talked about Rajba all night, and that the Rana is fuming. You know well whether or not the Rana can be trusted. After Kalavati’s departure, he sent a note to Shathrai. Who knows what he wrote in that note? He was heard muttering, “These can’t all be lies,” and he spoke about “Ramabai” or some such person, and said that even she had told him the same thing.’ Buddhidhan heard Jaymal’s warning and sent him back to the palace with the message that he would follow shortly. He could not decide whether the Rana was being devious with him or with Shathrai. But he had no time to deliberate upon this now. He had deliberated and plotted enough. Suddenly, another thought came to him. In the short time that he had observed Navinchandra, Buddhidhan had realised that his guest was trustworthy. Navinchandra had no dealings with Shathrai and no selfish motives in the palace; and for this reason, Buddhidhan found he could trust him even more than Narbheram. He sent for Navinchandra and Alak Kishori the moment Jaymalshankar had left. ‘Get the breakfast ready soon and send it up here,’ he said to Alak and sent her off. The Counsellor then placed a hand on Navinchandra’s shoulder, looked him straight in the eye and said, ‘Navinchandra, I need to assign you a responsibility today. It is a matter of absolute trust and must be kept secret. It is as if I am placing my most invaluable jewels in your custody. You are learned, appear to be high-born, and I consider you honest in every respect. I believe you will remain steadfast in these qualities even when I may no longer be around.’ Navinchandra was surprised. ‘It is not proper for one to speak about oneself; but yes, have the confidence that the trust reposed in me will not be wasted. I am grateful for your generosity, and am bound to you. For me, any service rendered to you is the same as an act in the name of God.’ ‘You know that tumultuous events are expected to take place at the palace today.’ ‘Yes, but I do not know the details.’ ‘Details you will know later. For the moment, you should know that today either Shathrai will prevail, or I. God willing, the outcome will be good. But times are strange. At the court, if you should perceive that I am in any danger, or upon a sign from me, you should rush home and take my entire family to Lilapur, rent a house and stay there. Alak Kishori knows where my money and jewellery are kept. In that matter, you should seek Dayashankar Kaka’s advice. On reaching Lilapur, you should meet Russell Sahib and inform him about my situation here. You should also write to Vidya Chatura and act as per his counsel. Pramad is still childish; it is your responsibility to look after him and guide him. I have kept carts waiting for you in the house adjacent, in case the need arises. You should take Samar Sen with you or the armed escort sent by him. Do not trust Shathrai, his son, or any stranger for that matter. And you should march out fast; their thoughts are utterly evil and depraved. I believe it will not be beyond your capacity to accomplish this.’ The Counsellor looked at the young man anxiously. Navinchandra was too astonished for words. This scenario was beyond his imagination. He would never have thought that in a strange land, someone could repose so much trust in him, and in such circumstances. But he quickly regained his poise and said: ‘Have no fear: this is the first time that God has tested my virtue and lineage. I shall not fail.’ The Counsellor’s hand moved from his forehead to his eyes and face, and suppressing a deep sigh, he said, ‘Navinchandra, I leave in your custody my dearest, most precious jewels. Never before in my life have I been through such trying times.’ ‘Bhai Sahib, consider me a brother—a son in fact. I touch your feet. I feel no distance from your family. What more can I say? Deeds are better than words. Your wealth to me is like offerings made to God. Devi is like a mother to me, and Alak is my sister.’ ‘I have other friends, but their interests are tied to the State. Shathrai is a wealthy and powerful man.’ ‘Bhai Sahib, you have trusted me completely; I am not unworthy of your trust. No one can buy me with money. I will share a secret with you, too: my father is a millionaire.’ The Counsellor seemed unconvinced. Navinchandra saw this, and felt a tinge of sadness. ‘I have this ring as proof. Take a look.’ He had tied a diamond ring to his janeu thread and hidden it in the folds of his dhoti. He took it out. Buddhidhan took the ring in his hand and stared at it; the diamond was worth at least seven or eight thousand rupees. ‘Bhai Sahib, I also know a few other things which are supposed to be secret. I know that Shathrai intends to kill you. I know about Kalavati.’ Now it was Buddhidhan who was startled. He squared his shoulders and looked Navinchandra full in the face: ‘What!’ ‘Bhai Sahib, please do not be startled. I will tell you later how I came to know of these matters. I know a lot, but haven’t said a word to anyone, not even Pramadbhai—God is my witness. I can keep secrets. I have not made use of any secrets that I know. I say this only to prove that I am worthy of your trust.’ Buddhidhan fell deep into thought. Seeing him in a quandary, Navinchandra continued, ‘If you have any doubts about me, I am not keen to take on this responsibility. I am a foreigner, a wanderer, a free bird. If you prefer, I am ready to leave for someplace else this very moment, and no one will ever know about it. You can assign this responsibility to anyone else you please.’ ‘No, no—it isn’t like that. Come, you are like a brother to me. This is your responsibility. But remember that the teeth do not have to be told to protect the tongue.’ ‘Please do not worry, Bhai Sahib.’ Alak Kishori called them for breakfast. The son-in-law joined them; Dayashankar also came in and sat down on a stool. Not wanting to frighten them, Buddhidhan had not yet spoken to the women about the political intrigues of the palace. But it had now become imperative to do so. He told them what he had said to Navinchandra, and requested them to do exactly as they were asked. They were taken aback and apprehensive, but there was no time to waste. The Counsellor went to his bedroom to change his clothes; Saubhagya Devi followed him. ‘Devi, there are some papers in this box. If it becomes necessary to leave for Lilapur with Navinchandra, open it once you are there, and do what is written in these notes.’ ‘But what is all this?’ Devi demanded to know. ‘Nothing. Do not be afraid, Devi. Until I return, let Dayashankar Kaka not leave the house.’ ‘You have never kept anything from me till date. Have I done something wrong that you no longer trust me?’ Devi asked, wiping anguished tears from her eyes. ‘No, no, it is nothing. I will tell you everything later. Is this the time to talk? It is just that the assembly will be stormy today and ...’ ‘I see from your face that you are very afraid of something.’ Buddhidhan made an attempt to laugh, ‘No, what should I be afraid of! I have told you what it is, haven’t I?’

‘Yes, there is a scare. But my heart tells me that all will be well. I am not afraid; it must be something else.’ Just then, Alak Kishori entered the room. Buddhidhan said to Alak, ‘Be brave, if the time comes to leave with Navinchandra. Look how brave your sister-in-law is.’ Pramaddhan came to inform them that everyone was ready, and that messengers from the palace had come asking after them twice. Saubhagya Devi sent Alak Kishori to fetch kumkum. Dressed for the palace, Buddhidhan emerged from his room and as he hurriedly made his way down the stairs, he met Alak midway. ‘Victory to you, father! I met you halfway. Let me apply the tilak. Today, triumph will be yours!’ And Alak put a tilak of red kumkum paste on his forehead. Everyone assembled in the courtyard and put on their footwear, eager to leave. Navinchandra was ready, too; Buddhidhan had asked Pramaddhan to lend him appropriate clothes for the occasion. The Counsellor now took Navinchandra by the hand. Vanleela was on her way to her maternal home. But hearing rumours of intrigue from her husband, she had called Kumud Sundari to the door to talk about it. They stood talking on the threshold. Vanleela left, and as Kumud Sundari entered the house, she ran into the Counsellor and his entourage on their way out. She shrank to one side and allowed them to pass before entering the house. ‘Navinchandra, the omens are auspicious. We met Alak Kishori on the stairs, and now Kumud Sundari near the door,’ the Counsellor said. ‘Yes, the omens are auspicious. Let us proceed.’ Everyone congratulated the Counsellor on the good omen, and they all proceeded for the palace. And yet, Buddhidhan’s mind was full of misgivings. Will I ever get to see this house again? Will I meet my family again, or is this the last time we are together? I could not even embrace Devi as I left. Oh God! What is to happen? Will I ever meet my Alak and Kumud again? My son Pramaddhan ...? Such thoughts crowded his mind as he looked at the beautiful women of his household gathered at the door to see him off. But the body moved on and dragged the mind with it. And as he left his home behind, he became immersed in thoughts about the palace. Buddhidhan, who was born poor, could see many obstacles between him and the Karbhar. He could also see the various means and instruments he had employed to remove them. He was accompanied by his strange party, all differently attired, preoccupied in their own thoughts. En route, they met Shathrai and his entourage. They all walked together, and yet they were visibly distinct. With them walked Navinchandra, a part of the procession, and yet distanced from them all. He attracted everyone’s gaze, and yet remained unrecognised. He observed this whole new world with new eyes.
chapters.summary: Shathrai's household buzzes with lewd plots for court, contrasting with Buddhidhan's solemn preparations and his deep foreboding about the impending legal confrontation.

chapters.title: The King, Palace and Administration
paragraphs: King, Palace and Administration The moon behind the western mount is sinking; The eastern sun is heralded by dawn; From heaven’s twin lights, their fall and glory linking; Brave lessons of submission may be drawn.⟨fn:13⟩ Rana Bhupsinh’s palace was situated at the centre of a sprawling garden, which was encircled by a high wall. The wall, built to resemble the ramparts of a fortress, was about ten yards high. The lime-wash on the wall had gone black in some places and was patchy in others. Masons on raised platforms were busy repairing it. A canopy of green leaves could be seen protruding over the wall. Some trees in the garden had dried up or shed their leaves; their bare brown branches grazed against the green leafy ones, as if to render them barren, too. Some mango trees were in bloom; they glistened and swayed in the morning sun. Like a white bud emerging from dense foliage, the upper stories of the palace could be seen rising from amidst this green copse. The palace was better looked after than the garden or the walls. The original palace had been a two-storied building. Bhupsinh had added two more levels to it and they were visible from the garden. The upper stories were smaller than the original two floors, with a view to giving stability to the structure. The third floor was smaller than the second floor, while the fourth was the smallest of them all. The fourth floor contained only one large bed chamber. It had been decorated in what Buddhidhan imagined to be ‘Bombay style’. The walls of the bedroom were made of small pieces of glass. Each piece was smaller than the width of two palms and was set in a rosewood frame. Some were square, some oval, while others were hexagonal in shape. Deep red curtains covered the glass walls and were kept open at some of the windows. The openings in the curtain were square or triangular in shape. Some pieces of glass were coloured and reflected the sun’s rays. The reflection dazzled the eyes of those who gazed at it even from outside the palace walls. The palace looked like a lissome Kathiawadi woman who insisted on wearing skirts and silken blouses even after girlhood was left far behind. The surrounding walls were like the block-hemming of a flared white chaniya. The trees reached beyond the walls like a blouse with red patterns and gathers that came down to meet the skirt. Their green branches and round tree tops resembled breasts straining against a tight blouse. The upper floors of the palace were like a head emerging from the torso, and the glass palace shone like two sharp, gleaming eyes. Like a piece of jewellery in the parting of a woman’s hair, a parrot came and sat atop the glass palace. The coloured glass looked like tattoos on the woman’s face. The palace, a solitary imposing figure, stood under the blazing summer sky. The procession which approached it in the heat of Chaitra was drenched in sweat, their faces red in the heat and their clothes wet with perspiration. They walked faster as the palace came closer. The approaching shade gave their legs new vigour. Just like a child playing in the heat runs home to the mother when hungry, leaving its playmates behind, the men thought of the Rana as they left town and neared the palace. Their minds craved intrigue and hungered for the fruits of their machinations. The courtiers now rapidly made their way towards the palace, like a king’s chariot surging ahead, leaving the others behind. The crowds of citizens thronging near the palace made way for the courtiers.

The palace gate was large enough to accommodate the approaching procession. Its two thick doors were covered with strips of metal. There was a room on top of the gate for the palace drummers who made announcements regarding the passage of time, important events and ceremonial days for the citizens. A raised platform on which canons could be placed ran along the length of the wall. There were steps leading up to the platform from several points. The room above the gate had doors that led to it. Behind the doors were two large platforms where the soldiers sat, slept, chatted, polished their swords, lined up their guns and guarded the palace. Today, they stood in line near the gate and saluted the officials as they entered the palace. Two soldiers on horseback moved between the palace and the gate and passed on instructions. Beyond the gate, there was a thick cover of trees and bushes on either side of the avenue and waterways filled with clean, sparkling water. Sparrows and pigeons quenched their thirst, splashed and dipped into these canals and flapped their wings dry. The rhythmic drone of the wheels that drew out this water filled the air. The bare feet and dark, stout, sweat-soaked bodies of the labourers and gardeners toiling in the garden and the waterways were not incongruent with the surrounding garden. Navinchandra, raised amidst the artificial landscape of Bombay, realised as soon as he entered the gate that man had not tried to impose his artifice over God’s creation here and traditional wisdom was not yet forgotten. He could see descriptions that he had read in old books come alive before his eyes. All around them, guava, pomegranate and custard-apple trees were to be seen in abundance, laden with fruits. Flowers of many different colours, shapes and fragrances filled the eyes and nostrils with God’s munificence. Parrots, peacocks, cuckoos, sparrows and pigeons flew from tree to tree, pecking at the fruits. The flapping of their wings and their sharp calls filled the ears. Navinchandra recalled with pity the landscaped gardens of Bombay that delighted only the eyes. He grew contemplative. Amidst the tall, solitary trees, the lonely statuesque palace and the endless coppery sky above, Navinchandra was filled with the sense of his own insignificance, his smallness, and he was duly humbled. He understood the desires felt by Raja Dushyant in the forest abode. Cowper’s description of the deep, long whistle of a soaring kite came back to him. He could feel the sense of quiet take possession of the others as well. He suddenly felt very lonely, and the absence of his parents and the home he had left behind in Bombay seemed to crush him like an immense weight. Remote, unfriended, melancholy, slow, Or by the lazy Scheldt, or wandering Po; Or onward, where the rude Carinthian boor Against the houseless stranger shuts the door; Or where Campania’s plain forsaken lies, A weary waste expanding to the skies: Where’er I roam, whatever realms to see, My heart untravell’d fondly turns to thee; Still to my brother turns, with ceaseless pain, And drags at each remove a lengthening chain. Eternal blessings crown my earliest friend, And round his dwelling guardian saints attend: Bless’d be that spot, where cheerful guests retire To pause from toil, and trim their ev’ning fire; Bless’d that abode, where want and pain repair, And every stranger finds a ready chair; Bless’d be those feasts with simple plenty crown’d, Where all the ruddy family around Laugh at the jests or pranks that never fail, Or sigh with pity at some mournful tale, Or press the bashful stranger to his food, And learn the luxury of doing good.⟨fn:14⟩ He murmured softly to himself: Oh, Kumud Sundari! I shunned you. But you came even closer. Am I now to be charged with your well- being? Home. Friendship. Love. Can these ever be forgotten? The beauty of a pure mind. Beauty imbued with knowledge! Is my craving for you inevitable? No ... No! Suddenly, the drummers began to beat their drums, and Navinchandra looked up, startled. He saw the flag flutter proudly atop the palace, and the procession came alive. His reverie broken, the surrounding scenes rushed into his consciousness. The traveller remembered where he was. Never before had such thoughts come to anyone whilst walking through the palace gardens of Suvarnapur; and if they had, no one would have had any inkling of it. No one was capable of comprehending or fathoming his thoughts; and for the world that was Suvarnapur, this was best. With this realisation, his mind became quiet again. A path with trees on either side led to a circular grove. From its centre, a path led to the royal palace. The palace faced the east, but it also had entrances on other sides. At the eastern entrance, Vijay Sen and his troop of soldiers stood with their swords drawn. An old but powerful elephant also stood there. His large domed head swayed from side to side as he looked at the passers-by with grave but curious eyes. The small bell hung around his neck tinkled when he moved his head. The horses were acquainted with him and stood quietly beside him without fidgeting, but their ears would perk up every time the little bell rang. The grandeur and intelligence of this animal greatly impressed those entering the palace. Rana Bhupsinh had just arrived at the court riding upon this beast. Matangraj, the elephant, had served many rulers previously and was also familiar with the Karbharis. He raised his ash-smeared trunk and lowered his head as Shathrai and Buddhidhan approached him. Shathrai walked past him. Buddhidhan went up to Matangraj, patted him on his trunk, spoke kindly with his keeper to inquire after the elephant’s health, and rejoined his group. Matangraj looked at Buddhidhan. Navinchandra noticed, and was surprised, and he entered the palace with his mind crowded with all kinds of thoughts. The court was to assemble on the first floor of the palace. A wide staircase, covered with an embroidered carpet, with a brass balustrade led up to the first floor. Removing their shoes in a heap on the ground floor, the procession climbed up and entered the palace stateroom. The stateroom was immense—enough to accommodate between fifteen hundred and two thousand persons. An expensive woollen carpet covered the floor. A gold and silver-plated throne was placed at one end of the stateroom. Its armrests were shaped after lions; silk cushions with gold embroidery had been kept on it. A thick intricately patterned carpet with gold embroidery covered the area in front of the throne, extending almost halfway across the hall. The sun’s rays filtered through large, multi-coloured windows into brass-lattice doors, filling the huge hall with light. On the opposite wall were artificial windows of similar colour and shape. There were also large cupboards that created a similar effect. In the alcoves of the windows, plain glass tables were placed on which figurines, bone china and other such fine objects were kept. The walls of the stateroom were sky blue, painted to resemble the curtains of a playhouse. The roof was decorated with bright red paint, glass chandeliers, and other bits and baubles. A curtain with gathers made from embroidered cloth hung from the skirting of the roof. Seen from below and around, the stateroom resembled an enormous bed— it stupefied the mind and induced an infatuated sleep; those caught in this delusionary slumber saw dreams of regal grandeur, forgot their reality, and thus struggled fiercely with the desire for power. The Karbharis and officials gathered in the stateroom. Some moved around, some stood at the windows, some looked into the mirrors, some looked up, some looked down, some joined in chatter, some moved about busily in preparation for the assembly, some stood, some sat, some waited, some reflected, some stared, some strained their ears, some looked on stupefied, some asked for news, some gossiped, some passed on information, some predicted the outcome of the day’s events, some pondered their own future, some conjectured the future of others, some were enthused, some were anxious, some were dejected, some tried to hide their sentiments, some tried to gauge those of others, some veiled their animosity and spoke affably, some saw through this, some were taken in by it, some matched wits, some spoke bluntly, some were intent on revenge; and all of this was reflected in the myriad glass bulbs, the cut-glass, the shining brass, and also in the eyes, ears, words and minds of all those who observed, heard and thought to a greater or a lesser degree; some reflections were big, others small, some clear, others hazy, some shallow, others deep; their form and colours were different and so was their constancy. This entire scene made a profound impact on Navinchandra who stayed close to Buddhidhan all this while, and for that reason attracted the attention of everyone present. As if he were at an exhibition of English goods, or watching statues that moved and spoke, or in a marketplace where a foreign tongue was spoken, Navinchandra stood aloof and distanced from it all; he was like an ascetic in a world of householders. He looked intently at all this activity and grandeur, astonished, observant and analytical. He likened himself to the multi-faceted, multi-hued glass that refracted the sun’s rays, and smiled at his own comparison. The humble, ordinary denizens of Suvarnapur crowded onto the rich woollen carpet, pushing and jostling, and settled down noisily. Some stood and stared like rustics, some stood apart gravely, some came forward as if they had a rightful place at court, some saluted court officials, some excitedly pointed out known officials to their kin, some puffed up with pride when some official returned their salutations. Thus, the people, who should have been the ones to be saluted and honoured by the rulers, who should have been the boon- granting Kamdhenu of Kings and all their officials, they surrendered their pride to officialdom and became meek and enthused and awed in the face of such majestic splendour. Navinchandra’s eyes were focused on their simple enthusiasm. When he turned around, he saw Shathrai and Buddhidhan standing at a far window by themselves, talking and smiling at each other like old friends. He was astonished. Suddenly, there came a solemn call from the hall adjacent: ‘Your kindness be upon all, Your Grace!’ The assembly was as startled as a muster of peacocks surprised by thundering clouds, and then everyone scrambled to their appointed places. Shathrai sat to the right of the throne. Next to him sat Karvatrai, followed by Dushtarai, after whom the other officials and functionaries took their place by rank. Some even took a place higher than their rank, leaving others to grumble. Buddhidhan took his seat to the left of the throne, and Pramaddhan sat next to him. Navinchandra sat behind Pramaddhan. Samar Sen, his sword tied at his waist, stood behind the throne to the left. The group that had accompanied Buddhidhan, including the school headmaster, also took its place. The Bhayats sat at some distance behind the Counsellor and his son: their beards and moustaches were shaped differently; they wore headgears woven in golden thread and had daggers and swords at their waists. Just then, Kalavati walked in with a party of musicians. She shone bright as a jewel, her lips stained red with betel leaf juice. She and her musicians sat in the centre of the vast stateroom. The assembly was entranced, their eyelids grew heavy as if they were about to surrender to sleep. They gazed at Kalavati with lascivious eyes, as if where she sat was in fact a bed, and she the lone waiting woman on it. At that moment, there were scarcely two or three people there who saw anything else. Navinchandra observed the movements of the assembly’s eyes. Jaymalshankar whispered something to Buddhidhan, who leaned back to hear him. Narbheram, who sat behind Shathrai, looked intently at Jaymal and Buddhidhan. ‘Dushtarai was in Kalavati’s room checking on something,’ said Jaymal, sounding out of breath. ‘What for?’ the Counsellor asked, concealing his eagerness to know. ‘I do not know, but he was fooling around with her.’ ‘Right here, in the palace?’ the Counsellor asked, as if surprised. ‘Yes. Narbherambhai and I were with Ranaji at the time. Narbheram was reading out today’s English newspaper to him. Suddenly, he saw something through these new, English-fashioned louvers, and stopped reading the newspaper.’ ‘Then?’ ‘Ranaji asked, Why did you stop? What are you looking at? Narbherambhai pretended that nothing was the matter and replied,

Nothing at all. But Ranaji insisted on knowing and he looked through the louvers himself, and then he lost his head.’ It was as if nectar was poured into Buddhidhan’s ears, but nothing in his outward demeanour betrayed this. ‘Did Ranaji say anything?’ ‘His hand went to his sword and he rushed to the door, his eyes breathing fire.’ ‘Oh!’ ‘But Narbherambhai went and held Ranaji back, whispered something to him, and sent me away from there.’ Buddhidhan thought it over briefly and said, ‘All right, go take your place.’ In a little while, he signalled to Jaymal again, called him close and said, ‘Go up to the top floor window and look out for the horse-carriage that is to come from Lilapur. The moment you see it approach, come and tell me. No one else should know about this.’ ‘Very well,’ said Jaymal and quietly left the assembly. Narbheram did not understand what had transpired and stared at Jaymal’s receding back. He returned his gaze to the Counsellor and then, like everyone else, focused his eyes on Kalavati and the two courtesans who flanked her on either side. He engaged Shathrai and Karvatrai in a conversation about which of them was more beautiful. Just then, the door behind the throne opened and chants of ‘Maharana, your kindness be upon all!’ and suchlike rang out. The assembly stopped looking at Kalavati and turned towards the Rana instead, like a gust of wind. It was as if the entire stateroom rose up as one man—all the surrounding mirrors attested to this, as did the hearts and minds of those present. Two thousand persons bowed low in greeting. Salutations rained and countless hands went up to as many foreheads in greeting. The Rana’s garments were woven of gold and silver threads. He wore diamond and pearl ornaments. The gold handle of his sword was studded with a diamond. His crown, worn over embroidered headgear, was also bedecked with diamonds. The Rana’s body was redolent with perfumes. He was a feast for the senses. He walked in regally, looking joyous, his chest thrust out. He looked at Shathrai, smiled at him, and took his seat on the throne. Everyone else took their seats as well. The royal ushers crowded in behind the Rana. On either side, servants fanned him with gold-embroidered fans. On one side stood Vijay Sen, his sword drawn. He served as the Rana’s bodyguard. This was the tradition of Suvarnapur palace at times when the court was in session. On the other side stood Ranjit, with the golden regal standard. Roses and other flowers, perfumes, rosewater, paan wrapped in gold and silver foil were placed in front of the Rana in large plates of silver. A sarangi player set the tone and Kalavati began to sing in her sweet, melodious voice; mridangam and sitar accompanied her. Spring was nearly over, but she sang spring compositions which were the Rana’s favourites. She also sang a Hori, usually sung at the time of Holi. I will not live in your city Krishna robs me in broad daylight! The assembly was delighted, captivated not only by the singing but also by the ardour of the beautiful courtesan. The soulful notes of the sarangi and the chords of the sitar moved them. The gathering was entranced. Kalavati came to the last stanza: No one dare question his tyranny There is no justice in this city The Rana, seething inwardly, composed an unpoetic response to Kalavati’s song in his head: Then don’t live in my city Whore: in broad daylight, you cheat me! Jaymalshankar returned just as Kalavati was singing the last lines. He whispered something into Buddhidhan’s ear. In a few minutes, the assembly heard a horse-carriage screeching to a halt and was jolted out of its trance. Russell Sahib’s Shirastidar, Ramchandra Rao, entered the hall accompanied by a soldier. The singing stopped as people made way for him to pass. Buddhidhan got up to receive him, and Shathrai stood up to shake his hand. The Rana accepted the Shirastidar’s salutations while remaining seated. Ramchandra Rao took his seat between the Rana and his Counsellor. The Rana enquired after the Sahib, and Shathrai asked the purpose of his visit. The Shirastidar replied, ‘I will tell you after the assembly has dispersed. It is nothing urgent.’ Kalavati took advantage of this interruption, got up and went to change her costume. In the meanwhile, a soldier had come up to Ranjit and whispered something to him. Ranjit called Dushtarai to a corner and said, ‘Bhai Sahib, do forgive me, God knows I am true to my salt. But do you know your Merulo? Do you know him at all?’ ‘He is better than you.’ ‘Indeed. Bhai Sahib, this opportunity will never come again. He knows that you are stuck here, and he is at home with ...’ ‘Rascal, I will cut out your tongue!’ Dushtarai would have hit him if they were not in court. Ranjit fixed Dushtarai with his good eye and said, ‘Bhai Sahib, this has to be done right now. Go home quietly, and see with your own eyes. If I am lying, put your sword to my neck.’ The Faujdar returned to his seat, but his mind was in a whirl. He fumed and fretted, but could not betray his emotions. Peace eludes those who doubt. He decided he must go home under some pretext. But nothing could possibly be more important than what was to happen in the assembly. Dushtarai took his father’s leave, saying that someone at home had taken very ill, and promised to return soon. In his anxiety, he forgot to take any soldiers with him. The soldiers were engrossed in the courtly spectacle, so they did not see him leave, and no one offered to accompany him. The Faujdar left the assembly alone. When Kalavati went in to change her costume, her place was taken by other courtesans. Some of them sang better than her, but the courtiers naturally praised the Rana’s favourite. These courtesans sang beautiful tappas and thumris much to the delight of the citizens. But the courtiers chose to neglect them and loudly talked amongst themselves instead. The singers felt angry and insulted, but were helpless. They sang even louder and more melodiously in the hope of catching the Rana’s ears. Buddhidhan quietly asked the Shirastidar for the Sahib’s letter, and read it. Shathrai asked for it, too. Buddhidhan gave it back to Ramchandra Rao and signalled that it should be sent to Shathrai by the ‘long’ route. The Rana asked for it, read it, and handed it to Shathrai. Karvatrai also leaned forward to read it. Ramchandrabhau had been sent by Russell Sahib to ascertain facts about the bania who was Karvatrai’s victim; he had to examine and report if the bania was still imprisoned and what his family’s condition was. The Sahib had written to the Rana to request him to facilitate Rambhau’s mission. The letter was read and discussed in whispers. Shathrai returned the letter to Rambhau, and looked around for Dushtarai who had not yet returned. Narbheram realised that Shathrai was worried. Buddhidhan and Narbheram exchanged a pointed look. Shathrai would have liked to give the task to Karvatrai, but Karvatrai was himself the object of inquiry. So he finally decided on Narbheram. Leaning close, Shathrai spoke into his ear, ‘After the assembly, we have to take up the matter of Rajba. But this obstacle has to be removed before that. Go out, write a note to the jailor that the bania should be released immediately. He should be given money and frightened into giving suitable answers to Rambhau. See to this, and return soon. Meanwhile the assembly will also wind to an end, after which Rambhau can begin his inquiry.’ ‘Whom shall I send the note with? Can Jaymal be trusted?’ ‘Yes, send him; he is one of our own. You be where you are required to be.’ Narbheram got up and left, but not unnoticed by Rambhau. The Shirastidar had been Buddhidhan’s subordinate in Lilapur, and had good relations with the previous Shirastidar, Sadashiv Pant. Buddhidhan had therefore cultivated his acquaintance. There were two or three contenders for the position of Shirastidar when Buddhidhan left the post. Rambhau was the likely choice and Buddhidhan had supported his claim. Shathrai was in favour of another candidate. When Rambhau had still occupied a low post, Shathrai and men from his office had ill-treated him. Rambhau had taken this insult to heart. Therefore, while he might have accepted bribes from Shathrai, he still wanted to get even with him. Rambhau did not see the bribes as any favour done unto him. He believed that Buddhidhan would also pay him, if he became the Karbhari. Moreover, bribes were paid because they needed favours from him. Buddhidhan knew Rambhau well and he also knew how to keep an upper hand in their dealings. Buddhidhan had cultivated proximity with Russell Sahib, which allowed him to exercise authority over Rambhau. Buddhidhan had also used his relations with the Sahib to Rambhau’s advantage. This apparent selflessness had helped Buddhidhan forge closer ties with the Shirastidar. This Dakshini brahmin was sharp. The moment he saw Narbheram leave the court, he became restless. He addressed Shathrai, ‘Karbharisahib, I will go and complete some personal work while the assembly is underway. I wish to return to Lilapur soon, upon fulfilling the Sahib’s order.’ ‘Very well.’ Rambhau discreetly asked Buddhidhan, ‘Who supervises the functioning of the prison?’ ‘Tark Prasad,’ Buddhidhan whispered in response. Rambhau got up and said, ‘Ranaji, I seek your leave. I will take Tark Prasad with me for company.’ No one could say no. The judge got up to leave with Rambhau. Shathrai and Karvatrai were both worried. They felt the bania should have been made to disappear without a trace, but the time for that was over. In hindsight, this appeared to them the best solution, and they sorely regretted the missed opportunity. What will be will be. We will deal with what comes. But doesn’t this Dakshini brahmin love his money! This thought emboldened Shathrai, who appeared quite at ease now. All this while, Navinchandra had been deep in conversation with the schoolteacher. The teacher pointed out and described all the officials of the state to him. The state of Suvarnapur was divided into twenty revenue divisions called mahals. Each mahal had officials such as the mahalkari or mahal administrator, the judge and the faujdar.

Suvarnapur was also the administrative headquarters of a mahal, and the officials who governed it resided in town. Moreover, it was also home to city officials such as the city judge, the collector of taxes and the head of city police. Official titles were a hotchpotch of Peshwai, Mughlai and English administrative titles. The titles did not give an indication of either the position or the responsibilities of these officials. For example, Dushtarai’s title was Faujdar, but he was the ‘Police Commissioner’ of the entire state. ‘The man seated next to the Karbhari is his brother Karvatrai. He gets paid two thousands rupees per annum. He has been in service for fifteen years. Their father had left them nothing. Today he is worth at least ten lakhs.’ ‘How so?’ ‘My dear sir, it is not our tradition to speak of such things. Now look, the one next to him is Dushtarai’s father-in-law. His house shines and glitters because of his daughter, Rupali. It is considered acceptable among us to seek a position when one gives one’s daughter in marriage. He has served the son-in-law well. He exercises the greatest influence and is wealthy. God has made the use of intelligence redundant for him. At present he is an official in the recovery of dues department.’ ‘Who is that?’ ‘That fat man? He wields a lot of power. People dread him. He is the Karbhari’s brother-in-law; he knows everything there is to know. To begin with, he was in the police department where he tyrannised people, both for money and for women. Buskin Sahib pressed for his removal and considering him unfit for the police department, he was anointed on the seat of justice. My dear sir, he always wished well for both parties. He never fails to return a favour. The Counsellor has made him in-charge of this mahal; now he milks both the king and his subjects.’ ‘Is there no one to check him?’ The schoolteacher chuckled. ‘Why, would your elder brother pay heed if I were to complain against you to him? Who has the guts to lodge a complaint?’

‘But irregularities and wrongdoing in the administration of a mahal would surely come to light very easily?’ ‘No, dear sir, no. You have no experience in such matters. If the Karbhari’s cook were to be made assistant Karbhari, he would be praised from the very first day. He would receive appreciation. But if some rascal were to acquire a position on his own steam, his shortcomings would be revealed immediately. Such a man cannot be capable. All right sir, do you know that man?’ ‘Yes, he is Narbheram. I know something of him. Tell me about his past.’ ‘He and the Karbhari work together to malign the Counsellor. Narbheram can plummet to the lowest level to flatter. That is his skill.’ ‘But there will be many like him.’ ‘True. But he was sent by Buskin Sahib. The Rana trusts him to an extent, and therefore, the Karbhari gives him some respect.’ ‘Hmm.’ Many officials were thus described and discussed in a similar vein. Tark Prasad had been quietly listening to them talk, when he was abruptly summoned. As he got up to leave, he put a hand on Navinchandra’s shoulder and said: ‘Now listen to my short description. All those who sit here, grave and sombre in their red pagdis, have committed such vile deeds that their punishment, if they were ever to be brought to justice, would range from monetary fines to hanging. These gentlemen who hide behind fine clothes are corrupt, thieves, debauched, deceitful, murderers, and possess many other such fine capabilities besides. They enjoy power and are entrusted with the protection of poor, innocent people, whom they devour. They mislead the world, keep the Sahibs happy through their petty politics and retain their authority. Power of money and status is the key to their success. I have said little, but you will have grasped all you need to know.’ And Tark Prasad gave Navinchandra a sly smile as he left in company of Rambhau. Navinchandra felt like someone who suddenly discovers that the person who was sitting by his side was not human but a ghost. His
chapters.summary: Navinchandra enters Rana Bhupsinh's magnificent palace, where he contemplates nature's grandeur, before Tark Prasad hints at the true, unsettling character of the assembled court officials.

chapters.title: On the Way
paragraphs: King, Palace and Administration attention now shifted to the singers. They sang unhurriedly. At times they clapped, they swayed, opened their mouths wide, made faces, lowered their eyelids in feigned coyness, rolled their large eyes, winked and gesticulated to the rhythm of their song. The assembly sat still as if in a trance, like people in a painting. Navinchandra observed the goings on, his mind preoccupied with thoughts of what the schoolteacher and the city judge had just told him. His eyes moved from face to face. He looked at Buddhidhan and felt sorry for him. The tales of the Arabian Nights he had read seemed to be coming true before his very eyes, and he felt like Aladdin trapped inside the demon’s palace. Kalavati now made her grand re-entry into the assembly, and the other courtesans stopped singing. She was dressed like one of Lord Krishna’s gopis of her imagination. She wore a broad skirt of blue silk with deep red patterns brightly embroidered on the hemming. The skirt was gathered in at the waist by drawstrings. A gauzy odhni bright as moonlight covered her head, coming down to her slender waist. Shiny anklets and fish-shaped toe rings gleamed on her feet. These and other tiny ornaments as well as her finely cut nails shone like seashells as she began her dance, to the accompaniment of the sarangi and the mridangam. Her entire ensemble gave the impression of sparkling foamy waves. The ornaments, her fair knees, the taut veins of her feet, her nails and her heels drew attention to themselves. The gaze moved to her costume only when other parts of her body were still. Her hair was like dark clouds on the horizon. Gold, diamond and pearl ornaments adorned her neck and her supple arms. She sparkled like a sky studded with stars. The sight of her fair glittering body produced a haze before the mind’s eye. Her large kohl-lined eyes came alive as she met the gaze of the assembly. Her anklets, her swirling skirt, her odhni, everything danced in rhythm as her delicate feet moved rapidly before the stunned audience. She was like lightning in a still sky. Her movements, swift and fluid, were akin to a small fish swimming in the quiet waters of a lake. She was the only one who moved. The audience sat still. She seamlessly danced into their mind’s eye, arousing fierce passions that she herself did not feel. Her flat, delicate stomach revealed itself ever so slightly as she whirled and twirled, her breasts heaved and shook, and the assembly stared at her transfixed, their passions enflamed, their breathing heavy. Her charming lotus-like face swayed like a snake’s hood, the sweet poison of her breath spread all around her. The assembly surrendered its manhood to her, and she played with them as if they were children or puppets. They waited impatiently for her song. Her eyes widened, her lips quivered, and the desires made manifest and aroused by her dance now tumbled out as a song. Let me go, O’ let me go now, Ghanshyam, It is evening now, my Lord I came in the afternoon An aeon has since passed My mother-in-law will scold My husband will ask questions People will sully my name She sang, quite impervious to the emotions embodied in the words of the song. But the assembly was captivated, and swayed to her melody as one. Bhupsinh appeared to be entranced like everyone else, but inwardly his displeasure mounted. Watching Kalavati, he thought to himself, Bitch, go, leave now! Why wait till tomorrow? She was singing the last stanza of the song. Daya Pritam says, Listen, O’ beloved we must stop here Let me go, O’ let me go now, Ghanshyam. The Rana could no longer keep up his façade—he got up abruptly as if possessed by a ghost and stormed out of the door through which he had entered. The assembly was astonished and anxious at this unexpected turn of events. The ushers shouted their customary calls which were drowned out by the sudden flurry of movement and commotion. People got up, made way, came together to enquire, and generally made noise. Buddhidhan, Shathrai and other principal court officials hurriedly followed the Rana. In the rush, rank and prestige were forgotten. The spell was broken, the mood interrupted. Kalavati

King, Palace and Administration stopped her song and dance and stood still as the entire hall milled around her and her accompanists. Some pushed past them, while others were careful not to brush against them. In the melee, Navinchandra somehow managed to hold fast onto Buddhidhan’s hand and follow him out, wondering what came over the Rana suddenly, but he had no time to indulge his thoughts as he was shoved and jostled and pushed and dragged along by the crowd. They followed the Rana down a flight of stairs to his personal drawing room. The room was large enough to accommodate a hundred to a hundred and fifty persons. A chandelier hung from the ceiling, the walls were adorned with mythical figures painted in the Jaipur miniature style, and there were paintings in the English and Chinese styles as well. There were mirrors with golden frames. There were ‘wall sets’ containing two or three frames. A mechanical music box was kept on a beautiful semi-circular table. On one wall hung a full length coloured portrait of Rana Bhupsinh. Facing the portrait, a bolster and embroidered square cushions were kept on a mattress. Bhupsinh sat down and, leaning upon the bolster, stretched his legs out. He sat there, biting his lips and frowning. His hookah was brought to him; it was intricately inlaid, one side was made of silver, the other of gold. He began to puff on it pensively. Others sat around him in silence on the carpet. ‘Maharaj, are you not feeling well?’ Shathrai asked with folded hands. They waited tensely for his response. The Rana removed the hookah pipe from his mouth and blew smoke. He seemed agitated and preoccupied. He drew another puff and said, ‘Yes. I wish to be left alone.’ Everyone got up to leave and hurried towards the door. ‘Kamdar, you stay back’, he said to Shathrai. Shathrai turned back. Buddhidhan saw this, and he looked at the Rana—their eyes met for a fleeting moment, and he went out with the others. The Rana and Shathrai were left alone in the drawing room. Shathrai sat facing the Rana. ‘Kamdar, I wish to take up the matter of these letters.’

‘Ji, very good. But what happened to you suddenly?’ ‘Don’t you know there is a limit to a man’s patience! How long can I carry this doubt in my head?’ Shathrai was pleased. ‘Ji, you are absolutely right. It must be resolved. Such behaviour is unbecoming of Rana’s trusted advisor.’ ‘Is everything in place? There is no need to make it known to all; after all the disgrace is mine as well. You go and send in the Counsellor alone.’ ‘Everything is in place. Narbheram has gone out; he will be back soon,’ and Shathrai got up to leave. The Rana looked at him; Shathrai appeared perturbed and sympathetic to the Rana’s distress, but he was of course delighted at the turn of events. In a while, Buddhidhan came in alone. He was acutely apprehensive, even frightened as he entered. Never before had he experienced such a state. But masking his fear, he put on a grave mien and waited for the Rana to relate to him his conversation with Shathrai. He needed to show courage. As soon as Buddhidhan entered the drawing room, the Rana burst forth. His conversation with Shathrai was either swept aside, or the Rana deliberately chose not to mention it. The Counsellor could not fathom the reason. ‘Buddhidhan, your counsel for patience must be drowned in a well now. I cannot contain myself any longer and wait for the assembly to be over. My mind is not in my control.’ ‘Why, Ranaji? What could be so serious?’ Buddhidhan asked with evident concern, but the cause of his concern was something quite different. ‘This man, your Dushtarai, was flirting with Kalavati in my palace—behind my back!’ ‘Oh! When? Ranaji would recall what I had said: a courtesan cannot have only one paramour.’ ‘Yes, yes. What all will I have to recall, Buddhidhan? So many of your predictions have come true, but we are barely in our right mind to reflect on them at this moment. I would have finished both of them today—this fellow Narbheram stopped me. I still doubt if he is

King, Palace and Administration your man. How long can I tolerate if that bitch sings in my assembly? Buddhidhan, I want to finish them off, I tell you, there is murder on my mind. I could not bear to sit a moment longer in the court. You must act fast. That is why I got up. Any further delay, and you and I shall not get along.’ The Rana spoke agitatedly, and he puffed on his hookah, kept shifting on his seat, unfolded his legs and folded them again—his unease was all too apparent. Buddhidhan’s hope was restored, but a shadow of doubt still lingered. The Rana had still not told him of his conversation with Shathrai. ‘Ranaji, the resolution you seek from me is very much within your grasp. I am here to carry out your wishes.’ ‘Yes, that is so, but what do you intend to do? Where is that rascal Dushtarai?’ ‘Shathrai is also anxious; he has sent messengers to fetch him.’ ‘All right, but what have you decided?’ the Rana pressed him for an answer. Buddhidhan hesitated for a fraction, he was still not fully confident of the Rana. ‘Maharana, you have yourself read the letter brought by Russell Sahib’s Shirastidar, Rambhau. Other skeletons will also tumble out. I hope that a remedy for Shathrai will emerge from them.’ ‘How?’ ‘You are aware of the discussions I have had with the Sahib. How can I be certain before I know of the contents of his letter? But Ranaji, rest assured your wish will triumph.’ ‘But Kalavati’s bluff has to be called today! Both of them will be made to ride a donkey—that is for sure!’ ‘You take that up on my signal.’ ‘But, today itself, Buddhidhan.’ ‘Yes, of course, Ranaji.’ Just then, an out of breath Mahvo rushed in through one of the side doors. The Rana was enraged. ‘Mahvo, you rascal, don’t you know that I have asked to be left alone?!’

‘Ji Maharanaji, I know, and that is why I came in. I am your servant; I would not want that your disgrace be made public. It should be dealt with in secrecy.’ Buddhidhan looked up in fright. He saw Mahvo carrying a bundle of letters. Mahvo flung them at the Rana’s feet and stood with folded hands. Rana’s eyebrows were raised as he skimmed through the letters. Buddhidhan calmly asked, ‘Mahvo, what is it?’ ‘Bhai Sahib, what right do wretches like me have to speak when the letters are with the Rana? Are you yourself not a confidant of the Rana?’ ‘Very well,’ said Buddhidhan and turned towards the Rana. He recognised the letters. Mahvo looked on with supreme disdain as he saw that the Counsellor’s authority was paralysed. The Rana threw the letters at Buddhidhan, and snarled, ‘What vile ploy is this, Mahvo? You should be hanged! Have you no shame in bringing such a charge against my trusted Counsellor? Have you no fear? Do you think I am so naïve and foolish as to be deceived? Buddhidhan, my friend, have no fear about the letters.’ Mahvo smiled ingratiatingly and said, ‘O Saviour of the poor, we poor are always wretched. Would I have the courage to bring before you forged letters? The Counsellor is your trusted man. He has done me good as well. But your kindness has been immense. If I did not believe that my duty towards you is foremost and paramount, I would not have done anything to harm the Counsellor. God alone knows the mental agony I have endured while doing this.’ Buddhidhan stared at Mahvo during this little speech. ‘Mahvobhai, it is quite unnecessary to state how faithful and loyal you are to the Rana. That you also remember my kindness speaks well of you. The good deeds of the past must for now be put aside. But do be fair to me, and furnish proof that I am indeed the author of these letters. Do also tell us as to how you came to be in possession of them.’ The Rana, who had been biting his lips in anger, now banged his fist and thundered, ‘Enough! I need no proof from you, you wily rascal!

King, Palace and Administration I am not going to believe your fabricated lies. Such brazen depravity! Go, go and blacken your face, miserable wretch. Shathrai! Kamdar!’ Shathrai rushed in. ‘Kamdar, have this rascal Mahvo arrested at once and hand him over to Dushtarai. Where is he?’ ‘He is on his way, Ranaji.’ Shathrai sat down next to Buddhidhan and asked him softly what the matter was, but before he could answer, Bhupsinh thundered, ‘Kamdar, look at these poisonous letters! This worthless lowlife has taken on our own Counsellor! Incredible! If Dushtarai is not present, call a soldier, take this wretch away! Who is guarding the door?’ This was the first time ever that the Rana had to himself shout for a soldier; the officials waiting outside cringed. ‘Ji, Huzoor!’ Vijay Sen entered the room, and holding Mahvo by the arm, took him away. The Rana slumped back on the bolster, exhausted. Buddhidhan protested, ‘Ranaji, this is not right. You should view the proof that Mahvo has. To you I may be innocent, but I must be so for the world as well.’ ‘Forget the proof. What was done is correct. To glorify the wicked is to make them swollen-headed. If we seek proof from them, they assume even greater airs and participate in other intrigues,’ Shathrai said solemnly. ‘Ranaji, my plea must be accepted.’ The Rana sat up straight and said in a low voice, ‘Shathrai, the Counsellor is right. There is a reason why I scolded Mahvo; the lowly should not be given much importance. But I have heard such rumours from other sources as well. I do not believe in them. But Buddhidhan, do not take it amiss, I too am human. If not today, I may doubt you tomorrow. That would not be good; yes, I think we must do as you have suggested.’ ‘Ji, Ranaji.’ ‘Kamdar, have the matter examined. Meanwhile, I will go to the queen’s quarter. The queen knows something about the matter which I must now ascertain for myself.’

Buddhidhan was unsurprised by this deep-rooted conspiracy of Shathrai. But he knew that the Rana trusted the queen, and that worried him. The Rana got up with an air of finality and walked towards an internal door. As soon as the door opened, there was a loud crack, like a gunshot. Bhupsinh hesitated and looked around in surprise and alarm. ‘Oh! God save the King!’ Shathrai and Buddhidhan shouted as they rushed towards the Rana. Suddenly, the floor beneath the Rana’s feet gave away, and he fell through it. But Buddhidhan ran and caught the Rana firmly in his arms, and both of them managed to come out and stand aside on secure ground. In seconds, the floor began to cave in from all sides and the hole widened to expose a large tunnel, four or five feet wide. The marble came loose and fell into the gaping cavity. The beautifully inlaid marble floor looked like it had been ravaged by an earthquake. The heavy wooden frame of the door balanced on the gaping hole like a bridge. Others now rushed in, excited, frightened, apprehensive. Suggestions, possibilities, theories flew thick and fast. ‘Intrigue! Treachery! Trap!’ shouted Buddhidhan as he encircled the Rana with both arms. Samar Sen, Vijay Sen, Pramaddhan, Jaymalshankar, Navinchandra and others who had come with them swiftly encircled the Counsellor and the Rana. Samar Sen and Vijay Sen drew their swords and stood prepared on either side. Navinchandra waited for a sign from Buddhidhan. The palace soldiers rushed in. Shathrai, who knew nothing, was momentarily stupefied. His eyes searched desperately for Dushtarai. ‘What ever happened?’ he asked and rushed to the Rana’s side. Karvatrai and other officials followed him. ‘What are you staring at! This is a crime against the State! The work of some vile traitor! Maharana, God preserve you! Ranaji, are you hurt? Vijay Sen, commence an investigation at once! Remove this debris and go into the tunnel, be careful, and keep your weapons in readiness ... Be careful, the floor is caving in!’ Buddhidhan shouted out instructions like a man crazed, but all the while he held on firmly to the Rana. The effect was dramatic.

King, Palace and Administration ‘What is it, Buddhidhan? Let go of me! What has possessed you? Let them all go to hell. What is that? A light inside the tunnel?’ Bhupsinh, recovering from his initial shock, tried to enter the tunnel. But Buddidhan was adamant and forcefully held him back, ‘No, no, Maharanaji! The fate of Suvarnapur cannot be endangered at any cost. Please stand back. There are many others to do this. Kamdar, you come along with me!’ Buddhidhan ordered Shathrai who was standing there looking dazed. Bhupsinh was glad to see Buddhidhan’s loyalty for him being exemplified, he was reassured. He looked at Shathrai, his mind crammed with doubts. Meanwhile, Vijay Sen, Samar Sen and other court officials were hard at work like labourers trying to remove the heavy debris. A path was soon cleared, and they entered the tunnel through a narrow gap in the floor. Inside the neatly dug tunnel that lay before them, they now saw two figures dimly silhouetted by the light of a lantern. Jamal Khan and Ranjit. Jamal held the lantern, while Ranjit’s sword was drawn. ‘Catch them! Arrest the traitors! Bring them up!’ loud shouts were heard from inside the tunnel, which were echoed by those anxiously waiting on the outside. As the news spread like fire, many others now rushed to the spot, guards, court officials, townspeople. Soldiers and palace guards caught the two and dragged them out of the tunnel.
