People were surprised to see the duo, especially Jamal Khan, who was himself a soldier in service of the palace Karbhari. They began to thrash them. As he watched all this unfold before his eyes, Shathrai was too crestfallen for words. He observed Buddhidhan, as if from a great distance, and submitted to the overwhelming numbness that was coming over him. The Rana knew quite well that Jamal Khan was Shathrai’s confidant. Questions flooded Shathrai’s mind, but no answers. How will I explain Jamal’s presence? Will the Rana believe me? Can the Rana’s rage be contained? What will be the outcome of his wrath? I had searched for that wretched Jamal everywhere, in every possible nook and cranny. How, why, and on whose instructions did he resurface today? And of all places here in this tunnel? Where on earth is Dushtarai? Why has he not returned? Is all of this related to Rambhau’s mission? Buddhidhan must have orchestrated all these events ... Who else but he could be behind this? Even as he searched in desperation for a last ray of hope, the wise, old and experienced Karbhari of Suvarnapur could see his fate sealed. Like the waning moon that disappears as the first rays of a new sun light up the skies, his heart could see no light, darkness enveloped him. He could no longer think clearly as an ominous foreboding and fear gripped his mind. Anticipating the impending disaster, his intellect was the first to take leave of him, and then his patience. He knew, his other faculties and people would also leave him. Like a fortune teller, he could read his own future. He felt weak. Dark thoughts clouded his imagination, he saw a macabre dance of the dead. All the sins of his past now caught up with him. He had failed to fathom the import of the Rana’s order of having Mahvo arrested—the truth of it now dawned upon him in all its frightful dimensions. He could see all his wealth destroyed before him. He thought of his son Dushtarai, and his mind froze like blood in the veins of the dead. Even the tremendous excitement and commotion of his surroundings failed to stir him, and Shathrai slumped down exhausted like a yoked bull upon the nearest chair. The Karbhari of Suvarnapur, known for his formidable political acumen, his all-encompassing capacity for intrigue, his razor-sharp intellect to which even kings submitted, that Karbhari now sat impotent and numb. His mind blank, his virility drained, Shathrai looked and felt like an old man as he sat helplessly on a chair, his hands folded across his lap. He felt that all the means and resources available to him were now futile. Kaba had robbed Arjun of his bow and arrows. Navinchandra, too, had been surprised to see Jamal Khan emerge from the tunnel. As the day’s astonishing events played out, he could suddenly see things quite differently. Various fragments and pieces of the grand puzzle fell into place the moment he saw Jamal. Navinchandra now knew that he would not need to carry out the instructions that Buddhidhan had given him that morning. Shathrai had indeed planned for something, but the events had overrun his plans. Thinking of all this, Navinchandra recited to himself:

King, Palace and Administration He comes full of desire but he will leave head shaven, Name besmirched, rolling in dirt. He was amused that such couplets came to him, and at such times. He had heard Vanleela sing parts of Rukmani Vivah to Kumud Sundari, and the verses had stayed with him. Kumud Sundari came to his mind, too. Like him, she too had witnessed the Counsellor spend many sleepless nights. All those sleepless nights are now about to bear fruit, he thought—what strategy, what intellect! Buddhidhan, you found an ingenious way of punishing the offender without any discredit to your own family. And Jamal Khan, if you had not done what you did, I, Navinchandra, would never have gained this invaluable experience. Buddhidhan, you turned adversity into opportunity, difficulty into possibility. From where did you learn this? Certainly not in school! Astonishing! Navinchandra’s mind whirred and hummed busily with his thoughts and observations of people in positions of power and political intrigue. The courtiers enthusiastically came together to beat Jamal and one-eyed Ranjit. The Rana had to intervene and stop them. Buddhidhan ordered: ‘Samar Sen, take some men with you and trace the origin of this tunnel. But be careful. Ranaji, please hand over Jamal Khan and Ranjit to Vijay Sen. This investigation should proceed in complete secrecy—am I right, Kamdar Sahib?’ Buddhidhan looked around for Shathrai. Hidden behind the crowd, Shathrai responded from a far corner, ‘Yes.’ ‘Come here, Kamdar! Why do you sit alone at the back? What is wrong with you today?’ said the Rana, looking in the direction from which Shathrai’s voice came. People moved aside to clear a passage between Shathrai and the Rana. The Rana walked towards Shathrai. Speculation was already rife ever since Jamal’s capture from the tunnel, and Shathrai’s subsequent and evident despair. Shathrai finally got up from his chair and walked in slow, dejected steps towards the Rana. It was not as if he was slow, or his walk unusually hesitant, but his face lacked all lustre, all hope. The preceding events had coloured the perception of observers and their minds had already arrived at certain conclusions. The courtesy shown by the Rana, and his cordiality, thus seemed artificial to many. The Rana held the Karbhari by the arm, and said, ‘My most experienced, most devoted and loyal Kamdar, your help is of utmost importance now. You know (and Bhupsinh looked towards Buddhidhan) I can no longer trust my old confidants. But if you too remain despondent, whom shall I look towards? Now, do reveal the full intent of this play—call Dushtarai immediately.’ As he spoke, the Rana neither let go of Shathrai’s hand, nor did he remove his eagle eyes from the Karbhari for a moment. ‘Oh yes, trusted and truthful Karbharis are required on just such occasions. Their true worth is recognised only at such trying times,’ Bhupsinh said, twirling his moustache. Each word that the Rana spoke singed Shathrai, each syllable uttered was like a snake bite. The sky and the earth collapsed into each other. Shathrai no longer knew whom he could trust, whom he could turn to. Then, suddenly, he saw the man. Narbheram had just returned and stood whispering in Karvatrai’s ears. Karvatrai looked at Shathrai, and he felt sorry for him. The judge’s capacity for intrigue was nowhere close to Shathrai’s. Karvatrai was not as imposing as his brother, but had a stout physique. Shathrai’s hair had greyed and signs of age were visible on his body. Karvatrai was young and strong; his moustaches were firm and black, he had dyed his hair to hide a few grey strands. He was more courageous, his mind was less rational compared to his elder brother and hence he had greater capacity to bear suffering. His eyes knew no shame; compassion and goodness were strangers to his heart. His intellect grasped no need to follow the path of truth and justice. But he loved his family, and he was moved by his brother’s plight. He had seen and followed what others had seen, but he had not fathomed even half of what his brother had. He was bold and strong in his belief that nothing could possibly go wrong for him and his brother. Karvatrai now went and stood next to Shathrai in solidarity, and turning to the Rana, said: ‘Maharanaji, our police will get to the

King, Palace and Administration root of this rebellion and the traitors will be duly punished. The dust of your feet is glorious. This task would be accomplished in a moment. The enemies of the Ruler of Suvarnapur are certain to be destroyed.’ ‘Without a doubt,’ Shathrai spoke up; his brother’s presence gave him the courage. ‘Buddhidhan, call Dushtarai! Remember the words of the Karbhari. My enemies are certain to be destroyed!’ the Rana smiled at his Counsellor. The Counsellor returned his smile, and replied, ‘Ranaji, you say your enemies are certain to be destroyed. But I know they already are.’ ‘But where is Dushtarai? Buddhidhan, words speak louder than deeds, at least those uttered in the presence of rulers.’ ‘Most certainly they do, Ranaji.’ Observers were perplexed by these cryptic exchanges. Karvatrai sensed victory; he felt the Rana was about to bring up the matter relating to Rajba. Shathrai’s understanding was quite the contrary; he glared at Buddhidhan, hatred evident in his eyes. He brought the small exchange between the Rana and the Counsellor to an end. ‘Maharana, at this moment, we need to act, not talk. We must get to the root of this. My brother and I, along with some other officials, must leave the palace at once. Buddhidhan, come with us. We must investigate; your presence will be useful.’ As an escape route flashed before him, Shathrai felt the blood flow back into his veins. He felt he must quickly escape the Rana’s clutches, and leave him with Kalavati and Narbheram. If matters went out of hand, Bhupsinh could be killed, or Shathrai himself could flee Suvarnapur with his family and wealth. This was his new plan. In any case, Buddhidhan should not be allowed to stay with the Rana. Sharp enough to recognise that Shathrai was clutching at the last straw, Bhupsinh did not allow him to get away. ‘No, Kamdar, I cannot let you go. I am deeply disturbed by today’s incidents. You must stay with me and give me solace.’ The Karbhari had thrown his dice. He was disappointed that the outcome was not to his liking.

‘Kamdar, call Dushtarai. Why do you not follow my command?’ Before Shathrai could formulate his response, Karvatrai said, ‘Ranaji, Narbheram has just returned from home. His news is that Dushtarai is unable to come, his physical condition does not permit it.’ ‘Oh! What happened to him? He was here a while ago? Has there been some treachery at your house, too?’ ‘Ji, Ranaji, there is some such matter,’ Narbheram replied. Shathrai and the others were startled. ‘What is the matter? Narbheram, what has happened?’ ‘I cannot speak of it. Please forgive me.’ ‘Will you not obey my command?’ ‘Here is the man who can speak!’ and Merulo rushed in, breathless and wounded, his arm covered in a bloodstained bandage. He fell at the Rana’s feet, howling, ‘Tyranny, cruelty, O Maharana! There is tyranny under your rule! Please save me, oh my saviour!’ He wept loudly. The soldiers knew that Merulo was a favourite of the Faujdar, and one of them tried to lift him up. Just then, some noises in the tunnel drew their attention. Samar Sen and his troop could be seen herding Raghi, Nichdas and Khoda out of the tunnel. Everyone looked at them. Karvatrai could see his fate eclipse. He had lost heart after hearing Narbheram’s report, but he put up a brave face. Merulo’s presence frightened him about the home front. Samar Sen’s captives scared him even more. Dushtarai had rushed home. He was alone. He saw the soldiers posted at home chatting outside. He went in. The door was shut. He climbed up on the first floor and looked down into the courtyard. He was blinded by what he saw. Some game was on. Merulo was dressed up like a Muslim man and Rupali and Khalaknanda were dressed as his wives—they were acting out their parts. Having hitherto restrained themselves in the presence of others, they had now abandoned the last vestiges of shame. Khalaknanda heard some noises on the terrace and, startled, she hid inside. Enraged beyond belief, Dushtarai drew his sword and came down to the courtyard by another staircase. Taking Merulo by surprise, he cut him on the arm with his sword. Wounded,

King, Palace and Administration Merulo promptly gave up all qualms and engaged his master in a fierce wrestling bout. He snatched away Dushtarai’s sword. Dushtarai called out to the guards outside for help and opened the doors. The soldiers rushed in. But before that, Merulo wounded Dushtarai with his own sword and ran out from the back door, throwing the sword towards Rupali as he ran, shouting, that she should either save him or kill him. The sword fell in a corner. Dushtarai’s wound was deep and he fell down. Khalaknanda saw her brother being injured, but feigned complete ignorance and lay down on a swing. Rupali was at her histrionic best, weeping and beating her breast. The soldiers considered arresting Rupali, but decided against it. They shut the doors and placed guards on them. They told her: ‘Woman, we will tell the Karbhari of your deeds, we won’t let you off.’ Rupali went up, dressed up as a man, took Dushtarai’s sword and jumped onto the roof of the adjacent house. The surprised neighbours followed her, but she managed to escape and rushed out onto the street, and a few streets later, she was indistinguishable in the crowd. She walked unhurriedly to Merulo’s house. Merulo’s brother was at home; she spoke to him, gave him all the information and sent him out to look for Merulo. Narbheram had left the assembly on pretext of doing the work assigned by Shathrai, but he followed Dushtarai instead. Narbheram wanted to witness the fun and also report it back to the Counsellor, who would find the information useful. He met Merulo on the way, who was trying to run away. Narbheram stopped him and advised: ‘Go to the palace this instant and lodge a complaint against Dushtarai. Their sun is about to set; you would be believed. If you hide, you will only prove your own guilt.’ Narbheram taught him what he should say to the Rana. Merulo said: ‘I will first go home and only then to the palace. No one has seen me except Dushtarai, who is about to die. The one who has seen me will not report me. I should go and alert my brother.’ He met his brother on the way. Both of them went home and met the waiting Rupali. Merulo sent her off with his brother to a village that was within the territory of another state. He then proceeded to the palace. Narbheram went to the prison, but found Rambhau and

Tark Prasad already there. These two had travelled by a horse-drawn carriage. They found the bania in the prison. Rambhau was quick to gauge things. Narbheram heard him and rushed back to the palace. Shathrai was busy talking to the Rana, so Narbheram narrated the events to Karvatrai. He told Karvatrai he had met Merulo who was going to lodge a complaint against Dushtarai, and also the events that had led to Merulo’s injury. Karvatrai was sorry to learn of the family’s disgrace; he certainly did not want his family to be shamed in court. Merulo was about to complain about Dushtarai, which could not be countered without divulging details. A thief was about to punish his guards, and Karvatrai did not know how to counter Merulo’s charge, since Narbheram had not told him that Merulo had grievously injured Dushtarai as well. People were stunned to see Merulo wounded. They asked him about the cause of the wound. Shathrai was clueless. He went up to Merulo, still believing him to be the family’s confidant. ‘Kamdar Sahib, you can no longer save me. My complaint is against the Faujdar.’ Shathrai drew back as if stung. ‘Ranaji, I have eaten the Kamdar’s salt. It is not right for me to badmouth his family. But I have no option left. I came to know some secret matters relating to the palace and the court in which the Faujdar was a party. He came to know that I knew. He believed I would not be able to keep his secret. See what he has done to me. He would have killed me if I had not run away. I am afraid to go back home, hence I have come here seeking refuge.’ ‘What was that secret?’ asked the Rana. ‘Oh Maharanaji! How can I speak of it before you? Such things happen. It is nothing but some intrigue. But, my Provider, I am not as lowly as Mota Bhai Dushtarai took me to be. Please protect me until my complaint is resolved or till such time as I leave for my native village. Please ensure that I am under the protection of your trusted men so that the policemen do not harass me. I do not want anything else. I am a poor man.’

King, Palace and Administration ‘But what was the secret matter? How do I know if you are right or wrong? Such a rascal—you evaded my question!’ ‘Maharanaji, I will tell you if you insist, but only you.’ Merulo looked at Shathrai as if frightened. ‘The Kamdar, too, has a right to hear your lies, so speak up. A lie, and you will be killed.’ ‘Ranaji, I have invited trouble for myself. Please forgive me, Kamdar Sahib, I have no option but to tell. Ranaji, there was something about a tunnel to be built between that pond in your garden and Kamdar Sahib’s office room. It was to be built on the Kamdar’s orders. I came to know of it. Kamdar Sahib, I tremble, please do not be angry. Oh, even Jamal is here! Ranaji, Jamal knows all about it! Please ask him. Let me go, my provider. Please do not ask me anything more. Jamal will tell you everything.’ ‘Lowly rascal! Vijay Sen, take him away!’ ‘O Maharana, is it your way to punish those who seek justice! I made a mistake. Never again will I complain. You are our provider. You protect us. Please let me go home. My house is better than your prison. The policemen will harass me, but let that be. But I have done no crime to deserve imprisonment.’ The Rana was surprised at Merulo’s courage and loquaciousness. ‘Fine. Go home. Vijay Sen let him go. Investigate his complaint, and report back to me.’ Merulo happily saluted the Rana and left. ‘My dear Kamdar, so do you see how cunning men can be? People who work for us, be it at home or in the state, must be faithful and rooted; or else, you have seen the result. He did not hesitate while placing a charge against my trusted officials. How could he break into his master’s house? How could he have the heart for it? What is even more surprising is that he ate your salt, but has none of your qualities.’ The Rana looked at Shathrai gravely. Meanwhile, Rambhau and Tark Prasad had returned from the prison. Shathrai realised he could no longer bribe Rambhau. Rambhau had met the bania in the prison and had all the facts in his possession. If Russell Sahib alone had to be tricked in this matter, it could have been done by bribing Rambhau. Shathrai realised that the Rana would be eager to take advantage of the matter. He sighed deeply and thought to himself, When the sky bursts, it cannot be patched up. Things were different when Rambhau had left the court earlier today. I was still the Karbhari. But the situation is now changed—Shathrai, the time when you could get things done with money is past. Formally accusing Shathrai and Karvatrai in the matter, Rambhau said: ‘Ranaji, Russell Sahib holds you in high esteem. But such Karbharis would cause you immense harm. It is true that he has been Karbhari for long now—but he is like an old disease. The Sahib knows well about the tyranny and cruelty in your state. He has said nothing hitherto and hoped for reform. But his hope has proved to be false. If the Sahib were convinced that no reform is possible, he would have taken different measures. He is convinced that the Karbhari does not allow complaints and pleas to reach you. You are not the one to tolerate tyranny if you were aware of it. If the Sahib were convinced that you do not have any able person in your service, he would most certainly recommend some outsider. But he knows well that you do have able and honest officials for whom the interest of the people is paramount. But the Karbhari has rendered them ineffective. However, the Sahib also believes that when you realise the true condition of your state, these officials will be ascendant and people will be happy. I am not authorised to say anything more. I place before you all the complaints that the Sahib and the Government have received about your administration. You are requested to have the matters properly investigated. The Sahib has sent these English newspapers which describe good and bad officials of your administration, and has left the comparison to you. He generally does not rely upon newspapers, but in this matter, his views match with those of the newspapers. Hence, the Sahib has sent them. Please have them read to you by some honest, English educated person and acquaint yourself with the details. And yes, I am asked to communicate a message from the Sahib. He believes that one should not fall behind the times. You must bear this in mind.

King, Palace and Administration You should employ English educated persons who can help you keep abreast of our times, persons who know English statecraft, laws and ethics. The Sahib’s letter deals with other issues also. I have nothing more to report as his representative. But I have a personal request. It is not a secret and hence it is not improper to mention it in the presence of the assembly. I am a well-wisher of your state. I am unfit to give counsel but if you will be so kind as to hear me, I wish to say that rarely is an officer as good and just as Russell Sahib posted in the native states. His advice is worth its value in gold. Your Counsellor knows the Sahib well, and would be able to speak with greater eloquence and experience and substantiate what I have said. The Counsellor has worked in the Agency, he has served you, and the Sahib is well acquainted with him. The Agent Sahib is pleased that you trust the Counsellor. He believes that so long as such individuals are part of your administration, both the people and you will benefit. The Counsellor would tell you the advantages of accepting the Sahib’s advice. Ultimately, it is within your powers to accept or reject all such advice. The good and evil results of your actions are also your responsibility. We can only advise. You hold the reins of the administration. The results are a prerogative of the Gods. I have nothing more to add. Kamdar Sahib, pray do not blame me. I am merely a messenger.’ The Shirastidar’s solemn speech came to an end. The assembly had frozen while he was speaking; it remained frozen like an image a little while longer. Rambhau took out wads of papers and newspapers from a cane basket carried by a soldier and gave them to Buddhidhan who stood beside the Rana. The officials looked at each other quizzically, whispered questions and guessed what the letters had in store for them and others. Finally, Rambhau handed to the Rana a square envelop that contained a letter from the Sahib. The Rana immediately opened the envelop, read the letter and responded after some thought: ‘Ramchandra Rao, there is no need to say that the Sahib is my well-wisher. His affection is evident in the letter. The Sahib’s advice is proper; there have been incidents today itself that prove that his assessment is correct. My eyes have opened. I am sorry that I bestowed my trust on one who was unworthy of it. Please go to the rest house and have your meals. I will send my response within an hour or two.’ Rambhau saluted the Rana and left. Shathrai could not look up. Buddhidhan looked at the Rana intently, awaiting orders. Other officials were also eager to hear the Rana’s decision. Rana Bhupsinh scratched his forehead, smoothed his moustaches and began: ‘Buddhidhan, I am confused. Kamdar, I am very sorry. Your fate is beyond my control until all these papers and newspapers are read, the matters examined and the root of rebellion and treachery found. But yes, it is time for me to remove all illusion. Kamdar, you and your cronies are vile, wicked and faithless—of that I have now no doubt. I know well that the letters given to me by Mahva, intended for Buddhidhan’s destruction, are forged. I know the author of those letters, and I also know that you are the source of the intrigue. You must be punished for it. I am very sorry. I am also extremely angry. How different can people be! Buddhidhan is of one kind, and you Shathrai are quite another. Have I done any less for you? Have I deprived you of anything ever? Have I not trusted you enough? No, the fruits of my deeds cannot be such!’ and the Rana shook his head gravely. ‘I have no more compassion left for you, Shathrai. Buddhidhan, you have counseled me thousands of times to be kind, to be liberal, to forget enmity and be good. And I have curbed my instincts and submitted to your advice. But no longer. The very men you were trying to save from my wrath have perpetuated such vile treachery to cause your downfall! Thank God that He showed me the right path, or else what would have become of you? But this demon did not even stop at that. This stupid fool, in my own palace, tried to ... But no, it is not worth mentioning. Is there anyone so blind who cannot see what is apparent to all? Officers, if you are wise, learn your lessons. Your ruler is not blind like others—he sees with his own eyes. Russell Sahib is naïve. He thought that Shathrai had truly deceived me. He does not know that I knew everything all along, but that I deliberately kept quiet. I have not been in the dark about the tyranny and cruelty faced by my poor people. Shathrai would have ceased to be a Karbhari

King, Palace and Administration long ago, but for Buddhidhan. But enough is enough. His evils have caught up with him. He is crushed under the weight of his own sins. Buddhidhan, I will no longer accept your advice on this matter. Vijay Sen! Vijay Sen! Arrest the Kamdar and his brother and keep them as under trial prisoners under your charge. Arrest Dushtarai as well, and keep the three of them separate. Be on your guard. None of them should be allowed to escape or talk to anyone else. Your own life is at stake here. Lock up their houses and place your guards there.’ Buddhidhan suddenly fell at the Rana’s feet and said with folded hands, ‘O Saviour of the poor! I have a humble request to make!’ ‘Get up! What is all this drama? Get up and ask. Have I ever denied you anything?’ The Rana caught Buddhidhan’s hands and tried to lift him up. ‘No, Ranaji, no. I will get up only after you hear and accept my plea. Shathrai is my caste brother and also a distant relative. Please do not send them to prison, their religion cannot be observed in prison. You cannot be like them, Ranaji.’ ‘All right, all right. Vijay Sen take them to some other place, but keep a strict watch over them. Ensure that they are provided with food and drink. Anything else? Shall I arrange for sweets to be sent to them? Tell me, Buddhidhan!’ ‘No, Ranaji, you are most kind. All else can wait.’ The Rana ordered: ‘Vijay Sen, arrest that bitch Kalavati and drag her to the prison. I want to see her dragged though the dusty streets in her silken and embroidered garments, her ornaments strewn on the streets to be found by beggars. Vijay Sen, I want to see a man who is the most wicked, the darkest among the dark, the ugliest among the ugly and the filthiest among the filthy, an outcaste, rub dust, ash and black soot all over her body, face and hair. Detain all the others involved in this treachery. All of them will face an investigation and be duly judged.’ The Rana then asked Jaymal to come closer, and whispered to him, ‘I am going to assign you a difficult task. I do not want to see the queen’s face. Take her to the old palace and keep her there.

‘Officers, you know that today is my birthday. The day did not begin joyously. That does not matter. My people have been freed from suffering and tyranny. They would celebrate. That is for me a matter of festivity. Moreover, the court will assemble as scheduled at five in the evening. I will give you enough reason to celebrate. The Counsellor and I will together plan as to how that is to be effected. ‘Shathrai, we are about to part ways. I am sorry that we had to see this day. But do not incur the wrath of Gods by putting the blame on me. The kingdom of God allows each one of us to earn merit by our good deeds. ‘Buddhidhan, come with me. You are the only one who can show me a way out of this morass.’ The Rana took the Counsellor’s hand, and they walked away together. Before leaving with the Rana, Buddhidhan signaled to Pramaddhan and Navinchandra that they should go home. Shathrai had no strength left to formulate a response even in his mind. The clothes on his body were the same, his body was the same, he was the same man. He had entered the palace of Suvarnapur in full glory that morning like the midday sun; but the sun had set when he was about to leave the palace. He was dethroned. But pride shone on his face like the last flicker of a dying lamp. A pride that was incongruous to the moment, barren, bereft of light and impotent. No one noticed his pride. Everyone looked at this Karbhari whose power and glory had waned. He took his leave of the royal palace where for years he had ruled uninhibited over kings. Officials and people had believed his authority to be eternal. He would not return to the palace. Shathrai felt a terrible void. The palace suddenly seemed like a dense and dangerous forest. Shathrai emerged from the palace, forlorn, and looked around with vacant unseeing eyes. The pride and glory of being the royal Karbhari, that had once been his, accompanied Shathrai upto the gates of the palace garden, and then turned back in search of the man who would take his place. A single tear glistened in his eye. He almost had to run to keep pace with the new guards that Vijay Sen had posted. For the first time, he was required to keep pace with the

King, Palace and Administration soldiers, instead of the soldiers keeping pace with him. His condition was like that of an impoverished and failed student. People pointed fingers at him, some with pity, and this momentary attention passed on to discussion about impending changes in the administration. People seemed to rejoice at his fall. His only companion was his brother Karvatrai. Finally, they disappeared from the sight of onlookers. He was soon out of people’s minds as well. Talk about the tumultuous events of the morning turned to eager anticipation of the court to be held that evening. People had entered the palace noisily. They emerged from it in silence, as quiet as midnight. No one said a word. Each face looked grave and pensive, as if they had emerged after a reading of the Ramayana or the Mahabharata, or were returning from a crematorium having consigned a body to flames, having collected the ashes and dried their eyes. The only sound was the crunch of their feet. They had followed Shathrai to the palace; they left it without him. Navinchandra and Pramaddhan were among the last to leave, accompanied by two or three soldiers. Their faces looked peaceful and free of fear. The group that had come with them also left for their respective homes. As Navinchandra’s eyes trailed after Shathrai, these words rose to his lips: Time ordains both strength and weakness: For one in the spring of his youth Time turns the sweet call of the swan Into the harsh cry of the peacock. Yes. Time ordains both strength and weakness. Time alone arbiters between power and the loss of power—nothing else but Time can do this. Man, your pride is incongruent. Shathrai, it is not that your conspiracy has failed, but your time has been defeated, mused Navinchandra as he walked. They had barely reached the gates of the palace garden when Samar Sen came running, and breathlessly urged, ‘Pramaddhan, Bhai

Sahib has called for you! Navinchandrabhai, please go home quickly; Bhai Sahib and Pramaddhan will be there soon. Ramsen, accompany Navinchandrabhai.’ Samar Sen and Pramaddhan went off in one direction. Navinchandra and Ramsen went another way. New thoughts swirled in Navinchandra’s mind like sparrows flying overhead, and he walked at a brisk pace.

Navinchandra was among the last to leave the palace. A guard walked behind him. They walked back in silence like two shadows on the long desolate road surrounded by vast fields under the blazing summer sky. Navinchandra was exhausted, and ravenously hungry. It was noon; the road was fiery hot. The unrelenting sun beat down upon him, draining his tired mind and body. He was drenched in sweat. Sweat poured in streams from under his pagdi. His eyes and cheeks were red with the heat. Why are you in this state, Navinchandra, he asked himself. Images of the inviting cool and quiet of the Counsellor’s house, still far, were suppressed by the tumultuous and fiery scenes he had just witnessed at the palace. He had seen, experienced and learnt a great many things, both at the Counsellor’s house and at the Suvarnapur palace assembly. The one in search of experience had been presented with rich learning opportunities. Yes, that could not be denied. But the satisfaction and pleasure of having learnt from these new experiences were not uppermost in his fatigued mind just then. He thought of home. He was hundreds of miles away from home, and yet all at once thoughts of his parents and friends filled his mind, bringing a rush of memories in their wake, and a sharp yearning. From the road, he could see the point where the river Bhadra met the sea. For an instant, he felt a strong impulse to take a boat. He became oblivious of his surroundings, of the presence of fellow travelers; he did not know where the road led or why he was walking upon it. ‘His eyes were in his heart, and that was far away.’⟨fn:15⟩ His heart was at home, and home was in his heart. Nothing of Suvarnapur, not one object, not one individual had come to belong in his mind. And yet, there was one person in Suvarnapur who had a place in it. Kumud Sundari, the daughter-in-law of the Counsellor’s family, occupied a central place in his world. Kumud Sundari, why are you here? Navinchandra, what is the matter with you? You remembered home when you entered the palace gardens. And now again. Why? Why do you think of Kumud Sundari and home inseparably? These and other similar questions rose sky high like tidal waves in his mind. Some incidents of the Counsellor’s family interspersed his thoughts. Navinchandra, are those events responsible for the present condition of your mind? Dear reader, you should be acquainted with those incidents. While he was recovering from his injuries at the Counsellor’s house, Navinchandra had observed and experienced much. He had been wounded trying to protect Alak Kishori’s virtue; Alak was immensely grateful for this. She had sat by his bed, attending to him, till his wounds had healed and he had fully recovered. She had no respect for her husband whatsoever. She treated the whole world with derision, and her husband was no exception. She showed no deference to anyone except her parents. She did not however believe her mother to be intelligent. She wielded power over her friends. She did not consider anyone, including her husband, to be her equal. She did not know what it was to love someone as an equal. But yes, Alak Kishori was capable of affection. She was true to her word and compassionate. It never occurred to her that any one could be worthy of deference or respect, that she could set aside her arrogance, be that of money, beauty, virtue, wisdom, intelligence, status or family, and be amiable, be affectionate and cultivate an equal friendship. This quality was dormant in her father. Buddhidhan’s daughter, and not the son, had inherited this quality. Her brusque and haughty demeanour was on account of it. She had been able to protect her virtues because of this quality. Whenever she looked at any man, her inevitable response was: Who is he? How dare he compare with me? Who am I, and who is he? Do I succumb to anyone? Is anyone fit to be my equal? Her pride had thus remained undiminished. Ultimately, it was two individuals who vanquished her pride. Affection that she had hitherto given to none, she gave to her sister-in-law. Kumud Sundari drew warmth unasked from her; Alak felt affectionate towards Kumud. One reason was Kumud’s gentle and loving disposition; the other reason was that she was Alak Kishori’s choice. Alak would become effusive and sentimental whenever she was with her sister-in-law. People would laugh at her. Her mother, too, would laugh at her daughter’s exuberance. Alak Kishori knew this, but she disregarded what others said. She even scolded her mother: ‘What is it to you? I will be what I like with my sister-in-law! You do what you have to do.’ She could even forget her own beauty in the presence of Kumud and sat meekly when Kumud read out passages from books and explained them to her. Alak was not even conscious of not being haughty around her sister-in-law. Kumud allowed Alak to run the household, was deferential to her in public and followed her around; this satisfied Alak Kishori’s ego, and her affection for her sister-in-law deepened. But those who observed them closely realised that it was Kumud who ruled over Alak, and that it was she who followed Kumud. It was Kumud’s subtlety that did not allow Alak to realise that she was under Kumud’s influence. Alak’s pride melted before Kumud. The other person who robbed Alak Kishori of her pride and hauteur was Navinchandra. She was beholden to him. She never left his bedside. She looked after his medication and comfort and all his other needs. She sat by his side even when he had visitors. Her friends also sat in Navinchandra’s room. Concerned, her mother advised and cautioned her: ‘It is good that you care for him, but it is not good for you to sit by his bed all day long alone, or in the presence of visitors. People will gossip. After all, he is a man and a stranger. Have a servant sit there with him, and you supervise from afar.’ In response, Alak snapped at her, made a face and said, knitting her brows, ‘Oh, I know how people are. Who cares about people! As if they are the only ones possessed of wisdom and virtue! They can ridicule me all they like. I don’t care!’ Resigned, her mother could only respond, ‘All right. Do what pleases you.’ So Alak continued to sit by Navinchandra’s bedside, freely mocking people and their interfering, over wise nature. She also received her visitors in his room. Kumud, shy as she was, would always hesitate to enter Navinchandra’s room, though her room was adjacent to his. Alak would often drag her to his room, saying: ‘Bhabhi, he is like a member of the family. Why should you be shy of being in his room? He is educated, and so are you. Sit here and read something nice. I will listen to you read, and so will he. He could even explain things that you may not understand. And since I am there, it shouldn’t be a problem for you.’ She would catch Kumud by the hand and make her sit. Kumud experienced thousands of inarticulate desires. She read when forced to. She listened, but not once did she allow herself to smile, converse or engage with Navinchandra in any way. In all the days she spent there, not once—not even for a moment—did she gaze straight at Navinchandra. If either she or Navinchandra wished to say or ask anything of each other, they did so through Alak Kishori. Even as Alak tended to him night and day, Navinchandra was aware that such overzealous care, even if sincere, was contrary to social conduct. He also recognised that by her insistence, Alak had put Kumud in a difficult situation; but he felt helpless in the face of his illness and Alak’s stubborn disposition. Gradually, women began to gossip about Alak Kishori. It was blown out of proportion by those jealous of the Counsellor’s growing power and influence. People enjoy gossiping about prominent families. Vanleela told Kumud about it, but Kumud treated it with disdain. Vidurprasad too heard the whispers and braced up to confront Alak Kishori, but was duly subdued after she lashed out at him angrily. He was subdued, but not convinced. One day Garbaddas was invited to their house for a meal. Alak Kishori bathed before entering the kitchen to cook. The bathing area was dark. Garbaddas took advantage of it and made a pass at her. In response, Alak threw a ladle full of boiling dal on his face and ensured that the lecherous man never entered their house again after that day. Garbaddas stopped harassing women. Vidurprasad was convinced of Alak’s chastity. Alak Kishori’s unfettered conduct thus emerged unscathed and victorious. She was so proud of her chastity and autonomy that she was unafraid of associating with those of loose morals. She would say: ‘A buffalo has to bear the burden of her horns—if others have low morals, what is it to us?’ She had among her friends some unchaste women and some who were brazenly sensuous. And Alak Kishori was particularly fond of them for this reason. Alak’s sensuality and physical desires may have remained unexpressed with her husband; but with her friends, she was completely frank and free. They also reciprocated her emotions. This was the reason for Alak’s excessive fondness and partiality for Krishna Kalika. No one had the courage to tell her to give up the company of such friends. This base association did not remain fallow for long. Krishna Kalika became infatuated with Navinchandra. But she could not, on her own, fulfill her desires. So she decided to make the Counsellor’s daughter an accomplice. Alak frowned upon licentious behaviour. Let alone men, she did not permit any lascivious praise of women. Krishna Kalika saw that Navinchandra had made a pure and immaculate impression on Alak, and decided to use this to her own advantage. She would praise Navinchandra’s good nature, his virtues, his learning. She also praised his handsome looks. Alak Kishori was overwhelmed by Navinchandra’s chivalry in saving her from dishonour. She heard his praise with pleasure. Krishna Kalika surreptitiously introduced vile thoughts in her praise of him. One day she spoke of his physical beauty and moved on to talk about mismatched couples. Then, emboldened, Krishna Kalika said: ‘Behn, you truly deserve a husband like Navinchandra; Vidurprasad is all right, but just so. It is like a crow that got the sweet dahitharu.’ Alak Kishori scolded her for her foolishness, and the matter ended there. She too forgot about it. After an hour or two, Alak went into Navinchandra’s room. He was fast asleep. He had to be administered his medicines. She stood there, uncertain if she should wake him. His wounds were healing, but they needed to be dressed afresh and bandaged. His fever had subsided now, but he needed to be given medication. He was advised not to exert himself, and had gradually regained some of his former strength. His face looked brighter, his cheeks glowed. A fine film of perspiration glistened on the broad forehead of the sleeping man. Manmatha, the God of Passion, sat unseen and formless between Navinchandra’s dark, manly eyebrows. His arrows pierced the heart of the helpless woman, who all at once trembled with an unknown desire. She, Alak Kishori who dazzled everyone who set eyes upon her, was herself dazzled. She watched in wondrous awe as his lips quivered in sleep and opened ever so slightly in a pout, as if ready to drink nectar from her lips. Alak could not fathom what was happening to her. She had never before experienced such emotions. She had not even heard of them. Whom could she have asked? Breathless and confused, she sat down on the floor by the side of his bed. She watched him breathe to a gentle rhythm. What was this man doing to her? Why did he seem so strangely transformed today? A vicious and potent desire possessed Alak, subduing even her pride and chastity. She stifled a deep moan in her throat. There was a mirror on the wall. In this mirror her face appeared adjacent to his. She looked up at their reflected faces. Krishna Kalika’s words now rang through her ears. The mirrored image gave testimony to her words. She recalled how she had tightly held on to Navinchandra the day Jamal was captured. The memory of that touch tickled her imagination, she liked the sensation. Alak who had fought Jamal like Ma Chandi and robbed Garbaddas of his dignity, Alak who was fiercely proud and free now appeared powerless to resist the charm of the sleeping Navinchandra. She lost her capacity to think. The image of the sleeping man rode upon the turbulent waves rising in her heart like the full bright moon. Her heart churned. No one could see her turmoil. Fantasy is like a monkey. Krishna Kalika had stoked her imagination. The fantasy moved unbridled between her mind and heart, it petrified the pure and chaste Counsellor’s daughter. It laid bare the wounds inflicted upon her by passion. She could no longer bear it. She mumbled, ‘Har, Har, Shiv, Shiv’ to calm herself, but to no avail. There are many who desire, even worship this state of inflamed uncontrolled passion. It gives pleasure to many. But it turned Alak Kishori frail and weak. There was no escaping its power. Navinchandra! Are you asleep? The virtuous woman could not plead for release. Tears rolled down her eyes. Just then Navinchandra turned on his side. As he turned, his hand moved and came to rest on Alak’s shoulder, startling her. The sudden unexpected touch was pleasurable. She felt at last she was about to be freed from the terrible pangs of desire. Her lips trembled in a smile. But her conscience, too, fought to the last—she felt agonised that she allowed his hand to rest upon her, that she did not remove it. It was as if Alak Kishori’s strong virtues propelled her hitherto unexpressed desires to manifest themselves even more strongly. She was not content with this slight touch and hungered for more. Desire, in the guise of gratification, exerted greater force. The touch did not bring a sense of release but of bondage and it sapped her mind and body. It spread through her like poison. This excruciating agony took the form of tears that refused to dry. Navinchandra’s unsteady hand slipped further down and came to rest where all desires are harboured. Alak Kishori’s warm tears fell on his hand. Sensitive to the wetness of tears, his hand moved. Pushed beyond endurance and willing to break all limits, Alak recklessly caught his hand in her own and pressed it to her wildly beating heart. Navinchandra opened his eyes partially, yet he remained in slumber. His eyes could not believe these dream-like scenes. What! Even he does not remove his hand? Did his mind, too, echo her desires, then? Or did he think it was a dream? What a great fall! Lowly company allowed this base fantasy to flourish. Fantasies of the mind became bodily passions. A body inflamed with desire permitted an illicit touch. A touch she had no right to, but one she accepted, allowed it to linger, to grow on her, to rest on a part of her beyond the scope of a stranger’s touch. She held on to his sleeping hand when it moved as if by a divine command. Oh, most virtuous woman—you have lost your chastity by just this one act. Many times while administering medication, you inadvertently touched him. And still you were virtuous. But the touch of the same body makes you a fallen woman today. You are impure! One friendship, one fantasy. What consequences! Like you, has Navinchandra also become sullied? Did the Gods witness this? Did the walls register it? Did either of them realise that someone else had witnessed them? Or was it that others could see, but the two of them had been blinded? Strange are the ways of God. Hitherto, Alak Kishori had never felt the need to close the doors of the room. Her mind was pure, so was her conscience. Like always, the doors were wide open, for she had entered the room with an entirely different mind. She had her back to it. Unknown to her, a pair of eyes watched her intently. Who? Women, especially young women of the same inclination and age, are quick to form a friendship. Krishna Kalika and Alak Kishori were friends while Vanleela and Kumud Sundari had grown fond of each other. Vanleela was playful but wise, lustful but virtuous; she was fond of reading and singing, and though not given to vilification, she did enjoy watching others being compromised. She had learnt singing from Saubhagya Devi; she possessed a high-pitched voice and wanted to scale it up further. She was always ready for a lively debate in Alak Kishori’s company. Vanleela visited Kumud daily. They would converse privately, play chess, sing to each other, and Kumud would read out interesting passages from books or poetry to her. Like always, after finishing her meals and household chores, that day too, Vanleela had come to meet Kumud. She had glanced into Navinchandra’s room in passing, and seen his hand on Alak’s shoulder. Startled, she had stopped to take a closer look, and then rushed to tell Kumud who had always scorned at the rumours. ‘Bhabhi, you refused to believe them; now come and see with your own eyes!’ ‘Vanleela, you haven’t changed. Let them be. Why should we bother about them? Don’t we have anything else to do?’

‘Oh, why such indifference! Can’t we even look? Come on. They are so engrossed in each other, they won’t notice us if we stood there for half an hour. Come!’ and Vanleela caught Kumud’s hand. But she had no clue how pained Kumud was, what turmoil it caused her heart and soul. Could Vanleela be speaking the truth? Oh learned Sarasvatichandra! What is this? What am I being told? Did you forsake me for this? Or are you in fact Navinchandra? Are you not Sarasvatichandra? You cannot be him. My Sarasvatichandra—though mine no longer—was pure. No, you cannot be him. Kumud Sundari freed her hand. ‘Vanleela, you may go. I will not come.’ ‘What will you do here?’ ‘I will sing and play my sarangi.’ ‘Would you rather sing than see them? I never knew anyone like you!’ ‘So be it. You go on.’ Vanleela was surprised at Kumud’s indifference and lack of curiosity. She went and stood near the door. Having rid herself of Vanleela, Kumud returned to her place. Her eyes brimmed over with tears. It was as if she had seen her husband with another woman, or as if she herself had been violated. She flung herself on the bed and cried her heart out. Then as abruptly, she got up, wiped her tears and stood in the middle of the room. How can I allow you to be so disgraced, Sarasvatichandra? I will not let you tread this path. You have erred, but I shall reawaken your virtues. You will come to your senses. If you walk such a vile path, what will the world come to? How can my heart bear to see you like this? How will my heart hold? Can Gorakhnath bear to see his disciple Macchandra beguiled by lust? O Baba Gorakhnath, come to my aid. Give me your strength. Sarasvatichandra, why have you come to such a pass? Water, if you want to flow downhill, who can stop you!’ Her eyes full of tears, she picked up the sarangi. She sat down on a chair that was close to Navinchandra’s room, and began to sing. Her voice carried to the room adjacent.

She who resides in the heavens white Fell down onto the Lord’s head Having fallen once, she fell again Not being contained by the Lord She fell onto the mountains And thence further, even lower Twisting and turning, she fell onto the earth Gathering dust and grime in her wake Sullied Ganga eventually entered the salty sea She who falls is destined to meet such an end A fallen mind is destined for dissolution Never before was Kumud Sundari’s song heard outside her room. Today, she broke free. Her voice opened up. Tears flowed down her cheeks as she sang. Her sarangi was wet with tears. She poured all of her pain into the song. Sapped of her strength, as she sang the last lines, she fainted, and the sarangi fell to the ground. Kumud’s lotus eyes closed and her mouth parted slightly, revealing her pearl like teeth. Her arms hung limp, her body became lifeless and inert, her tears dried on her pale face; only her tender breasts, witnessed by the lifeless walls of Pramaddhan’s bed chamber alone, moved to the rhythm of her beating heart. There was no one to see this. In a house full of people, you were alone. There was no one to care for you, Kumud Sundari. In the next room, Navinchandra had woken up, but he was still in-between sleep and wakefulness and incapable of recognising either state. Alak Kishori’s touch had induced a pleasant dream. This was his first ever experience of such a touch. Even when his eyes opened, he felt he had woken from one dream into another. He gazed at Alak Kishori with partially open, dreamy, playful and lusting eyes, as if she were a part of his dream. He did not withdraw his hand, and for a moment, he was filled with pleasure. Just then Kumud Sundari’s soulful song wafted into his ears. As his ears sensed the sublime pleasure of music, the pleasure of touch numbed. His eyes shut again. Kumud’s song carried her pain as well. They suffused his heart. This was the first time he had heard Kumud sing; the timbre and melody of her voice was divine like that of apsaras. He was enveloped by a pure joy. To Vanleela’s eyes, it appeared as if Alak Kishori and Navinchandra were engrossed in each other, their steady gaze fixed upon each other. They were still as an image. Vanleela had no doubt that their desire was mutual. Suddenly, both the sarangi and the song stopped. As Kumud’s sarangi fell with a sharp thud, it broke a string and let out a long shrill sound, mingling with her broken voice and a heart-wrenching sob. It jolted Navinchandra out of his dreamy state. He was now fully awake and alert. He gently freed his hand from Alak’s clasp, and looked at her with sad yet censorial eyes. Then, in a voice that redeems one from purgatory, he said softly but clearly: ‘Behn Alak Kishori, I am like a brother to you.’ Shamed beyond words, Alak could not meet his eyes and looked down, silently beseeching mother earth to swallow her. Like a drop of water evaporates from a heated pan, her passion, her desires vanished. She neither knew how to respond nor could she move a limb; she just sat there frozen with her eyes glued to the floor. There was only one thought in her mind: Oh God! What have I done! Her head throbbed painfully. She could not look up at him. She told herself, I should either bite my tongue and take my life this instant or stop breathing. Navinchandra saw her turmoil. He solaced her and said, ‘Behn, do not be so distressed. Even Brahma erred once. Do not make the same error again. I know your conscience is pure. I am not a simpleton. What has happened cannot be undone. Put it out of your mind. Your dharma was upheld; praise the merciful God for it.’ Alak Kishori was overwhelmed and speechless with emotion. ‘Behn, get up. Please give me my medicines.’ ‘Bhai, you are truly my brother,’ Alak found her voice at last and mustered the courage to speak. ‘Navinbhai, the blessing you have given me today is far more valuable than the time you saved me from dishonour. Oh, how I have fallen and tainted myself! What have I done! My life is futile. I am worth less than dust.’ She looked up at him, her eyes brimming with tears.

‘Behn, do calm yourself.’ ‘My virtue has been compromised, and by my own hand. I cannot bear the shame of it! What face will I show the others now?’ ‘People know nothing. God alone was witness. He is most compassionate.’ ‘True; but this disgrace, this ignominy is beyond endurance—I, Alak Kishori, fallen! I can no longer live.’ And she ran out of his door, weeping. Vanleela had seen Navinchandra withdraw his hand and also heard the words that gave testimony to his purity. But before she could hear Alak Kishori’s response, her attention was diverted. She heard the sarangi fall and rushed to Kumud’s room. She saw that Kumud had fainted. ‘Bhabhi, what happened?’ she cried out as she rushed to her aid. Saubhagya Devi had seen Vanleela crouching at Navinchandra’s door. Pained and angry, she had come up to admonish her daughter, to ascertain for herself the truth of the rumours, and to find out details of the matter from Vanleela. Saubhagya Devi was also worried about the family’s prestige. As she came up, there was no sign of Vanleela, but she saw Alak tearfully leaving the room and stared after her in surprise; she felt that perhaps she had erred in thinking ill of her daughter. Alak Kishori was also startled to see her mother at the door, and scared that she had witnessed what happened. Saubhagya Devi was about to ask her something, when Vanleela shouted from the next room, ‘Oh someone come and help! Devi, Alak behn, come, look! Bhabhi has fainted!’ ‘What!’ cried Saubhagya Devi and she ran; in her haste she stumbled and fell, but before anyone could come to her help, she picked herself up and rushed again. Alak Kishori forgot all about her distress and hurried after her mother. Her mind was numb and so were her feet. Navinchandra forgot his illness and wounds, jumped out of bed and rushed to Kumud Sundari’s room. This was the first time he had entered her room. He stood behind everyone else, perplexed and anxious.

Kumud was still slumped unconscious on the chair. Everyone crowded around her. Saubhagya Devi asked, ‘Vanleela, what happened?’ Vanleela was scared. Kumud had fainted while she was at the door of Navinchandra’s room. What was she to say if asked where she had been? She replied, ‘Who knows. She was singing and playing the sarangi, and suddenly she fainted.’ Navinchandra came forward. It was his responsibility to plead patience with the women and find a way of reviving Kumud Sundari. He looked at Kumud’s face, remembered her song, and guessed the reason for her condition. Concealing his anguish, he said, ‘Devi, do not worry. Please help me lift her and put her on the bed. She will revive soon. Alak behn, call for some rosewater.’ Alak Kishori hurried out, and on her way, she instructed Samar Sen: ‘Send someone to fetch father and another to get the vaidya.’ Vanleela followed Alak and said, ‘I think bhabhi had an epileptic fit. At my home there is a bottle of medicine we had got from Bombay. Have that fetched as well.’ One person was sent to get that. Samar Sen stood guard at the door but his attention was on Kumud’s room. Saubhagya Devi held Kumud’s head in one hand and caressed her face with the other, entreating her to open her eyes. ‘Kumud! Kumud, my daughter ... Oh do say something! Why are you so silent?’ Navinchandra turned his face and wiped his tears unnoticed. He said, ‘Devi, let us lay her upon the bed. She will not speak now.’ Saubhagya Devi was aghast. ‘She won’t speak? Will Kumud never speak again? Navinchandra what makes you say such things! She is the light of my house!’ she said, almost delirious. Alak returned with the rosewater, followed by Vanleela. Navinchandra splashed seven or eight handfuls of it on Kumud’s face. The others watched anxiously. Like the lotus bud that opens each morning, Kumud Sundari stirred ever so slightly. ‘Devi, look, bhabhi moved!’ Alak said. But in vain. Kumud Sundari did not regain consciousness even after half a bottle of rosewater was poured. Navinchandra was helpless and again said, ‘Devi, let us lay her upon the bed and wait for the vaidya.’ Alak Kishori and Vanleela lifted Kumud from the waist and legs, while Navinchandra supported her head and back. Saubhagya Devi tried to give them a hand, but she felt as if she were lifting Kumud’s dead body and she fell backwards in horror against the wall. She cried out, ‘Hai! Oh, my dearest Kumud!’ Navinchandra’s face came close to Kumud’s as he supported her head and shoulders with both arms. His tears rolled down his cheeks and fell onto her eyes and face; he was unable to wipe them. Slowly and carefully they lowered her onto the bed. Saubhagya Devi came and sat by her, she kissed Kumud’s face, ran her fingers through her hair, weeping. Navinchandra put on a brave act and tried to console the women. Devi’s breath seemed to momentarily revive Kumud, and she opened her eyes, but they remained unseeing and vacant. She had not regained full consciousness, and blabbered  intermittently in her delirium: ‘You are my life, you are my second heart/You are the moonlight to my eyes and the ambrosia to my limbs/You flattered your guileless wife with hundreds of such loving expressions/Why talk more of this?’⟨fn:16⟩ Then her voice cracked and she fell back unconscious. No one understood what had happened. They were shocked. Navinchandra gave up his attempts to comfort them. He got up and went and stood at a desk that had some books and drawings kept on it. Making a valiant effort to stop his tears, he murmured softly to himself. Damn me! My wanton ways Made her leave in anger. What will she do, what will she say to me For deserting her this long? I have little use for wealth or people Or my life or my house. Damn me! My wanton ways Made her leave in anger. I brood on her brow curving Over her anger-shadowed face,

Like a red lotus Shadowed by a bee hovering above. Damn me! My wanton ways Made her leave in anger.⟨fn:17⟩ She is gone, he said, and wept like a woman. It mattered not that he was in a house of strangers. His eyes fell on some drawings kept on Kumud’s table. She had drawn them. One drawing depicted a scene from the third act of Uttararamacharita in which Sita looks at Ram with moist yet admonishing eyes. Another depicted Dushyant looking at a flower-bedecked Shakuntala approach him. A volume of Shakespeare was on the table in which the pages of All’s Well That Ends Well and The Winter’s Tale were marked with book markers. Navinchandra observed what was before him, and grew pensive. Meanwhile, unconscious Kumud kept murmuring snatches of songs. ‘Oh learning, Oh Sarasvati, you have slipped away ...’ And then: ‘Oh bee, why did you fly away?’ There was a pause. Then, as they listened, the two songs merged into one another. Your name has slipped away You have slipped away from me But not from my heart You have not slipped out of my heart Why, bee? Navinchandra turned around and looked at her unconscious face. Kumud was laid on her back. Her thick black hair lay about her head like the spread feathers of a peacock. The flowers strung in her hair were now crushed and dishevelled. Everyone sat around her in silence not knowing what to do. At last the vaidya arrived, followed by Buddhidhan and Pramaddhan. Alak Kishori narrated the sequence of events. The vaidya began to administer to Kumud. He diagnosed that she had an epileptic fit. His efforts bore fruit. Kumud regained consciousness. Buddhidhan asked Alak Kishori, ‘Don’t you take her for outings these days?’ ‘No, we have not been able to go of late.’ ‘That is the cause. Take her out. Take the carriage and go today itself. Is there any difficulty?’ ‘No, none whatsoever.’ The elder’s command was obeyed. Ever since Navinchandra had entered their house as a guest, Kumud Sundari had never looked at him directly in the eyes. Later that day, just as she was about to climb into the carriage, she looked at him, breaking her own self-imposed rule. Her eyes betrayed anger, pity and anguish. From that day on, whenever she met his gaze, there was a silent censure in her eyes. After this incident, Navinchandra’s mind wavered between the strong desire to return home and to wander away to newer places. He had resolved that he must leave Buddhidhan’s house. He was held back only by his curiosity to witness the much anticipated fallout of the palace intrigues. On the morning of the palace assembly, Buddhidhan entrusted him with a great responsibility, and Navinchandra felt that his desire to leave was unlikely to be fulfilled soon. However, as soon as he stepped out of the palace, the thought came back to him. His wanderlust resurfaced and it excited and intensified his imagination; even the grand spectacle of the palace assembly paled before it. The afternoon heat made the restless images in his mind even more vivid. In the distance he could see boats out on the sea, and was drawn to them like a drunken man to a beacon. As he walked under that merciless sun, many thoughts flooded his mind. Sarasvatichandra, do you realise what delirious Kumud Sundari babbled? ‘Sarasvati ... You have slipped away from me, but not from my heart ...’ Oh! It was cruel, cruel on my part, and callous! My beloved has turned heartless The signs of love have turned

This tender heart will be torn apart O’ foolish, ill-fated one Oh God! Whose sin is it? Sarasvatichandra, do you realise what you have done?! A pure and virtuous woman—sacrificed in the fire of her husband’s stupidity, lasciviousness and debauchery. A virtuous woman unable to forget her past. She cannot forget the one to whom she gave her heart, and she cannot commit adultery, either of the mind or the body, forsaking the one she is married to. A strong-willed child-woman. Your desire for the man you wanted as a husband is so intense, and yet you wouldn’t even look at him! What self-control! Man, of the two, you are the woman; Woman—you are the man. Your sarangi restored him to his senses when he foolishly desired a woman not his own; you steadied his mind by your sublime song. What power! Oh Kumud, I was about to defile myself! Can a man know what difficulties lie ahead of him? I am a sinner. But, if you really are a sinner and a weakling, why did you then let go of her? Poor, wretched Alak Kishori! How can I berate you? Was I in my senses that I could admonish you? And Kumud—your eyes were filled with rage! Her glance is straight; her eyes are flashing red; Her speech is harsh, not drawling well-bred Her whole lip quivers, seems to shake with cold; Her frown has straightened eyebrows arching bold.⟨fn:18⟩ Undoubtedly, your heart is shattered—your song, your drawings, the books you read, your speech, they all point to that. Oh sweet and melodious sarangi! Your strings play the same mournful tune. The ways of God are indiscernible. What happened? Why did I lapse, even if for a moment, even if not fully awake? How did you fathom that? Why were you required to endanger yourself to save me from deluge? Oh sinful mind! Your debasement became manifest. Is learning not sufficient to uplift the base instincts? What if Kumud had not warned me? Would all my learning have been to no avail? Are the instincts of the illiterate and the learned, the cultured and the uncultured similar, then? Yes. Yes, most certainly they are. Alak Kishori you are illiterate, but it is you who became my teacher. You do not want a blot upon your virtue. Neither do I. Why is the mind subject to passions? Food tempts even those who have delicacies to eat; even the wealthy cannot refrain from stealing from others. Is the desire for flesh similar? Is lust so powerful that it subjugates the intellect and turns man into a beast? If it is so, then what is human volition, human will? Why did King Pandu allow his lust to overpower him in full knowledge that it would result in his death? I learnt the true meaning of King Pandu’s story through this one incident with Alak Kishori. Just as a matchstick is fire itself, lust lurks within each person, ready to manifest itself at every opportunity. It must be so for everyone. It must have been so with Alak Kishori. Does not this wise, sagacious, accomplished exponent of political intrigue, Buddhidhan, also submit to his instinct at a mere touch of his woman? And Saubhagya Devi, I have witnessed the power you wield over the mighty Counsellor. You are pure and virtuous. Your virtues remind me of Saibya. Covering her head with her sari, Her face acquires a demureness of its own She speaks a few words softly, intoning them sweetly She walks slowly, with eyes downcast O goddess mine: these are the Marks of a pure and noble lineage Saubhagya Devi, you are an embodiment of virtue. You are pure. O Arya woman, your pious image is etched in the minds of all whom you meet. I have read virtue described, but I never could comprehend the power and attraction of your piety. Travel to England, wander in America, the vineyards of Persia, or roam around in Armenia, it is impossible to find a woman as virtuous as the Arya woman. But even in this our land, you are becoming imaginary and rare; the arrogance of English knowledge has wrought destruction upon you. Saubhagya Devi, you embody the Arya woman. You are as revered and lovely to behold as the land of our country. How fortunate is Buddhidhan to have a jewel like you. Buddhidhan, enshrine this woman in your heart and hold her dearer than you do your power. But the question is: Why does the most pious and pure Saubhagya Devi desire Buddhidhan? Navinchandra suddenly laughed out aloud. Oh, the celebration of the body! It is so wrong to make assumptions about a person’s instincts from their outward appearances. Imagination misleads—it is not good to have a very active imagination. A person obtains an M.A. degree, fills his mind with lofty ‘philosophy’, and his hands per chance come to rest upon a woman’s breasts, and he behaves as if he is mindless! Is this not illogical? If someone else were to paint this picture before me, I would certainly dismiss it as improbable and laugh it off. If such a thing happened once, it could not be said that it would never happen again. Vanleela was at some distance from me; unknown to her my eyes were drawn to her. I turned my gaze away, but I did feel an attraction, I wanted to look at her. How can I dismiss this experience? But for the experience, would I even admit to it? Even to myself? What could be the reason for dismissing it even as a probability? It is like this: a man observing constellations in the sky falls into a ditch; lofty imagination is not well grounded. A man crossing the seas does not count every wave he rides upon. Those who reflect on the condition of the country, the world and its Creator forget the existence of hunger and passions. But hunger and passions catch us by the ears, grab us by the neck and bring us back to our senses and reality. One is forced to put the book aside and eat. Even the likes of John Mill and Wordsworth had to marry. Did they marry only for companionship of the mind? They might well respond to such a query in the affirmative, but that is deceit. I, Sarasvatichandra, have come to that recognition today. If it were only about companionship of the mind, why do they marry at all? Why are they not satisfied with conversations alone? Love, we are told, is companionship of the mind, marriage a union of minds; but these definitions are partial. I realise this today. Alak Kishori, you are my teacher in this. If I had known this four months ago, Kumud Sundari, I would never have put you in such a state. But what has happened has indeed happened. Can it be undone? I cannot marry. Is it possible for me to not submit to passion again? I should not keep the company of those who pander to the senses. I should stay miles away from women. I must leave Buddhidhan’s house. This would also make Kumud Sundari happy. If I am no longer around, she will eventually forget me. But where shall I go? Who can say ‘Thus far, no further’ to the tide of his own nature? Who can mould the spirit’s fashion to the counsel of his will? Square his being by enactment—shape his soul to legislature. Be himself his law of living: his own art of good and ill?⟨fn:19⟩ Oh heartless poet, are your cruel words true? Oh heartless poet, is it true that instinct is more powerful than will? Do desires of sensual pleasure rule over a man, dance over his head and chest and beat him into subjugation? Oh why are our senses not in our control? Does desire have more force than intellect? Cannot the intellect rule over the body? Navinchandra sighed deeply. Tears rolled down his cheeks unrestrained and unseen, and were dried by the harsh sun. He had not yet covered half the distance to Buddhidhan’s house. The road forked ahead of him. He took the path they had taken that morning. Ramsen, walking behind him, stopped him and said, ‘Bhai, take the other route, from that lane.’ His reverie broken, Navinchandra asked, ‘Ramsen, didn’t we take the other road in the morning?’ ‘Bhai, this is a shorter route.’ ‘Oh, is that so? Fine. Let us go.’ And he lapsed back into his cogitations. If marriage were only for the sake of the body, Kumud Sundari should be content with Pramaddhan and Sarasvatichandra’s memories should not haunt her.

If marriage were to mean nothing but bodily union, and if Kumud is still haunted by memories of Sarasvatichandra, it would imply that her chastity is compromised. His thoughts were interrupted once again. In the lane they had turned into, there was a small, beautiful house. The windows on the first floor were open. Glass chandeliers and mirrors could be seen from outside. Flowerpots and decorative plants had been kept on the otalo. The door was open but the latticed door behind it was shut. A fair complexioned, beautiful girl of fifteen or sixteen opened the latticed door as Navinchandra and Ramsen approached the house. Navinchandra did not so much as glance at her and walked past, preoccupied. She seemed hurt by this. Ramsen said, ‘Bhai, you go on ahead or else wait for me.’ He went up to the girl, spoke to her in whispers, then hurried back and joined Navinchandra. ‘Bhai, did you see her?’ Navinchandra turned back in surprise and asked, ‘What?’ ‘Nothing. That was Padma’s house.’ ‘Who is Padma?’ ‘Don’t you know her? Since you are friendly with Pramaddhan, I assumed you knew her.’ ‘Who is she?’ ‘She is the courtesan, Padma. Didn’t you see her? How beautiful she is! Come, let’s go if you wish to see her, we can eat a paan made by her.’ ‘No, what do we have to do with her. Now I understand; we took this route because of her.’ ‘Yes. I had to give her a message.’ ‘What message would you need to give her?’ ‘Nothing important.’ ‘There must be something. Do tell me.’ ‘All right. But only if you can keep a secret. Or else I will lose my job.’ ‘You will not lose your job; why would I need to tell anyone? Do tell.’ ‘Pramaddhan visits her in the company of friends.’

‘Pramaddhanbhai!?’ ‘Yes, Bhai, please do not tell anyone. He visits her even in the afternoons.’ ‘Does he have no affection for Kumud Sundari?’ ‘No, no! He loves her a lot! He goes mad even at the mention of her name. But Bhai, she is there every day. What is the use of all this wealth if he has to look at and be satisfied with the same thing every day?’ ‘Are there other such places that he visits?’ ‘No. Come, let’s go in. She will be hospitable; after all you are a friend.’ ‘Is Buddhidhanbhai aware of all this?’ ‘No, sir, no! It would be death for Pramadbhai and all of us. Buddhidhanbhai would not even look at other women.’ ‘Are you certain of that?’ ‘Yes. Without a doubt. Only those blessed with great fortune would have Buddhidhanbhai and Devi as parents.’ ‘Then why has Pramadbhai become wayward?’ ‘Bhai, he was raised by the likes of me. We took care of him, and now he spends some leisure time here. Hence, he is pleased with us. His friends also have fun, and we too earn some money in the bargain.’ ‘Does Kumud Sundari know?’ ‘She knew nothing until recently. A few days ago, she went to the Rajeshwar Mahadev. That fool Murkhdutt blabbered something.’ ‘How does Murkhdutt know this?’ ‘On some nights, Pramaddhan takes Padma to the Rajeshwar Mahadev for fun and frolic. So Murkhdutt knows. A few days ago, Bhabhisahib visited the temple and she saw Padma’s blouse drying in the courtyard. She asked Murkhdutt about it. The fool got frightened, lost his nerve and blurted out that Pramadbhai had come for a visit, and that Padma must have forgotten to take it.’ ‘Did she not throw a tantrum?’ ‘That is what is so surprising! If it were any other woman, all hell would have broken loose. But Bhabhisahib took the blouse home, gave it to Pramaddhan without any fuss and told him that someone had left it at the Mahadev temple, and that he should return it to whom it belonged. Pramadbhai was really scared and said he knew nothing about it. Bhabhisahib said: You are resourceful and wield power. Find out to whom it belongs, or else keep it with you.’ ‘And then?’ ‘Pramadbhai has not been able to visit Padma of late because of all these palace intrigues.’ Navinchandra heaved a deep sigh. They had come out of the lane and were back on the main road. ‘Bhai, please don’t tell anyone,’ pleaded Ramsen. ‘Why did you bring me into this lane?’ ‘I came to give her the good news that she will now find a place in the palace. I told you, I thought you knew all about her.’ ‘You made a mistake; not I.’ ‘Navinbhai, you are most generous. You are not innocent of these things. Have mercy on a poor man. What more can I say?’ ‘You needn’t worry. I won’t speak about what you have told me. At any rate, no one will know that you have spoken about it to me.’ Conversation stopped, and Navinchandra became immersed in his thoughts once again. Kumud Sundari, pure, virtuous and innocent Kumud ... This is the height of torture! Sarasvatichandra, this is all your doing. Your sin. Unthinking adventurer, you have tormented her! How unfortunate are the children of the high and mighty. Blameless Buddhidhan. Pious Saubhagya Devi. The foremost consequence of your power is that your son was raised by servants. A child raised by servants is bound to go wrong. How much attention can the father pay? Pramaddhan is not by nature wicked. He has been spoilt by servants and friends. Life in the households of the powerful tends to be unnatural. Those who run the politics of the state have darkness in their homes. But look at the power of the virtuous! Even this lowly servant recognises what good fortune it is to have them as parents. What really separates me and Pramaddhan? What is the difference between the learned and the illiterate? His conduct is impure, but there is impurity in my thoughts. The disease in me was stymied before it could spread. He continues to be debauched, perhaps more so now. Is that not the difference between knowledge and the lack of it? But how did such vile thoughts even enter my mind? Only because I came here. One must associate with equals. Yes, certainly the company of the higher is to be desired. Just as the lowly benefit by association with the high, the high are degraded by association with the lowly. I have already experienced the fruits of proximity with Alak Kishori. I walked with a servant and he brought me to a prostitute’s house. And a past association with Kumud ... She saved me from a great sin just by playing her sarangi and singing. Yes, I must now leave Buddhidhan’s house ... It is time. They had reached the Counsellor’s house. A messenger came up to Navinchandra and handed him a letter. He opened the letter as he entered the house.
chapters.summary: Navinchandra observes Kalavati's mesmerizing dance and Rana Bhupsinh's fury, then receives a mysterious letter, hinting at new paths and unresolved tensions.

chapters.title: Destiny Fulfilled
paragraphs: Destiny Fulfilled Before leaving for the palace, Buddhidhan had left two faithful soldiers to guard the house. Saubhagya Devi bathed again, smeared sacred ash on her forehead, lit silver lamps and incense sticks and sat down to pray before the household deity. She recited the verses that her mother-in-law had taught her. Old Dayashankar sat in the courtyard enjoying the mild morning breeze of Chaitra. Alak Kishori and Kumud Sundari sat with him, listening to his reminiscences of the palace, the Rana, Shathrai, stories of Buddhidhan’s youth, his mother, and legends surrounding the Karbhari family. Dayashankar, like Sanjay of Mahabharata, satisfied their curiosity with great verve and pleasure, recalling the days of Buddhidhan’s long illness, his pledge, the plight of his widowed mother, and adolescent Saubhagya Devi. The two young women heard the stories, and felt the hardship and suffering of days gone by. Even their worst enemy should not have to see such days, they said. This re-telling brought back painful memories for Saubhagya Devi. She remembered the affection of her dear mother-in-law, and could no longer concentrate on her puja as tears streamed down her eyes.
