She wiped her tears, got up and joined Dayashankar in remembering the old days. She said, ‘Dayashankar Kaka, Mataji should have been around to see such good days. There can be no one like her. I weep every time I am reminded of her affection and her patience. It was her lot to suffer. She hardly knew any happiness. She was born only to raise and nurture us.’ And so it was on the day of the big assembly, as events in Rana Bhupsinh’s court unfolded according to Buddhidhan’s plan, such were the noble and uplifting scenes unfolding in his household. After the Jamal episode, Alak Kishori had sobered down. She had also matured greatly after the incident with Navinchandra. She had become less haughty in the company of the kind, intelligent and sensitive Kumud who had also turned Alak’s mind more and more towards Vidurprasad. Stories of the suffering and humiliation that her own parents had endured had mellowed Alak further. Vanleela had clearly heard Navinchandra say: ‘Behn Alak, I am like a brother to you.’ She was convinced of Navinchandra’s purity. This had removed a thorn from Kumud’s heart. Vanleela repeated to Kumud the lines she had sung in her delirium. Kumud could imagine the intense agony she must have caused Navinchandra and felt that her conduct had been heartless. She knew that her attraction and infatuation for him was contrary to her conduct as a chaste wife. Aware of her own weakness, and battling conflicting emotions, Kumud had counselled Alak. She realised her folly and resolved to curb her desire for Navinchandra. The episode of Padma’s blouse also served as a lesson for her—Kumud realised that in some ways it captured her innermost desires; if she did not crave for Sarasvatichandra, her husband, too, would not have sought Padma’s comfort. Kumud became determined to banish the man who possessed her mind and soul. This was difficult. She focused her attention on the good qualities in Pramaddhan and made a conscious attempt to make place for him in her heart. Dayashankar’s stories made her feel emotionally attached to the Counsellor’s family. For the first time, Kumud Sundari felt proud of her marriage to a scion of this family. She felt a new energy in the belief that if she were to purge her mind, she would be able to reform her husband as well. A new light enveloped her as the noon sun blazed outside, penetrating the darkness within. The family was destined to receive the bounty of good fortune. Though unaware of it, they could feel the soothing presence of divine grace in their midst. The Counsellor’s family thus prepared itself to be worthy of this bounty. Alak Kishori’s conscience was duly purified. Her haughtiness gave way to humility, her arrogance to maturity, and her indifference and contempt gave way to a newfound regard for her husband. Kumud Sundari’s conjugal disaffection and discontent, known only to her, had the potential to destroy the family. By her own firm resolve and sincere efforts, even this was being gradually replaced by affection for Pramaddhan, and a certain inner quiet. Was this not a sign of good fortune, too? Was it any less significant or valuable than Buddhidhan being entrusted with the Karbhar? All of this contributed to the bliss that Buddhidhan and Saubhagya Devi were about to experience, and enhanced the glory of Buddhidhan’s triumph. It was about ten in the morning. The sun was already sharp. The women and Dayashankar moved out of the courtyard. Dayashankar went into the drawing room to repose in an armchair. Saubhagya Devi sat on the swing in the shade, moving gently to and fro, eagerly awaiting news of her husband. Kumud Sundari went up to her room. Alak Kishori went to the kitchen to instruct the cooks about preparation of food for the day, and then went up to join Kumud. ‘Bhabhi, what will be the outcome at the palace assembly today?’ Alak asked Kumud. ‘It will all be good, I feel, and besides, our worrying about it is not going to help matters. Oh, it is ten already! Someone should be coming from the palace soon. Perhaps Navinchandra.’ Kumud blushed despite herself as she uttered the name. ‘Bhabhi, Navinchandra will come only if things go wrong.’ ‘Oh, is that so? Then the news must be good.’ ‘Navinchandra is a good human being,’ Alak said, smiling. She had already forgotten the past. Alak’s heart was transparent. In many ways, she was childlike in her simple-mindedness, and the incident and agonising shame over which she had resolved to take her own life was barely a blur in her mind now. She lived in the present. She no longer felt any desire or attraction for Navinchandra. She remembered only his goodness and purity. Kumud Sundari did not respond.

‘Bhabhi, he has been here for so long. No one knows why he came here, or why he left his home. What do you think?’ ‘Ask Devi about it. They decided to send us to Lilapur in his care. They must know something about him,’ replied Kumud, eager to change the subject. She calmed herself by looking at Pramaddhan’s photograph. ‘Behn, I feel that news from the palace will be good, and that your brother will come to tell us so. Although, he may not come if he is detained by more important work.’ ‘Oh, you are crazy about your husband! You bring my brother into everything!’ laughed Alak. ‘Look who is telling me!’ ‘I am certainly not as bad as you!’ ‘All right. But is it wrong to be crazy about one’s husband?’ ‘Of course! All day long you think of nothing but him.’ ‘Tell me, what can be more important for a wife than her husband?’ ‘That is true. But do we need to talk about him all day long?’ ‘Some time ago, you weren’t even ready to admit this. Every time someone mentioned your husband, you would snarl.’ ‘That is also true. But it is no longer so. Do I do that now?’ ‘No. Did I say that you do! Did you hear what Dayashankar Kaka had to say?’ ‘Yes, my hair stood on end just listening to him. How Pitaji and Devi have suffered!’ ‘That bitch Khalaknanda insulted our grandmother, and that wicked Dushtarai sent such a vile message! Did you hear about that?’ ‘Oh yes. Today, they will all get the fruits of their deeds.’ ‘Pitaji harboured that insult for so many years. But today will be his day.’ ‘Bhabhi, it is so hard for him. He worries so much, constantly; it shows on him.’ ‘Now tell me, Alak behn, is Deviji wrong when she worries about Pitaji all the time?’ ‘No, of course not. How can it be wrong?’ ‘Is it ever wrong for a woman to worry about her husband?’

‘No. It can never be enough.’ ‘Now you have got it right. So tell me, is it wrong if you think and talk about Vidurprasadji all the time? It is perfectly good and desirable to be crazy about the husband. Those who are not are in fact guilty in the eyes of God.’ Alak Kishori blushed. Kumud Sundari was stunned by her own words: ‘... guilty in the eyes of God’. She looked at Pramaddhan’s photograph. Kumud felt a sudden surge of blissful relief along with the realisation that Sarasvatichandra now belonged to the past. She gazed at Pramaddhan’s photograph with longing. ‘Bhabhi, you are right. In that book you have given me, Lalita says: “Whether good or bad, naming him my beloved husband, I give solace to my mind. Such are my thoughts. But my heart refuses to fall in line. Restless, I yearn to be with him.” Perhaps I have mixed up the lines. But Lalita desires Nandkumar even though he is undeserving of her.’ ‘Yes, she cannot take her mind off her husband.’ Even Kumud felt that the example of the fictional and semi-literate Lalita was worthy of emulation. Alak said with a mischievous glint in her eye, ‘Yes, henceforth even I shall yearn for my husband and think of him all the time!’ ‘You and I and all other women will craze for our husbands! We shall settle a new village for crazy women like us!’ Both of them burst out laughing. Buddhidhan’s household was being purged of impurities. Kumud was changing Alak. Just then Vanleela came up. She hesitated for a moment, but entered the room nevertheless. ‘Come in. Why did you hesitate, Vanleela?’ ‘How come you are here at this time?’ asked Alak. ‘I have come to tell you all the gossip. Merulo has wounded Dushtarai, and Rupali has run away disguised as a man! Khalaknanda is hiding and cannot be traced!’ ‘What!’ Alak stood up and excitedly caught hold of Vanleela’s shoulder. Kumud remained seated but looked at them with curiosity. Vanleela relayed all that she knew without pausing to catch her breath.

Krishna Kalika and Radha joined them with the news that Jamal had been found and captured in the palace. They all went to Saubhagya Devi, and the gossip was recounted to her with undiminished interest and fervour. Then Vidurprasad arrived with full details of the day’s events at the palace. Alak Kishori’s joy was limitless. She could barely restrain herself from dancing about the house. Kumud was most impressed with her father-in-law’s brilliance, and felt proud to be a part of the Counsellor’s family; the family’s victory was a victory for Kumud as well. Joy brought sobriety to Saubhagya Devi. God had willed victory for her husband and defeat for his enemies—Saubhagya Devi seemed overwhelmed by this and could only weep in joy. The entire story was retold to Dayashankar. The listeners were no less interested in the narration on account of repetition. All of them moved to the drawing room. Vidyurprasad’s narration became more detailed as his audience increased and he held them captive for quite some time. This was a novel experience for Alak Kishori; never before had she felt captivated by Vidurprasad. Time passed in excited chatter. Then Navinchandra arrived, shoving a letter into his pocket. While the group eagerly turned to him for more details, Kumud’s attention was instantly drawn to the letter in his pocket. She was curious to read the handwriting on the letter. She reasoned that the letter would throw more light on him and his antecedents. She felt there was a chance her curiosity may at last be satisfied. She had resolved with all her strength to put him out of her mind. But seeing Navinchandra, she felt her resolve weaken. Navinchandra had made up his mind to leave. As he entered the house, he wanted one last glimpse of Kumud Sundari. He looked at her once, twice, thrice, but his desire was undiminished. Kumud Sundari, this is our last meeting, he said to himself as he was besieged by questions from his onlookers. His thoughts interrupted his responses and narration, but no one noticed. He was overcome by emotion with the thought that he would no longer be able to even look at Kumud; and that she was given in marriage to a man who visited Padma. Kumud saw these images fleeting before Navinchandra’s eyes, the pain and turmoil on his face, and the letter peeping out of his pocket. What could it possibly be? she asked herself. Hitherto she had remained firm and not responded to his searching eyes. Her resolve weakened with every passing moment. There was no way out of this predicament. Krishna Kalika had failed in her attempt to make Alak Kishori an instrument of her lust. She now stared at Navinchandra. She saw the two pairs of eyes gazing intently at each other, and was singed by envy. She pictured the pleasure that Kumud Sundari would have received from Navinchandra, and determined to bring that pleasure to an end. She quietly drew Alak Kishori’s attention to this union of eyes. ‘Rand! I will skin you alive if you ever mention this again!’ Alak Kishori shoved Krishna Kalika away and became engrossed in the conversation again. Just then, a big ruckus and uproar was heard from outside. Everyone rushed to the windows. They saw a terrified Khalaknanda running in the street, chased by an angry, abusive mob that pelted stones at her. Shathrai’s house had been seized. His daughter had been driven out from it. Buddhidhan had ordered that Shathrai’s house and women of that family should not be touched or harmed. Khalaknanda’s husband’s family had refused to shelter her. People who knew of her licentious and evil deeds ran after her. Those delighted at the fall of Shathrai and Dushtarai joined the mob. They clapped and jeered at her. There was no compassion in any eye for the plight of the former Karbhari’s family. Khalaknanda had nowhere to go. She should have run away with her sister-in-law Rupali, she felt. It was too late now. There was no escape for her. Frightened for her life, she ran around the streets, pursued by the stone-throwing, abusive mob. She cried out for help, stumbled and fell several times, got up and ran again. Followed by the mob, she reached Buddhidhan’s house. Alak Kishori and the others watched the scene from the window. Alak Kishori taunted, ‘Devi, look at this wretched rand! Neither Jamal nor Mahva can save her now. You bitch, you deserve it!’ Saubhagya Devi glared at her daughter to hear such words from her tongue. She came downstairs and stood on the otalo; the other women followed. Seeing them, Khalaknanda became even more frightened. Her defeat was total. She felt that the mob that was following her like a pack of bloodthirsty hounds would incite Saubhagya Devi to revenge. She knew that Alak Kishori would want to avenge the Jamal episode. There could be no better opportunity. Shathrai’s daughter burned within; fear brought back memories of her many misdeeds. She remembered how she had insulted Buddhidhan’s mother all those years ago, and the vile suggestions she had made about Saubhagya Devi, a young bride then. These and countless such misdeeds danced before her eyes like a rotting carcass infested with vermin. She made an attempt to run away from Buddhidhan’s house, but it was foiled. She was exhausted from all the running. Someone pushed her and Dushtarai’s sister fell flat on her face at Saubhagya Devi’s feet. A man pushed his way to the front of the crowd, shouting, ‘Beat up the rand!’ and he put his foot on her back. A policeman, once close to Dushtarai, stood watching the spectacle; he made no attempt to stop the man. In a moment, people would have started kicking her. As Khalaknanda fell, Alak Kishori incited the mob, ‘Yes! Beat her up! Thrash the rand! She deserves it!’. She provoked them by reminding them of Khalaknanda’s misdeeds. Ramsen came forward, eager to obey Buddhidhan’s daughter. Krishna Kalika, Vanleela and Radha silently enjoyed the farce. Dayashankar Kaka tried to stop Alak Kishori, but she did not heed him. Vidurprasad and Navinchandra also tried to restrain the people, but in vain. Finally Saubhagya Devi stepped forward and spoke up in anger: ‘Alak, stop this at once! Do you want us to be like them!’ She told the people commandingly, ‘Turn back. Go home. What harm has she done to you? You kick a woman! Aren’t you ashamed! Ramsen, take her away.’ The mob retreated a little but kept up the excited cacophony of murmurs and whispers. ‘She is the Counsellor’s wife, Saubhagya Devi. Devi is right, we should let the miserable bitch go. But how can we let her go! She deserves a beating and worse! She has ruined so many lives! Well said, Alak behn! She truly deserves to be punished! Oh, she is Alak Kishori? Yes, and that one there is Pramaddhan’s wife, Kumud Sundari.’ Alak argued with her mother, ‘Devi, I will not listen to you today. You will never change! You know perfectly well that this woman deserves no compassion. Ramsen, hold the bitch tight by her hair!’ Ramsen could not decide whom to obey. The other soldiers were keen to obey Alak Kishori, but it was not a small matter to disregard Saubhagya Devi’s wishes. In desperation, Saubhagya Devi turned to Kumud Sundari. ‘Kumud, this girl will not listen to me. You only talk some sense into her.’ She knew of her daughter-in-law’s persuasive skills and of her daughter’s soft spot for her. Kumud came forward, gently put a hand on her sister-in-law’s shoulder and said, ‘Alak behn let her go. Why flog the dead?’ ‘So you, too, are on Devi’s side,’ Alak said half accusingly. ‘Of course. Has she said anything wrong?’ ‘You heard what Dayashankar Kaka recounted for us this morning.’ ‘If anyone has the right to bear a grudge, it is Devi, not us.’ ‘No, she would never bear a grudge. She is the kind who would bless even those wanting her dead.’ ‘Why do you hold a grudge?’ ‘Why shouldn’t I! Should I forget what that bitch did to me— using that lowly Jamal? And what about the insult to Devi? She is my mother!’ Alak barely stopped herself from saying: To you she is mother-in-law, but to me she is mother. But Kumud heard what was left unsaid and continued regardless in a voice at once gentle and firm: ‘I don’t deny that, do I? You can feel hurt and angry, and so can I. Even so, what Devi says is right. We must follow her advice. You will get what you want in the end. Alak behn, please do as I am asking of you. I will explain all this to you later.’

Alak Kishori softened a little and said, ‘All right. Ramsen, do what Devi wants you to. But bhabhisahib, you are making a mistake. How will Khalaknanda ever realise the consequences of her evil deeds?’ The man who was standing with his foot on Khalaknanda moved away. Ramsen and some other soldiers of the Counsellor made a cordon around her. Khalaknanda now stood up. Alak turned to her mother, ‘Devi, now tell us, what should we do with her? If you permit me, I will tell father and have her beheaded.’ ‘Yes, yes! She deserves death! Have her beheaded!’ shouted the mob. ‘Alak Kishori, prove that you can do it!’, someone shouted and hurled a sharp stone at Khalaknanda that hit her on the back and she screamed in terror and pain. The sight of her blood incited the crowd even more. ‘Ramsen, what are they doing! Stop them!’ said Saubhagya Devi with a weary and pained expression. Then, several voices in the crowd addressed the Counsellor’s wife: ‘Devi, do not compel us to speak up. The misdeeds of this bitch are so vile we are ashamed to mention them. She had no compunction in committing those deeds, but we hesitate even to speak of them before you. Behnji, your revered mother-in-law is no more, or else she would have told you all about this woman here.’ Khalaknanda was an accomplice of her brother Dushtarai, the Faujdar. She had ensnared many sisters, young daughters and wives in her vicious net of vice; she had lured them, cajoled and threatened them and brought them under her power to satisfy her brother’s lust. Many innocent and pure women had become her unsuspecting victims. Saubhagya Devi had never concerned herself with anything that did not concern her husband. Hence, such vile words and deeds had never before fallen upon her pious ears. She was stunned beyond belief. She had remained completely ignorant of the venomous power that Khalaknanda had wielded. She had forgiven Khalaknanda’s insult of her years ago. Irate and impatient, Alak Kishori said, ‘Bhabhi, Devi refuses to say anything. You tell me, what do you want me to do?’ ‘It is not as if you do not know what Devi wants.’

‘Of course I know what Devi wants! She would want us to rescue this rand, take her into our home, give her shelter and feed her. That would make Devi really happy!’ Helpless in face of her daughter’s wrath and acerbic taunts, Saubhagya Devi again turned to wise Kumud: ‘Kumud, you tell me, would such a thing be wrong?’ Kumud looked at Alak and softly said, ‘Behn, a daughter must do what the mother wants.’ ‘No. I do not understand such things. And I see that you too have joined Devi,’ Alak retorted in anger. Kumud calmly replied, ‘No, that was just an aside. Devi, I think Khalaknanda should be kept under guard at some safe place. We can give her food. Let Pitaji deal with her when he returns.’ ‘Yes, that is all right.’ Alak, who revered her father, did not find anything objectionable in Kumud’s suggestion. Devi welcomed it. The mob was satisfied as well. Khalaknanda did not look up or meet anyone’s gaze; her eyes remained fixed on the ground. Following Alak Kishori’s instructions, Ramsen and two other soldiers took Shathrai’s daughter to an unoccupied house in the neighbourhood. The mob dispersed noisily. As Khalaknanda was taken away, Alak Kishori taunted her, ‘Rand Khalki! See, this is the difference between your administration and ours. Go. Take your black face away from this place!’ And she turned her back on her and entered the house followed by her friends. Saubhagya Devi quietly asked Kumud to send a woman servant to cook and care for Khalaknanda and keep her company while she was watched over by male guards. Kumud immediately made arrangements. As mother and daughter-in-law entered the house, a tearful Saubhagya Devi took Kumud’s hand and said, ‘See how the wheel turns, my daughter. What power she had once. You were not even born when she was young, haughty and beautiful. How her youth and beauty have frayed. And how she has come to this pass today. Such is the will of God!’ Kumud Sundari was drawn to her compassionate mother-in-law. She was the last one to enter the house. Everyone else was already on the first floor. Navinchandra had dropped the letter on the staircase. Kumud saw it and picked it up. Everyone was busy talking about Khalaknanda, debating what would have been the best thing to do. They could hear foot falls. Someone looked out and saw a group of men approaching the house. The officials and functionaries of the state knew that Shathrai’s long rule had finally come to an end, and that Buddhidhan would be the new Karbhari of Suvarnapur. All those wanting to be in attendance, and curious about the happenings at court, now gathered outside Buddhidhan’s house. Alak Kishori asked, ‘Why are all these people here now?’ Various explanations were provided. Finally Vidurprasad said, ‘What can they do but stand in attendance before the new Karbhari? The house of the Karbhari has changed.’ Vanleela said, ‘Alak behn, you will now have to vacate this room. This will become an office, and the officials will wait here.’ The soldiers opened the doors for the officials, and the women moved to Navinchandra’s room. The officials climbed up. Dayashankar closed the door after the women. He recited to himself: ‘Welcome Lakshmi, wealth and glory. You bring friends and relatives. Some say I am a cousin, the other says I am a bosom friend.’ Vidurprasad chuckled listening to him, and went out to receive the officials. The rustle of the heavily starched and ironed clothes of the officials, the squeaking of their footwear, their hushed murmurs, the respect with which they uttered the name, ‘Buddhidhanbhai’, all these sounds fell on Saubhagya Devi’s eager ears as she sat on the swing. Years ago, during the reign of Rana Jadsinh, the son of a poor widow would sit right at the back of the assembly, near the pile of footwear. He would come home and meekly narrate the stories of Shathrai’s power and influence to his mother and young wife. Those scenes played before Saubhagya Devi’s eyes now. She compared those days with the scenes that were unfolding before her right now. She did not despise the old days, she was not bitter, and yet she was overjoyed at the turn of events. Her face was wet with tears of happiness. When she pictured the high office that her husband would adorn, a shiver of pleasure ran through her body. The sound of all these officials reverentially taking her husband’s name gave her a pleasure akin to bathing in a lake filled with nectar. She tried to imagine her husband resplendent in his new glory, his new stature, his newfound power, and still as affectionate and attentive towards her as before. Her waiting eyes yearned for his return. Drawn by the scent of a shift in power, these officials had gathered together, just as a sign of rain draws peacocks. Saubhagya Devi had remained a steadfast companion through Buddhidhan’s worst years. She sat alone today, feeling blessed at her good fortune. Today, her bliss was replete. Today, nothing marred her joy. A little while later, Buddhidhan appeared at the doorstep. His eyes instantly searched for Devi, their eyes met, and conveyed the shared joy and good fortune. They smiled at each other. He climbed up, followed by his retinue, as Saubhagya Devi went into the kitchen. Her daughter held court there. There were many more hangers-on than usual. Alak Kishori’s splendour and power were a sight to behold. Only Kumud Sundari was not there.
chapters.summary: Kumud Sundari grapples with her heart's desires, resolving to embrace her husband Pramaddhan while palace news stirs the household with dramatic revelations.

chapters.title: Sarasvatichandra
paragraphs: Sarasvatichandra The women went down as the men trooped up to the drawing room. Kumud Sundari went to her room to examine the letter that Navinchandra had received. She had also received a letter that day, from her younger sister, Kusum Sundari. The letter was about Sarasvatichandra. Kusum Sundari had sent it to Vanleela, who was related to the sisters, with strict instructions to hand it over to Kumud in secret. Vanleela had done so. Now alone in her room, Kumud read the letter. And she was filled with sorrow. Kumud had resolved, with a tremendous effort of will, not to let her mind waver from Pramaddhan. But as she read of the suffering and ignominy endured by Sarasvatichandra, she found her resolve melting. Sarasvatichandra’s father Laxminandan was a wealthy merchant of Bombay. He was reputed to have assets worth ten to twelve lakhs of rupees. He was not educated beyond what most ordinary merchants are. Sarasvatichandra’s mother Chandralaxmi was a wise and virtuous woman. Her good conduct and nature had influenced Laxminandan as well. Chandralaxmi’s mother-in-law Ishwarkaur was a bitter woman. She could not bear her son being under his wife’s influence. Ishwarkaur ruled over the household, and did so with intent to slight the daughter-in-law. Chandralaxmi was large-hearted and disregarded the mother-in-law’s insults. Laxminandan loved her all the more because of it. Things changed with Sarasvatichandra’s birth. The old woman softened up, and her regard for the daughter-in-law increased. Chandralaxmi died when Sarasvatichandra was four or five years old. On the same day, Laxminandan was betrothed to an adolescent Guman. Sarasvatichandra was raised by his father and grandmother, till such time as Guman came to live in the house. Laxminandan had a photograph taken with his son in his lap, and Chandralaxmi by his side. As a wealthy resident of Bombay, he could dare such an act. When Ishwarkaur came to know of it, she had fought with the daughter-in-law for months for this brazenness. She naturally did not think that her son was at fault. There is a saying among the village folk that a dead buffalo is worth more than a living one. Ishwarkaur realised the virtues of her daughter-in-law once she died. She cried a lot. She had the photograph brought out; Laxminandan kept it in his room. Ishwarkaur would point out Chandralaxmi in that photograph to young Sarasvatichandra. And then Guman entered the household. She was from a lowly family and harboured ill-will towards the stepson and her mother-in-law who doted on him. Guman’s mother had taught her that it would be wrong for her to love the stepson. Sheth Laxminandan was wealthy as well as influential. He was a well known patron of scholars and learning. There were many who had benefited from his patronage. His home was a meeting ground for scholars of diverse fields; men of letters and academically inclined young people would gather there for discussions and debate. He was well liked and respected by them. The Sheth’s sensibility, too, had been cultured and refined by his association with scholars. And thus it was that infant Sarasvatichandra played in the laps of scholars. They inculcated in him a love of learning at a young age. His bright face was reminiscent of Chandralaxmi’s luminosity. The clerks and servants who wished to curry favour with Guman tended to ignore Chandralaxmi’s son. Children of the wealthy are most often deprived of a cultured upbringing. But God granted this boon to the fortunate son of Laxminandan who was thus saved from the curse of being raised and influenced by servants. At a tender age, Sarasvatichandra became friends with an extremely poor and intelligent boy named Chandrakant. Chandrakant had a great thirst for knowledge. They both studied together. This mutually nourishing friendship grew deeper over the years. Sarasvatichandra formed other associations as he grew older, which proved short-lived; but his friendship with Chandrakant remained steadfast and solid as a rock. Sheth Laxminandan, owing to the company he kept, had learnt to speak and write some English. He was a member of the Reformist Society of Bombay. He managed the business and running of a few weaving mills. He was also involved in several public and private philanthropic activities. His philanthropy was motivated by self- interest; he was eager for public applause. He cultivated contact with English merchants and officials and invented occasions to invite them home and play host to them. In return, they bestowed him with honours. He was invited to the Governor’s evening parties. Such news never failed to make its way to the newspapers. The famous and learned editor of The Bombay Light Bulwer Sahib, the editor of Gurjar Vartik Uddhatlal, Bombay’s favourite city poet Tarang Shankar, the impoverished and upcoming writer Shanti Sharma, the famous Marathi patriot Virrao Dhampate, and well known Parsi public speaker Shamsherji were among his friends. Sheth Laxminandan was honoured with the title of ‘Justice of Peace’, courtesy an influential officer of the Secretariat who was known to him. All this power and influence also accorded the Bombay merchant prestige in the native states. Whenever the Minister of Ratnanagari, Vidya Chatura, came to Bombay, he preferred to be Sheth Laxminandan’s houseguest. They were also caste fellows. Vidya Chatura was deeply impressed by young Sarasvatichandra’s intelligence, his quest for knowledge, his humility, civility, his pure conscience, his friends and mellow nature. The Minister grew fond of the boy’s radiant and smiling face. The son of a wealthy merchant should ideally have been betrothed in infancy; but for some reason, four or five years went by without Sarasvatichandra’s marriage being fixed. Once Guman arrived, she consistently spurned all marriage proposals for the stepson without consulting Laxminandan. Ishwarkaur tried hard to find a match for her grandson, but all proposals fell through because of Guman. Finally, Ishwarkaur spoke to Laxminandan. He told her there was no need to tie down the boy at such a young age. When Sarasvatichandra was about fifteen years old, Guman gave birth to a son, whose marriage was fixed immediately. Laxminandan did not consider this either objectionable or unusual. But his mother lost her head and lashed out at him in anger; and so he was shamed into finding a match for his firstborn. Around that time, Vidya Chatura was on a visit to Bombay and was Laxminandan’s guest. He observed that Sarasvatichandra had progressed well in his studies, his intellect had matured, that he was fond of reading, and had acquired a refined sensibility and was appreciative of all the arts. His attachment and regard for the boy grew. Vidya Chatura was in search of a good match for his daughter. He felt it would be inappropriate to broach the matter directly with a man as prominent as Sheth Laxminandan. Instead, he sought his mother Ishwarkaur’s advice. The grandmother was delighted; Laxminandan, too, gladly accepted the proposal. Guman felt insanely jealous, but the men decided between themselves without consulting her. Ishwarkaur’s joy was boundless. A family like Vidya Chatura’s and a girl like Kumud Sundari were worth more than the wait of fifteen long years. She expressed her joy all the more effusively in Guman’s presence and showered love and blessings over her precious grandson. Guman seethed inwardly, but kept quiet. Ishwarkaur wanted an early marriage. She often wondered, Why does Vidya Chatura delay the marriage? Will I have the good fortune to bless the couple? She also sent messages to Vidya Chatura. Not eager for an early marriage, but anxious not to displease the old woman, the Minister made vague promises. Sarasvatichandra’s studies progressed well. He passed his M.A. at the young age of seventeen or eighteen. The following year he passed his legal examinations. Thereafter, he passed many examinations, wrote prize-winning essays for which he was awarded scholarships and medals. In every field he emerged at the top. University professors and well known scholars loved him. It was said that he had an original mind. His aesthetic ability was regarded to be of a high standard. Combining learning and wealth, he had all the good qualities of those born high, but none of the ills. He was tall, fair, well-built, and handsome to look at. His face was bright, his features delicate. His friends were given to saying that even if Sarasvatichandra were not learned or wealthy, his well-proportioned body, handsome and masculine bearing would have attracted others to him. As Kumud Sundari grew in age and maturity, she heard with interest her parents talk about Sarasvatichandra. Vidya Chatura and Sarasvatichandra regularly corresponded with each other through letters. Vidya Chatura often discussed Sarasvatichandra’s letters with his wife Gunasundari. Kumud wondered what this man was like, who came in for so much praise from her learned and affectionate father. Vidya Chatura also made it a point to talk of Sarasvatichandra when he knew Kumud was certain to be listening. He wanted her impressionable mind to develop a genuine affection for her husband- to-be; his wish was fulfilled. It also gave rise to unknown desires and passions in adolescent Kumud. In the first blush of her youth, she was anxious to see the man she was to wed, to get to know him. Such anticipation excited her imagination. One day, she saw one of his letters to her father. Vidya Chatura had left it on the table. She so wanted to read it. But how could she, without her father’s permission? Should she be brazen and ask him for it? Ultimately, curiosity got the better of her. There was no one else in the room. She went up to the table. Her eyes searched out the letter from a pile just as the first rays of dawn pick out a white lotus about to bloom. Her small fair hand emerged from the folds of her soft sky-blue sari and picked up the letter. She anxiously looked around for prying eyes, smiled, concealed the letter quickly in the folds of her sari and walked back to her room as if nothing had happened. For a moment she felt like a thief, but the thought did not stay with her long. She read the letter once, twice, thrice, and yet she was insatiable. Sarasvatichandra’s beautiful handwriting, his poetic language, his articulate and mature thoughts captivated her. She came under his spell. Excited, she pressed the letter to her chest. Her eyes had the vacant look of one looking into the distance. She murmured, My beloved, my dear, my life, you write so beautifully! Oh why won’t you write to me? In anticipation of a response, she eagerly began writing him a letter. But she suddenly felt bashful and could not decide how she should address him. She considered and rejected many adjectives. Finally, her letter began with: ‘My Chandra’ and ended with ‘Yours, Kumud’. The letter—her heart itself, her anticipation and waiting— reached Sheth Laxminandan’s house. Laxminandan picked it up from a pile of letters. He was surprised by the handwriting. He gave it to a servant. The servant showed it to Guman and then brought it to Sarasvatichandra as he sat talking to Chandrakant. The servant, as instructed by Guman, waited to find out the sender’s name. Sarasvatichandra was surprised by the unfamiliar handwriting. He tore open the letter, and was pleased to see the sender’s name at the bottom. He handed the letter with a smile to Chandrakant without telling him who it was from. He waited to see what his friend’s response would be. Chandrakant read the letter wide-eyed and said, smiling, ‘Bhai, this is indeed your good fortune. Among us, it would take another lifetime to find such a wife!’ Sarasvatichandra laughed aloud. ‘Chandrakant, tell me is this really such good fortune?’ ‘Then what else! Do Hindus ever find such rare gems? Bhai, this match is truly a divine blessing. You should thank God for it.’ ‘Your ideas have not progressed. Your English education makes you believe that the sum total of life is a good wife. The worldly efforts of men are not subsumed in a wife, Chandrakant.’ ‘I truly cannot fathom this ascetic trait in an aesthete like you!’ ‘But I have not spoken of asceticism.’ ‘What else is this! See the one I have at home, and then tell me how different our fortunes are! This letter itself is proof.’ ‘You are dissatisfied with your wife. Ganga bhabhi is simple- minded. Why such disaffection on account of her?’

‘You are the only one I know who has one measure for himself and another for others. You are not satisfied with a woman like Kumud Sundari, and you accuse me of disaffection! Bravo! Bravo! You are not happy even after receiving such a loving letter from your adolescent bride-to-be, and charge me of disaffection. I am quite happy Ganga is mine! But do think about what I’ve said. Here, read the letter at least.’ Sarasvatichandra got up and, walking about the room, said with a smile, ‘Chandrakant, do you really believe that I do not value this letter?’ ‘I am only going by your words.’ ‘If anyone knows my mind, it is you, Chandrakant. If you, too, make such a mistake, I cannot blame the others.’ ‘Was all that you said a lie, then?’ ‘No, what I said was true. And so is this. A body without a soul is useless; our body is more than the soul. How can one’s fortune be measured solely by whom one is married to?’ They chatted and argued amiably for a long time, after which Chandrakant went home. He was as well educated as Sarasvatichandra. But being poor, he could study only because of his friend’s help. Sarasvatichandra closed the door of his room, picked up the letter and read it again. What can an adolescent bride-to-be write to her chosen husband? Dear reader, pay attention. It was a short letter. My Chandra, I do not know what to write. I write because I could no longer contain myself. I wanted somehow to reach out to you, and hence this letter. You would laugh at this worthless piece of paper. But you are Chandra—you are the moon in the sky. It is the duty of the moon so high to nourish the Kumud that grows upon the earth. So the world says. And why should I not believe the same? I do not know what more to write. What if I should ask for your photograph? It is not I but my heart which has dictated this letter. You have inspired it. I have nothing more to say. Yours, Kumud.

Solitude opened Sarasvatichandra’s heart and softened it somewhat, made it tender. He believed that women were unnecessary in his life. He considered marriage a lifelong encumbrance. He saw a life without progeny as the epitome of renunciation. He preferred a love of the mind and its pursuits and believed that only fools desired bodily pleasures. He felt it was possible to keep the mind free of desires. He felt that worldly life was lowly, worthless and barren. He did not wish to hurt his affectionate grandmother by going against the worldly norms, and so he had accepted the marriage with Kumud Sundari. He was indifferent to Kumud’s virtues and follies. But mercury encased in glass does not remain unaffected by the temperature outside for long. His passions, buried under ascetic inclinations, came to the fore under the power of her unsullied beauty. His cold heart was drenched by the waves of simple affection that Kumud had unleashed. His desires, hitherto caged, flew out like freed birds as soon as Chandrakant left. Faced with her letter, his distance, his resolve melted, and he slumped into a chair, gazing intently at the delicate curves and whorls of Kumud’s words, running his fingers over them. What is this? What is this, Sarasvatichandra? What strange power is this? How you would laugh at me, Chandrakant, if you could see me now! He gazed at the writing on the letter for a long time. He was no longer ashamed to admit the salience of women. Then he began to write a response to Kumud. Beauteous, beloved Kumud, Your letter has become most precious to me. It is true that the moon in the sky remains unaffected by the lotus, but your letter has proved to me that the two of us are mutually dependent and share the same ground. If I had to describe your influence over someone as hard-hearted as me, I would describe it through this verse. O Vaidarbhi! You are blessed with so many virtues That even Naishadha is drawn to you Why should one praise the moon just because It makes the ocean turbulent with tide

Dear Kumud, my friend Chandrakant knows how stone- hearted I am. But I cannot even begin to describe the turmoil in my heart after receiving just one letter from you! I was too ashamed to bare my heart even to him. He still thinks I am cold and unfeeling. What if you should ask for my photograph? I am sending it, without your having to ask for it. And I will come to you—to gaze upon you. Dear Kumud, I dislike verbose, convoluted expressions of love. I do not know you at all, and yet I am compelled to write such a letter. My mind, hitherto self-content, now eagerly anticipates your response. Is this what people call love? Is this what is known as self-emanating, born of the mind? Is this desire? Desire has implanted itself even in my cold heart. Is it not true? Yours forever, Sarasvatichandra. Sarasvatichandra began to realise that human experience was constituted quite differently from knowledge and thought. This realisation was both exhilarating and unnerving. His carefully nurtured ascetic resolve melted and it was as if he was born anew, body and soul. His mind was possessed by a single thought: Kumud is mine, and I am hers. The romance of love triumphed over his ponderous knowledge and ideals. Sarasvatichandra found a reason to visit Ratnanagari, and was received affectionately by Vidya Chatura. He recognised Kumud at first glance. After Vidya Chatura left for the palace, Kumud, driven by curiosity, desire, love, stealthily walked up to Sarasvatichandra’s room. It did not even occur to her then to seek her mother’s consent. Sarasvatichandra was seated at a table with his back to her, writing a letter to Chandrakant. He remained unaware of her presence. Kumud pressed herself against the wall and stood to the right of the table. She was in his line of vision, but engrossed in writing, he did not look up. Tongue-tied, painfully shy, Kumud constricted herself even more, wanting to disappear into the wall. Her bangles tinkled softly against the wall and, startled, Sarasvatichandra looked up. He looked at her, elated. The famous scholar of Bombay, the son of wealthy Sheth Laxminandan, the toast of learned men, suddenly turned speechless before this delicate rose petal-like figure that stood before him, shrinking in her own skin. For long moments, neither of them could utter a word or blink; the world outside of them seemed to blur and vanish as they forgot all else, except for the eyes that remained intensely riveted upon each other. The girl was a mere adolescent. But even the scholarly man of letters was in the same state of speechless ecstasy. Then, as if awakened from a daze, Sarasvatichandra mumbled, ‘I have written a few books ...’ and he handed them to her. Kumud took the books from his hands and pressed them to her heart; her searching eyes withdrew, now fixing themselves upon her toes and his. She said nothing. During the exchange of books, their fingers had fleetingly brushed against each other; they were both acutely aware of this. His face lit up like the sun breaking through rain clouds. Her cheeks flushed a slow red just as the eastern horizon flushes crimson with the rising sun. She could not lift her eyes. The youth at last found his tongue and something to say. ‘God willing, you will come and live in Bombay very soon.’ No response. ‘Have you seen any of these books before?’ Silence again. ‘You wrote me such beautiful letters, and today, not a word out of you!’ She stood mute like a statue. ‘Kumud! My dearest Kumud!’ Sarasvatichandra got up from the chair. Hearing him speak her name, a sharp thrill coursed through her body as she had never before experienced. Her face turned a deep warm red, her knees felt weak. She mustered all her courage and said, barely audible, ‘You are here for a very short while, isn’t it?’ Her voice was soft as the tinkle of tiny silver anklets and sweet as a sarangi. These few words escaped her pearl-like teeth and along with her sweet-scented breath etched themselves upon Sarasvatichandra’s mind and heart. He felt an intense joy flood his being. His eyes came to rest upon her gentle and radiant face and he slumped back into the arm chair as if inebriated. They conversed for a brief hour or so, she standing before him while he sat in his chair. The hour passed much too quickly, and the spell was broken when young Kusum Sundari called for her sister. Sarasvatichandra remained seated for a long time after she left the room, with his eyes closed, trying to ascertain for himself whether these magically beautiful moments that had just passed were for real or part of a daydream. He spent a few days in this dreamlike state, after which he returned to Bombay and immediately wrote to her. In response to his letter from Bombay she wrote: ‘After you left, the poem “He stole my heart” keeps playing upon my lips. I recite it to myself and your image comes before me. I understand now what love is. My father has fixed the date of our marriage for the next month of Magha. My excitement is boundless. I cannot wait.’ Many such letters were exchanged. Some may feel it is useless to write letters without a purpose. One writes, I am going crazy without you, the other responds, I am possessed by you! Sombre people say that ‘the toys of children and the coquettishness of lovelorn lovers’ are similar. But wealth, prestige, power and suchlike which are dear to others are worthless to lovers who deepen their love for one another only by its constant expression and reiteration. Who between the two sides is right? The things that fascinate both groups are similar in nature: they are products of the imagination; they guide thought, word and deed. They are powerful and dear to those who hanker for them, but despised by those who have rejected them. They give joy as well as sorrow. They are real for those who believe in them, but a mere momentary mirage for those who do not. What is the difference between a heartfelt infatuation and the hoarding of wealth that one is certain to leave behind, or hankering after prestige or glory and the desire to commit to memory what is certain to be forgotten and craving for those who are certain to die? Sarasvatichandra’s mind which had once shown ascetic tendencies was now under the sway of entirely new emotions. He discoursed endlessly with himself about what he could see was changing within him everyday, and why. He could not understand that if asceticism was also a form of desire, why should he then shun this other powerful desire which he now experienced? Why cannot both exist simultaneously? Why should the soul remain untouched by the world if the body does not remain untouched? Sarasvatichandra also discussed these and other existential predicaments with Chandrakant, and wrote about them in his letters to Kumud. One responded as a worldly wise practical man would, while the other responded as a young woman deeply and irreversibly in love. He learnt much from both, and educated both in turn. He was immersed in a heady emotional and spiritual churning of sorts. Searching for answers to his own questions, Sarasvatichandra found himself shedding his old ideas like a snake sheds its skin, and being born into a new one. He wanted to possess Kumud Sundari’s tender, impressionable mind and heart. When Chandrakant reminded him of his earlier ascetic predisposition, he would say that renunciation meant being completely immersed in one thing, and shunning all else. And by that logic, he was still an ascetic. But the dreamlike state he was in did not leave him. His letters to Kumud were a reflection of his thoughts. Just as the reflection of the sky remains in the waters of a river, Sarasvatichandra’s thoughts were reflected in Kumud’s nascent mind. He was ever present in her mind, consciously and unconsciously. On one hand God set up this play, while on the other, He laid out an entirely different one. Human beings desire one thing, God wills something else. Guman’s son was no longer an infant. As a young bride, Guman had seen the affection that Sarasvatichandra had been given as a child. She wished similar affection to be showered upon her son Dhananandan. But for several reasons, her wish did not come true. As Sarasvatichandra matured in age and learning, the scholars who had previously collected around his father now sought his company. Over the years, they had become self-sufficient and were no longer dependent on the Sheth for patronage or money. They were grateful to him, but were no longer drawn to him as bees are to flowers. Moreover, wealth and status no longer enamoured and enticed them as easily as before. These scholars had more occasions to associate with Sarasvatichandra. Sarasvatichandra had become a lawyer of the Bombay High Court after passing his law examinations. He was studying to be a Council Barrister, albeit he did not intend to use his learning to secure a livelihood. He viewed the position of the Council Barrister as ornamental. He assisted his father in his business alongside his studies. Sarasvatichandra was acquainted with many learned and influential men of his times and was a member of several societies. These gave him the opportunity to make new associations. What was advantageous for the son was disadvantageous for the father. Sheth Laxminandan’s associates were newly wealthy men or those who sought wealth. The scholars preferred his son’s company; and so in scholarly circles, Sheth Laxminandan came to be known as ‘Sarasvatichandra’s father’. Guman was never fond of her stepson; now she had even less reason to be so. She seethed in jealousy. Guman saw Sarasvatichandra’s rise as detrimental to her son Dhananandan. In time, Sarasvatichandra passed the Council Barrister’s examination. Laxminandan was full of praise for his elder son, and made him a partner in his business. Guman’s woes multiplied. Old Ishwarkaur would fan Guman’s jealousy by unabashedly expressing her joy at her first grandson’s achievements. Much to Guman’s fury and vexation, even her little son was drawn to Sarasvatichandra; he would seek him out and climb into his lap, despite her instructions to the contrary. Guman would berate Laxminandan at every available opportunity. But the best time was after dinner when he came to bed, tired. She would say whatever she liked, and the man would meekly submit to her tongue-lashing, shamelessly accepting all the untruths he was told. Her inflammatory words had greater impact on his tired body and mind. She found something new to complain about every day. She had an inexhaustible supply of tears, taunts and rage. Her similes were more evocative than Kalidas, her power of narration tighter than that of Bana! But just as Guman had her faithfuls amongst the servants, Ishwarkaur had them, too. All that Guman said about Sarasvatichandra to Laxminandan was reported to Ishwarkaur, who would relate it to the grandson, who would, without any feeling of rancour or rage, pacify her. In a short time, Sarasvatichandra developed good business acumen. His courteousness impressed outsiders as well as those who worked under him. They all called him ‘Bhai’ and submitted to him with affection and respect. Soon, he began to take on the responsibilities of his father. This gave Guman one more reason to be unhappy. Complaints about ‘Bhai’ erupted like so many ants on Guman’s bed. ‘Wonderful! No one heeds you in this house anymore! It is Bhai’s rule inside and Bhai’s rule outside. Whatever Bhai wants happens. I am of no consequence at all, but that is hardly new. But you? You were once worshipped like a god; now they treat you like a stone. Are you at all concerned? They barely acknowledge your presence. Such is my state when you are around, who knows what awaits me later! Bhai will become the master of the house and we shall be his servants. Whom shall I blame? When you are so meek, to whom shall I take my complaints? Mark my words, Bhai will reduce you to a sorry state one day. You trust him so easily because he is your son, but these English educated sons are not true even to their parents. He will capture the house, the jewellery and the business—and leave you with nothing to do but count beads! You will be subservient to him. And who will care for poor me and my Dhan!’ she sobbed. ‘If you were so uncaring, why did you marry me! I would have toiled and ground grain for others and filled my stomach somehow. But I would not have seen such days at least. Nothing moves here without Bhai. No one can be so submissive even to one’s own son. ‘Listen to me. He knows the law—everyone will support him. Journalists and High Court judges are his friends. He will know all your tricks and then capture the business. If you object, he will file a complaint and seek his share. Beware, wake up before it is too late. There is still something to be salvaged. Instead of him giving us a share, you give Bhai his share and settle the matter so that we don’t have to worry about tomorrow. But I know, you can never love us as much as you love him. For you he is made of gold, and we of ash. Are you at all concerned about what will happen to me as a poor, wretched widow?’ Over time, these nightly discourses had their impact. They broke Laxminandan’s resistance just as waves break a rock and turn it into sand. During the day, Laxminandan had little time to worry about such matters. But at night, despite his resolve not to listen, these complaints would raise their ugly head. He despised his wife for it; but he neither had the time and energy to ascertain the truth, nor the courage to shut her up. All these things were said behind Sarasvatichandra’s back, which gave him no opportunity to explain himself. As termites eat through wood, ultimately, the woman bore a hole in Laxminandan’s head and made him powerless. The son through his generosity, courtesy and ability wielded authority; but the father could not see this. Instead, he imagined the worst possible picture as painted by his wife. He began to believe Guman. One evening Laxminandan came home exhausted. He was hugely relieved not to find Guman in the bedroom. He slumped into an easy chair and asked a servant to bring him his food. He put his feet up and relaxed. Suddenly, he found Guman facing him. Oh God! What new war will she wage now, he thought nervously. She stood there in silence. Laxminandan began to eat. Even when tired and irritated, the Sheth thought of his son and couldn’t help but ask, ‘Is Bhai back? Has he eaten?’ A demonic power does not forgive even a single misstep. Sheth Laxminandan realised that his innocent question was about to unleash a barrage of abuse. He knew he had invited trouble. Guman burst forth: ‘So much affection for Bhai? Bhai has come home and eaten without worrying about his father. The father can think of nothing but Bhai. Bhai does not even bother about you. He is engrossed in reading his wife’s letters—even before they are married! You don’t bother about the one you married. People are wrong when they sing: Happy are those who marry the twice-married!’

The English charge that Hindu women enjoy no freedom. But was Guman any less free if she could scold an elderly man as wealthy and powerful as Sheth Laxminandan? A clerk, who had come in to deliver a telegram from England for Laxminandan, went back considering this question. The Sheth had just finished his meal. Guman went in to keep his soiled plate while Laxminandan read the telegram. She returned and stood leaning against a window railing; then she took out a letter. ‘Whose is it?’ ‘Have a look. It is Bhai’s letter to Kumud. Did you ever write such things to me?’ Guman said, handing him the letter stolen from Sarasvatichandra’s desk. Laxminandan took the letter and looked up at her incredulously. For once, he was both perturbed and enraged. ‘Where did you get this letter from? How could you do this? And you have the gall to give it to me! Are you not ashamed?’ Guman was not the least put out and calmly replied, ‘I know I should not have given his letter to you. I also know that I should not have read it. I have brought it only to show you Bhai’s true character. I have not stolen it. The wind brought it to my room. If I return it now, he will accuse me of prying. Therefore, I gave it to you. You do what you like with it. We also married, and I am only a few years older than Bhai. But it is not proper to write such letters before marriage. It is not as if he is the first one to get married.’ Laxminandan’s anger subsided. He read a few words of the letter, then said, ‘Let him write what he wants, what it is to you? He is young. He has not written it to someone else’s wife, has he!’ ‘That is true. But if I am at fault, I am treated as an elder, but when Bhai does something wrong, he is just a young boy! I gave it to you for a reason; read it if you want to. Who bothers about me in any case!’ Guman left the room in a feigned huff, sobbing. The Sheth did not bother about her and went back to his telegram, muttering to himself, Oh why on earth did God create women? Why? They are so stupid, so utterly stupid—stupid from head to toe! The Sheth knew that Guman was stupid, but his natural affinity for her convinced him that she was not wicked or malicious. He was inclined to pardon her stupidity, though he found her most tiresome at times. Guman realised the Sheth was in no mood to placate her. She re-entered the room on pretext of some work. Sheth was preoccupied with the telegram. She tried to draw his attention by opening and closing the doors noisily, and feigning as if she were suppressing sobs. The Sheth looked up and soothingly asked, ‘Why are you standing there? Come, come here. Now stop crying. Do not do such things in future, all right? What is there to cry about? See, what did you gain by bringing his letter to me?’ Guman came in and sat on a chair facing him, her eyes red with crying. The Sheth took pity on her. He got up, closed the door and came and sat next to her, trying to placate her. Guman saw that her plan was coming to fruition. At first she played hard to get, then meekly said, ‘What is it to me? I gave you a letter. But this Kumud is truly a match for Bhai. By mistake the postman gave me a letter addressed to Bhai, and I opened it, believing it was for me. But just see how clever this woman is! Her roots are deep. Simple men like you won’t understand a woman’s character. We do. Bhai has become her captive already. If she has such a hold on him now, what would she not do later? We will have no place to go to. We will also have to be subservient to her. Bhai also writes to his father-in-law. You were only telling me the other day how cunning these people from the native states tend to be. Moreover, those who have received an English education remain faithful to no one. They will show their true colours at the right time. Now you run the business. So you should be in control outside, and I should rule over the house. Instead, we have a different story. And you still trust Bhai!’ Guman spoke submissively without aggression. This softened the Sheth further. He said, ‘All right. But is this such a big problem?’ He read the letters because Guman wanted him to. Then he remarked, ‘But what is so objectionable about these letters? They are what all young people write to each other.’

‘You will hand over everything to Bhai. Have you ever considered what will happen to my Dhan and me?’ ‘Oh. So is that what it is?’ ‘Yes. Is that not a problem? For you it is all very trivial.’ ‘All right. That will be taken care of,’ the Sheth placated Guman, made her laugh, fooled around with her for a while and went out. Sarasvatichandra’s thoughts were all about Kumud Sundari. She played on his mind constantly. As the day of marriage came closer, his joy increased manyfold. He controlled his father’s business. He knew that no questions would be asked if he were to spend money from its accounts. His mother Chandralaxmi had received close to a lakh of rupees from her parents and from Laxminandan in jewellery and money. Sarasvatichandra inherited it when he became an adult. He preferred to spend money from this amount rather than spend his father’s money. His father owned two or three bungalows on the Walkeshwar hill. He was given one of them for his use. The bungalow had a large drawing room. Sarasvatichandra decorated it to his taste, for which he spent five to six thousand rupees. He had a large portrait of Kumud painted and had it framed in an intricately carved ivory frame, spending another three, four thousand rupees on it. Sarasvatichandra liked to gaze at this portrait for long hours in company of his friend Chandrakant. Chandrakant often reminded him of his former ascetic nature and teased him. Sarasvatichandra’s response was always laughter. He believed that his love and devotion for his wife was true, praiseworthy, and considered it his moral duty to further this emotion. Thoughts are guided by disposition. To top it all, Sarasvatichandra got an exquisite diamond ring made. A large diamond, pure as water, set in an intricate gold base. The base could be opened by pressing a key, supported by a tiny hinge. On the inside of the base was painted a beautiful image of Sarasvatichandra’s face, which could be seen only when the base was open. The ring was for Kumud. It cost five thousand. For this millionaire’s son who did not hesitate before spending fifteen or twenty thousand rupees, this expenditure on the love of his life was paltry. Chandrakant teased him on his face, but secretly he admired

Sarasvatichandra’s devotion to Kumud and sincerely wished his friend good luck. Oh, the wealthy are most fortunate! A mind so pure and noble despite so much wealth! Such deep learning, such prestige, and the blessing of a union with such a loving and beautiful woman! And so much love and devotion! My good friend is fortunate indeed! May God protect his luck! Chandrakant did not know that the wheels of fortune can turn in a moment. In the game of dice that is life, luck and misfortune are two sides of the same dice. These stories travelled to Guman, who naturally related them to Laxminandan, furnishing proof that Bhai in his infatuation would squander all the family wealth on his wife. Laxminandan had never spent money on such things; even he felt that his son’s expenditure was unjustified. Guman said, ‘We know of this expenditure—it has been spent from the wealth that you have entrusted to him. But we do not know where else he has spent the money. How can we know? This is the outcome of your trust.’ It never occurred to the Sheth that Sarasvatichandra could have spent the money from his own inheritance from Chandralaxmi. Ishwarkaur knew of Guman’s machinations. She would tell Sarasvatichandra, who would listen to her without comment, and try and solace her as best as he could. But he was pained by Guman’s evil doings, and by his own father’s unsteady mind. Ishwarkaur was convinced that Laxminandan would disinherit Sarasvatichandra someday. She could do little about it, but she had about a lakh of rupees which she wanted to give to Sarasvatichandra. Sarasvatichandra smiled at the suggestion and said, ‘Grandmother, God will take care for me, as He does for everyone else. If we were to implement this suggestion, parents would become even angrier and the conflict would escalate. The best option is to will this money to the younger brother. The money will remain with you for your lifetime, the parents will be happy, and these hurtful schemes and machinations will also stop.’ Ishwarkaur was not convinced. She was certain that neither Laxminandan nor Guman would be grateful to Sarasvatichandra; moreover, this was too small a sum to turn Guman benevolent. Ishwarkaur knew that her grandson was quite capable of charting his own course. But she was sad that the most worthy son of the family was likely to receive nothing from the ancestral wealth, and felt helpless as Sarasvatichandra himself opposed her plans. Ishwarkaur called Chandrakant and sought his assistance. Chandrakant approved of the old woman’s plan, but he knew it would be extremely difficult to fructify. There was a time when Sarasvatichandra had different plans. He wanted to give away Chandralaxmi’s wealth for activities dedicated to the country’s progress. His father’s wealth was ancestral property. He wanted to renounce his claims over it. His desire was to mingle with the common folk without donning the saffron robes of a mendicant. He wanted to travel across the length and width of the country in search of new experiences, and God. He wanted to spend three, four years as a wanderer, then settle down someplace and use his experience and knowledge for the social and spiritual uplift of the people. Sarasvatichandra realised that the reformist classes would decry his actions, and also that his father would be terribly pained by it. He was not going to be deterred by any direct or indirect criticism that might come his way while adopting a path he  strongly believed in. But Sarasvatichandra abandoned his plan knowing how his father would feel. Chandrakant knew of these plans. He knew from his own knowledge that Sarasvatichandra himself was the biggest obstacle in actualising his grandmother’s plans. Chandrakant was a pragmatic man; he had known extreme poverty first-hand, he knew the pain, the ignominy and desperation of poverty. He loved Sarasvatichandra even more for his self- sacrificing tendencies. But he was afraid that these very inclinations would someday lead this gem of a man to an obscure life. He did not want his dear friend to abandon such wealth and adopt poverty. He was pained by the thought that his learned friend would invite the censure of the reformists because of his renunciation. The deep bond between Kumud Sundari and Sarasvatichandra had assuaged his fears somewhat. And yet he saw some strange similarities between Sarasvatichandra’s fierce idealism, his strongly ascetic predisposition, and his intense love for Kumud. Chandrakant feared that someday Sarasvatichandra, accompanied by Kumud Sundari, would renounce the world. For all these reasons he was keen to put Ishwarkaur’s plan into action. Chandrakant wanted a solution that could be kept secret from Sarasvatichandra, and one that was irreversible. Chandrakant advised Ishwarkaur to appoint someone she trusted as an administrator of her wealth, who would manage her property and give her the profits accruing from it. After her death, the property would vest in Sarasvatichandra and his wife, and in case of Sarasvatichandra being without his wife, then in him alone. Chandrakant was certain that Sarasvatichandra would never use this wealth for selfish purposes. They could not decide who the administrator should be. Ishwarkaur asked Chandrakant to accept the responsibility. He accepted, as there was no other way of securing his friend’s interest. A deed was drafted; some prestigious persons were called in as witnesses. Sarasvatichandra had no inkling of all this. Finally, when it was ready, Ishwarkaur summoned Laxminandan one day and handed him the deed in the presence of everyone. She chose not to explain her decision. She merely asked him to write his assent on the deed. She knew her son would have no option but to sign. Laxminandan read the deed, but appeared hesitant to sign. Ishwarkaur commanded, ‘Bhai, sign the deed.’ Wealthy, influential and prestigious Sheth Laxminandan saw a different facet of his mother that day— there was no plea in her voice. He had no option but to submit to her wishes. Laxminandan felt he was being punished for his subservience to Guman. His mother appeared to him then as a divine avenger. He signed the deed and handed it back to his mother. All those present solemnly signed as witnesses. No one spoke a word. There hung a photograph of Chandralaxmi near the door of Ishwarkaur’s room. Laxminandan looked up at it and felt as if Chandralaxmi approved of his actions. He could almost hear her say, ‘What you have done is worthy of my love.’ Laxminandan felt that Chandralaxmi was content. Looking at her photograph, he remembered the love, the simple pleasures and joys that the two of them had shared in the past. And for a while, he forgot Guman. Then he got up and went to his room. He found Guman sitting there. Sheth Laxminandan felt like the aged King Dashrath must have felt as he left Queen Kaushalya’s palace after proclaiming that Ram would be king, and entered Queen Kaikayi’s chamber. Laxminandan put his hand on Guman’s shoulder. Faced with the stark reality of his present, his blissful unsullied dream shattered. ‘So you are back. What did she want?’ Guman began her slow interrogation and got her husband to divulge everything. She was convinced this entire plan was hatched by Sarasvatichandra. She could now prove the vile influence of English education. The Sheth felt obliged to compensate her for the perceived injustice done to Dhananandan. Guman sieved his fatherly joy into doubt and despair. Where once stood a secure tree that generously showered affection, a weak and poisonous weed took root. How did my innocent son suddenly conceive of this deed? It must be the machinations of Kumud, or her father, reasoned the Sheth. He became convinced that his son had betrayed him, and sorely repented having signed the deed. He began to look at each of Sarasvatichandra’s business decisions with jealousy and suspicion. The son’s judgements were pure as gold, but to the father’s clouded eyes they seemed impure as brass. There were differences in their thinking, as there are wont to be between the old and the new. Innocent and undoubting, the son acted in good faith, believing he still enjoyed the right of disputation, and that his view would prevail. But the Sheth cross-examined each act minutely, and saw only what he chose to see. He came to be haunted by the thought that, My son will take over everything and reduce me to nothing. The Sheth devised a ploy to ascertain his suspicions. Guman’s brother Dhurtalal exercised considerable influence over his sister. He had hitherto been unable to get a foothold into Laxminandan’s house. He now saw that the fish was about to bite the bait and seized the moment. Guman’s acerbic tongue was Dhurtalal’s source of power. The Sheth reasoned with himself: I reposed full trust in my son, but Guman’s charges are proving to be true. How can I not believe her now? My confidence in Sarasvati was false. The response of the haunted mind was the one that he chose to believe. Sheth Laxminandan was the managing director of a cotton weaving mill. A few years ago he had entrusted this position to Sarasvatichandra. Laxminandan devised a plan to enrol Dhurtalal as an assistant to Sarasvatichandra and, over time, make them joint managing directors. He argued that it would protect Dhananandan’s interests. If Sarasvatichandra could have seen through his father, he would have seen that the plan was to clip his wings. But that is not what he saw. His were the eyes of a trusting son. Sarasvatichandra knew about the sayings of worldly wise men that all machinations begin with a breach of trust and one person’s goodness can be the peg from which the wicked gain a foothold. He was also told that one person’s trust can be the source of strength for another. He had been cautioned that one should trust others only after they have proven their trustworthiness. But Sarasvatichandra had hitherto not felt the need to put these into practice. How can a loving and devoted son ever feel that, my own father is playing a treacherous game with me? Sarasvatichandra responded to his father with a pure conscience. ‘Pitaji, Dhurtalal is our relative, and we should try and do him good to the extent possible. However, you are not unaware of his attitude and conduct. We can only deal with honest and sincere persons, or else we shall have to face the consequences. Monetary loss is insignificant, but we can ill afford the loss of trust and prestige or a loss to the shareholders of our mill. If you want him to join a business, we can easily accommodate him in any of our personal businesses, can’t we? There are other ways to ensure Gumanba’s happiness, an honest income for Dhurtalal, and no injury to our reputation.’ But the Sheth who had already made up his mind did not like this intervention. His suspicion deepened. ‘Bhai, but I have decided. It must be done.’ ‘But there must be a good reason for it.’ ‘My wish is reason enough.’

‘If that is so, your wish is my command. I only suggested what I thought was in the interest of the family.’ ‘That is all right. Make sure this is done.’ ‘Yes.’ For the first time, Sarasvatichandra heard a different tone in his father’s voice. He could not fathom the reason for it. But he felt no need to dwell upon it further. It must be one of those things, he said to himself. He could never imagine that his father wanted to eliminate him from business. The Sheth thought: That was easy! Around this time one day, old Ishwarkaur died while counting the beads. Laxminandan felt sad for a while, but not for long because of the grudge he bore her. He joined in with the laughter and chatter at the crematorium and did not think that his behaviour was unnatural. When he returned from the cremation, Guman was all dressed up to mourn, and he remarked on her attractiveness without any feeling of sadness. But for Sarasvatichandra, the loss was immense, and for a while he felt that with her passing away, he no longer had any more ties with the family. His grandmother had lavished much care and affection in raising him. He moved Chandralaxmi’s photograph and a few other memorabilia from Ishwarkaur’s room to his own. He would look at them and remember vividly his grandmother’s stories, her affection. Forlorn, he sought solace at work. He never once thought about her wealth, and remained ignorant of the arrangement that she had made for him. Laxminandan had set aside a large sum of money for Guman just about the time that Sarasvatichandra had joined his business. He had wanted to invest the money in some good shares. He had then trusted the elder son and sought his advice. Sarasvatichandra believed that women’s wealth should not be invested in shares and had advised his father to instead invest it in secure government ‘loans’. Laxminandan had  accepted this advice. Sarasvatichandra had inherited Chandralaxmi’s wealth, which was also invested in government loans. He decided to redeem the loan and invested the proceeds in shares. Those days, there were rumours of a possible

Russian aggression. The sale and purchase of government loans was stopped, and consequentially their market price also fell. The shares in which Sarasvatichandra had invested rose in value, from which he made huge profits. Laxminandan now suspected that Sarasvatichandra had deliberately misguided him. He had done one thing for himself and offered contrary advice for Guman. What could it mean? Love and trust prompt one to find benevolence even in a malicious deed, but disaffection and mistrust give rise to suspicion even in benevolent acts. One day after lunch, father and son went to office in their two- horse drawn carriage. Guman had tutored Laxminandan. He was angry about Ishwarkaur’s money, the imagined influence of Kumud’s family on Sarasvatichandra, and the seemingly harmful advice he had given on the financial market. Guman added salt to the wound. The Sheth broached the matter in the carriage. ‘Bhai, are you keeping track of the market prices?’ ‘Yes, the prices are good,’ and he told his father of the profits he had made. ‘But the government note is trading weak.’ ‘Yes, it will bounce back once these rumours subside.’ ‘And what if the Russians invade?’ The son laughed and said, ‘Father, it will take a while.’ ‘You sold your government notes?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Oh, I see,’ Laxminandan looked at his son askance. ‘Bhai, I am very disappointed in you. I must speak frankly with you.’ This unusual and illogical opening surprised Sarasvatichandra considerably. ‘Of course! If you do not tell me, who will!’ ‘Listen carefully. For many days I have observed you but said nothing. You have changed, though I cannot fathom why. But it is my considered opinion that your views are no longer independent. Your marriage has been fixed to make you happy. But it is your duty to ensure that it does not lead to conflict within the family. Some youngsters become totally besotted with their wives, who never fail to take advantage of it. Such women are eager to destroy the household by using their husbands as tools. Those who influence their husbands before marriage will stop at nothing after marriage. But if the husband’s heart is in the right place, such a situation will never arise. I am not suggesting that you are one of them. Only that if you are aware, you can be careful.’ If Sarasvatichandra had any intention to respond, it vanished. Laxminandan had crossed limits, but he could not do likewise. The only thought in his head was, My pure, innocent Kumud! He was profoundly hurt and angered by this vile and baseless allegation against her. Oh father! You do not know what you have said! It does not deserve a response. Dearest Kumud, in my heart and before God, your purity remains unsullied. This allegation in fact makes you shine forth even brighter. Sarasvatichandra had great reserves of forbearance, but only with regard to his own self. Every pore in his being felt outraged at this unjust accusation of Kumud, that too by his own father. My own Kumud! Why should I accept this vile and false charge against you? Is it not a crime before God? His face turned a deep red, but he somehow controlled his rage. He did not show the anguish he felt and allowed his father to speak without a pause. Under Guman’s inexorable and unforgiving influence, Laxminandan had completely lost his power to discriminate between good and bad,  right and wrong, rational and irrational. He said everything he could have and more. He said he had faltered in his assessment of Vidya Chatura. He said Guman was vulnerable, and reminded Sarasvatichandra of his duties towards his stepmother. He accused him of being bewitched by Kumud Sundari and told him that men who submit to their wife and father-in-law are called effeminate. He expressed his displeasure at the huge sums of money that Sarasvatichandra had wasted in decorating the Walkeshwar bungalow and said he was worried about the future of a son as profligate as him. He charged Sarasvatichandra of profiteering from shares while ensuring losses for Guman. He also pointed out his own generosity in signing Ishwarkaur’s deed, and said, ‘But you should not have plotted such a thing against me.’ He taunted him about Dhurtalal’s inclusion in business, saying, ‘You refused, but gave in only because I stood firm.
