You should be beholden to me, always.’ He did not spare Sarasvatichandra’s education and learning. ‘You cannot earn a living simply by putting on airs of your English education,’ he said. He said Sarasvatichandra was wrong to believe that he, Sheth Laxminandan, would cower before his knowledge of law. He said this and many such unbearable things. He picked holes in his son’s business dealings to show that Sarasvatichandra lacked intelligence, experience, ability, judgement, in practical dealings and analytical faculties. He also gave him a long lecture on how his devotion to his father was found lacking. Sarasvatichandra could not understand many of the things that were said to him, or even begin to gauge their intent. He was utterly and completely taken by surprise. He saw Guman’s absolute control over his father and began to realise the extent of the situation he now found himself in. He witnessed the full force of his father’s disaffection and the limitless injustice that was meted out to him, and recognised with sadness that his father was the epitome of weakness, insecurity and stupidity. He did not respond, since a retort would have been contrary to his understanding of his duties as a son, and of his upbringing. He knew that words were now futile. Even to reveal his mind was beneath his dignity and he chose to remain silent. He no longer pondered over his father’s stupidity; his only concern now was the dilemma: What is my duty at present? What should I do now? He was so engrossed in this contemplation that Laxminandan’s words no longer penetrated his ears. His face had turned red, he was drenched in sweat, he trembled with hurt, rage and indignation, his heart was filled with anguish and a bottomless despair, he could not think, his stomach was one tight knot, and hot tears gradually welled up in his eyes. No one saw him shed a tear. Sheth’s interminable umbrage abruptly came to an end as he had nothing more left to say, and was exhausted besides. They reached office. Laxminandan got down with the air of a judge who had meted out just punishment. Sarasvatichandra followed him like a man just awakened from a ten-year long sleep. From now on, he was on his own. His head had turned.

Sarasvatichandra wrote a note and called for Dhurtalal. He spent the day familiarising Dhurtalal about all business matters. At the end of the day he took Dhurtalal to Laxminandan. Dhurtalal related the day’s events to Laxminandan, who was happy at the turn of events. The next day Sarasvatichandra reported to his father on all the matters that he dealt with. Laxminandan was pleasantly surprised and asked what the matter was. Sarasvatichandra replied, ‘Nothing. Just like that.’ That evening he went home with his father and left soon afterwards, saying, ‘Tonight I will eat and sleep at the Walkeshwar bungalow.’ The home bustled with regular hangers-on and activities, but he remained indifferent to it. When the evening lamps were lit, he took the carriage and went out. He picked up Chandrakant on the way. The cool sea breeze on the Chowpaty beach did not assuage his state of mind. He felt no joy at the sight of the dark hills in the distance. He did not exchange a word with his friend on the way. As the horses pulled the carriage up the hill, Sarasvatichandra was suddenly pushed against his friend by this sudden movement, and it broke his reverie. They had passed by the colourful cosmopolitan crowds of Bombay, horse drawn carriages, lazy merchants, laughing children unattached to worldly concerns, friends sitting on the rocks with arms around each other, worshipful Parsis and European couples riding in free abandon— Sarasvatichandra’s eyes had not seen any of them. The expression in them was peculiarly intense and distant. As if wanting to ask a question of the huge orange sun setting between the beacon at Colaba and the hills of Walkeshwar. As if searching for some spot far out on the limitless grey-green sea. As if wanting to measure the depths of the darkness now descending upon them. At last the carriage approached the bungalow. The purebred horses turned into the driveway, neighing. The coachman put aside his whip. The cool green of the darkening garden welcomed them. The gravel crunched crisply under the horses’ hooves. The carriage came to a halt at the doorsteps. The two friends got down. They entered the newly decorated drawing room, and stood facing Kumud Sundari’s portrait. Sarasvatichandra leaned upon his friend’s shoulder and gazed at the portrait. He went up close to it, then turned around and led his friend to a couch covered with brocade cushions. He sat down beside him, rested his head on Chandrakant’s shoulder and broke down. He wept and sobbed like a child. Chandrakant was astonished and perturbed. He tried to comfort him, ‘Bhai, Bhai! What is this! What is wrong? Have courage. What ever happened?’ ‘Chandrakant ... Chandrakant. No. There is nothing to be said. I am perfectly calm. What can happen? Nothing. Nothing whatsoever.’ ‘What is it then?’ Chandrakant’s heart beat faster. ‘I will tell you.’ Sarasvatichandra wiped his tears, sat upright and patiently narrated the incident with his father. He also told him that he had handed over the business to Dhurtalal. His head had now cleared. ‘Chandrakant, I am ashamed that for a while I allowed my emotions to run riot. But what could I do? I had no inkling that things had come to such a pass. It is God’s will.’ ‘Bhai, the fault is not yours. But you have acted in haste; it was not right.’ ‘Chandrakant, from today on, I shall treat my father’s wealth like wealth gifted to a temple. I shall not touch it.’ ‘Calm down! Why say such things? It is not as if you do not have options.’ ‘No, I do not want any options. Sacrifice by one who has no options is like the chastity of an aged woman. My father believes that I relate to him for his wealth alone. He no longer cares for me. Nor does he trust me. It is good that he does not care for me. His mistrust I will remove. I shall bequeath all my wealth to Gumanba and Dhanbhai, may God grant them eternal wealth. Poverty is not too difficult for me.’ ‘Why do you persist with such unreason! Has God not granted you enough learning?’ ‘I do not wish to hawk my learning. I am not worried about a livelihood. I do not need wealth—it is useless for me. You know well that I remained a householder only for the sake of my father’s love. That love no longer holds. So I am now a free man!’

‘Who says wealth is useless?’ ‘I know your views. But the good of the country, the good of the people and the good of the self can all be attained without wealth. What can others do if we are found to be lacking?’ ‘You could practice before the High Court. Are you not qualified?’ ‘Fool, don’t you know that I have always despised it! Do you really think I would soil myself in a world I find so repugnant just for the sake of filling my belly!’ ‘But what about engaging with the practical aspects of life? Aren’t you running away from those?’ ‘Chandrakant, stop it. I do not want to have this debate.’ ‘But it is not as if you have to earn your livelihood. You have one lakh rupees. Your grandmother has left it for you, and Kumud Sundari.’ Sarasvatichandra was speechless. Chandrakant apprised him of Ishwarkaur’s deed. Some of Laxminandan’s long litany of accusations now began to make sense. Sarasvatichandra was greatly displeased, but there was nothing he could do. He had no right to gift away Kumud Sundari’s share. ‘Chandrakant, I do not care. I do not want that money.’ ‘You are mad, Sarasvatichandra! It is your own money. Set up your own household. Augment your learning, do good unto the world, give joy to Kumud, and be happy yourself! Can’t you do that much?’ ‘But I cannot set up my own household. My father now believes that Vidya Chatura proposed the marriage only for his wealth. What can be done? The engagement cannot be called off on that ground.’ ‘You are being as wise as the God’s bull. Vidya Chatura was impressed by you and nothing else.’ ‘Chandrakant, I desire to observe the pain and joys of poverty, experience the state of a vagabond, search out gems obscured by poverty and ignorance. I now have that opportunity.’ ‘But what will people say?’

‘I do not fear opprobrium. Prestige and ignominy are both false measures of human effort; they are but dreams. They are not tangible objects that can be grasped.’ ‘All right. But have you even spared a thought for Kumud Sundari?’ ‘I leave her care to God. Her love, the outcome of a short acquaintance, will wane. She will forget me once she finds a good husband.’ ‘You are making a mistake. You will repent deeply if you hurt that young woman. You will commit a crime before God. She, too, is not going to be erased from your mind and conscience.’ ‘I know myself.’ ‘Indeed! If you really do, what else is needed! All you can then do is to aspire for the dreams of a deranged man. What others suppress, you not only articulate but also wish to experience. To me, this is a sign of pure idiocy and irrationality.’ ‘You have said enough.’ ‘Have I? I merely speak, but you are about to destroy everything! You became a barrister, gained so much learning, prestige, cultivated a love so profound and mutual, you have so much wealth and learning. Just think, what have you set out to do? This is the height of foolishness! Just imagine, what would you have said if some other barrister had brought this unto himself?’ ‘What else can I do?’ ‘You can and must put to good use the ability, the resources, and the virtue that is uniquely yours. Do not think like a cowardly ascetic and withdraw from the world just because it is difficult! Consider what would then happen to more ordinary mortals like the rest of us.’ Sarasvatichandra became pensive. He rested his head upon the couch. His half-closed eyes were for a while vacant. After a long silence, he reached out a hand to touch Chandrakant on the shoulder and began to speak in a voice grave and sad. ‘Chandrakant, my dear Chandrakant! I cannot ever repay you for your friendship. A judge hears arguments of both sides before making up his mind. But a man takes an extreme decision privately; very rarely does he have friend to argue with. You have said much, you have even argued against me, but I know you have always thought for me, for my best interest. Nevertheless, my resolve does not leave me. ‘Dear pure Kumud, I have had to hear words that abased you. And keep silent. Those words have left wounds in my heart which will not heal. I know my duty towards my father. But if in fulfilling that duty, I am required to torment or neglect my wife, this is not acceptable to me. A wife considers her duties to her husband primary as compared to her obligations to her parents. Once married, she accepts the husband’s primacy. Why should the duties of a husband be any different, then? If a scripture says that I should torture my wife to make my parents happy, I reject such a scripture. One eye should be on parents and the other on the wife; more preferably, both eyes should look at them with equanimity—such is the duty of a son and husband. A virtuous wife and a Respected lord. Are each to either all—kindred And friends, Wealth, love and life, and all The heart should covet.⟨fn:20⟩ ‘Yes, I think it is best that parents do not marry their sons if they want the son to neglect his wife and not share her joys and sorrows. My father wants me to be such a son even before marriage. After marriage, I would never have fulfilled his desires. It would have aggrieved us both. Marriage would have united Kumud and me. But what about my father? I am a son to him, but who is Kumud to him? Chandrakant, I know such logic can be nauseating. Kumud will never cease to reside in my mind. The beauty and purity of her heart has come to possess me, and it always will. I know well that separation from her would mean great suffering for both of us. But my father is my father and will remain so. It is therefore best that this marriage does not take place. I will, for his sake, bear the agony. Kumud will marry someone else and forget me in time. A marriage to me will not make her happy. No one will let her be in peace—and hence ...’ Sarasvatichandra was overcome with emotion; but he quickly regained composure and continued: ‘You would argue that I should build our own house where Kumud and I would be happy. But why should that be necessary? If I have my own house, Pitaji would see me as a competitor—that thought itself is painful to me. Painful because it would make him unhappy and I would be forced to be party to his embarrassment. His happiness is also my goal. ‘No. It is better to be unknown rather than to live apart from him. If it brings censure, it would be of my conduct. I am not afraid of that. Dhanbhai will ensure that my father does not miss having a son. The wedge of fear and envy in Gumanba’s mind will also be removed. My father will regain his composure. Pitaji does not love me anymore, and so he will not feel the pain of my absence. I will not be worried on his account because he is a wealthy man. But I will never be able to forget him. It pains me that Kumud will always be present before me. And you, Chandrakant! How am I ever going to forget you! Chandrakant, the web of household obligations and service to the country, and your learning will help you forget me. If my father were to ever miss me, do comfort him, care for him. I will never forget you, Chandrakant.’ Chandrakant became emotional. He held Sarasvatichandra’s hand in his and said, ‘Dear friend, why do you say these things? Why are you being so cruel?’ Chandrakant had practical sense. He hoped that by diverting Sarasvatichandra, his agitation and turmoil would subside. They talked of other things. Sarasvatichandra appeared quite calm. Finally, it was eleven in the night when the two friends parted. Sarasvatichandra ran after him with a bag, saying ‘Chandrakant, take this bag with you. I will tell you in the morning what is to be done with it.’ ‘Friend, I think I shall also sleep here at the bungalow.’ ‘No, no! Go home, or Ganga bhabhi will curse me.’

‘No, that she will not do. I do not trust your intentions.’ Sarasvatichandra laughed. ‘Go now, don’t be so suspicious. What will you do if my mind becomes uncontrollable?’ ‘You are audacious and impossible. That is why I’m concerned.’ ‘Now go home.’ ‘But you will be careful and not do anything rash.’ ‘All right. Send the carriage for me in the morning.’ Chandrakant took the bag and went home in the carriage, reassured that Sarasvatichandra would meet him next morning to give him instructions about the contents of the bag. Next morning, he waited for the carriage. There was no sign of it till eight. Chandrakant grew anxious. He hired a carriage and went to the bungalow. There was no one there except the gardener who told him, ‘Bhai left early in the morning for a walk to Chowpaty.’ Chandrakant rushed in the carriage to Chowpaty beach, a favourite spot of Bombay residents. A long paved road curves along the seashore. A little ahead, there is a railway crossing and station. Chandrakant saw Sarasvatichandra’s carriage parked on the seashore. The coachman told him, ‘Bhai went for a walk quite a while ago and has not yet returned. He gave me this note with instructions to give it to you.’ Chandrakant’s heart sank. He read the note. Dear Chandrakant, You soothed and consoled me before going home. I felt calm. But I spent the night walking around the garden. I thought a lot. Ultimately, my thoughts prevailed over your counsel. I am putting it into action. Do not mourn the separation from me. All living things are destined to enter the darkness of death alone. To live an obscure life is to prepare for death. I have decided to abandon illusory light and to seek darkness without any remorse. I shall never forget you. At the right moment we shall meet again, directly or indirectly. I leave you behind, but can my heart go without you? Do not search for me. Console Ganga bhabhi. I will not be able to forget her.

Sooner or later, everyone will forsake me So if I were to leave you behind, dear friend It wouldn’t be a fault The sun will set, the birds will fly away The night too shall pass And so shall the rising moon fade I know that your deep affection would have tied me down and weakened my resolve. So I have decided to embark upon this adventure. Namesake of Sarasvatichandra. What else can I call myself? A forlorn sigh escaped Chandrakant. He held his head in his hand and read the letter addressed to Sheth Laxminandan. Dear Father, If my action opens up the path of your happiness, it would not be considered a crime. But if you were to think of it as a crime, your son would not be further dejected in seeking your forgiveness. I have, as you desired, handed over the functioning of the mill to Dhurtalal. I have shown you all the records as well. Brahma lacks nothing. There is no reason for you to miss me. I pray to God that Dhananandbhai gives you every possible joy and satisfaction. Please use all your wealth for his welfare. If you have any occasion to remember me, that alone is wealth enough for me. I believe you will not object to my decision of adopting the path of renunciation. Hence, this decision. I will now lead a life of obscurity. It is not necessary to take leave of others prior to the act of renunciation. The renouncer has no one to take leave of. I have been innocent of any wrongdoing, my conscience is clear. But if Gumanba believes me to be guilty, please ask her to pardon me. Once I leave, you will have no more reason to feel distressed and wronged. You shall no longer feel cheated in your estimation of Vidya Chatura’s family. May your bliss be eternal! Pitaji, do not worry about me. Do not grieve for me. Everyone must take leave sooner or later. Those who leave do not return.

Chandraba left; I too am leaving. She went one way; I am going another way. Just as you erased her memory, forget me as well. The wise are those who do not remember those who have left. From now on, What does the world care for my sorrows and joys There are so many souls upon this earth Some distraught, some joyous One cannot cry for them all There would be no end to tears So father, for one such as I Why should you cry? Do not remember me Do not weep for me Why these futile tears? Why not forget one who has forsaken and left? What does the world care for my sorrows and joys Father, what more can I write. If you find anything missing from your house, do tell Chandrakant. He shall pay for it. One who, for the sake of your happiness, wishes to be erased even from memory, Sarasvatichandra. Chandrakant read both the letters. A sea of sorrow engulfed him. He sat down on a boulder and said to Sarasvatichandra’s coachman, ‘Go and tell your Sheth, Bhai has left home. For good.’ The coachman was startled. ‘What! Where did he go?’ ‘Who knows? Go tell him that he has left the city.’ ‘What has he written in the letter?’ ‘Just that.’ The coachman sped off and disappeared behind a line of trees on Charni Road. Chandrakant got up, took the hired coach and went to the railway station to make enquiries. No one could tell him anything. The station master, the ticket master and others crowded around him. They checked tickets issued on mail and passenger trains, but it told them nothing. Dejected, disheartened, Chandrakant returned home.

He sat alone at his writing table in the bedroom. He could no longer hold back his tears. He confided in his wife. ‘Oh what shall I do now, Ganga? He is gone! Sarasvatichandra, what have you done? You can be angry with the Sheth, but what about me? What will happen to poor Kumud Sundari now? Where shall I look for you? Nothing is certain about these romantic idealists.’ The news spread like wild fire. After some time, Laxminandan’s clerk came to fetch Chandrakant. Chandrakant once again read Sarasvatichandra’s letter to Laxminandan and pondered over the statement: ‘Please use all your wealth for Dhananandan’s welfare’. He decided not to hand over the letter immediately to the Sheth. Guman and Dhurtalal were with Laxminandan when the coachman brought him the news. Guman turned pale and Laxminandan looked stunned. Dhurtalal whispered to Guman, ‘Make sure he hasn’t walked away with things. He is cunning.’ Guman gathered courage and told the Sheth, ‘Get the house checked.’ Laxminandan snarled at her, ‘Checked? For what? My son has left home, and you want the house checked!’ ‘Look here, Bhai is not an innocent child. He is playacting to frighten us. He must be hiding somewhere just to send us on a wild goose chase. A man who owns two lakh rupees is not about to run away like this. Most likely, he must have gone to meet his father-in-law and bride-to-be. But first make sure he has not run away with things. This is just a ploy to secure my brother’s removal. It is apparent even to me. Don’t you smell a rat?’ Laxminandan turned red with rage and said, ‘Careful! Today I am not going to listen to you. You may not care, but my heart is in agony.’ When Chandrakant arrived at the house, Laxminandan got up and took him to another room. Guman followed them, but he turned her away at the door, latched it, and came and sat with Chandrakant. He was overcome by emotions. The virtues of his firstborn son came back to him. He realised he had handed over charge to Dhurtalal in haste, and that he had been harsh on Sarasvatichandra and unjust. The anguish was evident on his face.

‘Chandrakant! You know everything! Your face tells me that you know. Do tell me, what possessed him? I will not live without him! I will take poison.’ Sheth Laxminandan suddenly looked old, and he beat his head helplessly upon the table. Chandrakant consoled him. He told him Sarasvatichandra had objected to the deed that Ishwarkaur had made, and that the deed had been drafted without Sarasvatichandra’s knowledge. He also told him how much pain Laxminandan’s words had caused his son. As he spoke, Chandrakant wondered what to do with Sarasvatichandra’s letter. It would be dishonest not to give the letter to the Sheth. But once he gave it, he could not take it back; there would be a finality to the act. The Sheth could easily disown Sarasvatichandra if his mind changed once again, and Guman’s ploy would then succeed. Chandrakant decided to deal with issues as and when they arose. He gave the letter to Laxminandan. As he read it, Laxminandan’s emotions were somewhat similar to how King Munj felt when King Bhoj had sent him a letter written in his own blood. Tears flowed from his eyes. He understood his son’s noble sentiments, and felt nothing but abhorrence and contempt for Guman and Dhurtalal. He put the letter aside and said, anguished, ‘Chandrakant, you know where he is. Do anything, but bring him back. I cannot live without Sarasvatichandra!’ Chandrakant picked up the letter and tore it up into small pieces. He said, ‘Sheth, I told you that I do not know. And that is the truth.’ The Sheth saw him tear up the letter, but he did not ask him why, nor did he think about it. Chandrakant suddenly felt as if his heart would boil over and he spoke up fearlessly. His words tore into the father’s heart. ‘Sheth, you are an important and powerful man. But you should also be concerned about those under your care. If you want to arrange your son’s marriage, you should also desire that the two love each other, and are happy. By accusing innocent Kumud Sundari, you thrust a dagger into your son’s heart. God alone knows how much suffering you would cause them both. Is our society so regressive that parents cannot bear the son and the daughter-in-law to be in love? But what can you do? Such are the ways of God. One has not heard of a son reared by a stepmother to be happy. It is true that you desire your wife more than your son. Why would you accept that your son was without blemish? He was possessed by the thought that his father did not love him, and he left home. The man who always travelled by horse-drawn carriage, who never walked without shoes and socks, a man raised in the lap of luxury that you provided, is today roaming God knows where, alone, unknown and friendless. Where is the man who held sway over erudite audiences, a favourite of scholars and benefactor of so many like me? Sheth, his condition is like that of Dhruva. Oh God! What will Kumud Sundari’s state be? Sheth, the light has gone out of your home. But what do you care. ‘I must tell you a story. Listen. A man and his wife loved each other dearly. Their minds were one. A pair of sparrows made a nest in their house. The female laid eggs. Both the male and the female sparrow looked after the chicks with great love. One day the female sparrow died. The male sparrow brought another female to the nest. Together they pushed the chicks out. The chicks had not yet learnt to fly. They would have hit the floor and died, but for the woman of the house who caught them mid-air. The woman held the chicks to her breast and cried. ‘Meanwhile, her husband came home. He asked her the reason for her tears. She did not reply. When he insisted, she finally showed him the chicks, told him what had happened and said, If such a thing can happen to birds, why not to us? There is no certainty about life. Today you love me dearly. But what would happen to my young children if I were to die tomorrow? It is this thought that brings me to tears. Her loving husband tried to console her, made her many promises, but the woman was not convinced. And the tears flowed unceasing from her eyes. What would happen to my children? She could think of nothing else. At last her husband told her that if such a thing ever happened, her children should bring him to this nest and remind him of this story. Would I ever forget our love? ‘Days passed and that fortunate woman died. The man remarried. He had a son and a daughter from his first wife. The new wife slowly began to turn the husband away from the children. Every day she had a new complaint. She spoke ill of the children. But how could the motherless children speak ill of their stepmother? Ultimately, the new wife declared she could no longer live with the children, and the man would have to choose between them and her. How can a man love motherless children more than a new wife? The children can look after themselves, but where will the poor woman go? So the man called his children aside and told them that he did not want them anymore and that they should leave. ‘The children looked pitiable. But who would take pity on them? Father, where shall we go? they asked. But alas, he was no longer a father to them. That demon replied, Why ask me? Go wherever you please. Go throw yourselves in a ditch! The orphaned children wept and left the house. That demon felt no pity for them. The girl was wise. Suddenly she remembered what her mother had taught her. She told her brother amidst tears, bhai, let us do what our mother taught us. Both of them turned back. ‘Why have you come back? Go away! The man barked at them. Trembling with fright, the girl replied, Father, we will go away. But our mother had taught us that if such a thing ever happened, we should remind you of something. Will you listen to us? That heartless man took pity on them and agreed. The children reminded him the story of the sparrows and how their mother had wept that day. That demon melted. He remembered his past as also his promise. He wept and embraced his children and took them back into the house. ‘Sheth, your condition is like that man. But Chandralaxmi did not teach any such thing to Sarasvatichandra. He has left home. You do not have the choice of assuaging his hurt. You thought that he loved you for your money? Even that relationship no longer holds. You are a father to him, but he is no longer your son. Yes, such is the truth. Do not worry that he has taken anything from you. Check all your valuables in the house. If you find anything missing, do let me know, and I will pay for it. Shethji, I must go now. You are an important man.

Pardon me if I have said things I should not have. I take your leave.’ Chandrakant put his pagdi on his head and got up to leave. Sheth Laxminandan caught his hand and made him sit down. ‘Chandrakant! Chandrakant, why are you doing this to me? Please tell me where he is. You have brought me back to my senses. But I cannot bear to be separated from my son! I will go insane!’ ‘Shethji, there are others in your house who shall bring you back to your senses. Honestly, I do not know where Bhai is. If I had known, I would never have allowed him to go. I will with my own resources search for him. I will wander like him. I will do whatever comes to my mind. What is it to anyone? You enjoy yourself. A thorn from your side has now been removed. Stop worrying. I cannot endure this any longer. Please let me go!’ Chandrakant jerked his hand free, opened the door and left. Guman entered. The Sheth was delirious like a man possessed. ‘What does the world care for my sorrows? One cannot cry for everyone! What? Does your pain mean nothing to me? Do not remember me, do not weep for me. Why these futile tears? For one such as I, father why should you cry? Oh, it is all my fault! It is all my doing. Chandrakant, bring Bhai back for me!’ He looked up, Chandrakant had gone. ‘Bhai! Bhai!’ he screamed. Guman, standing close to him, said, ‘Bhai is gone.’ Sheth got up and kicked her so hard that she rolled upon the floor and hit the door, howling. Dhurtalal and others rushed into the room. Brother and sister realised that Laxminandan was no longer under their control. Just like grass that bends to let powerful gusts of wind pass, everyone submitted to the Sheth’s wishes, or acted as if they did. All his instructions regarding the search for Sarasvatichandra were apparently carried out. Many days passed, many persons were engaged in the search, much money was spent. But there was no trace of Sarasvatichandra. With every passing day, Laxminandan became less anxious, and Guman, freer from fear. She bribed the Sheth’s men with money and promises to ensure that the search for Sarasvatichandra did not bear fruit. The Sheth was told that this stupendous effort had proved futile.

Meanwhile, Chandrakant did his utmost to find Sarasvatichandra. As his rage subsided, it was replaced by pity for Laxminandan. He recognised that the search mounted by the Sheth was feeble and persisted with his own efforts. One day Chandrakant received a letter from Bulwer Sahib of The Bombay Light. He immediately rushed to meet the editor. Bulwer Sahib received many letters from other towns. One of them appeared to have been written in Sarasvatichandra’s hand. He showed it to Chandrakant. Chandrakant recognised the writing, the familiar language and thoughts. His joy was limitless. The cover had a postmark, it was marked ‘Suvarnapur’. They decided to keep this news a secret between Bulwer Sahib and him. Chandrakant decided that he himself would go to Suvarnapur. Vidya Chatura and the Counsellor of Suvarnapur were related. He therefore decided to go to Ratnanagari, obtain a letter of introduction from Vidya Chatura and then go to Suvarnapur. In his excitement and anticipation, Chandrakant felt he was already in Ratnanagari. Vidya Chatura and Gunasundari welcomed Sarasvatichandra’s friend warmly. They were most curious to know about Sarasvatichandra. Chandrakant told them all about Sheth Laxminandan and Guman’s doings. Affection and sorrow gave him the powers of a poet, and he lucidly captured the workings of his friend’s noble, unselfish heart. Vidya Chatura and Gunasundari keenly felt his despair, and were taken aback by Sarasvatichandra’s decision. Both of them felt he ought not to have taken such an extreme step. Vidya Chatura said, ‘Chandrakant, I must say that the English education we impart has one major shortcoming: it makes rational thinking go asunder. We can also say that this is characteristic of Western knowledge itself. The West is motivated by a deep sense of discontent. All action and effort stems from it, furthers engagement with the world, and promises immediately recognisable fruits. This makes one impatient and eager to attain these fruits of action. In the natural course of things, such fruits are slow to come by, which goes contrary to this sense of discontent. One is never satisfied with one goal but must hastily pursue one goal after another, which makes the mind like that of a speculator. The impatient mind looks towards the future without any basis in its past experiences or any assessment of the future. It seeks ends without means. A mind discontented with the present grasps images of the future fleeting before it; but when the possible future lurking behind these fleeting images become clear, it shudders. Sarasvatichandra exemplifies this. Look how he wants to understand the world by renouncing it! Look how he wants to do good unto others by renouncing his own wealth! You will realise the worth of my words when you will yourself see the pitiable condition in which your friend is likely to be. ‘The youth of today considers forbearance to be slavery and submission to others’ thoughts cowardice. They seek independence to follow their own whims. For them bravery consists of expressing their ideas and actualising them. They mock at experience. They despise the lack of activity and consider the conduct of elders lowly. Many fathers would have spoken to their sons in the same vein as Laxminandan, but it is only your friend who took such a step. You men of Bombay should be forced to work among the most foolish and serve under acerbic, egoistic and malevolent superiors for a few years, tolerate their taunts and experience servitude. This would bring you all to your senses. I am not suggesting that such servitude is without its problems. But it is necessary to learn to be accommodating of other persons, of their experiences, and all kinds of situations in which one may find oneself. One must also learn to keep one’s impulses under check.’ Chandrakant had seen much of the vicissitudes of life himself, and would not have allowed such proud words to go unchallenged. But he needed Vidya Chatura’s help to find his friend. He also knew that Vidya Chatura had been hurt by Sarasvatichandra’s decision, and needed a vent for his feelings. Various such considerations taught Chandrakant the virtues of submission and silence. He would not suffer even Lord Indra calling his friend a fool; but his eagerness and anxiety to meet his friend gave him the forbearance. Vidya Chatura continued, ‘Chandrakant, what has happened has happened. It is not good to brand those already scalded. Now you must search him out. This adventure would have taught him something. He would be better for the experience. The position of Chief Justice will fall vacant in my state in some months. He can be given that post. My younger daughter Kusum is not yet betrothed. I would be happy to arrange this match. It does not bother me that he is no longer wealthy. But I would insist that he takes up a profession. If he wants me to help him, I would do so gladly. But I can do nothing if he keeps wandering.’ Chandrakant attempted in vain to keep his temper in check. He said, ‘Minister Sir, I am most grateful to you, but the wisdom that you desire in my friend he is incapable of. And that wisdom will elude him even more if this is your condition. Do not for a moment entertain the thought that he will abide by your condition in order to attain Kusum Sundari in marriage. I do not believe that suffering would soften him. Therefore, you should consider someone else. I am certain that the qualities you seek in him he will never acquire. All I need from you is help in my search for him. I would be grateful for it. You are also free to refuse. I must leave this evening.’ Chandrakant had lived in extreme poverty; but just as grass can grow from stones, he too had struggled to uplift himself, and with great effort, had overcome the burden of poverty. Sarasvatichandra had supported him, and that was no mean support. But Chandrakant did not seek help; he only accepted it when it came without his having to ask for it. Suffering and hardship were acceptable to him, but his pride and self-respect would never allow him to ask for help. He would never flatter his wealthy and more learned friend, nor did he think it necessary to say things that would please him. Sarasvatichandra loved Chandrakant even more for his fierce sense of autonomy, pride and self-respect. Vidya Chatura, on the other hand, albeit most learned and occupying a high office himself, was raised to believe that he must always please his superiors. He considered it imperative to conduct himself in a way that pleased the powers that be, as long as such action did not invite the wrath of the Gods. He had cultivated the fine art of submission to the wishes of others and action in conformity with social beliefs. The office he occupied had also made him accustomed to receiving favourable responses. He was surrounded by people who took his every wish as a command. He did not permit obvious flattery, but those around him were past masters in that art. Hence, they wouldn’t say this or that was a virtue and that he was an embodiment of it. Instead, they would gauge the qualities that Vidya Chatura most cherished in himself, and praise those. They would point out the expertise and novelty of his decisions and mock those who said or believed otherwise. This worked even better than flattery. Vidya Chatura, though weary of flattery, did erroneously believe that his thinking was acceptable to all, and perhaps even superior. A man so conditioned would naturally be astonished at Chandrakant’s response. The minister thought Chandrakant was arrogant, childish and extremely discourteous. But there was nothing he could do. Chandrakant was not his subordinate. He laughed at him inwardly and thought, What can I do with him? What can be said to him? It would be pointless. And anyway, what is it to me? He will falter and learn from it. ‘Advice should not be given to just any person. For, one with a good home was rendered homeless by an inconsiderate ape.’⟨fn:21⟩ Vidya Chatura reasoned with himself, Why get into an argument with him? These Bombayites are like apes. And this one is educated to boot! Let them be. I treated that Parsi so well, and the fool went and published what was shared in private in the newspaper. This one is of the same mould. It is not my job to teach the whole world. The Minister of Ratnanagari had momentarily forgotten his diplomatic nature and spoken harshly. He now became his sophisticated self again and spoke kindly: ‘Chandrakant, do not be upset. Your friend was once to be my son-in-law, and I am still fond of him. Even you would accept that he should not have done this. Let him be. What can he do if God willed something else? I said what I said believing that if you were to ever meet him, he may not listen to you, but my words might persuade him. But, as you say, you know Sarasvatichandra far better, so do what you think is best. Whatever you need will be arranged by this evening.’ The storm subsided and the sailing was smooth thereafter. Chandrakant was pacified, and he apologised for his outburst. Vidya Chatura responded in the manner of a man who did not want the other to know if the apology was accepted or not and still wanted him to feel pacified. ‘Do not worry, what was the apology for?’ But Chandrakant was no longer listening and did not respond. That evening, he set out for Suvarnapur in a large coach provided by Vidya Chatura. As he lay down to rest, his thoughts were only about his friend. The letter to Bulwer Sahib had been signed by one Navinchandra. They were not certain if this was in fact Sarasvatichandra. Navinchandra’s father’s name and address were unknown; but in the hope that a letter would somehow reach him, Chandrakant wrote him a letter. This was the letter that Navinchandra had received, dropped on the stairs, and which was picked up by Kumud Sundari. Unseen by anyone, Kumud’s sister Kusum Sundari had heard Chandrakant’s entire conversation with her parents. This precocious young woman had written down Sarasvatichandra’s story as told by Chandrakant in the form of a letter to her sister. She had not sent it by post, fearing that it might fall into Pramaddhan’s hands. She had instead found a messenger who carried it to Vanleela, who had given it to Kumud. Dear reader, now reorient your memory a little. We had briefly left Suvarnapur behind, if you will recall, to acquaint ourselves with the world of Sarasvatichandra, and had seen vignettes of Bombay and Ratnanagari. Now wake up from that dream and return your gaze to the world of Suvarnapur. The main protagonist of the grand play enacted in Rana Bhupsinh’s palace returned home with pomp and glory. Officials had already gathered there to felicitate the new rising sun in his drawing room. An overjoyed Saubhagya Devi was anxiously awaiting her husband’s return on the swing. As soon as Buddhidhan entered, their eyes met, shared the mutual joy and triumph, and as he went up to his drawing room accompanied by court officials, Devi busied herself in the kitchen where Alak Kishori, imitating her father’s style, held court with her friends. Only Kumud Sundari sat alone in her room, reading the letter from her sister, and weeping silent tears. Dear reader, bring all of these images back into your mind. Behold! Even in a wakeful state you are adept at moving from one lucid dream world to another! Kumud first read the letter from her sister. Her thoughts and emotions overwhelmed her. Dear Chandra, must you endure and suffer so much on my account? Is it no longer possible for me to address you as ‘dear’? Cannot a husband remember his departed wife as dear? You were my beloved husband in the life that passed us by. You are no longer. I have submitted my body to my husband, as well as my mind. If it is proper for me to address God, my parents and other loved ones as dear, why then should it be improper for me to remember Sarasvatichandra as a dear one? You suffer so much for me. And we shared such a deep bond once. Kumud was well and truly caught in the web of love. She could no longer hold back her tears, which fell onto the letter. She put her head down on the table and wept copiously. Towards the end of her letter, Kusum Sundari had mentioned that Chandrakant was on his way to Suvarnapur to enlist Buddhidhan’s help in search of Sarasvatichandra, and that he was carrying a note for Buddhidhan from Vidya Chatura. The letter also mentioned that Gunasundari was about to set off on a pilgrimage to Bhadreshwar Mahadev near Lilapur, and that a decision to invite Kumud to join the pilgrimage had been taken; therefore, ‘You should obtain everyone’s consent and be ready’ to accompany a messenger. These gave rise to further conflicting emotions and confusion, and Kumud cried even more helplessly. Chandrakant’s letter to Navinchandra was somewhat strange. It was written in English. Unhappy life: date, day and night are all the same. Dear Chandra, You can live without Chandrakant, but Chandrakant cannot live without you. Even when Chandra forsakes Chandrakant and hides in the antipodes, his actions, however discreet, reveal him. I did you no wrong. It was cruel of you to forsake me. In doing so, you also compromised your honesty. What did you tell me at night, and what were your actions the next morning? God’s will. But now be kind. I have fought many a battle with fate, and you were the one who took me to victory. But now, you are the cause of my defeat. The day that is spent without you, may it perish This human frailty like a mirage Takes me further away from where you are My state is like that of the cuckoo. You have been heartless with all. You felt no pity for your father, your friend, not even for that delicate soul! Such heartlessness! So be it. You may pretend to be heartless, Chandra, but your soul is not, and can never be heartless. Let me give you an example. I believe that you have in truth gone to look for the one you abandoned, and to repent. Compassion and heartlessness, wisdom and foolishness, delicacy and adamantine hardness, pleasure and renunciation; you harbour many such contradictions within you. Do not be perturbed. Be kind to me, and stay where you are for a few days. Thereafter you will be free. If it is my destiny to roam endlessly after you, so be it. Eager to be with you—one whom you are not incapable of recognising. Kumud Sundari’s heart ached. Just then she was called in for lunch. She wiped her tears, composed herself, kept the letters carefully in her cupboard between layers of clothes and went down. On the staircase she sang to herself, I saw the world In all its futility today Emotions like the colours of the rainbow are short-lived. Alak Kishori had insisted that on this joyous and auspicious occasion, all the women also eat together. Her word was accepted even by those who had
chapters.summary: Kumud Sundari reads a secret letter detailing Sarasvatichandra's difficult past and current suffering, deeply affecting her resolve and stirring complex emotions about her betrothed.

chapters.title: Buddhidhan and Saubhagya Devi
paragraphs: already eaten. Amidst all these celebrations, Kumud’s sombre mood also turned celebratory. Saubhagya Devi was to eat in Buddhidhan’s plate, similarly Alak Kishori would eat in Vidurprasad’s plate, Kumud Sundari in Pramaddhan’s plate and Jamnakaki in Dayashankar’s plate. No plates had to be set for these fortunate ones. For all others, plates were being arranged. Meanwhile, Vanleela composed a song on a sheet of paper and showed it to Saubhagya Devi. Alak Kishori demanded that it be sung. She also said the song would be considered good only if it passed Kumud Sundari’s test. As Kumud came down, all the women made way for her. She sat down, Alak Kishori and Vanleela sat on either side of her; Kumud held Vanleela’s composition in her hand. Other friends sat around them. Saubhagya Devi and Jamnakaki, who had taken the seats previously occupied by their husbands, now turned their attention to Kumud. The cook ready to serve their meals also paused and looked up. The three women sang in their soft and melodious voices. What would mortals know of Godly play? The oil He pours shapes the burning flame The days of sorrow are now past Joyous times are upon us, behold He who troubled the meek and good The evil Shath stumbled and fell at last In this chess, we have beaten you, ungodly ones The Rana of Suvarnapur was alert and just May his glory all ages outlast May we prove worthy of our victory Prays Vanleela with folded hands May this glorious dream forever last All the assembled women attentively heard the song. They awaited Kumud Sundari’s verdict. ‘It is well composed,’ Kumud said with a smile, and the women got up to begin their meal. One said, ‘The words flow in a rhythm’; the other remarked, ‘Yes, the meaning is also very clear’. One of them went up to Vanleela and asked, ‘What does beaten in chess mean?’. Vanleela was enthusiastically pulled in all directions.

Sarasvatichandra Alak Kishori caught Vanleela by the arm and sat her down beside her. All the women sat down to eat. They joked and laughed during the meal. Thus the past, the present and the future were forgotten in the unfolding of the present.

Before Kumud Sundari came down for lunch with the rest of the women, all the men assembled at the Counsellor’s residence went up to Pramaddhan’s drawing room. Buddhidhan moved around, talking to the officials. Those whom he spoke to, or even acknowledged by merely looking in their direction, felt especially privileged. Vidurprasad passed around paan. Pramaddhan reclined in an armchair, grandly issued orders, chatted with his friends, and laughed loudly and incessantly. Navinchandra sat quietly in a corner, torn between his decision to leave Suvarnapur and his desire to observe the unfolding developments. Finally, at around two in the afternoon, all the officials and other guests began to leave in groups. Buddhidhan was exhausted and wanted to rest after the heavy meal. He retired to his room. Pramaddhan also went into his room. Navinchandra fell asleep on a couch in the drawing room. The court was to assemble again that evening at five. But the general assembly was postponed to the next morning. Only trusted aides were to meet and confer that evening. It was decided to send Pramaddhan and Tark Prasad to Lilapur to brief Russell Sahib of that day’s events and obtain his consent for future plans. They were asked to return before the assembly convened the next morning. Russell Sahib’s Shirastidar Rambhau had, through Tark Prasad, made certain inappropriate demands on Buddhidhan. He had also threatened to ferment trouble with the Sahib if his demands were not met. This new problem had caused the postponement of the assembly.

Buddhidhan went to his room and found Saubhagya Devi waiting for him. Just looking at her face, all his troubles vanished for a while. He took her hand in his and asked her how she had passed the day. Devi did not reply. Buddhidhan said, ‘Today is a festive day. God willing, tomorrow, too, shall be a day of celebration. Devi, do you recall my delirious words during my long sickness? I will touch Dayashankar Kaka’s feet as soon as I receive the robes of my new office tomorrow. He has been like a father to me.’ This pleased Devi. ‘In our days of poverty in Lilapur, once when we were standing at the window, we saw an English madam pass by in her closed carriage. Devi, do you recall what you had said that day? I did not tell you this, but I have got a carriage made for you. From tomorrow, you must travel in it every morning to pray at the Rajeshwar Mahadev. We have seen this auspicious day only because of His blessings.’ Devi’s joy climbed a notch higher. She said, ‘Alak told me that Kumud has made the temple garden look even more beautiful. We should spend some more money on the temple. Kumud has a sense for these things. We should let her and Alak decide.’ ‘Yes, of course. Our wealth is for our children.’ Husband and wife took delight in each other. Buddhidhan looked at her fondly and with desire. Devi’s body seemed different to him. He sensed there was going to be an addition to his family. Her shyness confirmed his belief. Their children were married and old enough to be parents themselves. Devi’s joy at being a mother again was shadowed by doubt and perplexity as to what her children would think when the news became known. Saubhagya Devi, like a good Arya woman, expressed a noble desire. And Buddhidhan, like a good Arya husband, accepted. ‘We should adopt Vanaprastha even while remaining householders. The responsibilities of being a householder should now be passed on to the children,’ she said. Her wish fulfilled, Saubhagya Devi’s joy knew no limit.⟨fn:22⟩

Arth, the pursuit of worldly desires, is the preserve of men; but the pursuit of amorous desire and moksha are enjoined upon both women and men. Saubhagya Devi’s pursuit of sexual desire had reached its end. She had matured from being a girl to a woman. Today, she freed herself from the bond of desire that had given her youthful pleasures, and chose a bond of piety and abstinence. It was not for her to contemplate moksha—her moksha was her husband, in this life as in the next, in this world as in the world to come; its location was insignificant for her. She would travel as her husband’s shadow in all his pursuits of artha, dharma, karma and moksha, and partake in the fruits of all his efforts. The husband accepted his wife’s wish to be freed of sexual desire, and also the new basis of their relationship. What more could she want? Her moksha was her husband, as voiced in the song: Vraj is dear, Vaikunth I would not go, For how would I find my Nand Kunwar there? Oh, you pious women of India! Your instincts are noble indeed. Saubhagya Devi had cultivated a sense of religious duty by listening to the instructive tales of the Shastras and Puranas, thousands of years old, which have brought noble aspirations to the illiterate masses of India, surrounded them with examples of good morals and right conduct, and guided them to lead lives devoid of wealth, prestige and ego, and yet made their minds aglow with an inner light. These instructions are now mocked by stupid, arrogant reformers, and neglected by the passage of time. Saubhagya Devi’s husband had become the Karbhari of Suvarnapur, and her desire to lead a religious life was fulfilled the moment she expressed it. She was no longer a conjugal partner to her husband, but a spiritual companion. Devi felt blissful, and thought, If I were to die this very moment, with my eyes on my husband and my heart filled with pure joy, I would be truly blessed. She continued to hold his hands but her eyes lowered reverentially to Buddhidhan’s feet. Her gaze turned inward. Just as the quiet flow of the river captures the reflection of the moon, her heart reflected the image of her husband.

With the new boon she had been granted, she felt only an emotional attachment towards him. She felt as if she were standing on the shore, watching, while he churned the sea of Suvarnapur’s administration. She pictured him, Krishna-like, riding on the serpent Kalia that was Shathrai, while she was the gopi who witnessed his triumph from the banks. She continued to hold his hands, but her bejewelled toe moved to some inner rhythm. Her youthful passions were leaving her just as a new phase of her life was about to begin. She wept joyous tears as she bid farewell to a dear friend and welcomed new joys. Unaware of her tears, Devi was aware only of her husband’s radiant face etched deep in her heart. She was in a trance. Her eyes were focused on his feet. A song escaped from her lips, as if on its own. Gone is my churner, gone is my churner How do I churn the milk? The water dances, the wind dances This whole world dances Upon the now tamed Shesha, The very universe plays As if swaying to tinkling anklets The milk brims over So do my sobs O’ thief of Govardhana, O’ son of Nand Seeing my reflection in the water, I weep As the dawn eclipses the moon Says Kabir, Listen O’ you sadhus The world sings of the joy in The house of Nand But gone is my churner, my churner is gone The beauty of her song enveloped Buddhidhan. He was filled with a joy pure and intense and, for a brief while, he was freed from the bondage of life.
chapters.summary: Buddhidhan and Saubhagya Devi share a profound, intimate moment, discussing their future and embracing a new spiritual path amidst the day's political complexities.

chapters.title: Pramaddhan and Kumud Sundari
paragraphs: Pramaddhan and Kumud Sundari The men had dispersed, but the women were to spend the day with Alak Kishori. Kumud Sundari was in that group of women. And, Pramaddhan? What was he doing? Buddhidhan’s son could not sleep that afternoon. His head was full of excitement, of dreams of a new life. His authority was absolute, that is, as long as Kumud Sundari was not present. He respected his educated wife but lacked the courage to respond to her. Kumud tried her best to further his education and mould him in her own image. This he did not like. He wanted passion and desire from his wife, not learning. He also grew tired of her superior aesthetic sensibility. Love for him was animal passion. He felt constrained in Kumud’s presence as one often feels in the presence of elders or superiors. He sought enjoyment with equals among his friends and flatterers, and with Padma. As the days passed, he grew even less fond of Kumud. Moreover, his position in the palace had now altered, he was flattered by all. He did not like feeling insignificant and inferior before his own wife. He felt it was degrading for an important official like him to have to suppress his desires in the presence of his wife. That afternoon, since Kumud Sundari was not there in the room, Pramaddhan felt a great sense of freedom and abundant joy. He talked to himself, paced restlessly about the room, lay down upon the bed for a while, then got up again and went and stood at the window overlooking the street. He played with the gold buttons of his starched kurta, impressed passers-by with his imposing mien. He went into the room, picked up a mirror, twirled his moustache and admired himself. Meeting his own proud eyes in the mirror, he said: Now you watch me, Pramaddhan! Now I am an officer with a salary of two hundred rupees. Navinchandra, despite his lofty education will only get a paltry hundred rupees, while I will get two hundred! I will occupy the post hitherto occupied by Narbheram. And what shall I do with the money? Pitaji has said that I must maintain dignity. That means I must be proud. I will promote my friends. Won’t Pitaji agree even to this much? But how am I to spend these two hundred rupees? I don’t have to worry about household expenses. I don’t have to worry about savings, Pitaji saves enough. All right then, I should allocate my expenditure. I must give fifty rupees a month to Padma. I have to spend at least twenty five rupees on perfumes and suchlike if I am to visit her. I will need to spend another fifty rupees on clothes and other sundry expenses. So how much is it then? Fifty, and twenty five, and fifty more—that makes it hundred and fifty. So I still have fifty rupees to spare. That Kumud never says or asks for anything. But do I have a choice of giving her nothing? The rest will go to her. It is because she says nothing that I am free to spend without accounting for it. So that makes it two hundred. Thus the budget was allocated, the money accounted for. British officers who are paid thousands make mistakes of crores of rupees while making budgets for India. So why should it bother anyone if illiterate Pramaddhan should forget to account for twenty five rupees in his excitement and exhilaration! He put aside the mirror and sat on a chair near the table. Kumud Sundari’s things were on the table. On one side were books of English poets, next to it was Sanskrit poetry; on the other side there were books on physics and the Manusmriti in Gujarati, and facing him were pages of the Ramayana with a book mark placed in it. Pramaddhan stretched his legs under the table and picked up the Ramayana. He looked at the image on the first page, made an attempt to read a page, but gave up. He kept it carefully back in its place. He had bought all these books for Kumud. She spent the difficult hours of the day reading them. He stared at the books for a while, and felt as if he were looking down a deep well. He made a face and got up from the chair. Next, he picked up Kumud’s sarangi and idly plucked a few strings. He liked Kumud’s playing but found her singing dry, for unlike Padma she did not sing songs of Krishna and love. How can there be a song without Krishna! He put away the sarangi and stood with a finger on his lip, solemnly admiring his own portrait on the wall. Then he turned around and, facing the bed, saw a philosophical book in English lying on a pillow. What’s this? God knows why, but she needs to read and read and read! Otherwise she is listless. A book can be kept upon the table. But on the bed! Pramaddhan promptly picked it up and put it on the table. He felt like reading something, but didn’t know what. He opened a cupboard and looked, but found nothing to match his taste. Eventually, he picked up an English novel, a romance that he had bought, and lying down upon the bed, he began to read it out aloud. Just then, he heard some noise in Navinchandra’s room. He got up, opened the door and found Krishna Kalika there, alone. What was she doing there? This young woman of loose morals had become infatuated with Navinchandra. Reader, as you already know, Krishna Kalika had tried to make Alak Kishori the instrument of her lust, and failed. For sometime after that incident, Alak Kishori remained cautious and tried to distance herself from Krishna Kalika. But true to her nature, before long she had forgotten all about it and regained her former affection for Krishna Kalika. Saubhagya Devi had doubted her daughter’s virtue and was worried. But by the time the episode of Kumud Sundari fainting, and coming to, was over, Saubhagya Devi had become aware of Alak Kishori’s repentance. Pious herself, she believed that her daughter could not but be chaste and pious, too, and she admonished herself for thinking otherwise even briefly. We also know that Kumud’s doubt and distress in the matter was resolved by Vanleela. Moreover, unable to keep it a secret from her beloved bhabhi, Alak Kishori had herself told Kumud all about it; she had abused Krishna Kalika, and gratefully praised Navinchandra. Taking advantage of the moment, Kumud counselled Alak, advising her to forsake such a degrading friendship with Krishna Kalika. One day in her naiveté, Alak went and told Krishna Kalika that Kumud had advised her to keep away from her. Thereafter, Krishna Kalika did her best to reduce the impact of Kumud’s counsel on Alak. Alak Kishori repented having told Kalika about Kumud’s advice. For some days she kept it to herself, but eventually she again told Kumud. Kumud became cautious, and her attempts to wean Alak away from Kalika’s influence became more subtle. She stopped giving her advice and instead became even more affectionate towards Alak. Gradually, Kumud turned Alak toward Vanleela. Vanleela was friendly, intelligent, and more playful than Alak Kishori, but she was also more mature. Kumud praised Vanleela before Alak, spoke of her virtues and thereby fostered warmth and affection for Vanleela. As Alak’s eyes opened to Vanleela’s virtues, Krishna Kalika appeared lowly in comparison. Thus Kumud Sundari managed to create a distance between Alak and Kalika without criticising her or even mentioning her vile name. Krishna Kalika was related to Shathrai. Alak Kishori suspected her of carrying stories of her household to Shathrai. She had made a conscious effort to distance herself but could not bring the old relationship to an abrupt end. Today, Alak Kishori publicly displayed affection for Vanleela and made her sit beside her at lunch. This was too much for Krishna Kalika; her pride was hurt and she glared at Vanleela. She resolved to find a way out of her situation. After lunch, as everyone sat talking, she got up unnoticed and sneaked up to Navinchandra’s room in the hope of finding him alone. Navinchandra was not in his room. She immediately thought of another plan. Let that rand Alak be, she told herself. I don’t need her. If I can take Pramad in my hands, I can get something for my husband. He will get him a good job, and I shall take my revenge on that bitch Kumud. She is after me with a vengeance, the rand! Just then Pramaddhan opened the door. Kumud Sundari had seen Krishna Kalika get up. Her eyes followed her as she climbed up and disappeared into Navinchandra’s room. Kumud made an excuse and got up. But she did not feel like shadowing Krishna Kalika. Let her be, she thought. Why should I watch over her debauched ways? But though she seemed engaged in the conversation around her, Kumud’s mind was on Krishna Kalika. There was no sign of her for a while. Finally Kumud grew anxious and impatient, and climbed up the stairs. She peeped into Navinchandra’s room. There was no one in it. The door to her room was shut. She tried to push it open. It was latched from within. ‘Who is it?’ Pramaddhan enquired. She again pushed at the door. He shouted, ‘Wait, I am opening it!’ After a few moments, Pramaddhan opened the door. He was alone in the room. Kumud did not enter. Pramaddhan asked her in. She replied, ‘I am coming,’ but she stood near the door. Her eyes were on the terrace. Soon enough, Krishna Kalika quietly sneaked out from Navinchandra’s room and crept down the stairs. But Kumud ran after her and caught her by the wrist. Pramaddhan turned pale and hid inside the room. Kumud seethed with anger, her cheeks flushing a deep red, and tears of indignation welled up in her eyes. Her eyes blazed, but she was speechless with hurt and rage. At first Krishna Kalika was frozen numb with shame and would not dare look up to meet Kumud’s eyes. But when she did not see a way out, she turned brazen and said in a cold flat voice, ‘Let me go’. ‘Aren’t you ashamed!’ ‘Why should I be ashamed? You should be.’ ‘Wretch, you are not even worthy of conversation. I will let you go today. But if I ever see you again in this house, you would not know where to run. This is not Shathrai’s house. Don’t you ever cast your eye on us again.’ Krishna Kalika was about to retort, when she remembered that things had changed now, the scales had tilted between Shathrai and Buddhidhan, and that Alak Kishori was no longer on her side. She knew Pramaddhan was powerless; she also knew the influence Kumud Sundari wielded on the household. Krishna Kalika was bathed in cold sweat. She hissed softly, ‘Will you let me go?’

‘Only on the promise that you will never enter this house again as long as you live.’ ‘What if someone calls me?’ ‘Not even then.’ ‘I cannot give any such promise.’ ‘Then I won’t let you go.’ ‘Do you want to imprison me? If yes, tell me so, woman.’ Kumud Sundari realised it was pointless to battle with this shameless woman. She could no longer bear to defile herself by her touch. ‘Go! Leave at once! But if you hold your life dear, do not enter this house ever again.’ And Kumud let go of Krishna Kalika’s hand and watched her run down the stairs. Kumud entered her room. Pramaddhan was sitting with his head on the table. He did not have the nerve to lift his head. Kumud Sundari went up to the window facing the street and looked out. She heard loud wailing and saw a dead body being carried, followed by a handful of ten or fifteen mourners. They were the closest relatives of Shathrai. The body was his son Dushtarai’s. Some women followed at a distance. Khalaknanda was among them, she was wailing the loudest. Kumud Sundari could not see Rupali, Dushtarai’s wife. Even Shathrai and Karvatrai were not among the mourners. Pramaddhan raised his head and asked, ‘Who has died?’ ‘Dushtarai’ replied Kumud. As Pramaddhan got up to come to the window, she turned away from it. Kumud stood in the middle of the room, pondering the destinies of Dushtarai and Pramaddhan. Are the sons of Karbharis all fated to be debauched? What Rupali did to Dushtarai, Krishna Kalika or Padma or some other woman may do to Pramaddhan. What would be her condition, then? As she stood thinking, she spotted something on her bed. She went closer and saw a flower from Krishna Kalika’s hair and buttons in a chain of her blouse. She picked them up and stood by the bed. Then she noticed that the latch on the door that led to Navinchandra’s room was open. Pramaddhan stood at the window and watched the women mourn and wail. Krishna Kalika had joined the mourners and stood facing him. As she beat her chest, she realised that the chained buttons of her blouse were missing, and was frightened. She was brazen enough to come back to Pramad’s room to retrieve them, but seeing Kumud’s livid face flash before her, she abandoned the thought. She wept both for her buttons and the dead relative. Her tears did not allow her to look up at Pramaddhan. Pale and nervous, Pramaddhan turned around to face Kumud. He tried to pretend that nothing had happened before her sudden arrival. Kumud stood leaning against the bed, toying with the flower and the chain, silently talking to herself. Dear God! Is it no longer within my power to reform him? Have all limits been crossed? I am in the room, and he stares at that woman from the window! He does not wish to even look at me. He is no longer restrained by my presence. Are all windows for change firmly shut? And then she thought, What is it to me? Why should I care? I was forsaken by a learned man before marriage, and then by an uneducated man after marriage. This thought pained her and she was overcome with emotion. She abruptly went to the window and flung the chain and the flower with some force at Krishna Kalika. Then she collapsed on the floor, put her head between her knees and wept her heart out. Pramaddhan looked at her, but neither moved nor said a word to comfort her. She felt even more violated and sobbed aloud. Fortunately, no one heard her crying. Pramaddhan was taught by his friends that a woman’s tears are only a ruse and should be ignored, a man should not give into such womanly traps. He remained at the window, unmoved. Kumud Sundari beat her head upon the floor in anguish. The beast felt some pity then and melted. Pramaddhan came and sat down beside her, and gently said, ‘Come, now. What is all this?’ He took her hand in his lap. The mere touch of her provoked in him a pure thought. He realised he had committed a crime and had hurt her. He again asked, ‘What happened?’ Kumud felt that she still occupied some space in her husband’s heart. She felt hopeful of changing him. This gave her solace. She wiped her tears, responded evasively, saying, ‘Nothing’. She freed her hand from his clasp, got up and sat on a chair.

Pramaddhan had been raised by servants. As he had grown up, selfish and debauched friends had led him down the path of vice. He had enjoyed much freedom, without the incumbent responsibility, from an early age. Even so, he was not untouched by the pious atmosphere of the house. He was Buddhidhan and Saubhagya Devi’s son, after all. The goodness latent in him was awakened. He pleaded with his hurt and angry wife. She remained silent, but he continued his attempts to engage her in conversation. He asked her questions, he tried to tell her of the day’s tumultuous events at the palace. But he did not once mention Krishna Kalika. Neither did Kumud. Pramaddhan gave her the news that he had been assigned the responsibility of going to Lilapur and that he had been appointed a salaried official. He told her about the postponement of the evening assembly due to some machinations of Rambhau. He talked about Navinchandra. He told her about Dayashankar Kaka’s advice that Buddhidhan should buy back his ancestral house at whatever cost and fulfil his father’s desire to build a Mahadev temple in memory of his mother. Pramaddhan talked on and on. Kumud Sundari sat there, gazing intently at the hands folded listlessly in her lap and paid no attention to his words. She only lifted her eyelids once ever so slightly at the mention of Navinchandra. Pramaddhan eventually did succeed in calming her passions somewhat. At last she looked up, happy that her husband had at least made an attempt to assuage her hurt. As she got up, Kumud felt a sudden rush of affection for her husband. No, she told herself firmly, It was a trap laid by that vile woman. My husband is simple-minded. She thought of his inherent goodness, his desire to make amends, and the guilt on his face. She surprised both of them by putting her delicate arms around his neck and embracing him and felt as if all her virtues had transmigrated into him. Oh Arya woman! Your heart has far greater capacity for happiness than what can be obtained from a divorce court! Let the joys of the divorce court remain the preserve of the foreigner alone! Kumud felt that her husband’s heart had become pure and transparent like glass. She tried to erase all traces of Krishna Kalika from it. Without disturbing the pleasure of innocent and affectionate conversation of these rare and joyous moments, Kumud also told Pramaddhan a few things. It was Krishna Kalika who informed Shathrai about the secret meeting between the Rana and Pitaji at the Rajeshwar Mahadev. She spied for Shathrai, and she also knew about Jamal Khan’s evil designs, she told him. Kumud, intelligent as she was, felt that with this startling information, this woman, an enemy of the family, should have been erased from her husband’s mind for good. Under the gentle ministrations of his left hand, her hair came undone. She looked up at him and sought his consent to visit her mother at Bhadreshwar. He gave his consent by a light caress of her face. She liked the sudden sensual warmth of this touch that had come after a long estrangement. But why and how did this happen? How did the bitter fight turn into affection and love? Did they both long for each other? Did she forget his sin? Did she whisper love to him? Do couples not communicate emotion without words? Are words necessary to respond to such messages? When did such love rise unspoken, unasked in Kumud? When did Pramaddhan become aware of it? How did they respond to each other’s touch? Where did uncultured Pramaddhan acquire this subtle art? Why did the learned and sensitive woman forget her insult and hurt and adopt the love of the unlettered? The answers to these questions are not to be found in the Puranas, this philosophy has not been discussed in the Vedas nor in the Vedanta, English learning is not about to discern its secrets, and it cannot be understood in everyday life. But the two hearts for whom it was meant understood it and responded intuitively. Such is the miracle of God’s creation. The Arya mind has the capacity to forget the past, be content in the present, and make the future beautiful even by force. May God preserve this capacity for ever.
chapters.summary: Pramaddhan revels in his newfound freedom and status, but Kumud Sundari's keen observation leads to a tense encounter with Krishna Kalika.

chapters.title: The Karbhari and his Administration
paragraphs: The Karbhari and his Administration The king who gives up the two vices of lust and rage, and allocates wealth where it is due, One who listens well and acts fast, such a king is seen as exemplary by all. One who can make men believe in him, and who punishes those whose crime is established beyond doubt, One who knows his limits and knows pardon, Lakshmi embraces such a king. One who remains unperturbed in crisis and with a clear mind pursues any enterprise he takes, One who, when the time comes, bears suffering and endures, for such a great soul, sagacious as he is, for a king like him, enemies are already won. And existing enmities he does not fan, nor does he quell them; he does not swell with pride, nor shrivel in dejection, One who does not do what should not be done, those who are noble call such a person as possessed of nobility.⟨fn:23⟩ It was evening. As the momentous day wound to a close, the excitement, too, had begun to ebb in Suvarnapur. Shathrai had become old news. Pramaddhan and Tark Prasad had left for Lilapur. At such a time, Buddhidhan walked about all by himself in the vast magnificent assembly hall of Suvarnapur palace, reciting to himself these verses. The soft lights from the chandeliers soothed his tired eyes. Until today, Buddhidhan had never felt completely at ease in the palace. The Rana’s trust in him was a matter of public knowledge now. With Shathrai out of the way, Buddhidhan no longer needed to play hide and seek, something he had always found distasteful. The Rana and his Karbhari for the first time experienced the joys of mutual trust and openness. A long journey had come to an end. The man who took pride in his Karbhari ancestors was now himself one—the Karbhari, the Chief Administrator of Suvarnapur. And the man who was the king was now a ruler in the true sense of the word. But the fate of Shathrai and his cohorts still remained to be decided. In the native states, factional power changes with a change in the administrator, and the new karbhari abhors all those who have served under the previous administration. Buddhidhan knew that when power is distributed in all factions, it gives the impression of a just administration, which is liked by the reform-minded individuals of Bombay, and those trained in the new education system. But he found that to maintain even the appearance of a balance of power was extraordinarily difficult. If power were vested in two, neither would be able to exercise it unhindered. It may prevent the abuse of power, but it may also not allow for the exercise of power for good ends. How could he trust the other faction? Pity or generosity may be taken as a sign of weakness; people of the state and opposing factions may both interpret such gestures as inability and ineptitude. Moreover, it would also allow them to continue their machinations and to pose a threat. Just as an uncouth woman does not respect a meek husband, subordinates do not respect superiors who seem timid of opponents, and given a chance, such subordinates would join the contending faction. What would be the implications of this? How should he administer the state? When two factions are mired in mutual mistrust and bias, it renders both ineffective and allows for a third view to prevail. This makes for uncertain politics. Who should be made responsible for the state? Who can be held accountable? Both factions would want praise and acknowledgement, but neither would accept criticism. The people would obviously blame the Karbhari, as they will only see a partial picture. They would be in the dark about who holds actual power, who wields authority, and whom to petition for redress. Power divided among various factions can only lead to the oppression of the people. Why do the English educated insist that there be no factions? Why do they say that all factions must have equal rights? Buddhidhan asked these and countless other questions of himself. In the absence of any worthwhile answers, he grew increasingly bewildered. What do they see in the British system? Isn’t the English Parliament also similar? One party rules. If people believe in one party, that party is right and the other is wrong. I think that these people just talk, they have no experience whatsoever. They can only talk. Among the reformist sections of Bombay, there are fads, and if they adopt one fad, they will not leave it until they get a new one. They just need someone to give them a fad. The Sahibs that I have worked with are not like them. From where did this lot pick these things up? They are neither Hindus nor English! But this Navinchandra seems learned. He says that in England there are parties and opinions, and the opinion that wins the trust of the people rules. But among our people, relations are more important than opinions. But Buskin Sahib told me that in England, individuals must follow the party discipline even if they hold a different opinion. He must be right. Navinchandra is wrong; he is inexperienced, he must have read it in some book. But Buskin Sahib has had personal experience of such things, so he would know. But what choice do I have anyway? Power should be vested in one person. Can two men share a wife? Can a woman have two husbands? We are better off than the English! If I hold one opinion and ‘vote’ for another—it is called a vote, isn’t it! Is that not tantamount to lying? Among us there is only one vote—that of the superior officer. All others have to follow instructions. Even then, can there be a state without factions? Even the Gods have factions—devs and rakshasas. Isn’t the religion of the English also like that? For their God, his angels are always right and Satan is always wrong. Satan is regarded as cunning, false, evil, and destined for perpetual hell. Our Gods are not so partial, even a rakshasa can be reformed—if not in this life then in the next one. Buddhidhan laughed at this thought as he lay down to rest. Ultimately, Buddhidhan came to the conclusion that the age-old ways were good and right. There could be no danger in following them.
