Now the problem is, he said to himself, who is in my faction and who is not? Then he laughed at his own stupidity. Those who are mine are with me, of course, and all the rest are in the other faction. How foolish of me to ask such a question! But then he remembered something, and his face fell. When he was ill, Dushtarai had insulted his mother. It was pointless to now seek redress against a dead son from his own father. What would happen, for instance, if his own people were to do wrong? The people of Suvarnapur will have nowhere to turn, they would be crushed. Intoxicated by power, even Pramaddhan could do wrong. Who will have the courage to bring his complaints to you, Buddhidhan? Now he was really perplexed. There will be so many impoverished like I was once; they would be crushed and insulted by my own people. Who will protect those orphans and widows? Oh God! Does the Karbhar involve so many problems? I do not want such a Karbhar. Why should I bear such burdens? My Goddess is my mother. I have fulfilled the pledge that I had taken. I have taught a lesson to Shathrai and Dushtarai. I have fulfilled the aspirations of my father. I have attained the highest office. They certainly did not say that I should hold the office forever! I did not take a pledge to be the Karbhari. Devi aspires to lead a life of renunciation—that aspiration remains to be fulfilled. God has given me enough to last a lifetime. The Rana can make anyone he wants the Karbhari. If he agrees, we could even invite Vidya Chatura. Then I won’t have to worry about Pramaddhan. I will hand over all responsibility to him; and Devi and I will take Vanaprastha and retire to the forest. Yes. That is final. For how long should I struggle and strive! What for!

Buddhidhan suddenly felt at peace with himself. He had no more desires. No new aspirations. He was ready to experience the joys of renunciation. He got up. The Rana had still not had his dinner. The assembly hall was warm, and he was perspiring. He told a servant, ‘Call me when the Rana is ready for me,’ and he went out to sit near a fountain in the garden. He looked up as the stars appeared one by one in the darkening sky and remembered some passages that he had learnt as a young boy. I wandered over the country rugged with numerous impassable tracts but did not gain anything; giving up the proper pride for race and lineage I served (but) to no purpose; banishing all sense of self-respect, I dined in strange houses, fearing like a crow (of being driven away at any moment); but thus waxed still, oh Greed—delighting in wicked deeds—and art not satisfied.⟨fn:24⟩ Buddhidhan remembered the days of his childhood when he had to take meals at Shathrai’s house. Tears welled up in his eyes. He came to a fountain. Some wrought iron benches purchased from Bombay had been placed around the fountain. He sat down on one of them. Intent upon propitiating them, I endured with great difficulty the taunting words of wicked men; checking in my tears I even laughed with vacant mind; I steadied my heart, and even bowed to the wicked. Disappointed Greed, in what other way wilt thou make me dance?⟨fn:25⟩ Shathrai kept coming back to his mind. The days gone by flashed before him like a dream. He lay down on the bench. The wind cooled by the fountain soothed him. Once he was impoverished; today he shared the wealth and luxuries of the ruler of Suvarnapur. But the future that lay before him was bereft of luxuries! Much of the glory and triumph of the morning assembly had lost its sheen and headiness.

That delightful city, that great king, and the circle of feudatory kings, and that assembly of eminent scholars at his side, the ladies (of the court) with their faces like the disc of the moon, and that group of haughty princes, those bards, and those stories—a bow to Death through whose (destructive) power all these things have become things of past.⟨fn:26⟩ The grand assembly of the morning was already a thing of the past. It had become memory. Did anything of it survive now? Is there not a delightful mansion for habitation; is not music [and company] pleasing to the ear; is not the happiness of the company of one as dear as life itself to (a man’s) great gratification? But wise men have resorted to a forest considering all this as unstable as the shadow of a small lamp flickering in the wind (caused by the wings) of a moth madly falling upon it.⟨fn:27⟩ Deep in thought, he shut his eyes. The cool breeze and the fragrance of flowers calmed him and lifted his worries away. Buddhidhan slipped into the world of dreams. He saw Saubhagya Devi looking at the reflection of the full moon in the pond at Rajeshwar Mahadev. He was seated next to her. They had both renounced the responsibilities of householders. He said to her, ‘Beloved Devi, do you not find our love as pure as this reflection? There are ripples in the water but not in the reflection. The reflection remains whole and sways with it. Our life is also like that. In the true sense, this reflection is false, it will disappear. The real moon is the one in the sky. Similarly, this worldly life is illusory; it will disappear. The true life is Brahma—it is moksha. You and I must finally attain that moksha. Devi, you are ignorant; but your conscience is clear and your mind is pure, just as you are beautiful and your complexion is unsullied. Chaste woman, knowledge for you consists of only one thing—chastity—and a soul as beautiful and pure as you must find moksha. You shall be one with Brahma. Devi, I too have contemplated none but you. I am with you. When you unite with Brahma, you will find me as a companion. Devi, everywhere you go, I shall be with you.’ As he dreamt, a soft smile played upon his lips. Vishnu, as he sleeps blissfully on the Shesh Nag, contains the whole universe within him. In his dream, Buddhidhan had touched the true meaning and higher goal of life. All his efforts from childhood had borne fruit. He slept a blissful sleep on the iron bench moist with dew. Rana Bhupsinh finished his dinner and instead of asking for Buddhidhan, he walked down to meet him at the fountain. A barber accompanying him raised the lantern he carried. The Rana saw his old friend fast asleep. Meanwhile, Narbheram, Navinchandra, Vidurprasad and Jaymal had also gathered there. Narbheram was about to wake up Buddhidhan, when the Rana stopped him. ‘Narbheram, Buddhidhan has stayed awake for long years. After many years he has slept so fitfully. Let him sleep undisturbed.’ Bhupsinh, too, had regained his peace and composure after long years. Shathrai’s removal had given him the sudden calmness of a man who becomes aware that what had passed before was only a nightmare. The Rana felt content that Buddhidhan who used to visit his small and bare house in Lilapur today walked about freely in his palace. The memories of days gone by and struggles shared quietened him. The affection he felt for his old friend worked as a balm on Buddhidhan as well. It soothed his mind much as the fountain soothed his body. ‘Jaymal, keep a pillow softly under his head so as not to wake him up, and also arrange for our seating here,’ the Rana ordered. His orders were immediately carried out. A silken pillow was slipped under Buddhidhan’s head. A couch with silk cushions was brought for the Rana. A carpet was brought for the others. Silver, golden and gilded lights were placed around them. The fountain shone and sparkled in the light of a myriad lamps. The Rana puffed on his hookah from a golden pipe. People sat around him. Servants stood at a distance, whispering amongst themselves. At the Rana’s command, a young singer presented himself, settled on the carpet, and began to strum his sitar softly. A servant brought baskets laden with flowers, their sweet heady fragrance filled the air. The wind, saturated with the fragrance of flowers from the baskets and the garden, merged with the droplets of cool water in the fountain and the crystal clear sounds of the sitar, sprayed the fragrance and music upon all those present there, much as an elephant sprays itself while bathing. The wind brushed against the trees in the dark and shook their branches, scattered the clouds high across the skies. The wind brought with it the rustle and deep green silences of distant forests. Turning soft and fragrant like a woman’s hands, it played upon the body, entering the elaborate folds of garments to caress and cool the skin. It touched all those present, touched their bodies and minds, showering them with joy and pleasure. Its only fault was that it did not make a distinction between the powerful and the lowly; it treated the Rana and his servant alike, just as it treated the sleeping and the awake. The wind, the lights, the fragrance, the music, the coolness of the fountain—all lifeless and yet moving—entered Buddhidhan’s subconscious, and they aided and nurtured his pleasant dreams. Buddhidhan moved from one dream into another. Then, as he gradually came awake through layers of sleep, all the thoughts he had just before he slept off came back to him. His eyes remained closed, and his hands lay unmoving upon his chest. Like birds who sing from their nests at the first rays of a new sun, thoughts crowded his mind afresh, though to the others he still appeared fast asleep. Sleep had erased the confusion that had clouded his mind. His thoughts were crystal clear now: I know what Karbhar is. I will be honest and will not hesitate to use my—the Rana’s—authority even over my own people. If the populace is convinced that though I grant my officers certain powers, I am open to any complaints about their misdeeds and eager to reprimand them if necessary, people will come to trust me, and the officers will also remain in their limits. They will expect neither encouragement nor forgiveness for their misdeeds. People will bring their complaints to me, and I shall give them justice. Granting authority and dispensing justice are two different things. One involves trust and a bond of closeness, while the other requires dispassionate neutrality. Do the English, who are so intent on doing the right thing, remain just while granting authority? I would commit a crime before God if I do not give authority to those who are trusted by my people. All those who appeared to be in Shathrai’s faction are not necessarily his men. The correct step would be to remove only the top men and retain all other officers, with a warning that henceforth competence will be the sole criteria of judging them, and that their past actions will be forgiven. It is not likely that all those who supported Shathrai when he wielded power would remain faithful to him even now. Those who sided with him out of necessity will now take my side for the same reason. I have no need for them, and I need not fear them either. They should only remain faithful to the Rana, not to Shathrai or me. If I ensure that all the top officials remain supremely efficient and incorruptible, the subordinate officers will also follow their example. The initial appointments will have to be made based on trust, but thereafter, they will all be judged by their virtues and by their work. It would be ungrateful indeed for me to desert the Rana at this stage, especially since he has shown so much trust and affection for so long. Once the administration has been set on course, I will be a free man, won’t I? Buddhidhan opened his eyes with this thought. A novel scene lay before him. He was quite alone when he had fallen asleep. And now, all these people here, this splendour, soft strains of music, all these beautiful lights ... Was he still dreaming then? He rubbed his eyes and looked around him. He recognised signs of the Rana’s affection and generosity. Rana Bhupsinh removed the pipe of the hookah from his mouth and said with an amused smile, ‘Buddhidhan, did you sleep well?’ A surprised Buddhidhan sat up hurriedly, ‘Ranaji, you? Here?’ ‘You were fast asleep and I did not wish to disturb you. So we all decided to wait for you to wake up.’ Like the old days, the Rana invited him to sit beside him on the couch. Buddhidhan opted to sit below. He signalled to the servants to withdraw. Once alone, they conversed at ease.

‘Buddhidhan, at long last, I am at peace today. If something still worries you, do tell me.’ Buddhidhan smiled. ‘Ranaji, do worries ever cease? Life itself is one big worry—one problem gets resolved and the other follows on its heels.’ Navinchandra was surprised to hear the worldly but uneducated Counsellor speak like a philosopher, and listened with interest. The Rana laughed and said, ‘Tell me, Buddhidhan, what troubles you? I know that all my troubles are gone. If there are any, they are now for you to resolve!’ ‘Ranaji, what shall we do with Shathrai?’ ‘What is to be done; a criminal deserves punishment.’ ‘Buddhidhan bhai, Dushtarai’s death has diverted attention from the real thing. Shathrai’s brother-in-law had gone to Lilapur. Garbaddas has disappeared; most likely he has gone to seek support from the outlaws of Dhirpur.’ It was Narbheram who gave this news. ‘Ranaji, did you hear that?’ ‘Yes. But it is not for me to worry about these things. I can give you a short and swift resolution if you like. We Rajputs do not know of any longwinded methods. Those are for the likes of you,’ said the Rana with a nonchalant puff on his hookah. Narbheram butted in, ‘I think they will try and take Rambhau on their side. They will give protection to the outlaws, which will bring a bad name to the new Karbhari. They will then carry tales to the new Sahib at Lilapur and try to prejudice him against us. Their plan would hinge upon what we do with Shathrai and Karvatrai.’ ‘Buddhidhan, let us for a moment accept that Rambhau succeeds in prejudicing the new Sahib against us. Should that worry us? Should we imagine that he will be unjust and not even give us a chance to present our views? Should we always be worried about what the Sahib or Rambhau or his soldiers do or think? The welfare of our people is no longer Shathrai’s responsibility. Should we not be concerned about our people rather than concern ourselves with such matters all our life?’ the Rana asked.

Buddhidhan replied, ‘Ranaji, what you say is absolutely right. But recall our old days. The engine of our train could not have moved without the Sahib’s help. Today, they are the masters—they have the power and they exercise it. That means that hitherto Shathrai ruled; and now the Sahib will rule. We are mere puppets. The Government should intervene and restrain us only when we oppress our people. That is their responsibility. But should they interfere in everything? Are we to accept even a lowly soldier as our master?’ Narbheram spoke, ‘Maharana, the newly appointed Sahib is from the army. He is a nephew of Dobak Sahib. He has a bad temper and harbours animosity. He can be easily swayed. He is not very enthused about his work and cannot tolerate any disregard of his orders. He is susceptible to flattery, though. All of Rambhau’s fingers will be in gravy now.’ The Rana’s brows knotted in irritation. ‘Buddhidhan, this means that they are the masters and we are their slaves. I do not wish to hear any further on this. We can be good to them. But if you want to be completely pliable, don’t mention it to me. You deal with them. Let us deal with what we have to. Tell me, what have you decided?’ Buddhidhan replied, ‘I do not think it would be a good idea to punish Shathrai.’ ‘What!’ The Rana stared at him. ‘So shall we honour and felicitate him tomorrow?’ ‘No, Ranaji, not that. It is not as if Shathrai has not been punished already. Dushtarai is dead. Rupali has brought dishonour to the family. His Karbhar is gone. The punishment now should just be sufficient to ensure that our administration can work unhindered.’ ‘Sure! And his brother-in-law will show you the way to run a smooth administration!’ retorted Bhupsinh. ‘Ranaji, anger will not benefit us. We must also realise that had we removed him in haste when all court officials were still faithful to him, how difficult it would have been for us. I have another plan that I think would be more suitable. The Mughal emperors of Delhi had devised a policy. Whenever some nobleman became overambitious, they sent him away from Delhi as a governor of some small region. He would wield absolute authority over that region, feel that he had some power, and so remain content. Once content, he would not be as ambitious as before and so would cease to be a threat. But, if we reduce the enemy to a mendicant, he has nothing more to lose, nor to fear. There is no one more dangerous than such an enemy. He may or may not be able to improve his lot, but he can harm others. Hence, I feel that we should allow Shathrai to retain his village, but we must draw up a new deed for it. The new deed should be made out to him personally, in which we must state that if he satisfies you, the village can become a hereditary holding. Moreover, we must make a condition that he and Karvatrai must reside in the village itself, work for its uplift, and that they should not leave the village without your consent. We must also stipulate that he should not meddle in the affairs of the state. His livelihood will be tied down to it and his self-interest will be to protect it. He will not risk cutting down his own livelihood. He will remain afraid and always remain under our control. Shathrai does not believe in God, but if he does so now, he will thank God. People will praise your mercy. Neither Rambhau nor the Sahib, and nor for that matter will anyone else be able to raise a finger of criticism against you. Those who oppose you will be silenced and will expect mercy for themselves as well. Most importantly, Ranaji, God shall be pleased with you. We will fulfil our objective, the animosity and bitterness will diminish, and you, the people and God, all will be pleased—What more can one hope to obtain with one action?’ The Rana listened to him quietly. His displeasure was clear in the beginning, but now he appeared to be deep in thought. He finally submitted, ‘All right, Buddhidhan. What you say makes sense. Do it your way.’ Navinchandra was pleasantly surprised. He thought to himself, A minister who combines mercy and wisdom must be applauded. A king who submits to the counsel of a wise and trusted minister must also be praised. A king so fiercely independent and stormy in temperament submitted so easily, like a child, to superior wisdom! Are all kings like him? If they were, what more could one desire? One has read that kings are incapable of recognising the wisdom of others, or worse, they prefer to sleep in ignorance rather than use their own or someone else’s intelligence. There must be numerous such examples in the world. God has created both men and monkeys. Narbheram spoke up, ‘Bhai Sahib, you have shown us the path of the good and the just—but I am certain that they will see this as a sign of weakness. They will say we are afraid of punishing them and that we are unable to clearly establish their crime.’ Buddhidhan laughed. ‘Narbheram, do you think I have not considered that? Pramad and Tark Prasad have gone to meet Russell Sahib. They will tell him everything. The opposition will have no basis to make any claims thereafter. Russell Sahib trusts us, and he will give the new Sahib a thorough briefing on Suvarnapur. After that, they can try all the games they want. We will deal with Rambhau and bring him around. But we should do nothing to Shathrai just now. Let all his attempts fail at Lilapur and elsewhere. He will recognise defeat when he sees it; and then, if he so wants, he will fall at the Rana’s feet and seek pardon. And Ranaji will pardon him. The mercy of the ruler of Suvarnapur cannot be obtained as easily as one finds things on the road. The world will also know that the Rana knows how to punish as well as how to pardon. The Maharana knows no fear from such people.’ Bhupsinh sat up erect, twirling his moustache with a smile—his pride and his Kshatriya ego were satisfied—and he looked upon his Counsellor with affection and respect. Ego boosting words have a magical effect on most people. Navinchandra witnessed such scenes for the first time. The Rana was not in full agreement with his Counsellor, but he restrained himself nevertheless. Narbheram had said things that should have made his displeasure even more pronounced. But Buddhidhan’s words swept away all his objections and doubts like the wind that sweeps the road clean of all dust. Not just that, the Rana felt that the Counsellor should do what he deemed best. Navinchandra was impressed by Buddhidhan’s ability to make his ruler do what he wanted him to do, while appearing to accommodate his desires. But he also pitied those who had to serve such a master, who had to spin a web of deceitful words to either please or not displease the master and hide their true feelings. Navinchandra felt that such a servile attitude corrupted one’s conscience, ultimately corroded one’s self-respect, and was hence destructive. This corruption and destruction appeared to him mutually supportive. He slipped into a world of his own, and then he heard these verses surface in his mind, he knew not from where. The man of virtuous soul commands not, nor obeys. Power like a desolating pestilence, pollutes whate’er it touches; and obedience, Bane of all genius, virtue, freedom, truth, Makes slaves of men, and of the human frame A mechanized automation.⟨fn:28⟩ Navinchandra leaned against a tree and recited the last lines of the poem. He felt as if he was back in his own house in Bombay. The passions of the English poet inebriated his mind as he conversed with himself. This was a ploy of the Counsellor to make the Rana pliable. Such is the desolation of corruption! Power made this charade an imperative. O Rana, this is the evil outcome of your power! One man commands another man, one man submits to another man—both these are undesirable. But as the power of these thoughts waned, his Indian upbringing came to the fore: God, such is Your will. Thy will be done! I think the fault lies in my own perspective. Such a good king and so wise a minister; when such great things transpire between them, it can be nothing but the will of God. If all were to think like me, how would the world ever function! Does it not happen that a subordinate suggests something as an equal and autonomous person, and that suggestion is accepted? What do friends and couples do? Does Saubhagya Devi conceal her true nature from Buddhidhan? Is she not independent? And despite that, does she not follow her husband? Is she compelled to conceal and hide in the face of Buddhidhan’s desires? And in doing so, does Devi deny herself? No—because the desires of both come together harmoniously. She does not desire anything contrary to what her husband desires; even when that happens, she openly expresses herself and finally their desires harmonise. Is such a thing not possible between a master and a servant? Was this charade by the Counsellor truly necessary? Was there no other way of meeting the same objective? But fear gives birth to untruth. Fear of the master makes his subordinates speak untruth. The master who is displeased with the truth and the subordinate who fears the master are both to be shunned. With this conclusion, Navinchandra snapped out of his reverie and turned his attention back to the immediate context. As he listened attentively to the Karbhari, his busily churning mind now occupied the zone between present reality and abstract thought. But once again, his recessive thoughts gave one last warning. His forehead creased as he said to himself: Masters in your speech, in your movements, in all your thoughts and actions, at every single moment—please remember that even the lowliest of your servants is a human being just like you. He deserves as much autonomy as you do. God placed you on a higher station not so that you can crush those below. ‘A dog wags its tail, falls at the feet of his master, and falling on the ground exhibits his mouth and maw; but the lordly elephant looks grave and eats after hundreds of flattering words.’⟨fn:29⟩ Masters, treat your servants not like dogs but like elephants. And servants, there are duties higher than those of filling your belly; the responsibility of securing a livelihood does not destroy your eternal obligations. With this thought, his mind at last quietened. The churning subsided. Meanwhile, the Rana and his trusted Counsellor had considered and debated many issues, and resolved a few. They had decided what they wanted to do with Shathrai. Narbheram spoke guardedly about Rupali and Khalaknanda. Buddhidhan did not engage in this conversation. He felt there was nothing to be gained by bringing Jamal Khan to trial and awarding him a punishment. Buddhidhan did not want to give Jamal the opportunity to even utter his daughter’s name during the trial or after his imprisonment term was over. And he was right. Moreover, the Maharana’s queens were involved, and however vile they may be, it was undesirable to discuss their affairs in public. This was why they decided to avoid a public trial and punishment for Raghi, Mahva and other accomplices of theirs. Ranjit was a confidant of the Counsellor. He did not deserve to be punished. Like Shathrai, Ranjit was privy to the secrets of the old tunnel and knew that it opened into the queen’s quarters in the palace. It was Ranjit who had informed Buddhidhan about machinations involving the queen. He had suggested a way of bringing this conspiracy out into the open. Jamal and others were thus sent into the tunnel. Ranjit was sent to lead the group to allay any suspicions that Shathrai might have. Once inside the tunnel, Ranjit threatened them with dire consequences if they refused to act according to his plan. As per the plan, the tunnel caved in and the entire group was captured by Vijay Sen. The assembly was dumbfounded. Nothing was said, leaving everyone to make their own conjectures and arrive at their own conclusions. The capture of Shathrai’s trusted men from the tunnel and the public knowledge that Shathrai resented the Rana’s growing power and his trust and affection for Buddhidhan, coupled with rumours about Shathrai’s involvement in Parvatsinh’s death—all these pointed to Shathrai’s guilt. This was an inevitable conclusion for most people. In case some dull minds still failed to grasp it, Merulo’s accusations sealed the case. The man who had seamlessly orchestrated all these events now tried to soothe his troubled conscience and absolve himself of any guilt. What am I to do if that is what the people choose to believe? I committed no crime. Nor did I force anyone to commit a crime. I did not ask anyone to lie. I only helped those who had dug their own grave to fall into it. I also did that to protect my own life, my family, and in order to fulfil my pledge. I followed the commands of my ruler. I did it for his sake. How was it wrong if I placed Shathrai’s men in the dark tunnel that was symbolic of his sins? The goal was accomplished. I am not going to have those involved punished wrongly. God, You are my witness—I have not sinned against You. If I have committed any wrong, I will ensure that innocent pawns are not punished. That is my repentance. Tomorrow, I could be in Shathrai’s place. If I show mercy now, I might be shown similar mercy in future. How long can any ruler be trusted? And thus, Buddhidhan tried to row his boat through the sullied and troubled waters of Karbhar. But the dark waters drenched him and filled his boat as well. Many seen and unseen markers guided his morality. No one else had any inkling of his troubled mind. God did not make our mind and conscience transparent to others. It must be for our own good. Pure soul and impure body—their union is somewhat apparent but largely concealed from human eyes. It is for the better. Purity and impurity are human artefacts. They have no place in the world of Gods. We must accept the time and space of the world we inhabit; east and west, north and south are irrelevant once we leave the earth. While dealing with this world, one must cultivate a penetrating, clear and unsullied this-worldliness. But while contemplating the highest truth, one must develop a holistic vision. O’ reader, be aware of this state and nurture a detached view to closely examine Man who combines aspects of purity and impurity and revolves like constellations around the antipodes. Reflect with equanimity on this human condition and learn from it. Because you, too, are human. There was a state guesthouse in the forest a few miles away from Suvarnapur. It was meant for the Sahibs. It was decided to send Jamal there as a caretaker on a reduced salary. He would be assured of a pay rise provided his conduct was good. Raghi was similarly sent away. Mahva was made a postman. He had to carry official letters to distant villages. Ranjit was made the police chief of the area under whose jurisdiction Shathrai’s village fell. This was a motivated move. Shathrai would feel happy that his man had been appointed. Ranjit was Buddhidhan’s trusted man and he was to keep a watch on Shathrai and his men. Ranjit was properly briefed on his responsibilities and was promised a gradual but substantial pay rise. Maharana was furious with his queen for her role in Shathrai’s plot, and determined never to look at her face again. But Buddhidhan advised against it. Instead he suggested that Bhupsinh should marry again and get a new queen. The old queen should be told that her prestige and position would be reconsidered based on her conduct. Indian mothers tend to cry after punishing their children. Indian people have a similar mentality. During the Mutiny, people had complained to the Sahibs about the cruelty of Malharrao; but when he was punished, the same people pleaded that he be shown mercy. Unaware of this mentality, the foreign rulers were perplexed by the people’s attitude. Buddhidhan was well acquainted with this mindset. He knew that there was an outcry against Shathrai, but that if Shathrai were to be imprisoned or otherwise punished, people would suddenly turn sympathetic and criticise the Rana and him. Brahmins and baniyas would not want even a man-eating tiger to be killed. Buddhidhan’s strategy was therefore to wisely ensure that the tide of public sympathy does not turn in favour of Shathrai. He and Bhupsinh decided on a plan that combined punishment with compassion and administered this concoction to the guilty. The Counsellor confidentially predicted that it would meet with the people’s approval as it would satisfy their desire for revenge as well as their expectation of compassion. He predicted that people would praise Bhupsinh for his actions. His confidence in his predictions inspired faith in others. Navinchandra recognised that Buddhidhan was an expert politician and possessed all the capabilities to be the chief administrator of the state despite his lack of English education. As he reflected on this, the topic of conversation changed. Decisions regarding the opponents had been taken. Now it was time to reward the supporters. Everyone was more interested in this pleasant duty. Buddhidhan began forming his ‘cabinet’. Everyone became attentive. There was no difficulty in giving Karvatrai’s position to Tark Prasad. In his time, Shathrai had also acted as the superior of all mahal officers. Buddhidhan separated this task from the office of the Karbhari, and appointed Narbheram as the superior of all mahal officers. Narbheram was pleased with such a high position. Buddhidhan wanted to ensure that Narbheram, although a trusted man, should not have the temptation to turn traitor. This objective was achieved. There was no possibility of a dispute about Narbheram’s suitability for the new position. Pramaddhan was given the position hitherto occupied by Narbheram. Jaymalshankar was to replace Dushtarai; Vijay Sen was made his assistant. Vidurprasad was made the representative at Lilapur; he was not too pleased with the posting and felt jealous of Jaymal, but he chose not to object. It was decided that Buddhidhan would be the new Karbhari. The old position of the Counsellor was abolished. The arrangement satisfied everyone. These appointments were to be made public. Buddhidhan had a soft corner for Navinchandra. But he did not think it fit to give an unknown, inexperienced outsider an independent position so soon. It was his plan to send Navinchandra to Lilapur along with Vidurprasad. He intended to call back Vidurprasad to Suvarnapur in a few months once Navinchandra became acquainted with the work and was known among the people. Buddhidhan had brought him to the assembly to read English newspaper reports concerning Rambhau to the Rana. Navinchandra was thus introduced as a man to be trusted. Buddhidhan wanted to keep Garbaddas in his old position. But Garbaddas had incited Rambhau, telling him: ‘You ask for your reward in the form of a position in the state. If they decline, threaten them that you would use your position in Lilapur to harm them. If they give you the desired position, accept it. I am not capable of being the Karbhari, but I can make efforts to obtain that position for someone as experienced and prestigious as you. Buddhidhan fulfilled his aspirations with my assistance, but now he refuses to show gratitude. With your support, I will take my revenge. You look after the arrangements at the Agency. The Rana and I trust each other fully.’ Rambhau liked this advice. He sent a message to Buddhidhan through Tark Prasad. If he wanted money, Buddhidhan would have readily met his demand. But his demand was dangerous. Buddhidhan clearly saw that Rambhau and Garbaddas were flexing their muscles and were in collusion with each other. He found a way of countering the duo. He realised that Garbad had acted from fear and he decided to allay his fears. He sent him a message that indicated his trust: ‘Tomorrow in the morning assembly, you will be asked to report on the treasury, and Shathrai’s mismanagement of it. Your assistance would be required in the future as well. Our efforts of many years have borne fruit. For all these years you have pretended, on my suggestion, to be on the other side. But now is the time for you to come out in the open. You must remove all traces of mistrust. Ranaji had taken a pledge to reward all those who have supported him and punish those who opposed him. You must not waste any more time.’ Buddhidhan decided that Garbaddas should be given the task of conveying the message to Rambhau. Garbaddas had cast his net. Now he was in a fix as to how to extricate himself. He had incited both Rambhau and the outlaws. Buddhidhan feared that it was beyond Garbad’s capacity to rein them in. Meanwhile, Navinchandra translated for the Rana a few letters that had arrived from the Sahib. But Rana did not want any more papers read to him; they held no interest for him. He impatiently asked, ‘Buddhidhan, almost everything is now settled. There are some minor matters, but you deal with those. I am only concerned with three things. One, how do you intend to accomplish your plan regarding Shathrai?—You have decided to wait for Tark Prasad to return. Second, you will be honoured with a presentation of robes tomorrow—that should be the first item in tomorrow morning’s assembly. Third, you mentioned that we should commence some work that would bring us glory all over the country. Now it is for you to decide what that should be. It should bring glory to our name and immortalise us. You must work towards it. The Sahibs submit to fame.’ They talked late into the night. The world was already asleep. Sleep drew the Rana to itself and sent him into the embrace of a queen he despised. Buddhidhan, Narbheram, Jaymal and Navinchandra got into their horse-drawn carriages and submitted themselves to the skills of the coach drivers. The sound of hooves and rumble of the carriages pierced the quiet of the night. All other senses were numbed by the enveloping darkness. Navinchandra’s mind cried out, Darkness! Darkness! Wretched citizens of Suvarnapur! They could not spare even fifteen minutes for you in the last four hours! Unless, I am making a mistake. But wasn’t everything they did for the people? Wasn’t the removal of a corrupt and cruel Karbhari for the good of the people? But somehow his mind did not accept this. A lantern faintly lit the passenger compartment of the carriage, almost hiding itself from the dark. Buddhidhan’s eyes shone in that light. They had left the palace grounds and were speeding through the night in silence. Buddhidhan spoke, his words seeming to emerge from the darkness itself, piercing it. Everyone listened carefully. ‘Narbheram, make sure everything goes smoothly tomorrow. Tark Prasad will return tomorrow morning. God willing, the Sahib would have given his consent to various things. We have not said a clear no to Rambhau. We have told him that his demand has been placed before Ranaji. Once all the major decisions receive the Sahib’s consent, the other functionaries for assisting the Karbhari will be appointed. Most likely you will be considered at this stage. It is another matter that we are not going to consider Rambhau—of course, we will not tell him that. We will give him hope and buy a month’s time. Eventually, we will get him out of Lilapur as well, just as we got rid of Sadashiv Pant. Rambhau is a snake who should not be nurtured; at the same time we also don’t want to make an enemy of him so soon. We will keep one important position vacant; so he will think it has been reserved for him. I have already told you of the arrangements regarding Garbaddas. You must go see him as soon as you reach home. You must have already alerted Vijay Sen regarding the outlaws.’ ‘Yes, sir,’ Narbheram replied. ‘Some of Shathrai’s friends are also part of that plot. In just six hours, they have created enough trouble. This news must have reached Lilapur.’ Jaymal said, ‘I have heard that Shathrai’s brother-in-law has rushed to meet Dobak Sahib.’

‘Is that so?’ asked Buddhidhan. No one spoke for a while. Jaymal broke the silence. ‘Ranaji said that once the matter about Shathrai is settled, he intends to gift you the village of Ujaliyu.’ Buddhidhan had himself prompted Jaymal to make this proposal to the Rana, which was accepted. But pretending to be unaware, he said, ‘Ranaji is very kind, but he should not act upon it right now. It would be justified once I have done something good for the state.’ Narbheram said, ‘Buddhidhan, it is not good to keep Goddess Laxmi waiting at the doorstep. One should never refuse wealth. Ranaji might change his mind tomorrow. One should not stop those who wish to be generous. I had thought about it, but as the saying goes, one has to ask even one’s mother for food. If this has occurred to Ranaji without anyone’s prompting, what could be better?’ ‘Narbheram, I feel that it may not be proper.’ ‘Let propriety be. Take my advice. If you don’t take it, you will have to live without it. An opportunity once gone does not return. Bhai Sahib, I am not a mendicant like you. Let me tell you, get something for me, too, at the right time. I speak straight from the heart. Don’t you trust me?’ Navinchandra was stunned by this cold, calculated plunder. But then he thought to himself, How can one blame these illiterates? What else do the educated English do? What do civil servants do except plunder? They annex native states for no reason. Every year crores of hard-earned rupees of poor Indians cross the seas like Hanuman! Even if it drowns in the sea, it is lost to us. But it causes so much harm. This plunder will at least be distributed among the people of Suvarnapur. It will be taken from the people, but it will stay with the people. But Navinchandra’s patriotic heart bled at the thought of this plunder. Tears rolled from his eyes in the dark. He thought, Buddhidhan, I do not blame you. But I desire that you be pure and unsullied. You cannot be a thief and a liar just because the world is made up of thieves and liars. Let those without learning turn demonic. But are you any less diabolic? Navinchandra felt overwhelmed by a profound despair, and a vast distance between himself and the administrators of Suvarnapur. ‘My poor countrymen! What can I do for you? I see no way forward!’ These words escaped him as if of their own volition. But those preoccupied with other concerns, driven by self-interest and immersed in machinations did not hear them. The rumbling and rattling of the carriage did not prevent Buddhidhan and Narbheram from holding their conversation effortlessly. They made plans and predictions, took decisions, plotted, granted favours, worried about things and also took pleasure at the turn of events. Their plans were such that they would fatigue the memory, exhaust the imagination and numb ordinary intellect. Hope and hopelessness, fear and fearlessness, joy and dejection, all these troubled them. Their shallow reason took giant steps. They considered favours to be dispensed and punishments to be awarded. They suspected many a fool and the cunning of many became apparent to them. Many good men were castigated for the company they kept. Someone who had said or done something out of place a long time ago was now denied a position for that wrong. Many such inadvertent actions were similarly punished or rewarded. Some deeds escaped their attention. Power and authority gave them the capacity to do good as well as harm. Darkness nurtured this authority. Narbheram got down at his house. Jaymal got down in front of his house, and found his old father Dayashankar patiently awaiting his return. Buddhidhan exchanged a few words with Dayashankar. He felt good that he was able to reward old Dayashankar’s son for all the support he had given in times of hardship. He ordered the coach driver to move on. The horses trotted off. Buddhidhan now addressed Navinchandra and said, ‘I have thought of a position for you.’ He told him of his plan. Navinchandra heard him patiently and turned pensive. He felt grateful for the trust and affection. But he did not want this position. And he did not know how to respond without sounding ungrateful. It was against his nature to show false gratitude, and it was against the norms of conduct in the native states not to appear overtly grateful. He finally said, ‘Bhai Sahib, your affection for me is deep, and so is your trust. I am grateful. But I am a wandering foreigner, as you well know.

A friend of mine is likely to visit us in a short time. I will await his arrival. I also wish to witness the honours ceremony for you tomorrow. After which, with your permission, I would like to resume my travels.’ Hitherto, no one had ever declined to accept a favour done to them by Buddhidhan. He felt deeply hurt and insulted. Navinchandra was a rank outsider after all. Buddhidhan felt that his trust and affection had been misplaced, and that he had erred in offering the job to him. It was a mistake unbecoming of a Karbhari, and Buddhidhan resolved never to repeat a similar mistake. But he felt relieved that Navinchandra, by his own stupidity, had prevented any potential damage. When one blows on a piece of hot iron, the breath produces a slight vapour. The blot of ill-feeling on Buddhidhan’s emotions corroded even his positive sentiments. He felt indifferent and cold towards a man who had hitherto been a recipient of much warmth, affection and trust. He felt he had nothing more to do with Navinchandra. Concealing his true feelings, Buddhidhan calmly asked him, ‘Navinchandra, who is it you expect? And where do you intend to go hereafter?’ And they talked of this and that, until they reached home. The carriage came to a halt and the passengers alighted from it and entered the house. Before Buddhidhan had left for the palace in the evening, Alak Kishori had met him on the way and said: ‘Father, I have something to ask of you. Do find a suitable position for Vanleela’s husband. She doesn’t ask for anything, but I think it should be done. That day you refused to help Krishna Kalika’s husband. But you can’t refuse me today. That bitch Kalika! I don’t like her anymore.’ Buddhidhan had replied: ‘If you don’t like her, how long will your affection for this one last?’ And Alak had said: ‘Father, the two are very different. That Kalika is an evil wretch. But even bhabhi likes Vanleela. You have to do this for me.’ Buddhidhan had replied: ‘All right. I will try and do something since you have brought your bhabhi into the picture.’ As he climbed the stairs, Buddhidhan suddenly remembered this conversation. He had been unable to decide as to who should replace Navinchandra. That decision was now made. The mere presence of Saubhagya Devi in the house freed his mind of all rancour. He said, ‘Navinchandra, no one in the family would like your decision to leave us. Alak would be the first one to pick up a fight with me about it.’ ‘Bhai Sahib, I too will never forget this affection. I have been received and looked after as if this were my own house. But what is to be done? Those who come must go.’ Samar Sen was guarding the door. Buddhidhan called him and said, ‘Samar Sen, Vidya Chatura has sent a letter to say that a gentleman called Chandrakant from Bombay is to visit us tomorrow. Most likely he will be here in the morning. I will be at the palace. Look after him well when he comes home.’ Navinchandra heard this. He thought for a while and said, ‘Bhai Sahib, I am somewhat acquainted with him. The way from Ratnanagari passes by Rajeshwar Mahadev, doesn’t it?’ ‘Yes, but the time of his arrival is uncertain, or else I would have kept someone to wait for him there.’ ‘I will go. I should be back before lunch.’ ‘There is no need. How long will you wait there?’ They went their separate ways. Navinchandra, absorbed by new thoughts, went to his room and closed the door behind him. It was midnight, but sleep eluded him. He opened a window, removed his formal clothes and sat down in a chair, contemplating the lonely sky and the dark night. Outside his room, the night held sway. He felt like a man drowning.
chapters.summary: Buddhidhan, as the new Karbhari, wrestles with the intricate burdens of administration and contemplates renunciation, while Navinchandra ponders his uncertain path.

chapters.title: Night Life: The Rising Curtain and the Ordeal by Fire
paragraphs: Night Life: The Rising Curtain and the Ordeal by Fire The Crescent-moon, the Star of Love, Glories of evening, as ye there are seen With but a span of sky between— Speak one of you, my doubts remove, Which is the attendant Page and which the Queen? —Evening Voluntaries, William Wordsworth. The chaste, virtuous woman did not harbour any ill will towards her husband. She attended to all his needs till he left for Lilapur. She then went down and joined the group of women gathered around her sister-in-law. Everyone teased her for the time she had spent with her husband in broad daylight. The banter gave her and others joy. They spent the day around Alak Kishori as if they had nothing else to do. Saubhagya Devi had made a practice of listening to a katha, a narration of Puranic tales, every afternoon. Today the Savitri Akhyan was being recited. There were more women in attendance than usual. Alak Kishori had no interest in such narrations. She and her group did not disperse even after the katha had commenced. Their chatter disturbed the listeners. Saubhagya Devi sent a message to Alak Kishori to go and sit somewhere else. They wanted to move to Kumud Sundari’s room. But she went and sat down to listen to the katha; so they moved out of the house and sat on an otalo meant for women, where Alak Kishori held court like a queen bee.

After the katha, Kumud tried to tiptoe back to her room. The pious tale of virtuous Savitri worked like a balm on her. But the nightmarish encounter with Krishna Kalika still haunted her. Her tears refused to dry up. People thought her tears were due to the tragic story of Savitri. Saubhagya Devi had observed Kumud through the day and she suspected something was wrong. She called Kumud and asked her to join the other women. Kumud feared she would break down and she made an excuse and declined the suggestion. She went up to her room, closed the door and latched it from inside. She sat down at the table and picked up her books. But she could not read, her mind would not focus. She looked all around her, at the bed, the window, the door connecting her room to Navinchandra’s room, the spot where she had sat crying, and at the door where she had stood, forlorn. Her heart was in turmoil; memories flashed before her, jealousy fired her imagination and she saw in her mind what she had not witnessed. Her eyes had the look of a woman crazed. Her breath came hard, her heart beat faster, her lips felt parched, and finally she slumped into the chair. She didn’t know how long she spent sitting there, motionless. Her reverie was broken when she heard knocks on the door and got up. It was Alak Kishori and Vanleela. It was five in the evening. All the other women had left; Vanleela had stayed back with Alak Kishori. Vanleela had noticed Kumud’s altered mental state. She had also heard some talk about some trinkets being flung at Krishna Kalika and suspected that she had a role to play in Kumud’s apparent distress. Concerned, she had come to visit her friend, but chose not to mention anything in Alak Kishori’s presence. Kumud’s face looked drawn. She somehow regained her composure and joined in their conversation. But she could not bring herself to smile; her heart was empty of any trace of joy. They climbed up to the terrace and cooled themselves in the evening breeze after a hot summer day. Vanleela said, ‘Bhabhi, you have spent the whole day in your room. You could do without our company, but we could not.’ Kumud could not think of a response. They took out a chess board, but she could not concentrate on the game. Kumud and Alak played. Alak, who was defeated by Kumud every day, easily won the game as Kumud made a series of rash moves. Vanleela had gone down to Kumud’s room while the game was in progress. She returned with a recent issue of Buddhiprakash from Kumud’s table and handed it to her saying, ‘Bhabhi, they have published a poem called “Chanda”. It is beautiful. But I cannot understand it fully. Please explain it to me.’ The crescent moon had risen in the sky. Melancholic clouds began to lift under its soft incandescent light. Kumud said to Alak Kishori, ‘Alak behn, the moon addresses the evening as her friend. The moon described in the poem is similar to one in the skies. Listen.’ Enticing the dusk, my dear friend, I bedeck myself and sail to meet you The evening breeze lovingly sweeps The courtyard, scattering Petals of a myriad hues Gazing upon his calm visage My river of joy runs over How beautiful she looks All draped in orange, A bright star dazzling upon her forehead Overcome with joy, I touch the star And so it is that I play with my friend But when she comes to embrace me I am startled and frightened For there stands a dark sorcerer Woe betide the night, she has Separated two loving friends My dear friend has flown away Fluttering her tiny wings While the sorcerer has me in a grapple hold Making sport of me in the palm Of her hand Then she swallowed me whole She does not know that I am Immortal in my own temple

As she softly sang the poem addressed to the moon, Kumud’s face seemed to glow with a hidden joy; but it also betrayed anxiety. An image of Krishna Kalika flashed before her eyes at the words ‘dark sorcerer’. She abruptly got up, agitated, and looked down at the road from the terrace. Then collecting herself, she returned to her seat. It was late in the evening when Alak Kishori and Vanleela left her. Kumud Sundari stayed on the terrace alone. She gazed at the darkening sky and recited the poem to herself over and over again. The words affected her deeply. ‘Krishna Kalika, what wrong have I done you!’ Kumud said out aloud in anguish. Her sorrow rose up like smoke from a burning volcano and turned the eyes of the Gods red. She lay down and fell into a disturbed sleep. The wise have said: Keep the women happy. Where women suffer, wealth and prosperity disappear. As if to prove them right, at that very moment, as he lay on the iron bench beside the fountain in the royal palace gardens, Buddhidhan was seriously debating refusing the Karbhari’s position. Kumud lay there on the terrace for about an hour. Her maid prepared her bed and came up looking for her, and she escorted Kumud to her bedroom. Just as the thought of renouncing the Karbhari’s position vanished from Buddhidhan’s mind, Kumud too forgot about Krishna Kalika. Back in her room, she picked up Buddhiprakash. She lit a lamp, put a protective glass over it and read the magazine. She re- read the poem ‘Chanda’, reading aloud the verses that described how the rain played with the moon. The mischievous rain clouds come To harass me Devising ways to wreck My happiness But I will never rage against The rain clouds She sang the lines over and over again. She reminded herself that she was no longer hurt or angry with Pramaddhan. Her heart filled with affection for him and a poem rose unasked to her lips.

Pramaddhan is my true husband All else is false Pramaddhan, he alone is mine All others are distant Pramaddhan is my true beloved All others are unloved She recited these lines repeatedly to herself, changed their sequence, even tried to set them to tune on her sarangi. Kumud felt a quiet joy as she recited these lines bereft of any poetic merit. She repeated with emphasis every syllable of Pramaddhan’s name. She felt shy repeating his name as if she were in the presence of others, as if she had uttered his name for the first time ever. She felt the romance of his first touch. The slow utterance of his name syllable by syllable filled her with a novel sensation of pleasure—she trembled and closed her eyes. She got up, and balancing one leg on the bed and the other on the window ledge, she brought down a framed photograph of Pramaddhan from the wall. She sat down on the chair and showered his photograph with kisses, pressing it close to her heart as if it held her very life. A shiver of excitement akin to the moment of union ran like a current through her body. Kumud Sundari, intelligent, sensitive, refined by education and her love of books and poetry, forgot all about her husband’s shortcomings, forgot her pain and misgivings, and focused her mind on his virtues. She became one with him. She romanced the photograph. She held it to her chest and sang: ‘Pramaddhan is my true beloved/All others are unloved’, moving her hand as she sang as if to brush aside ‘All others’. The Indian mind seeks happiness in that which is destined. The Indian land, despite the desultory influence of Western culture and learning, trembles at the thought of forsaking age-old ideas and norms of conduct imbibed through the affectionate nurture of parents. They continue to live in the joint family.⟨fn:30⟩ Those who play with ‘geography and astronomy’⟨fn:31⟩ are infatuated by illiterate women whose beauty radiates like the fire on which they cook. Such a couple in fact feels love for each other. Such a celebration of destiny is unknown to those whose intellect is lower than the Indian mind. Among the many resources that arrest the slide of this land of Aryas into a sea of sorrows is the Indian mind. This sensibility now flowered in Kumud Sundari’s heart like a lotus. She sang to herself a song so noble and pure that it is beyond the comprehension of non-Indians.⟨fn:32⟩ Gradually, her excited mind came to rest. She sensed the arrival of sleep slowly enfolding her in its arms. She decided to change her clothes and retire for the night. As she raised her arms to remove her blouse, the crumpled chit of paper with words written in a golden hand slipped out, brushing against her soft breasts, and got caught in the folds of her sari before falling onto her toes. She picked up the chit and read the familiar verse inscribed on it. Enchanting Night! Do not allow separation from the waning moon to blind you By day, holding the hands of the one you desire, Become a joyous bride.

Sleep evaporated as her mind awakened to her own moon. Sarasvatichandra! Sarasvatichandra! She moved to a different state; her resolve melted. Human life is like a twisted rope. Each thread has its own existence and there are times when they are not in harmony with each other. Superior intellect, deep learning and a refined sensibility make these threads and their enjoining more subtle and complex. Though engrossed in thoughts of Pramaddhan, Sarasvatichandra did not wane from her thoughts. Though chaste and faithful to her husband, she could not erase the man who was to be her husband. King Dashrath sacrificed Ram for the sake of truth; Ram abandoned Sita for the sake of his people. And yet Dashrath repeated Ram’s name until his last breath, and Ram could never forget Sita. Pious Kumud Sundari sincerely and with firm resolve strove to make her foolish and debauched husband the master of her heart, she joined her image with his and shut out all else. But just as light penetrates closed eyes, receding sounds echo in the ears, and dreams inhabit sleep, the image of Sarasvatichandra remained where it was, deep in the recesses of her mind. Kumud went to her cupboard and took out a bundle of letters from a golden box. She left the cupboard open and sat down on her chair. She carefully opened the bundle of letters bound in silk cloth. As, one by one, she read the letters she had received from him as a young bride-to-be, she forgot her present and slipped into her adolescent past. Sarasvatichandra’s learned discourses revived her thirst for knowledge and made her feel as if she was being educated once again, despite being in a family that did not value learning. She read his letters over and over again. And then his photograph came into her hand. She kept it on her table and gazed at it for long moments, her eyes caressing every feature on his face, looking into his eyes, drinking in his beauty. Memories flooded her mind. She looked at him reverentially one minute, and chided him the next as if she were his rightfully wedded wife, she smiled at him playfully, she talked to him aloud, she laughed; and then as her thoughts returned to his present state, she wept. She  pressed her palm upon her breasts to calm her racing heart. Years after abandoning her in the forest, when Ram met Sita again, he must have experienced similar emotions. Oh Kumud Sundari! Indifferent through despair, ruffled by harsh treatment, paralysed as it were on account of this long separation, pleased by its inherent goodness, and deeply affected by the touching words of your husband, your heart appears to melt with love, as it were, at this moment.⟨fn:33⟩ The bright flickering light of the tiny lamp was the only witness, the only friend that Kumud had on that dark and tumultuous night. The lamp became her refuge, her Tamasa river. Her beautiful liquid eyes reflected its flame. She closed her eyes and felt Sarasvatichandra’s presence. Her eyelids grew heavy with sleep and she slept off on the chair for a while, but she soon woke up feeling uncomfortable. She got up and lay down upon the bed, leaving the letters and the photograph on the table. Pramaddhan was not there to share her bed tonight. She slept alone. In sleep, her waking desires became her dreams. Time and orientation changed, and dream became reality for her. She experienced new joys and her heart rose beyond considerations of sin and virtue. In this dream world, Kumud Sundari became one with Sarasvatichandra in every respect. Buddhidhan had not yet come home. The soldiers sat talking on the otalo. One of them began to sing. When will my lover come home? Come home to me O’ when will my lover come home? O’ when? He sang aloud as the others shouted encouragement. Kumud Sundari’s dreams were disturbed by the noise. In the state between sleep and wakefulness, she sat up in bed and looked around for

Sarasvatichandra. She was jolted by the lines, ‘When will my lover come home?’ and felt hot tears roll down her cheeks. She did not want them to stop. She was fully awake now. She got up, sat down at the table, and poured her heart out on a paper. A sheet of paper is like the earth for many, it absorbs misery just like the earth absorbs rain. Sarasvatichandra’s ‘Enchanting Night’ came back to her, and her tears turned into words. The moon has gone, promising To rise again But the dark night persists Creating a deluge in my mind Woe be upon the life that Bears witness to this She paused, resting her chin on her hand. She thought of Sarasvatichandra’s present condition, her own desire for him, and the knowledge that this violated her virtue. She sighed deeply and continued. Leaving her husbandless and bereft, he journeys to a foreign land She holds his name close to her heart to keep despair at bay Refusing to submit to dejection She sets her heart asail Two lives lived as one: This playfulness now costs you dearly Tears filled her eyes. Oh! Sarasvatichandra! What was my crime? Even Nala left Damayanti in a better state. Oh God, Oh mother, Oh Goddess Amba! Kumud put her head down on the paper, her tears smudging her written words. She knew that as a chaste, married woman, this pining was wrong, but she could not control her emotions. She recited verses from the Uttararamacharita describing Ram’s condition. Verily you did not approve of the queen’s staying in my house and, therefore, I abandoned her in a forest like a straw; nor did

I mourn her loss. But the various objects of long familiarity move me; and so being helpless, I weep to-day; please forgive me.⟨fn:34⟩ O Ramchandraji, you are the embodiment of right conduct, you are the epitome of piety. If you too were subject to this state, pardon my transgression. I am an ignorant worm. I can no longer bear to be alive—it is beyond my endurance! Just then, she heard Buddhidhan and Navinchandra talking as they climbed the stairs. Navinchandra’s voice had a strange effect on Kumud. She was convinced that he was no one but Sarasvatichandra. Her past was indelibly etched upon her mind. She had shunned amorous desire, but she could not erase her love for him; she still feared her passions. Sarasvatichandra—Navinchandra—Sarasvatichandra—why are we fated to be bound thus? Oh my cruel heart, why can’t you accept the new reality and be at peace? Dear God, why are you angry with me? Her heart in turmoil, Kumud’s hand moved feverishly on the sheet of paper. The heart reincarnates bonds of love From a life past The vision falters upon a glimpse Of an idol once beloved The beloved, though proximate, Says nothing Where then do I lay bare my heart Torn asunder? A body held by morality can Remain still But the mind refuses to listen The mind will not submit to morality Two lives lived as one meet Like rivers And the helpless one caught In their midst Must seek her own salvation

Kumud was stunned by what she had written. She flung her pen away and stared at the darkness of her room and beyond. She read and re-read the lines. ‘The beloved, though proximate, says nothing.’ Sarasvatichandra, you belong to me, as I to you. And yet we cannot even speak to each other. How long can I endure this? She closed her eyes in torment, but found him standing before her—as she had seen him for the very first time. She recalled the verses in his very first letter to her. O Vaidarbhi! You are blessed with so many virtues That even Naishadha is drawn to you Why should one praise the moon just because It makes the ocean turbulent with tide Frightened yet thrilled by the immediacy of his image, she watched as he took her shy, hesitant hand in his, and was filled with pleasure at the touch. She recited these lines to herself: As the moon rises full, my heart smiles The ocean inheres in it It murmurs softly, filling me with joy Its waves dance within me.⟨fn:35⟩ She was delighted by the allegory of the ocean for Sarasvatichandra. Pleasant images came to her mind, and she smiled, her smile soothing as a moonbeam. Her agony vanished as she felt her joy overflow in all directions. This comparison is perfect: he is as vast as the ocean, while I am a wretch without virtue, she thought. The ocean softly murmurs, filling me with joy, its waves dance within me. It is true—what merit have I earned that I would possess a great soul like you? Even that momentary association was no less fortunate. Her heart sank. Her deep sigh extended itself to envelop the world in its melancholy, and the night became dark as before.

Navinchandra entered his room, closed his door and latched it. The noise startled Kumud. The human mind has the ability to find opportunities to fulfil its desires. In rare and fortuitous moments, such opportunities present themselves to match desires. Kumud’s eyes now turned towards the door that connected her room to his. The door was unlocked. Kumud Sundari, did the conviction that Navinchandra was in fact Sarasvatichandra turn your head? Did the incident between Pramaddhan and Krishna Kalika prompt you to forsake your chastity? Was it a fortuitous moment where solitude, opportunity and desire came together? Sometimes, inflamed passions are reined in by the question: Does he too desire me? Oh woman crazed by love, did that question occur to you? Did the thought come to you that, if he did not love you, why would he follow you here, forsaking his wealth and family? Did this question lessen your anxieties? Do not passions become unbridled when one believes that the other reciprocates the intensity of our desires? When you compared your husband with a man who was to be your husband, did not the one you desired to marry appear irresistibly attractive? Was not your heart flooded by the memories of previous encounters with him? Reader, ask your conscience, search your experience, and give an honest response to all these questions. Oh debauched ones, reveal your experiences and provide us the means to evaluate this situation. Oh pure ones, search your memory for a similar moment and reveal to us the weakness and the dangers of such a situation. Be kind and compassionate towards this young woman entrapped by circumstances and pray to God that good sense prevail. If a brahmin, recite the Gayatri mantra. A brahmin prays only for righteous conduct. His brahminhood is contained in this prayer. A brahmin desires nothing but rectitude. Oh pure Gayatri, give light to this daughter of a brahmin. Will you do this? That only the One who is omniscient knows. The world knows that not all desires of humans are fulfilled. Can purity remain eternal? Wealth is so very fickle. Is purity likewise? That is the will of God. Foolish and cunning man! Forsake your pride and pretence. Be humble and virtuous. Those who counsel others, examine your own conscience.

Poor Kumud! She got up and approached the unlatched door. She turned back. She went to the door twice, only to turn back. She considered her virtues. She imagined the dangers of her transgression. She sat down on her chair. She remembered the poems, ‘I despise this knowledge’⟨fn:36⟩ and ‘A shepherd without virtue gains no knowledge’.⟨fn:37⟩ She got up again, touched the door and came back to her chair. She put her head down on the table, unable to think. The lines comparing Sarasvatichandra to the ocean came back to her. She desired to be in his arms, to hide herself in his broad chest. The desire aroused her, tempted her and trapped her. All reason deserted her. She stood up, put one leg on the chair and the other on the floor, and tried to think what to do. Vanleela’s house was close to Buddhidhan’s. Vanleela did not have parents-in-law. She lived with her husband. At this moment, they were together on their terrace, his head was in her lap and she sang to him. In the silence of the night, her faint voice carried. The song drenched Kumud Sundari and sent a shiver through her body. If you stay awhile, I will tell you, Biharilal I have withered away for you, Biharilal My body is eager, Biharilal Day and night, I find no respite, Biharilal Tend to our love forever, Biharilal So we may be as the fish and the sea, Biharilal ⟨fn:38⟩ How can one describe the effect of Vanleela’s song? As she heard the song, Kumud Sundari understood her own unbearable pining. ‘Tend to our love forever’, these words echoed in her mind. She was gripped by a fierce yearning, and she surrendered her mind, heart and body to it. All her doubts disappeared. Her hesitation ended. She made up her mind and walked resolutely towards the unlocked door. With each deliberate step, her mind and body altered, new urges overwhelmed her, unseen dreams maddened her. She felt inebriated, she could see colours and fantastic apparitions dance before her eyes. Her desires overpowered her discerning mind just as Bhima had vanquished Duryodhana. Her passions were as fierce as the demon Hiranyaksha who subjugated the entire earth. Her yearning was fiery like the burning sun that scorches the earth. Virtuous and wise Kumud Sundari had lost all her autonomy. Strains of Vanleela’s song softly broke the silence of the night, impatient and urging. The night is alight O Kanha, your eyes are enchanting The song intermingled with sounds of laughter, and then the insistent voice became distant and receded altogether. Kumud Sundari, felt pangs of jealousy, and remembering the bewitching gaze of her own Kanha, she lost all control over herself. Torrential rains cause spates in a river calm and quiet, its uncontrollable force drags with it all impurities; a powerful gust of wind shakes a delicate creeper bedecked with flowers. Kumud Sundari felt an electrifying excitement course through her. The distance between them became unbearable. Her gaze became unsteady with passion as she saw his image before her. She felt possessed and powerless to resist. She murmured, My body is eager, Biharilal. Her eyes travelled beyond her body and beheld the beloved as if there were no doors and walls between them. She was drawn to him as the sea is drawn to the moon. She was propelled towards him like a fish riding on the crest of a tidal wave. She was like that fish of pure water hurtling towards capture as she thrashed in the nets of her own desire. She did not offer any resistance to the inexorable pull of her desires and allowed herself to be swept away by the waves. Her eyes closed themselves to everything except his image. They did not want any light, any knowledge or even a single rational thought to penetrate her conscience. They reflected only the bewitching eyes of the beloved. O Kanha, your eyes are enchanting, she murmured, biting into her lower lip, her body moving to the rhythm of her song. She sang it repeatedly, emphasising a different word each time.

Kumud stood near the door. The song had ceased to reverberate in her ears. She no longer murmured or even breathed. She was ready to lie down on the fiery bed of passion. She was now intent only upon her beloved. Like a soldier awaiting the clarion call to sacrifice his life on the battlefield. Her hands trembled like those of someone about to jump into a deep well. Her breasts, the seat of countless dreams and desires, throbbed with anticipation, the arousal of rushing blood made them painfully tender. Gripped by delirium, her delicate young body trembled. She knew fear, as if she had suddenly come face to face with death. The whites of her large eyes became prominent, her beauty deserted her and her soft features took on a harsh ghostly pallor. But Kumud Sundari could not see these changes; for bereft of self-awareness, though conscious, she was like a dead body. Then as if guided by some unseen power, she put her palms flat on the door and pushed. But, unused to such tasks, her hands lost their nerve and hung limp as if abruptly severed from the wrist. Krishna Kalika had left the other side of the door unlatched. This friendly act now seemed like a boon to Kumud. The door was waiting to be opened. Kumud Sundari, why don’t you push the door open? Why do you stand there petrified? How long will you wait? Are you not overcome by sleep and fatigue? What are you frightened of? Who? It is midnight. There is not a soul around to see you or judge you. Kumud stood still. But in the flickering light of the lamp her shadow moved, looming large over her. The shadow of the extended hand moved over hers as if to say: No! Kumud Sundari, are you without anchor, have you lost the ballast? Has your chastity run its course already? One night without Pramaddhan—and is your virtue shaken? Were you chaste until now only because an opportunity like tonight never arose before? Doesn’t even God help the virtuous? Will He remain a mute witness to your fall? Will He not extend a hand to stop you from falling into hell? Blinded by desire, she did not see the shadow. Disregarding all norms of this world and the next, brushing aside all limits and restraints, mocking her own fear and muting her conscience, her hand moved serpent-like to open the door. But the moment her hand touched the door, she was startled as if it had singed her. The shadow hand seemed to be stopping her from opening the door. She stood there transfixed, staring at the flickering shadow. It was as if Gunasundari’s loving soul had traversed space and time to rescue her daughter—to Kumud, the shadow seemed to embody her dear mother’s soul. She clasped her hands tightly together. The tide turned. Her conscience was reborn. Just as Lord Krishna had come to Draupadi’s rescue in Duryodhan’s assembly, Gunasundari had rescued Kumud’s chastity. Grateful tears flowed from her eyes, her sense of relief more profound than Draupadi’s in the unseen presence of her divine saviour. Words tumbled out of her, she knew not what she said or to whom. Oh Chastity, you have been saved from certain death! Oh mother, you have saved me from being sullied! Oh mother, I remain pure! Goddess Sarasvati bestowed her grace upon Kumud in form of a song, which rose to her tremulous lips. Saviour of the helpless, He rushes to their aid Startled, Sri Krishna suddenly awakens Lord of the fourteen worlds, He rises at once Rukmini asks: My Lord, who calls you? It is Panchali! Don’t you know her? Today, my devotee is in grievous anguish I must go to her at once! Govinda says: Bring Garuda, ask why later Garuda is on his way, lest the dark night set Lord Narasimha has set out With her eyes closed, Draupadi sees Him Saviour of the helpless, He rushes to their aid My Lord, You came to my rescue! Who else could have saved me? Kumud Sundari folded her hands in prayer. Her voice regained its sweet melodiousness, her eyes shone with a new light, and tears of joy and gratitude flowed down her cheeks as she sang. Lifted of its burden, her heart beat fervently and pure. She was suffused with new hope. She looked at the shadow and smiled through her tears. Her tears fell to the floor as if washing her mother’s feet. She felt perfectly calm. Her mind was clear. She rested against the doorframe and felt as if she were in her mother’s embrace. How can mere mortals like us know or fathom in what form God will come to our aid? With relief came repentance. Cleansed by tears, her heart regained its autonomy. Moving away from the door, she accidentally brushed against her sarangi which stood against the wall. As she looked at it, she felt as if the strings were playing of their own accord. Their sound reverberated through her. She then remembered the song she had sung to protect Navinchandra from committing a sin. She who resides in the heavens white Fell down onto the Lord’s head Having fallen once, she fell again ... A fallen mind is destined for dissolution Stunned by the truth of the last line, Kumud realised with horror the full import of what she had been intent upon doing, and stepped back, suddenly afraid of the sarangi as if it had admonished her. Dear God! What was I thinking? Oh pure Sarasvatichandra, I could never have been a true companion to you. It was just as well that you abandoned an unchaste woman like me! In life after life give me wisdom, O’ Lord Let my mind and body be pure and not stray Keep the desires of a hundred lifetimes at bay This is all I ask of you, O’ Lord Where passion and desire had possessed her, noble thoughts now swept her mind and heart. Kumud Sundari sat down on the chair and picked up the letters that had produced in her such potent yearning. She read them again with a tranquil, unsullied mind. They were memories of a life past, nothing more. She pressed them to her heart once, carefully folded them into the silken cloth, and put them back into the cupboard. The clock struck one past midnight. Returning to the table, she sat down and reflected upon her previous state of mind, the reasons that had led to her intense uncontrollable desire, and how God’s grace had saved her from a terrible disaster. She brought before her mind images of virtuous women: Gunasundari, Saubhagya Devi, Vanleela, Alak Kishori. Her pride melted with the sombre realisation that she had proved inferior to Alak Kishori. Kumud discovered a newfound affection for her impassioned, impulsive, arrogant, even somewhat stupid but unsullied sister-in-law. She felt fortunate that she had a friend in Vanleela, who, with all her playfulness and curiosity, was utterly devoted to her husband. Kumud had an intimation of the joys that Vanleela must have shared with her husband earlier that night, and she blessed her from her heart: Oh Vanleela, may your bliss be eternal! Kumud felt as if Saubhagya Devi, whose only desire was to follow her husband, had come to bless her and said: ‘Follow my example, Kumud’. Kumud even looked up to receive Devi’s blessings. Then she clearly heard her mother Gunasundari’s voice: ‘My own Kumud, hitherto, I have always been your guide. Now be on your guard and look after yourself. Ensure that you do not become a blot upon your father’s illustrious and virtuous family, and that you do not bring my nurturance to disrepute. Honour is important. You are wise; do not let your honour go to dust. You have been educated with great care; do not let it go waste. Do not bring disrepute to our age-old Sanskrit learning and wisdom. You were imparted English knowledge in the face of social opprobrium; do not allow it to be blamed for your conduct. Do not be counted among the impure and fallible, in this world or in the next. Do not surrender to your passions like ordinary people. Kumud, you are beautiful; do not become demonic. Do not lose your inner light. Never allow your pure and transparent conscience to be so sullied that even you would not wish to gaze into it. Daughter, my wise daughter, each of your actions must be deliberate and conscious. Today, we are. Tomorrow, we will not be. When we gave you away as a gift in marriage, we lost all claim upon you. But remember your mother’s love for you always, don’t ever forget your mother. No matter whether you are alone, among your husband’s family, in a distant land, or in the shelter of God, do not forget your mother’s counsel. Your conduct is known only to you and to your Maker. Who are we to do or say anything? God does everything; we are only His instruments. We gave you to that family. You do not belong to us anymore. We cannot advise you. But mine is a mother’s heart. It speaks of its own volition. Whether you heed my advice or not is for you to decide. But counsel you I must. Now you are an adult.
