Do what pleases you, but in this one matter, you must follow your mother. Joy and sorrow come and go; but what is once done can never be undone. Are you listening to me, Kumud?’ Kumud began to sob and felt as if her mother had put a loving hand upon her shoulder. She looked back and heard another voice. ‘Kumud, my daughter, God is your witness. I am a father only in name. He alone is the true Father to both you and me. Whatever you do, seek His advice. He shall never give you wrong advice. He shall always guide you. He is omnipresent, you shall find Him everywhere. You may forget me, but never Him. His wrath and grace are unique. They cannot be undone. I might have forgiven your transgressions, but you will recognise God’s wrath only when it visits you. You will not even be able to plead forgiveness.’ She saw her father’s affectionate yet stern face. She got up and looked around, and was startled. All around her, Kumud saw faces—her father, her mother, Vanleela, Alak Kishori; Buddhidhan seemed to be near the window facing the road, Saubhagya Devi appeared to be sitting at the window facing the terrace. She also saw Sarasvatichandra standing near Navinchandra’s room, looking at her quizzically as if questioning her chastity. She saw her younger sister Kusum Sundari seated next to her, a mocking smile on her face. She was frightened by all these apparitions. Are they all here to judge me today? Was it a dream or reality? Kumud ran around the room looking at the walls, at the ceiling, at the floor, on the table, on her bed. She heard Kusum Sundari sing a song teasingly. O’ sister mine, driven to madness by love Your deeds will come back to haunt you O’ sister mine, driven to madness by love

Kumud could bear it no longer and flopped down on the chair, crying, God, I will never entertain such thoughts ever again! She put her head down on the table and sobbed her heart out, her tears smudging the papers. Her divine punishment over and cleansed by repentance, Kumud felt calmer. She looked up. The apparitions had vanished. She was alone in the room once more. She knew that she had received God’s forgiveness. Her heart felt light. But her need for repentance still remained. She could not stop her tears. Eyes red with tears, yet how you weep Two streams course down your face Like the blood in your veins Vaidarbhi pines in the forest She was filled with self-loathing for having strayed even momentarily. She recalled her parents’ counsel. The wise truth of their words heard in a trance-like state now made her feel terrible. She felt alienated from everyone: husband, beloved, mother, father, chastity and God. She asked herself, Will I ever be worthy of my loved ones? How will I, a sinner, ever face them again? She pleaded with the earth, O’ Mother, forgive my transgressions and take me in your embrace. She searched for Goddess Amba in her mother’s image and tearfully sang. O’ Ma Amba, glance below your feet Take pity on me, judge not my deed You gave me this human body, Mother Do not forsake me, for without you I’m distraught I see you in all ten directions, Mother Without you, who can show me the way? O’ Ma Amba, without you, all is desolate Her tears cleansed her. She felt pure. Kumud felt in control of herself and stopped crying. Human essence, instinct and ability determine our modes of engaging with the world. Like everything else, they can be put to good use as well as bad. We are unable to fathom the will of the Creator. Human autonomy is subject to God’s will. Actions good and bad are decided by the orientation of this autonomous action. Abilities either aid or obstruct this process. Human ability tends to be either inert and passive or conscious and active. The inert tendency is governed by instincts, while conscious action is determined by intellect and tends to either support or hamper instincts. Vulgar people believe that autonomy is the unrestrained exercise of instincts. Others claim that autonomy is the unfettered play of intellect. Inert abilities are natural to animals and persons governed by animal passions; they are therefore easy to cultivate. The cultivation of a discerning intellect requires effort. The use of intellect for righteous ends is the ultimate grace of God. It is a state of bliss. The intellect emerges superior only through great conflict. Rare human beings remain pure without experiencing conflict; they are truly fortunate. In rare instances, the pure emerge triumphant despite undergoing many trials. Even before the final triumph, one has to face many blows and obstacles, but this is not seen as a blot. Most are unfamiliar with such trials. Oh ignoramus, see not the momentarily retreating steps or the wounds received while confronting the enemy. Do not consider the warrior to be a weakling. Consider instead the great courage of the warrior, respect him, worship him. Human frailty is limitless. Bear in mind that your resolve is yet untested and your weakness is not for all to see. Praise those who show some resolve and pray to God that He may grant you similar strength. Compassion for the weak and praise for the display of strength in the right manner is not possible without deeply felt experience and a generous and cultivated piety. Kumud Sundari proved to be momentarily weak, but her virtue finally triumphed. Oh those who aspire to test her noble and steadfast virtue, sharpen your intellect and put it to good use. Examine and judge yourself so that you may acquire the fitness to judge others. Those who shine by their own efforts and learn from their own imagination have a powerful conscience and possess virtue that triumphs over the most powerful of attractions. Sing their praise with abandon. Cleansed by tears, repentant and wiser, the ever growing light of Kumud Sundari’s heart illuminated her mind. A smile soft and grave returned to her now radiant face. Her eyes closed in contentment. A pure light enveloped her from head to toe, shattering the darkness that had engulfed her before. She rose and wondered what to do next. She felt exhausted and decided to sleep. As she lay down on the bed, her mind conversed with itself anew. Without doubt, I can claim no relationship with Sarasvatichandra. God, let not my impure heart sully that pure man by craving for him. Allow me to be imbued with the presence of my husband. Make me worthy of the husband I have. But I can still be of service to Sarasvatichandra. Can I not reason with him to return home to Bombay and perform his duties towards the country? Would it be right for me to approach him with this request? No. But will it also be right for me to allow this precious gem hiding from his father and friend to descend into the darkness of anonymity? No. Will it compromise my purity if I approach him? Yes. I can neither trust myself, nor him. Then I must not go to him. But what if he disappears before Chandrakant arrives? He may leave at daybreak. What must be done must be done tonight. It is my responsibility. But will he disappear? How can one be certain about a man as adventurous as him? Virtue need fear nothing. Men are weak when faced with women. If I am true to myself, there is no danger of passion overwhelming either his or my mind. No desire can overpower me now. God is my witness. It would be dangerous. But it is an imperative. No, I need not harbour any doubts regarding my chastity or my intentions. Mother, your counsel, your purity is my shield, and this shield is inviolable. I am your daughter. And my husband? No, I need not look at his deeds. I must be true to myself. Who am I? Who are my parents? What could be more vital than my chastity, my honour in this perishable, ephemeral world? Pious Devi, your blessings will not forsake me. All impure thoughts are now consigned to hell. Kumud got up and stood near the bed, lost in thought. Then suddenly she began to sing as if possessed, her tone pleading and worshipful. Come, Ma Amba, come soon Keep your hand on my head, O’ Mother of this world Purge me of these demonic passions And fill my heart with your pure light Shine it serenely upon my face Such that my Chandra is neither enchanted nor swayed I cannot bear to see him thus eclipsed My heart breaks to see the darkness engulf him It is midnight, and I have submitted neither to fear nor custom I have found the courage to accomplish this pious task We were enticed by love and the arrows of memory sharp Blunt though they may now be They should not pierce our hearts Cause this miracle to happen Hold me to your breast, Mother, help me keep my pledge Rest my head in your lap, keep my honour intact I seek release for my once beloved I seek that my virtue remains unsullied Whether I call you Father or Mother of the world You remain a mother to me As I enter this ordeal by fire Ma Amba, help me emerge unscathed She looked up at the sky framed by the window and said aloud: Ma Amba! Your power is miraculous. Men are mere playthings in your hands. You can rescue him from sorrow. You can bring him laughter or make him weep. The sun may or may not rise, but you as the dawn are the dispeller of darkness and the saviour of the world. Ma Amba! Ma Sarasvati! Laxmi! Vidhatri! The Goddess of Fate and Kalika are all your forms! Amba! I am your daughter. I feel your power rise within me. Sarasvatichandra, if demonic passions were to rise within you, my power will turn them to ashes. Sarasvatichandra, I pray that you accept my counsel. Allow me to offer you a service worthy of our former love. Oh pure intellect, come reside within me. Kumud sat down at her table. She inadvertently picked up the sheet on which she had previously scribbled her musings and wrote on the back of the same page. You who are no longer mine! I have no right to speak with you, but the mind conveys what it must through this note. If you have any pity left for this mind, if you feel anything at all for the heart that pines for you, heed this prayer. If you will, do what I pray you to do. A bat cannot see the light, such are the fruits of its deeds. But you can, so do open your eyes. As, The vapours that rise from the earth Return from the heavens as rain This world is such that our actions Are fated to remain small You soar above this earth on the Many-hued wings of Garuda Any wonder then that our time together was fleeting? Winged celestial who descended upon this earth Fly back. For this is no land for birds. Spread your golden wings and imbibe beauty Measure the skies and bathe in the pool of sunrays When you soar above the mountains, forests and skies Your light will be as one with the sun And we who are earth-bound Will worship your glory with all our hearts I may not be able to fly, but allow me To rejoice in beholding the flight of my beloved Or else, to weep in despair Love has the power to search out the beloved from the bottom of the earth. Eyes can be cheated, but the recognition of the heart is something else. Damayanti recognised Bahuk as Nala. I have said what I had to. When the boon-giver turns a stranger, who can measure his cruelty? The one who must suffer shall suffer. It is for you to decide what that suffering shall be. How does it matter to you who wrote this? She picked up the letter and told herself, I will put this into his pocket. If he is awake, I will drop it on him and return. I will not speak to him. I will not look at him. Ma Amba, be with me. So saying, Kumud got up. She held the letter that contained all her musings of that night, voluntary and involuntary. There was no hesitation in her step. She had moved heaven and earth to muster courage to open the door. Now she pushed it open easily with her foot and stood inside the other room. Was there anyone in the room? Who? What was he doing? What went on in his mind and what did he do when he found Kumud Sundari standing beside him? Navinchandra had returned late with Buddhidhan. He was in his room. The dramatic events of the day, first glimpses of Buddhidhan’s administration, thoughts of the day to come, memories of home, thoughts of Kumud, and plans of his impending departure all crowded his mind and kept sleep and peace at bay. He lay down exhausted, but was restless. He could hear Kumud Sundari’s faint soliloquy, her singing, and her intermittent sobs, which beat down on his ears torturously. Sleep eluded him. He got up from the bed and took out a piece of paper from his bundle of composed poems. He added a few more to the existing ones. He lay down again and read his new compositions by the light of the lamp placed on a chair at the head of the bed. Sleep crept in stealthily under his tired eyelids, and the pages fell onto his chest as he entered the world of dreams. Just then, Kumud Sundari opened the door. Sleep vanished that very instant. Who was that? Kumud Sundari? The question filled his mind. He was stunned. He did not know if what he saw was a dream. His imagination took over; he attributed various desires to Kumud Sundari, and found his own awakening. He felt his virtue was no longer steadfast. He struggled. The mind decided that the eyes shall not open, but the eyes decided that they wanted to observe her stealthily. The anxiety of anticipation gripped him, his heart pined as the body became petrified. Kumud Sundari entered the room and looked at him. He looked asleep. She carefully put her letter inside Navinchandra’s pocket, and turned back to leave. But then she saw the paper lying on his chest. Her curiosity surfaced. She tried to pull the paper free from his grip without waking him. Either because he let go of it or because of her dexterity, she managed to slip it out of his hand, untorn. She immediately recognised the writing. He was Sarasvatichandra! She looked at him intently, wanting to ascertain that he was asleep. It was the same body that she had joyously looked upon at her father’s house. He looked withered and pale. But that was to be expected. His ribs were clearly visible. His face had lost its ruddy glow. Kumud Sundari realised that this millionaire’s son had taken to wandering like a vagabond only for her sake. Her desire for him had turned to ashes. But her anguish at his suffering became unbearable. Tears coursed down her cheeks. She stifled her sobs in her throat, but they racked her body. She stood still for five minutes or ten; but the man remained steadfast to his decision and did not open his eyes. Finally she began to read the writing on the paper. The ink was still fresh. I left my father and mother, left my pure beloved Caring not for despair, I renounced them all For my father, I abandoned my love I heeded not your entreaties, o’ brother dearest friend I discounted your sighs and renounced the world I hardened my heart, futile were the signs of love Now all that is left for me to do is To watch her delicate heart break I have not the right to wipe her tears I cannot bear witness to this. O’ generous beloved do not waste away Forget that which cannot be forgotten Bear with that which is destined

O’ generous beloved, virtuous, pure and wise Bear with what cannot be forsaken Play the hand dealt to you O’ generous beloved, deeming it a dream Forget that which cannot be forgotten and Bear with reality. O’ generous beloved, destiny cannot be averted So drink deep from the well of destiny O’ generous beloved, o’ friend and true brother Close your affectionate eyes and Let the one who must leave go Consider our bond false and broken, forget this ingrate Let the one who must leave go. I had prosperity. I had a father. I had a beloved. I had a brother. None of them might I now take with me. O’ dear brother, erase me from memory Let me work for our wretched people O’ brother, this land is richer for your presence Why impoverish it by searching for me? Abandon this quest, cease thought of me I do not wish to live in this world I shall not return What I have renounced I shall not reclaim Even what remains I shall surrender What do I need of this world? O’ life mine, why did you poison my beloved? Discarding she who was dearest You cheated this naïve dear O’ life mine, why did you poison my beloved? What will become of her? You have killed her Now break cruel heart. Let my wretched eyes weep day and night Why should they have respite? O’ life mine, why did you poison my beloved?

You do not deserve to live in this world You deserve neither life’s pleasures nor The quietude of renunciation Body smeared with ash, heart in turmoil Such will be my renunciation. Abandoned, the river lies inert She will never break free of the mountain. Affixed to the earth, head in the skies The mountain may only watch the river weep. Unbound, I may don any garb I choose My path is as unbridled as kites that fly Like them, I too shall soar To be like the ocean waves Neither above nor below Is there succour to be found Destitute and formless am I I shall be like the forest breeze, invisible but Carrying aloft the fragrance called Kumud My forehead is inscribed with the wealth of the world And its renunciation I am the people, and I the king But in my heart, only you reside. The poem was smeared with the author’s tears. Some smudges appeared fresh. Kumud’s heart was torn asunder. Her anguish like an abyss knew no depth. Her tears flowed incessantly. Her pain became unbearable. She blabbered deliriously. Friend, unrecognised, he roams in the wilderness, He, burning like a volcano, shall not return, His wounds are countless, his memory cannot be erased, I occupy his heart and he is lonely, friendless, unknown, These bonds cannot be broken. Kumud forgot where she was. She felt dizzy and fell to the ground unconscious like a creeper struck by lightning. The paper fell from her hand. Blood drained from her face. Although he had decided not to open his eyes, hearing her fall Sarasvatichandra jumped up. At moments of crisis, the strongest of resolves melt. Lord Krishna picked up the Sudarshanchakra in the midst of battle for the sake of his devotee. Love respects its limits, but when faced with a crisis, its force dissolves all pledges. Such is the unfathomable play of God. She had come to plead with him to return to Bombay. She had her answer. Each stanza of his poem had scorched her heart. Sarasvatichandra’s undying and unsullied love, his sacrifice in spite of that love, his refusal to go away despite his renunciation, his pure and loving counsel expressed in the poem, his Bhishma-like resolve to remain steadfast to his decision, and the realisation that his resolve was because of his love for her. She was so overwhelmed by sadness that she fainted. Her unconscious body lay at Sarasvatichandra’s feet. He looked at her just as Lord Shiva had looked at the unconscious Uma at the sacrifice performed by Daksha. Many thoughts clouded his mind. Hitherto he had remained incognito. He had also concealed his feelings. Now he was no longer in hiding. His face betrayed his true emotions. He looked as if he were in his own house looking at the unconscious body of his own wife. His intellect had hitherto been clouded by romantic notions. He had concealed his sorrows by pretending to be an outsider. As his mask shattered, his intellect and emotions also ruptured. What if someone were to open the door right now and come in? He was after all a guest in another man’s house. This was not the time to ponder the appropriateness of his action. Kumud had snapped under the weight of pain like the levers of an overwrought clock. She had suffered enough through the day and the night, and now she lay unconscious at his feet. Sarasvatichandra was stunned. He could not think what he should do. He felt numbed by the harm he had caused. He sat next to Kumud who lay broken like a garland of flowers. He cast aside customary morality and took her head into his lap. He knew he was violating norms, but felt that everyday morality did not apply to the extraordinary situation he was faced with. And yet, he was able to restrain himself. His hand moved to caress her face, but stopped, continuing to hold her head. His mind provided no answers as to how he could give succour to the unconscious woman. How could he call anyone else for help? He felt completely helpless. Finally, he spoke softly into her ears, ‘Kumud! Kumud Sundari! Please wake up! Why do you do this? Both of us will be needlessly put to shame. False allegations will be levelled against us. No one will believe us!’ Confused and unable to think clearly, Sarasvatichandra kept repeating these words, but to no avail. Kumud remained unconscious. As time went by, the possibility of someone in the family rising early also increased. He became fearful. His mind could no longer be judicious. He impatiently caressed her face and shook her gently by the shoulders. But Kumud Sundari remained unconscious and incapable  of knowing what was happening to her. She lay there lifeless like a sparrow on a cold night. Her clothes had come undone like the small, delicate and dishevelled feathers of the sparrow. She had worn a soft, sheer malmal sari to sleep in for the night. It clung to her body, enticing his eyes. Her fair skin shone like a silvery cloud upon the horizon that concealed the young moon, mesmerising and frightening him. Her body was soft and silken under his tremulous hands, which tried desperately to massage her back to life. But her eyes remained closed like a stubborn flower bud. They dispelled any signs of desire. At last, the tragedy of the moment triumphed and guided the righteous effort. Ultimately, either by some great effort of will, or by the magical touch, Kumud Sundari regained consciousness and opened her eyes. She realised that her head was resting in Sarasvatichandra’s lap. She sat up and moved some distance away from him. For some reason, he held her hand as she tried to move away, but let it go just as suddenly. Kumud stared at him. This silent exchange continued for long moments. Finally, Sarasvatichandra got up and sat on the bed. Kumud Sundari also got up then and went and stood near the window, his poem still clutched in her fist. Both felt quite calm.

Unnatural resolves dictated by fear melted as those fears subsided. Kumud gathered the courage to speak. Just then, in the distance, some women labourers could be heard singing to the rhythm of their work. Stay eternal, unbroken, enchanting Intoxicating night For how will I pass the day Without my beloved? A shiver ran through Kumud when she heard their song. The words ‘intoxicating night’ echoed in her heart. A woman sang lustily in a voice rich and sonorous: Play with colours, my beloved Sun, we will worship you with pearls, delay your rising My beloved plays the hunter Riding on a steed of love Some offer diamonds and pearls I offer you my life Despite herself, something within Kumud responded to the simple allure of the song, and she felt angry at her own body for growing tense in anticipation. Her own weakness saddened her. She blamed her love for Sarasvatichandra for it. She knew it was her moral duty to purge herself of this love and sadness that had once again threatened her purity. She became resolute. She decided to speak her mind. The momentary weakness and frailty disappeared like lines drawn on sand, washed away by the waves of her determination. Sarasvatichandra was deep in thought, his eyes riveted upon the floor, pondering his action. I was sullied by wealth and prestige, he thought, and I allowed the moment that should have been pure to become blemished. I gave Kumud Sundari a reason to change the good opinion she might have had of me. He was quite annoyed with himself. Snatches of songs that people returning from a theatrical performance were singing also disturbed him. It would have been better had I not come to Suvarnapur at all. If I could fly, I would have flown away this very instant. He looked up and was filled with compassion for Kumud Sundari. He realised he had wronged her. He recalled the words that a repentant Dushyant had spoken to Shakuntala: ‘O fair-bodied one, let the unpleasant feeling caused by my repudiation pass from your heart’.⟨fn:39⟩ Just then, like the rustle of winds or a divine revelation, words began to flow out of Kumud Sundari. Sarasvatichandra could only see her piercing gaze. As her words fell upon his ears and impaled his heart, they became real. She spoke like a temple idol; her voice had the ring of silver bells, combining delicacy, beauty, purity and gravity. Kumud Sundari shone with a light never seen before. ‘You have snatched away from me the right to speak to you. But today for some reason not known to me, I speak. These are my final words to you. ‘You have lost by your own choice the right to know my past, or be concerned about my present and future. You wanted it so. It was your wish. It is not right for me to speak of myself. But I plead with you: do not put another unfortunate woman in a condition such as mine. ‘I have kept a letter in your pocket. In that I have written all I have to say to you. I do not believe you will do me even that favour of considering my plea. It was foolish of me to write that note. I wrote as I could not contain myself. ‘Sarasvatichandra, have mercy and return to Bombay. Are all learned men like you? Is cruelty integral to learning and intellect? Return to Bombay and meet your father, do not be so cruel. Be like a kite without strings, or like waves in the sea, or the forest breeze! No one can prevent you from being so heartless! I am alive but thrown amidst blazing flames. Is there any escape for me? I will burn, wither, weep or die—but I will bear my heartbreak. I will bear with all that befalls me. What is it to you? Your freedom will remain undiminished. That is all you care for.

‘I do not want you to respond. It is enough for me that you consider what I have said. May God show you the right path.’ Kumud choked on her tears which flowed despite herself. Her tormented eyes seemed to admonish him and say: ‘You have made it impossible for yourself to embrace me and comfort me even in moments of such intense suffering.’ She ran towards her room and locked the door without once looking back at him. She flung herself on the bed and cried her heart out. After a while, somewhat calmer, she got up, picked up Sarasvatichandra’s poems. She read them again. They were imprinted indelibly on her mind. It seemed futile to preserve the paper on which they were written. She tore up the paper. She then brought out all his letters. Her heart broke at the thought of destroying them. She pressed them to her heart, kissed them, bathed them in tears and stacked them as if she were laying her beloved’s body on the funeral pure. She set fire to them, and wept at this act of cremation. She carefully collected the ashes in a beautiful glass bottle, put a label on the bottle and wrote ‘Soul Ash’. She pressed the bottle to her heart, kissed it and kept it on the table where she could see it daily. She dried her tears and gazed at the bottle. At last she lay down. She lay awake until three o’clock. Kumud Sundari felt certain that she had finally erased Sarasvatichandra from her life for ever. She thought of her profound sacrifice and felt purged and purified once again. Her heart felt lighter. She had emerged unsullied by God’s grace and by a tremendous effort of her own will. Her ordeal by fire over, the strong-willed and virtuous Kumud Sundari at last surrendered herself to sleep.
chapters.summary: Kumud Sundari confronts her tumultuous emotions and past affections, undergoing a profound 'ordeal by fire' to embrace her destined path amidst haunting memories.

chapters.title: Leave Taking
paragraphs: Leave Taking After Kumud left his room, Sarasvatichandra felt as if some powerful force had gone, leaving a serene calm in its wake. He saw her retreating back, and the closing door. He slumped back into bed with a sigh. Was all of that a dream? Was that Kumud Sundari herself? How did she faint? Did he really hold her in his arms? Did he truly caress her face? What was it she said? Has she gone? Forever? Shouldn’t she be the one in a pitiable condition? Was his own frailty not proven? Many such thoughts crowded his mind. He was overwhelmed by a complex of emotions including love, sadness, helplessness, self- loathing, and compassion. It was all too much for his exhausted mind to bear. He fell asleep, and woke up at seven the next morning. Pramaddhan had returned from Lilapur, triumphant. The Rana, after this successful mission, had decided to present robes of honour to Buddhidhan the same day. Narbheram and Jaymal were given the responsibility of making the arrangements. Buddhidhan’s household was bustling with these activities when Sarasvatichandra woke up. He went down to the drawing room after brushing his teeth. Pramaddhan was boasting of his success in Lilapur to a group that had gathered around him. At the door, bards were reciting their compositions in praise of Buddhidhan. Charan women, tall and buxom, sang songs in beautiful melody, evoking feelings of pure devotion towards the Rana and his administration. As the day progressed, a large crowd gathered outside Buddhidhan’s house. The entire street was full of people. The house also had many visitors; administrators, friends, well-wishers, and anyone with a fleeting acquaintance with the family called to pay their respects. The drawing room was filled to capacity. Sarasvatichandra’s room was opened for visitors. The women occupied the courtyard and the surrounding rooms. They were decked up in beautiful brightly coloured sarees and adorned with gold and silver ornaments studded with diamonds and pearls. They looked like a garden in full bloom. Saubhagya Devi shone like the moon among the stars. Alak Kishori flashed through the gathering like lightning that eclipses the brightness of stars and the moon. Kumud Sundari was like the sombre and alluring Venus. Dayashankar Kaka and the old family priest were busy instructing the women in the preparation of things required for worship. Flaring red kumkum, fragrant and colourful flowers, incense sticks, silver and golden plates and other objects for worship added to the glory of Buddhidhan’s house. Meanwhile, the Rana sent a ceremonial procession to invite his appointed Karbhari to the palace. Drummers and trumpeters came first, followed by an elephant, followed by a horse carriage in which sat a bhayat, Narbheram and Jaymal; a troupe of riders on horseback and soldiers on foot followed the carriage. The procession stood outside Buddhidhan’s door, waiting to receive him. Sarasvatichandra moved around vacantly amid all this bustle. Kumud Sundari’s letter was still in his pocket. He wanted to read it, but found no spot where he could do so undisturbed. Last night he had fallen asleep without reading it. He knew that Chandrakant was on his way to Suvarnapur. Pensive, and fighting to contain a melancholy which threatened to overwhelm him, he remained untouched by the joyous and festive mood around him. On the street outside, the number of horse carriages had multiplied, the excitement in the air was feverish and palpable. Only Sarasvatichandra stood alone and aloof from it all. He realised it was desirable for both Kumud Sundari and him that he not be anywhere near her. But it was hard for him to let go of her. I had abandoned you, Kumud. But unbeknownst to you, you drew me to Suvarnapur. It is not easy for me to break free of you. How should I leave? When should I leave? Should I wait for Chandrakant? What should I do with him? Will I be able to shun him coldly when I see him? I do not desire to return to Bombay with him. His search for me has brought him here. Oh God! How many people have I made unhappy! Kumud Sundari, what fate awaits you now? If you can, do forgive me, my dearest Kumud. But I must leave—I cannot bear to see you lifeless again. Sarasvatichandra was not the only one who experienced a profound sadness in these festive moments. Vanleela had mentioned Pramaddhan’s transgression to Alak Kishori, who in turn had told Saubhagya Devi, and she had informed Buddhidhan last night. Buddhidhan was saddened by the degradation of his son. My daughter-in-law, defiled by my own son under my own roof! And I am powerless to do anything? How will I then bring other culprits to justice? No, this cannot be made public, and hence he cannot be punished. Buddhidhan saw Krishna Kalika’s husband outside on the street, and thought, This young man is now my responsibility. Will he dare bring this complaint to me? No, of course not. What punishment can be given which does not make the matter public? How can an aggrieved party be satisfied that justice has been done unless that justice is publicly awarded? If I do not have the capacity to satisfy a complainant, I should give up my Karbhar. Has anyone been able to give up the Karbhar? No one has shunned wealth, except under duress. No, I have decided—I will somehow punish Pramaddhan. The world shall see my justice. I do not want to go to hell. Mother, I have not forgotten the insults you had to bear. I will not allow such a thing to pass. Pramad, how shall I punish you? What should be your punishment? What if I punish myself? Just then Sarasvatichandra entered Buddhidhan’s room. Concealing his grief, he said, ‘Come, Navinchandra. How are you?’ ‘Bhai Sahib, servants from Ratnanagari have arrived to accompany Kumud Sundari back to her parents. They inform me that Chandrakant will spend a few days in Bhadreshwar. I need to see him urgently. I have come to seek your leave.’

‘Go tomorrow if you must, but you should attend the court today. There is also a celebration at home. Have lunch with us and leave at night; take a vehicle along. And isn’t Chandrakant supposed to come here?’ ‘Yes, but for some reasons I must leave immediately. I will have my lunch there. You have shown extraordinary kindness towards me, Bhai Sahib; you would naturally like me to extend my stay here. But please accept my request.’ Buddhidhan was worried about Pramaddhan. He was also preoccupied with palace matters. Since last night, he had felt differently towards Navinchandra. He did not want to insist when the other was so intent upon leaving, and so he said, ‘As you wish, Navinchandra.’ ‘Bhai Sahib, please do forgive me if I have ever hurt you by my words or deeds. You have been most generous to me.’ ‘Do not mention it.’ Sarasvatichandra took his leave. The Karbhari, engrossed in his own affairs, forgot to show the courtesy of arranging a vehicle for his departing guest. Sarasvatichandra sent his belongings to Rajeshwar Mahadev with Murkhdutt, who was a daily visitor to the house. He then went to Saubhagya Devi and Alak Kishori and sought their permission to leave. Quite naturally, they insisted that he stay back, at least for that day. He told them he had already obtained Buddhidhan’s permission. Hearing this, Saubhagya Devi gave up her attempts to persuade him and expressed her regret at his sudden decision. Alak Kishori said, ‘I will talk to Pitaji—you must stay for this one day. What could be so urgent?’ But finally, she too gave up. Sarasvatichandra looked once at Kumud Sundari, and turned to leave. Hot tears welled up in his eyes which he did not want seen, his legs refused to move, but he somehow dragged them on with slow deliberate steps, nearly stumbled at the threshold, and at last, stepped out of the house of Buddhidhan. Kumud Sundari was sad that her counsel had been futile. She had no opportunity of exchanging any last words with him. Watching his receding figure, her heart sank into an abyss. She was filled with dread about the future. Kumud moaned aloud as if in pain and fell backwards, but was caught by a woman standing behind her. The celebrations were abruptly halted. She was helped to her feet, given water, and surrounded by concerned eyes and questions. She said it was nothing but a painful knot in her stomach. She composed and becalmed herself by an effort of will, and joined in with the celebrations, which were then resumed. But her heart went with the wanderer. Sarasvatichandra walked past all the hustle and bustle and revelry. He walked invisible and silent through the jubilant crowds. He left his heart behind in the Karbhari’s home.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra, overwhelmed by sorrow and a letter in his pocket, struggles to leave the festive house, while Kumud Sundari collapses from heartbreak.

chapters.title: Walking Away
paragraphs: Walking Away Sarasvatichandra was eager to read Kumud Sundari’s letter. He hurried out of the house. If anyone had seen the letter, the consequences would have been disastrous for Kumud Sundari. Murkhdutt met him at Rajeshwar Mahadev. Sarasvatichandra had his lunch with him. During lunch, the two of them conversed. ‘Bhai Navinchandar, where will you go from here?’ ‘I intend going towards Bhadreshwar.’ ‘Have you arranged for a carriage?’ ‘I will take a ride in a passing cart.’ ‘Did not Bhai Sahib arrange a carriage for you?’ ‘I did not ask for it. I want to go alone.’ ‘Don’t tell anyone on the way that you have been his guest.’ ‘Why?’ ‘Shathrai’s outlaws are at large. They harass anyone who they take to be from Bhai Sahib’s faction. Kumud Sundari is also going to Bhadreshwar. I told Behn Alak Kishori that her departure should be delayed, or else there should be adequate protection arranged for her.’ ‘Let them be. What should I be afraid of? I will spend some time in the garden. Please stop any cart passing this way, and call me.’ Murkhdutt went out. Sarasvatichandra went into the garden. He sat on Murkhdutt’s bed and read the letter. He knew their separation was final. As he tried to clear his mind and think of a way ahead, the tears now coursed freely down his face. Kumud Sundari, what can I do for you? All you want is that I should return to Bombay. You are truly a pure woman. Some women are courageous and do not submit to men they dislike. Are they virtuous? But you kept your resolve despite such deep and abiding love for me. Is your virtue not superior? Sita felt no love for Ravana, naturally she turned away from him. But you did much more, Kumud Sundari. You counselled me. Until now, I was never aware of my own frailty. This was the second instance in which you have saved me. How fortunate and blessed I would have been had I not abandoned you! Now, it is my fate to leave you. Should I follow your advice? If you can, do pardon me, but I cannot do what you ask of me. I will not return to Bombay. I must atone for what I have done to you. I will roam the land, I will face what hardships come my way, and I will remember you. I do not desire prestige or worldly glory. For whom? I had agreed to be a householder for the sake of my father. You enticed me to worldly desires. But my father’s conduct gave me the liberty to break free from worldly bondage. I abandoned you and renounced the world. Why must I dream those dreams again? Dear Chandrakant, why did you have to go to Bhadreshwar? Am I to meet Kumud there again? Events of last night have forced me to leave Suvarnapur in haste. I cannot wait for you here. I cannot meet you here. And I do not want to be in Bhadreshwar. Then where shall I meet you? Can I not go away without meeting you? Do I have these attachments, still? Yes, let me go away somewhere else. I will send him a note. Isn’t that a cruel choice, Sarasvatichandra? How heartless of me. Have I not inflicted enough cruelty already? I wonder how father is. Did my leaving pain him? If I felt pained, why would he not feel likewise? God, be kind and let Chandrakant tell me that father has forgotten me. Chandrakant, I have hurt Ganga bhabhi as well. How many have suffered because of me? How many more will suffer? His reverie was disturbed by Pramaddhan’s confidant Ramsen.

‘Navinchandrabhai, you have to come back to Suvarnapur immediately.’ ‘Why?’ ‘Bhai Sahib has gone to the palace. But he has done something unexpected. He knows about Padma and Krishna Kalika.’ And Ramsen related the news in detail. Buddhidhan had been told about both these women, and was deeply pained by the debauchery of his degenerate son. Krishna Kalika’s husband was enraged. Buddhidhan had called him and promised to punish Pramaddhan. He had not yet awarded the punishment, but the rumours had already reached Pramaddhan. Frightened, he decided to seek his father’s forgiveness through Narbheram, but did not have the courage to open up before an elderly person. Pramaddhan thought of Navinchandra, and sent Ramsen to call him back. Sarasvatichandra heard him in silence, then said, ‘Bhai Ramsen, it is you who encouraged Bhai’s bad habits. You are responsible for things to have come to such a pass. If Pramadbhai fails to reform himself, he will get what he deserves. But you are certain to lose your livelihood. Go back and help Bhai to reform. I will not meddle in such affairs. Bhai Sahib will take action only after due deliberation. If I intervene, the first thing I would say is that you should be sacked. Hence, go back. My intervention will not benefit anyone. Tell Pramaddhan to change for the better, and be like his father. Whatever punishment Buddhidhan gives will be appropriate. Go back. I will not return.’ Ramsen went away without another word, his head hanging in shame. Murkhdutt had heard their conversation. He came forward and said, worried, ‘Something untoward will certainly happen. Bhai Sahib does not tolerate such things. Pramaddhan may take poison. Who is to say what should be done? Anyway, Navinchandrabhai, a cart is waiting outside. But it may not go to Bhadreshwar.’ Sarasvatichandra retorted, ‘Bhadreshwar can go to sleep! I just want to leave this place! I will go anywhere the cart takes me. I just want to leave!

They both came out of the temple. Sarasvatichandra stood at the temple gate; the cart was waiting there. Murkhdutt followed with his belongings. It was a large cart pulled by two bullocks. It was long and covered. The rear part was so low that it almost touched the ground. The driver’s side was raised. There were three other passengers, an old woman, an unhappy looking man of about forty, and a woman of about twenty. They seemed to be banias; the old woman was a brahmin. None of them were good looking or fair complexioned. Murkhdutt had found out that the cart was headed towards Ratnanagari. ‘Chandarbhai, you want to go to Bhadreshwar, but they are going to Ratnanagari. There is a village called Manoharia some ten miles away. The road forks there—one goes to Bhadreshwar and the other towards Ratnanagari.’ ‘All right, I will go with them.’ He took his belongings from Murkhdutt, and gave him five rupees. This was the first time that Sarasvatichandra was going to travel by such a cart. The cart was lined with hay which was covered by a thick cloth. Sarasvatichandra sat right at the back. It was ten in the morning and the sun was fierce. The millionaire’s son set out like Dhruva. But the sun showed him no mercy. For the unhappy man, the heat was the least of his worries. The slow-moving cart passed through dusty roads, taking a jewel among men as its load. Murkhdutt walked behind the cart for some distance, advised Sarasvatichandra to be cautious, requested the cart driver to take good care of him and took his leave. He turned back and soon disappeared from view. Sarasvatichandra lay down and covered himself with a dhoti. He was still unaccustomed to hardships. What with the discomfort of the noisy cart, the dust rising from the dirt road, the prickly hay, and the harsh blazing sun, he found strange thoughts and images filling his despondent mind. The road seemed like a tunnel and the clouds of dust took on strange forms. One moment they looked like the surrounding trees, one moment like the clouds, and a while later like the warp and weft of the dhoti with which he had covered himself. The clucking noises and harsh guttural sounds the cart driver produced from time to time, the sharp piercing calls of eagles circling high, the raucous cacophony of crows, the echoing calls of kabar, the excited chatter of sparrows, the high-pitched squeaks of squirrels on the trees, the grating sounds of reeds breaking under the cartwheels, and the rhythmic lurching and squeaking of the moving cart filled his ears. The sun’s rays pierced the thin dhoti and his closed eyes. He was bathed in perspiration. His body swayed as the cart laboriously made its way up a hill. Tired as he was, he could not sleep. His mind, too, had no respite. Kumud Sundari’s poem resonated through it. Will I be forced to meet her at Bhadreshwar? What if I do not go there at all? Should I not meet the man who has travelled so far to meet me? I will stay at Manohariya and meet him there; he is certain to pass that way. He will give me news of my father. Does my father remember me at all? What state would he be in? Should I return to Bombay? Should I not? What should I tell Chandrakant? I have seen for myself how the Karbhar is obtained, how the Karbharis operate. But I still need to see how the native states are administered, under what conditions people live. I have left behind Suvarnapur. Shall I go to Ratnanagari? In any case, the cart is headed towards it. It is good that Pramaddhan is to be punished. But why do I need to know about it? Oh, Kumud Sundari! One should be careful of the outlaws. It is good that Murkhdutt has warned the cart driver. As the cart lurched along, the cart driver sang lustily to himself. O’ beloved mine, your teeth are pearly white Come visit me, we will tie a secret knot O’ beloved mine, my home lies across that field Come visit me there, I will leave the door ajar O’ beloved mine, your hair is serpentine black Come visit me, we will spend an enchanting night Sarasvatichandra found the song absorbing. Kumud Sundari seemed to be knocking at his heart. The cart driver remembered he had women passengers and abruptly stopped singing. They moved on in silence in the oppressive heat and dust for a while. Then the old woman began to sing. The desire to live is high as the mountains But we die at the foothills When you die, you die alone No relations accompany you Sarasvatichandra was moved by the song and tears filled his eyes. His heart was wrenched between thoughts of death and Kumud Sundari. Eventually, he fell into a disturbed sleep. The cart moved on, unmindful of the beating heart, the many-layered dream world and the consciousness flowing through both the heart and the dreams. In his dream, Sarasvatichandra entered an unknown world. He knew where he wanted to go but did not know what he wanted to do there, he had no idea of what lay in store for him, what new experiences. How could a man about to be reborn possibly know? Three horse-riders followed the cart at some distance. They kept an eye on the cart even as they talked among themselves. The sounds of the trotting horses reached Sarasvatichandra’s ears. Far on the horizon, a cloud of dust rose. Sounds of beating drums and trumpets could be heard. The experienced cart driver grew increasingly nervous; the sounds could be a sign of the presence of outlaws from Dhirpur. He wondered if he should warn his passengers. Then he saw an ascetic walking beside the cart. The cart driver decided that silence was a sign of wisdom. The old woman sang songs of popular poets, snatches of which penetrated Sarasvatichandra’s subconscious. Countenance neither sorrow nor joy For each is formed by destiny No one can will either away For they are wrought by the Lord Forsaking bodily desires, a jogi inhabits the forest Disenchanted with the world, he is melancholic

He who once slept on soft beds, whose house was rich and vast Now has not even hay to lie on and shelters in the shade of trees Once rich embroidery and fine clothing adorned him Now he carries a coarse blanket to keep the chill away Once thousands rose at his call and armies marched That man now walks barefoot, that man now walks alone In his dream, Sarasvatichandra saw Kumud running after the cart, suspended in air. She seemed to be singing. The old woman sang another song. Attachment to the body is false It cannot remain yours Think it over, oh mad one Why has thought deserted you? He opened his eyes, and Kumud disappeared behind the clouds. The old woman continued her song. Deceiving the simpleton, the ash-smeared mendicant walks away Says Bhoja Bhagat: The sea of life drowns us all Sarasvatichandra felt as if Kumud’s grandmother had chided him. Saddened, he closed his eyes and slipped back into his dream world. The cart moved on at its slow lurching pace. It was noon. The sun beat down mercilessly on everything below it. He felt as if he was about to enter a dark cave bereft of sunlight. He felt he was sinking to the bottom of the sea. Surrounded by darkness and silence, he searched for light—for Kumud Sundari. The dense impenetrable darkness enveloped him like a snake’s coils. He was falling, falling, falling endlessly to the bottom of the sea. As he fell, an old English poem he had read in a life past came to his rescue. He could hear in it echoes of his own thoughts. While the sound whirls around, Down, down! As the fawn draws the hound, As the lightning the vapour,

As a weak moth the taper; Death, despair; love, sorrow; Time both; to-day, to-morrow; As steel obeys the spirit of the stone, Down, down! Through the gray, void abysm, Down, down! Where the air is no prism, And the moon and stars are not, And the cavern-crags wear not The radiance of Heaven, Nor the gloom to Earth given, Where there is One pervading, One alone, Down, down! In the depth of the deep, Down, down! Like veiled lightning asleep, Like the spark nursed in embers, The last look Love remembers, Like a diamond which shines On the dark wealth of mines, A spell is treasured but for thee alone. Down, down!⟨fn:40⟩ The cart moved on weighed down by the immeasurable sorrows of this man. It moved towards a fiery future, like oblations offered in a sacrifice. It moved on, like Sarasvatichandra’s fate, towards an uncertain, inexorable future.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra, heartbroken by Kumud Sundari's letter, embarks on a solitary, arduous bullock cart journey, grappling with his past and an uncertain, wandering future.
